docs.title: MongoDB Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

MongoDB is easy to start with and easy to misuse. You can store a JSON-like document in minutes, and many teams do — then discover months later that a list embedded in one document is approaching the 16 MB limit, that a counter loses increments under load, that a "successful" restore restored nothing, or that writes the database acknowledged were quietly rolled back after a failover. None of those are bugs in MongoDB. They are the consequences of decisions somebody made without knowing they were making them.

This course teaches MongoDB by making those decisions visible. Every lesson runs against a real server and measures what actually happens: how a document is encoded, how a query is planned, what an index costs, what a transaction retries, which writes survive which failures. It assumes you can program in some language and have used a database before; it doesn't assume any MongoDB experience.

Level 1 covers the foundations: a throwaway local lab and what lives in its data directory, mongosh, BSON and the types JSON doesn't have (and why 0.1 + 0.2 matters for prices), queries and update operators, arrays and embedded documents, bulk writes, the Python and Node.js drivers, and the import/export and dump/restore tools — ending with a tested data layer for a recipe app. Level 2 is data modeling and indexes: embed or reference, relationship patterns and schema design patterns, $jsonSchema validation, how B-tree indexes and compound key order work, special index types, reading explain(), the query planner, and time series collections — ending with a modeled, indexed store catalog. Level 3 covers the aggregation pipeline and application features: grouping and reshaping, $lookup joins, window functions, pipeline performance and $merge rollups, multi-document transactions, change streams, geospatial queries and text search — ending with an order analytics backend kept exact by a change-stream worker. Level 4 is production: replica sets and failover, write and read concerns, sharding and shard keys, security and TLS, backups and point-in-time recovery, monitoring, tuning and online migrations — ending with a secured sharded cluster accepted by an automated test script.

Every lesson has a How It Actually Works section — why an $inc is recorded in the oplog as an absolute value, why a compound index's field order can mean 71,514 keys examined or 219, why a transaction under contention fails instantly instead of waiting, why w: 3 can be faster than w: "majority", why a range of one shard-key value can never be split, and how a former primary decides which of its writes to throw away.

Versions and what was actually run

Every command, query and script in this course was run on MongoDB 9.0.2 Community Server (the official macOS tarball), and every output shown is the output it produced — including the errors, which are some of the most useful parts. Supporting tools: mongosh 2.13.0, MongoDB Database Tools 100.19.1 (mongodump, mongorestore, mongostat…), PyMongo 4.18.3 on Python 3.14, and the Node.js driver 7.7.0. Timings come from a laptop and show proportions, not benchmarks; where a lesson compares numbers, both sides were measured the same way on the same machine.

Things that were not run — MongoDB Atlas and other managed services, Ops Manager, Enterprise-only features such as auditing, encryption at rest and LDAP, Atlas Search and Vector Search — are described where relevant, never shown with invented output.

docs.title: How the program is organized
docs.text:
Level Focus Modules What you can do after 1 · MongoDB Foundations Server, mongosh, BSON, CRUD, arrays, updates, drivers, tools 10 Write correct application code against MongoDB 2 · Data Modeling & Indexes Embedding, patterns, validation, indexes, explain, the planner 10 Design schemas and indexes that stay fast as data grows 3 · Aggregation & Application Features Pipelines, joins, analytics, transactions, change streams, geo, text 10 Build reporting, real-time and transactional features 4 · Operations & Production Replication, concerns, sharding, security, backups, monitoring, tuning 10 Run MongoDB in production and recover when things go wrong

Each level has 9 teaching modules plus a hands-on project (module 10), for 40 lessons total.

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
• Run your own server. Level 1 · 01 sets up a lab you can delete and rebuild in seconds. Later lessons start several servers on different ports; a laptop is ideal, a shared company database is not.
  • Reproduce the outputs. Your ObjectIds, timings and sizes will differ; the behaviour should not. When something differs in kind, find out why — that is usually where the learning is.
  • Break things on purpose. Kill a primary, run two writers at once, restore without the oplog. Most of what matters about databases only shows up under concurrency and failure.
  • Do the projects. Each one combines its level into something you could adapt for real work, and each was tested end to end, failures included.

docs.title: Level 1 · MongoDB Foundations
docs.text:
Level 1 gets you from "I've heard MongoDB stores JSON" to writing correct application code against it. That takes more than learning find() and insertOne(). It means knowing what a document really is (BSON, with types JSON doesn't have), why {price: 0.1} adds up wrong, why a filter on an array matched a student who failed the test, why a read-then-write counter lost 80% of its increments, and why a mongorestore "succeeded" without restoring anything.

Every lesson is built from commands run against a real server — MongoDB 9.0.2 — and every output shown is what that server returned, errors included.

Prerequisites: basic programming in Python or JavaScript, and comfort at a terminal. No database experience is required, though if you know SQL you'll see where the two models differ.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. How MongoDB Is Built: mongod, Storage & a Local Lab — install from the official tarball, start a throwaway server, and look inside its data directory, log and cache.
  2. mongosh Like a Pro — connection strings, cursors and batches, scripts, JSON output modes, numbers, errors and .mongoshrc.js.
  3. Documents, BSON & Data Types — ObjectId anatomy, Decimal128 for money, real dates, null vs missing, mixed-type comparisons and the 16 MB limit.
  4. Inserting & Querying Documents — filters, comparison and logical operators, projection, sort/skip/limit, counts and $expr.
  5. Querying Arrays & Embedded Documents — "contains" semantics, $all, $size, why $elemMatch matters, and trimming arrays in projections.
  6. Update Operators, Upserts & Array Updates — atomic $inc vs lost updates, $push with $slice, positional and filtered updates, upserts, findOneAndUpdate.
  7. Deletes, Replaces & Bulk Writes — safe deletes, drop() vs deleteMany({}), ordered vs unordered batches and bulkWrite.
  8. Drivers: PyMongo & the Node.js Driver — one shared client, connection pools, type mapping, timeouts, errors and retryable writes.
  9. mongoimport, mongoexport, mongodump & mongorestore — typed CSV imports, Extended JSON, archives and namespace remapping.
  10. Project — Recipe Box Data Layer — a tested Python data layer with unique slugs, atomic ratings, array updates and keyset paging.

docs.title: After Level 1
docs.text: You can store and change data correctly. Level 2 is about doing it well: deciding what to embed and what to reference, enforcing a schema in a "schemaless" database, and designing the indexes that turn the collection scans you've been running into fast, targeted reads — with explain() to prove it.

docs.title: 01 · How MongoDB Is Built: mongod, Storage & a Local Lab
docs.text:
Before you write a single query it pays to know what you are talking to. MongoDB is not a library your program links against and it is not a file you open — it is a server process called mongod that owns a directory of files, listens on a TCP port, and answers commands sent to it in a binary wire protocol. Every tool you will use in this course — the mongosh shell, PyMongo, the Node.js driver, mongodump — is a client that opens a connection to that process and sends it commands.

This lesson builds a lab you can destroy and rebuild in seconds, and then looks inside it.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
Program What it is Used in mongod The database server. Stores data, runs queries, replicates. every lesson mongos A router that sits in front of a sharded cluster and forwards queries to the right shards. Level 4 mongosh The interactive JavaScript shell. Shipped separately from the server. every lesson Database tools mongodump, mongorestore, mongoimport, mongoexport, mongostat, mongotop, bsondump. Also shipped separately, with their own version numbers (100.x). Level 1 · 09, Level 4 Drivers Libraries for each language (PyMongo, the Node.js mongodb package, Java, Go, C#…). Level 1 · 08 onwards

The server, the shell and the tools are versioned independently. The versions used to produce every output in this course are listed on the home page.

docs.title: Getting the binaries
docs.text:
There are three common ways to get a server onto a development machine:

  1. Your OS package manager — MongoDB publishes its own repositories for the major Linux distributions and a Homebrew tap for macOS. (The server is not in Homebrew's core repository because of its license; the shell mongosh is, so brew install mongosh works directly.)
  2. A container — docker run -d -p 27017:27017 mongo:<version> with the official image. See the Docker Mastery Path if containers are new.
  3. The official tarball from fastdl.mongodb.org — nothing to install, just unpack and run.

This course uses option 3 because it leaves nothing behind. The download page publishes a SHA-256 checksum next to each archive; always compare it:

curl -sSLO https://fastdl.mongodb.org/osx/mongodb-macos-arm64-9.0.2.tgz
curl -sSLO https://fastdl.mongodb.org/osx/mongodb-macos-arm64-9.0.2.tgz.sha256
cat mongodb-macos-arm64-9.0.2.tgz.sha256
shasum -a 256 mongodb-macos-arm64-9.0.2.tgz
tar xzf mongodb-macos-arm64-9.0.2.tgz
ls mongodb-macos-aarch64--9.0.2/bin

9a30e942877445dc143d83671eba6cda2ec93a99160c8a8de57595853dc76de3  mongodb-macos-arm64-9.0.2.tgz
9a30e942877445dc143d83671eba6cda2ec93a99160c8a8de57595853dc76de3  mongodb-macos-arm64-9.0.2.tgz
install_compass
mongod
mongos

The two hashes match, so the archive is what MongoDB published. Swap osx/macos-arm64 for your platform (Linux archives are named after the distribution, e.g. ubuntu2404). Notice the archive contains only the server and the router — mongosh and the database tools are separate downloads.

docs.title: Starting a throwaway server
docs.text:
mkdir lab1
mongod --port 27100 --dbpath lab1 --bind_ip 127.0.0.1 --logpath lab1.log &

Each flag matters:

  • --dbpath is the directory mongod will own. It must exist and must not be shared with another running mongod.
  • --port defaults to 27017. Using a different port lets you run several servers side by side, which you will do constantly in Level 4.
  • --bind_ip 127.0.0.1 means only processes on this machine can connect. Since MongoDB 3.6 the default is already localhost-only, but writing it explicitly makes the intent obvious. Binding to 0.0.0.0 on a machine with a public address and no authentication is how many thousands of databases have been emptied by automated scanners.
  • --logpath sends the log to a file instead of the terminal.

If you are on macOS and reach for --fork (which daemonizes the process on Linux), this server version refuses:

BadValue: Server fork+exec via `--fork` or `processManagement.fork` is incompatible with macOS
try 'mongod --help' for more information

Run it in the background with your shell (&, nohup) or under a process manager (launchd, systemd) instead. On Linux in production you would normally let systemd manage mongod and leave fork off anyway.

Connect and confirm it answers:

mongosh --port 27100 --quiet --eval 'print(db.version())'

9.0.2

docs.title: What's in the data directory
docs.text:
After inserting one document into a shop.products collection, the data directory looked like this:

WiredTiger
WiredTiger.lock
WiredTiger.turtle
WiredTiger.wt
WiredTigerHS.wt
_mdb_catalog.wt
_tmp
collection-37409f2c-aed8-4003-8228-72c5b1010677.wt
collection-53ca67f9-bcf9-49d5-bb43-b0160f048f5c.wt
collection-577008e9-9fd2-4ab2-b218-a9abfcacabe3.wt
collection-6ebb04ca-b382-4752-b268-5a0e6e872948.wt
diagnostic.data
index-311b82c6-db79-4645-9170-04e30d948cf7.wt
index-35070c29-ef31-4d8c-93f7-6751d785721b.wt
index-a745ca20-aed7-4e00-af30-3f819d51a97a.wt
index-ab1ed0cf-8d97-4ba0-a4ab-4c1da99da13a.wt
index-dd646673-c3ea-4a74-8ded-3a924b7de804.wt
journal
mongod.lock
sizeStorer.wt
storage.bson

You can ask the server which file holds a collection:

db.getSiblingDB("shop").products.stats().wiredTiger.uri

statistics:table:collection-37409f2c-aed8-4003-8228-72c5b1010677

That is the new collection-…wt file that appeared after the insert, and the new index-…wt file next to it is the mandatory _id index. The other files:

File Role collection-*.wt, index-*.wt One WiredTiger table per collection and one per index. _mdb_catalog.wt MongoDB's catalog: which namespaces (db.collection) exist and which files back them. WiredTiger.wt, WiredTiger.turtle The storage engine's own metadata. WiredTigerHS.wt The history store: older versions of documents kept so long-running reads still see a consistent snapshot. journal/ The write-ahead log. Writes are recorded here before data files are updated, so a crash can be recovered. diagnostic.data/ FTDC — "full-time diagnostic data capture", compressed server metrics sampled every second. Support engineers ask for it; Level 4 · 07 looks at it. mongod.lock Non-empty while a mongod is running on this directory.

Do not edit, copy or delete files in a live data directory. The only safe ways to copy one are to stop mongod cleanly first, or to use a filesystem snapshot that captures the journal at the same instant (Level 4 · 06).

docs.title: Databases, collections and namespaces
docs.text:
Inside one mongod there are databases; inside a database, collections; inside a collection, documents. None of them have to be created in advance: the first insert into shop.products created both the shop database and the products collection.

db.adminCommand({ listDatabases: 1 }).databases.map(d => d.name)

[ 'admin', 'config', 'local', 'shop' ]

Three databases come with every server:

  • admin — users with cluster-wide roles, and the target of administrative commands.
  • local — never replicated. On a replica set member it holds the oplog (Level 4 · 01).
  • config — sessions and, on sharded clusters, the metadata about where data lives.

Leave all three alone unless a lesson tells you otherwise.

docs.title: The log is JSON
docs.text:
Every log line is a JSON document, which makes it easy to filter with jq or grep:

{"t":{"$date":"2026-10-11T22:52:53.729+05:30"},"s":"I",  "c":"NETWORK",  "id":23016,   "ctx":"listener","msg":"Waiting for connections","attr":{"port":27100,"ssl":"off"}}

s is severity (I info, W warning, E error, F fatal, D1–D5 debug), c the component, id a stable numeric message identifier (searchable across versions even when the text changes) and attr the structured details. A startup produced 132 lines on this machine; the one to look for is "Waiting for connections".

The server also keeps its startup warnings for you:

db.adminCommand({ getLog: "startupWarnings" }).log.forEach(l => print(JSON.parse(l).msg))

Access control is not enabled for the database. Read and write access to data and configuration is unrestricted

On a laptop lab that is acceptable. Anywhere else it is not — Level 4 · 05 turns authentication on.

docs.title: A configuration file
docs.text:
Command-line flags are fine for experiments. Real deployments use a YAML file, which maps one-to-one onto the flags. You can see the parsed options of a running server:

db.adminCommand({ getCmdLineOpts: 1 }).parsed

{
  net: { bindIp: '127.0.0.1', port: 27100 },
  storage: { dbPath: 'lab1' },
  systemLog: { destination: 'file', path: 'lab1.log' }
}

The equivalent mongod.conf:

net:
  port: 27100
  bindIp: 127.0.0.1
storage:
  dbPath: /var/lib/mongodb
systemLog:
  destination: file
  path: /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log
  logAppend: true

Start with mongod --config mongod.conf (or -f).

docs.title: Stopping cleanly
docs.text:
db.adminCommand({ shutdown: 1 })

The shell reports that its connection closed — that is expected, the server went away. A clean shutdown flushes everything to the data files and takes a final checkpoint. kill -9 does not, but thanks to the journal the next start replays recent writes and recovers; you will see that happen in Level 4. Pressing Ctrl+C on a foreground mongod, or sending SIGTERM, also triggers a clean shutdown.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When mongod starts, it opens the data directory with the WiredTiger storage engine (the only general-purpose engine since 4.2; buildInfo on this build listed ["devnull","wiredTiger"], and devnull discards everything — it exists for testing). WiredTiger reads WiredTiger.turtle to find its own metadata table, replays any journal records written after the last checkpoint, and then MongoDB reads _mdb_catalog.wt to rebuild its list of collections and indexes.

From then on, all reads and writes go through WiredTiger's cache in RAM. Documents live in B-tree pages; a read pulls the page into the cache if it isn't there; a write modifies the page in cache and appends a record to the journal. Roughly every 60 seconds a checkpoint writes all dirty pages to the data files as a consistent snapshot. If the process dies, the last checkpoint plus the journal is enough to get back to the last acknowledged write (with the default journaled write concern — Level 4 · 02 explains exactly what "acknowledged" means).

The cache size is the single most important memory setting. By default it is the larger of 256 MB or half of (RAM − 1 GB):

db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache["maximum bytes configured"]

Long('3758096384')

On this 8 GiB machine (sysctl -n hw.memsize → 8589934592) that is (8 − 1) / 2 = 3.5 GiB = 3,758,096,384 bytes, exactly the formula. The rest of the RAM is left to the operating system's file cache (which holds compressed data-file pages), to connections, and to query execution. Running two default-configured mongods on one machine means each thinks it may use half the memory — fine for a lab of tiny datasets, a real problem in production, which is why Level 4 sets --wiredTigerCacheSizeGB explicitly for multi-process labs.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Pointing two servers at one --dbpath. The second refuses to start because of mongod.lock; deleting the lock file to "fix" that while the first server is running corrupts data.
  • Exposing an unauthenticated server. bind_ip_all or 0.0.0.0 without access control is the classic way MongoDB data leaks. Keep labs on 127.0.0.1.
  • Mixing up client and server versions. mongosh --version tells you the shell version, not the server's. Use db.version().
  • Copying the data directory of a running server as a "backup". Use the tools in Level 1 · 09 and Level 4 · 06.
  • Assuming databases must be created first. They appear on first write — which also means a typo in a database name silently creates a new, empty database.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Download a server for your platform, verify its checksum, and start it on port 27100 with a fresh data directory and a log file.
  2. Insert one document into practice.notes. Find which .wt file holds the collection using stats().wiredTiger.uri and confirm the file exists on disk.
  3. Write a mongod.conf that reproduces your command-line flags, stop the server cleanly, and start it again with --config. Check getCmdLineOpts to confirm the file was used.
  4. Find the "Waiting for connections" line in the log and note its id. Then compute the default WiredTiger cache size for your machine by hand and compare it with serverStatus().

docs.title: 02 · mongosh Like a Pro
docs.text:
mongosh is a full Node.js-based JavaScript REPL with a MongoDB connection attached. That one fact explains most of its behaviour: you can declare variables, write loops and functions, require Node modules, and every db.collection.method() call is the Node.js driver underneath. Knowing the shell well saves you from writing throwaway scripts for every question you want to ask a database.

All examples run against the lab replica set from this course's setup (rs0 on port 27017).

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
mongosh                                         # mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017, database "test"
mongosh --port 27100                            # another local server
mongosh "mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/shell101"    # connection string with a default database
mongosh "mongodb://app:secret@db1:27017,db2:27017/shop?replicaSet=rs0&authSource=admin"

The connection string (URI) is the same format every driver accepts, so a URI that works in the shell will work in your application. The path part (/shell101) selects the starting database:

$ mongosh "mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/shell101" --quiet --eval 'db.getName()'
shell101

Never put real passwords on the command line on a shared machine — they show up in ps output and shell history. Use mongosh --username app and let it prompt, or a config file readable only by you.

docs.title: The prompt tells you where you are
docs.text:
rs0 [direct: primary] shell101>

That is: replica set rs0, connected directly to the member that is currently primary, using database shell101. If it says secondary, writes will fail — useful to notice before you paste a migration.

docs.title: Moving between databases
docs.text:
use shell101                 // REPL-only helper: switches the shell's `db`
db.getSiblingDB("shell101")  // works everywhere, including scripts and --eval
show dbs                     // REPL-only
show collections             // REPL-only
db.getCollectionNames()      // works everywhere

use and show are shell commands, not JavaScript, so they are not available inside a function or a .js file you load. Make a habit of getSiblingDB in anything you might save.

docs.title: Cursors and batches
docs.text:
find() does not return documents. It returns a cursor, and the shell prints the first batch of results (20 by default) when the cursor is the last expression in the line. With 45 documents in a collection:

rs0 [direct: primary] shell101> db.nums.find({}, {_id:0})
[
  { n: 1, sq: 1, even: false },
  ...
  { n: 20, sq: 400, even: true }
]
Type "it" for more
rs0 [direct: primary] shell101> it
[ ... n: 21 to 40 ... ]
Type "it" for more
rs0 [direct: primary] shell101> it
[
  { n: 41, sq: 1681, even: false },
  { n: 42, sq: 1764, even: true },
  { n: 43, sq: 1849, even: false },
  { n: 44, sq: 1936, even: true },
  { n: 45, sq: 2025, even: false }
]

You can change the page size, and the setting persists between sessions:

rs0 [direct: primary] shell101> config.set("displayBatchSize", 3)
Setting "displayBatchSize" has been changed
rs0 [direct: primary] shell101> db.nums.find({},{_id:0,n:1}).sort({n:1})
[ { n: 1 }, { n: 2 }, { n: 3 } ]
Type "it" for more

Other ways to consume a cursor:

db.nums.find({ even: true }).sort({ n: 1 }).toArray()   // everything, as an array
db.nums.find().itcount()                                // iterate and count client-side

const c = db.nums.find({ even: true }).sort({ n: 1 }).limit(3);
while (c.hasNext()) { const d = c.next(); print(d.n, d.sq); }

2 4
4 16
6 36

One trap: cursor.map() looks like Array.prototype.map but returns another cursor:

> const r = db.nums.find({even:true}).sort({n:1}).limit(4).map(d => d.n)
> r.constructor.name
Cursor
> db.nums.find({even:true}).map(d => d.n).slice(0, 5)
TypeError: db.nums.find({ ... =>d.n).slice is not a function
> r.toArray().join(",")
2,4,6,8

Call .toArray() when you want an array.

docs.title: Scripts: --eval and files
docs.text:
For anything you will run more than once, write a file:

// seed.js
const d = db.getSiblingDB("shell101");
d.dropDatabase();
const docs = [];
for (let i = 1; i <= 45; i++) docs.push({ n: i, sq: i * i, even: i % 2 === 0 });
d.nums.insertMany(docs);
print("inserted", d.nums.countDocuments());

$ mongosh --quiet seed.js
inserted 45

--quiet suppresses the connection banner. In a script, nothing is printed automatically — use print() for plain values or printjson() for documents. Inside the REPL you may also load("seed.js").

docs.title: Output formats for other tools
docs.text:
When another program will read the output, ask for real JSON instead of the shell's JavaScript-ish display. --json=relaxed gives readable JSON:

$ mongosh --quiet shell101 --json=relaxed --eval 'db.nums.find({n:{$lte:2}},{_id:0}).sort({n:1}).toArray()'
[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "sq": 1,
    "even": false
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "sq": 4,
    "even": true
  }
]

--json=canonical preserves every BSON type exactly, at the cost of verbosity — this is Extended JSON, which you will meet again with mongoexport:

$ mongosh --quiet shell101 --json=canonical --eval 'db.nums.findOne({n:3},{_id:0})'
{
  "n": {
    "$numberInt": "3"
  },
  "sq": {
    "$numberInt": "9"
  },
  "even": false
}

docs.title: Numbers in the shell
docs.text:
JavaScript has one number type; BSON has several. When the shell inserts a whole number that fits in 32 bits it sends an int, otherwise a double. Use the constructors when the type matters:

db.types.insertOne({ a: 1, b: 1.5, c: NumberInt(7), d: NumberLong("7"), e: new Date(0) })
db.types.aggregate([{ $project: { _id: 0, a: { $type: "$a" }, b: { $type: "$b" },
  c: { $type: "$c" }, d: { $type: "$d" }, e: { $type: "$e" } } }])

[ { a: 'int', b: 'double', c: 'int', d: 'long', e: 'date' } ]

Pass NumberLong a string. Passing a number works but the shell warns, because a JavaScript number above 2^53 has already lost precision before NumberLong sees it:

Warning: NumberLong: specifying a number as argument is deprecated and may lead to loss of precision, pass a string instead

Lesson 03 covers BSON types properly.

docs.title: Errors are exceptions
docs.text:
Server errors are thrown as MongoServerError with a numeric code, so you can handle them in scripts:

try {
  db.nums.insertOne({ _id: 1 });
  db.nums.insertOne({ _id: 1 });
} catch (e) {
  print(e.name, e.code, e.message);
}

MongoServerError 11000 E11000 duplicate key error collection: shell101.nums index: _id_ dup key: { _id: 1 }

Code 11000 (duplicate key) is the one you will catch most often in application code. Match on the code, never on the message text.

docs.title: Your own helpers: .mongoshrc.js
docs.text:
On start, mongosh runs ~/.mongoshrc.js if it exists (skip it with --norc). This one changes the prompt and adds a helper:

// ~/.mongoshrc.js
prompt = () => `${db.getName()}@${db.hello().me ?? "standalone"}> `;
function topN(coll, field, n = 3) {
  return db[coll].find({}, { _id: 0, [field]: 1 }).sort({ [field]: -1 }).limit(n).toArray();
}

test@127.0.0.1:27017> use shell101
switched to db shell101
shell101@127.0.0.1:27017> topN("nums","sq")
[ { sq: 2025 }, { sq: 1936 }, { sq: 1849 } ]

Keep anything destructive out of your rc file. A helper that drops a collection is one autocomplete away from a bad day.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
mongosh is a Node.js application. It wraps the official Node.js driver in a layer called the shell API that turns the asynchronous driver into something that looks synchronous: in the driver, collection.findOne() returns a Promise; in the shell you write db.nums.findOne() and get a document. The REPL inspects each line, and if an expression returns a Promise it awaits it for you before printing. That is why loops like while (c.hasNext()) work without await in the shell but the same code copied into a Node program does not.

db.nums.find() creates a cursor object but sends nothing yet. When the cursor is first iterated — by the REPL printer, toArray(), next() or forEach() — the driver sends a find command. The server replies with the first batch and a cursor id; to get more, the driver sends getMore with that id. Typing it is just one more getMore (or the next slice of an already-fetched batch). A server-side cursor that is not used for 10 minutes is closed by the server, which is why an old cursor in a forgotten shell eventually fails with "cursor not found".

Values are converted between JavaScript and BSON by the driver's BSON library. Integers in 32-bit range become int, other numbers double, Date objects become BSON date, and the wrapper classes (NumberLong, NumberDecimal, ObjectId, UUID…) map to their BSON types. On the way back, int and double become plain JavaScript numbers, and long becomes a Long object so no precision is lost — which is why you sometimes see Long('3758096384') instead of a bare number.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using use or show in a script. They are REPL commands; use getSiblingDB and getCollectionNames().
  • Expecting cursor.map() to return an array. It returns a cursor; add .toArray().
  • Reading from a cursor's printout as if it were complete. The REPL only shows one batch; a "result" of 20 documents may be 20 of 20 million.
  • Building numbers that need exact precision in JavaScript. Use NumberLong("…") and NumberDecimal("…") with string arguments.
  • Running ad-hoc writes against production in a REPL you also use for local work. Check the prompt before pasting, and consider a different prompt colour or text per environment in your rc file.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create a practice.squares collection with documents for 1–100 using a script file, run it with --quiet, and print the count.
  2. In the REPL, set displayBatchSize to 7 and page through the even squares with it. Reset it to 20 afterwards.
  3. Print the five largest squares as relaxed JSON with --json=relaxed --eval, and pipe the output into python3 -m json.tool (or jq) to prove it is valid JSON.
  4. Insert one document with NumberLong("9007199254740993") and another with the plain number 9007199254740993. Read both back and explain the difference.
  5. Add a helper to a .mongoshrc.js that prints every collection in the current database with its document count.

docs.title: 03 · Documents, BSON & Data Types
docs.text:
A MongoDB document looks like JSON, and most of the time you can think of it that way. But it is stored and sent as BSON — a binary format with more types than JSON, a defined comparison order across those types, and a hard size limit. The differences are small and the bugs they cause are large: totals that are off by a fraction of a cent, dates that sort wrong, queries that silently match nothing.

Everything below was run in mongosh against the lab server, in a database called bson.

docs.title: The types you will actually use
docs.text:
BSON type $type alias Shell / driver value Use it for Double "double" 1.5 Measurements, scores — anything where tiny rounding is fine 32-bit integer "int" 1, NumberInt(7) Counts, small whole numbers 64-bit integer "long" NumberLong("7") Large IDs, counters that can pass 2 billion Decimal128 "decimal" NumberDecimal("0.10") Money and anything that must be exact in base 10 String "string" "hi" UTF-8 text Boolean "bool" true Flags Date "date" new Date() Points in time (milliseconds since the Unix epoch, UTC) ObjectId "objectId" ObjectId() Default _id values Embedded document "object" { a: 1 } Grouping related fields Array "array" [1, 2] Lists — and they get special query and index behaviour (lesson 05) Null "null" null An explicitly empty value Binary "binData" BinData(...), UUID() Hashes, UUIDs, small files

There are others (timestamp, regex, minKey, maxKey, javascript) that you will rarely store yourself. The timestamp type in particular is internal — it is what the oplog uses — so store points in time as date.

docs.title: Size on disk, byte by byte
docs.text:
bsonsize() in the shell shows how many bytes a document takes:

print(bsonsize({}), bsonsize({a:1}), bsonsize({a:1.5}), bsonsize({a:"hi"}),
      bsonsize({a:NumberLong("1")}), bsonsize({a:NumberDecimal("1.5")}), bsonsize({_id:new ObjectId()}))

5 12 16 15 16 24 22

An empty document is 5 bytes: a 4-byte length and a terminating zero. {a:1} adds a type byte, the field name a plus its null terminator, and a 4-byte int: 12. The same value as a double needs 8 bytes, so 16. Decimal128 needs 16 bytes for the value. Note that the field name is stored in every document — a field called customer_shipping_address_line_1 costs 33 bytes in every document that has it, before any value. On a billion documents, naming matters. (Compression on disk reduces this, but the cache and the wire still carry the full names.)

docs.title: ObjectId: a timestamp in disguise
docs.text:
When you insert a document without _id, the driver generates an ObjectId. It is 12 bytes: a 4-byte timestamp (seconds since the epoch), 5 bytes of random value fixed per process, and a 3-byte counter.

const id = new ObjectId("6703a1f2c9e77a1b2c3d4e5f");
id.getTimestamp().toISOString()

2024-10-07T08:55:14.000Z

Two ObjectIds generated back to back in one process:

6acbc68a750685768b1b44d3
6acbc68a750685768b1b44d4

Same first 8 hex digits (the second they were made in), same random middle, counter incremented by one. Consequences:

  • ObjectIds are roughly increasing over time, so sorting by _id approximates insertion order across processes (only to the second; within a second, across machines, it is not exact).
  • You can recover a document's creation time from its _id without a separate field.
  • They are not secret: anyone holding one knows when it was created and can guess neighbours. Do not use them as unguessable tokens in URLs for password resets or private links.

docs.title: Numbers: why money needs Decimal128
docs.text:
db.money.insertMany([
  { k: "double", v: 0.1 }, { k: "double", v: 0.2 },
  { k: "dec", v: NumberDecimal("0.1") }, { k: "dec", v: NumberDecimal("0.2") }
]);
db.money.aggregate([{ $group: { _id: "$k", total: { $sum: "$v" } } }, { $sort: { _id: 1 } }])

[
  { _id: 'dec', total: Decimal128('0.3') },
  { _id: 'double', total: 0.30000000000000004 }
]

The double total is the classic binary floating-point result: 0.1 has no exact representation in base 2. For currency either store Decimal128 or store integer minor units (cents as long). Whichever you choose, choose once — a collection where some prices are doubles and some are decimals sorts and compares correctly (all numeric types compare by value) but adds up inconsistently.

docs.title: Dates belong in Date fields
docs.text:
db.dates.insertMany([
  { s: "2026-9-5",   t: new Date("2026-09-05") },
  { s: "2026-10-01", t: new Date("2026-10-01") }
]);
db.dates.find({}, { _id: 0, s: 1 }).sort({ s: -1 })   // "newest first" by the string
db.dates.find({}, { _id: 0, s: 1 }).sort({ t: -1 })   // newest first by the date

[ { s: '2026-9-5' }, { s: '2026-10-01' } ]
[ { s: '2026-10-01' }, { s: '2026-9-5' } ]

The string sort is wrong because strings compare character by character and "9" is greater than "1". A real Date also gives you date operators in aggregation ($dateTrunc, $dateDiff, time zones), TTL indexes (Level 2 · 06) and 8 bytes instead of 10–30. BSON dates are always UTC; convert to local time when displaying, not when storing.

docs.title: Null versus missing
docs.text:
db.mixed.insertMany([{_id:1,v:"10"},{_id:2,v:9},{_id:3,v:null},{_id:4},{_id:5,v:true},
  {_id:6,v:new Date(0)},{_id:7,v:[3]},{_id:8,v:{x:1}},{_id:9,v:ObjectId("000000000000000000000000")}]);
print(db.mixed.countDocuments({v:null}),
      db.mixed.countDocuments({v:{$exists:false}}),
      db.mixed.countDocuments({v:{$type:"null"}}));

2 1 1

{v: null} matches both the document where v is null and the one where v does not exist. When you need to tell them apart, use $exists or $type.

docs.title: Comparing values of different types
docs.text:
A field is allowed to hold different types in different documents. Sorting such a field follows a fixed order of type classes: null and missing, then numbers, then strings, then objects, arrays, binary data, ObjectId, booleans, dates, and so on:

db.mixed.find({}, { _id: 1 }).sort({ v: 1 }).toArray().map(x => x._id)

[ 3, 4, 7, 2, 1, 8, 9, 5, 6 ]

Null (3) and missing (4) first; then the numbers — [3] (7) sorts by its smallest element when ascending, so it lands among the numbers before 9 (2); then the string "10" (1); the object (8); the ObjectId (9); true (5); and the date (6).

Queries, on the other hand, only compare within the same type class ("type bracketing"):

print(db.mixed.countDocuments({v:{$gt:5}}), db.mixed.countDocuments({v:{$gt:"1"}}));

1 1

$gt: 5 matched only the number 9 — not the string "10", not the date. $gt: "1" matched only the string "10". This is why a field that is a number in some documents and a numeric string in others makes queries look broken: half the data is invisible to any one query.

docs.title: Embedded documents: field order matters for whole-document equality
docs.text:
db.emb.insertOne({ p: { a: 1, b: 2 } });
print(db.emb.countDocuments({ p: { a: 1, b: 2 } }),
      db.emb.countDocuments({ p: { b: 2, a: 1 } }),
      db.emb.countDocuments({ "p.a": 1, "p.b": 2 }));

1 0 1

Matching an entire embedded document compares it byte for byte, including field order — so {b:2, a:1} does not match. Dot notation ("p.a") matches individual fields and does not care about order. Prefer dot notation unless you really mean "exactly this sub-document".

docs.title: Field names with dots and dollars
docs.text:
Modern servers accept them, but they are awkward:

db.odd.insertOne({ "a.b": 1, "$x": 2 });
db.odd.countDocuments({ "a.b": 1 })                                    // 0 — dot means "path"
db.odd.countDocuments({ $expr: { $eq: [{ $getField: "a.b" }, 1] } })   // 1

0
1

The ordinary query treats "a.b" as the path a → b, which doesn't exist. Avoid dots and leading dollars in field names; they are the source of endless escaping problems. This matters most when you use user input (email addresses, URLs) as keys — store them as values instead.

docs.title: The 16 MB limit
docs.text:
for (const mb of [15.9, 16.0]) {
  try { db.big.insertOne({ blob: "x".repeat(Math.floor(mb * 1024 * 1024)) }); print(mb, "ok") }
  catch (e) { print(mb, e.name, e.code, e.message) }
}

15.9 ok
16 MongoServerError 10334 object to insert too large. size in bytes: 16777249, max size: 16777216

A single document can be at most 16 MiB (db.hello().maxBsonObjectSize returns 16777216). The limit is deliberate: a document is read and written as a unit, so a huge one makes every operation on it expensive. If you approach it you almost always have an unbounded array — comments, events, log lines appended forever — and the fix is a modeling change (Level 2 · 03), not a bigger limit. For genuinely large binary files there is GridFS, which splits a file across many documents.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A BSON document is a length-prefixed sequence of elements. Each element is: one type byte, the field name as a null-terminated C string, then the value encoded according to its type (4 bytes for an int, 8 for a double or date, 12 for an ObjectId, a length plus bytes for strings and binary, and a nested BSON document for objects and arrays). An array is literally an embedded document whose keys are the strings "0", "1", "2"…

The length prefixes make BSON fast to skip: to read field 30 the server can hop over fields 1–29 using their lengths without parsing their contents. The cost is that values are stored in document order, so finding a field is a linear scan of the document — another reason to keep documents reasonably sized.

Comparison is defined in two layers. First the type class order (MinKey, null, numbers, symbols and strings, objects, arrays, binary, ObjectId, booleans, dates, timestamps, regular expressions, MaxKey). Then, within a class, values compare naturally: numbers by value regardless of int, long, double or decimal; strings by simple binary comparison unless a collation says otherwise (Level 3 · 09). Sort uses the full order so every document has a place; query operators like $gt stay inside the type class of the value you gave them, which is why indexes can answer range queries with one contiguous scan.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Storing dates as strings. They sort wrong, can't use date operators or TTL, and take more space.
  • Storing money as doubles. Use Decimal128 or integer minor units, consistently.
  • Mixing types in one field ("42" here, 42 there). Queries see only one type at a time.
  • Using ObjectIds as secrets. They are timestamped and sequential.
  • Matching embedded documents whole when you meant to match some of their fields — use dot notation.
  • Long field names on high-volume collections. They're stored in every document.
  • Letting arrays grow forever until a write hits the 16 MB limit in production.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Generate three ObjectIds a second apart and decode their timestamps with getTimestamp(). Which bytes changed between them?
  2. Store ten prices as doubles and the same ten as Decimal128, then sum both with $group. Find a set of prices where the double total is visibly wrong.
  3. In one collection, store a qty field as 5, "5", 5.0, NumberLong("5") and NumberDecimal("5"). Which of them does {qty: 5} match? Which does {qty: "5"} match? Explain.
  4. Use bsonsize() to compare a document with the field name customerShippingAddressLine1 against one with addr1. Multiply the difference by 50 million documents.
  5. Write a query that finds documents where a field is missing but not where it is null.

docs.title: 04 · Inserting & Querying Documents
docs.text: This lesson covers the everyday half of MongoDB: putting documents in and getting the right ones back out. If you know SQL (the SQL Mastery Path covers it), most of the ideas map directly — find() is SELECT, the filter is WHERE, the projection is the column list — but the syntax is a document, and a few behaviours differ in ways that matter.

docs.title: A sample collection
docs.text:
Save this as books.js and run mongosh --quiet books.js. The rest of the lesson queries it.

const lib = db.getSiblingDB("library");
lib.books.drop();
lib.books.insertMany([
  { _id: 1, title: "The Pragmatic Programmer", author: "Hunt & Thomas", year: 1999, pages: 352, genres: ["software", "career"], rating: 4.6, inStock: true },
  { _id: 2, title: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications", author: "Kleppmann", year: 2017, pages: 616, genres: ["software", "databases"], rating: 4.8, inStock: true },
  { _id: 3, title: "Dune", author: "Herbert", year: 1965, pages: 688, genres: ["sci-fi"], rating: 4.5, inStock: false },
  { _id: 4, title: "Project Hail Mary", author: "Weir", year: 2021, pages: 496, genres: ["sci-fi"], rating: 4.7, inStock: true },
  { _id: 5, title: "The Martian", author: "Weir", year: 2011, pages: 384, genres: ["sci-fi"], rating: 4.6, inStock: true },
  { _id: 6, title: "Clean Code", author: "Martin", year: 2008, pages: 464, genres: ["software"], rating: 4.2, inStock: false },
  { _id: 7, title: "Database Internals", author: "Petrov", year: 2019, pages: 370, genres: ["databases"], rating: 4.5, inStock: true },
  { _id: 8, title: "Foundation", author: "Asimov", year: 1951, pages: 255, genres: ["sci-fi"], rating: 4.3, inStock: true },
  { _id: 9, title: "Refactoring", author: "Fowler", year: 2018, pages: 448, genres: ["software"], rating: 4.4 },
  { _id: 10, title: "Thinking in Systems", author: "Meadows", year: 2008, pages: 240, genres: ["systems"], rating: 4.3, inStock: true }
]);

The ratings and page counts are illustrative values for practice, not authoritative data. Note that book 9 has no inStock field at all — real collections are like that, and it will matter below.

docs.title: Inserting
docs.text:
const r = db.books.insertOne({ title: "Snow Crash", author: "Stephenson", year: 1992, genres: ["sci-fi"] });
r

{ acknowledged: true, insertedId: ObjectId('6acbc6dc40661aefb428093d') }

Every document has an _id, unique within its collection. If you don't supply one, the driver generates an ObjectId before sending the insert — which is why insertedId comes back immediately. Supply your own _id when the data has a natural unique key (an ISBN, an order number, a username): it saves an index and makes lookups by that key free.

insertMany() sends a batch in one round trip. What happens when one document in the batch fails is covered in lesson 07.

docs.title: Filters: equality and comparison
docs.text:
A filter is a document. Each field is a condition; several fields are combined with AND.

db.books.find({ year: { $gte: 2015 } }, { _id: 0, title: 1, year: 1 }).sort({ year: -1 })

[
  { title: 'Project Hail Mary', year: 2021 },
  { title: 'Database Internals', year: 2019 },
  { title: 'Refactoring', year: 2018 },
  { title: 'Designing Data-Intensive Applications', year: 2017 }
]
Operator Meaning Example (none) equals { author: "Weir" } $eq, $ne equals / not equals { inStock: { $ne: true } } $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte ranges { pages: { $lt: 300 } } $in, $nin in / not in a list { author: { $in: ["Weir", "Asimov"] } } $exists field present or not { inStock: { $exists: false } } $type BSON type { rating: { $type: "double" } } $regex pattern match { title: /^the /i }

Two conditions on different fields:

db.books.find({ author: { $in: ["Weir", "Asimov"] }, pages: { $lt: 450 } }, { _id: 0, title: 1 })

[ { title: 'The Martian' }, { title: 'Foundation' } ]

Two conditions on the same field go in one operator document:

db.books.find({ year: { $gte: 2000, $lt: 2010 } }, { _id: 0, title: 1, year: 1 })

[ { title: 'Clean Code', year: 2008 }, { title: 'Thinking in Systems', year: 2008 } ]

docs.title: The duplicate-key trap
docs.text:
This looks like "between 2000 and 1960" (which should match nothing) but it is not:

db.books.find({ year: { $gte: 2000 }, year: { $lt: 1960 } }, { _id: 0, title: 1, year: 1 })

[ { title: 'Foundation', year: 1951 } ]

A JavaScript (or Python, or JSON) object can't have two year keys — the second silently replaces the first, and the server only ever receives { year: { $lt: 1960 } }. Merge conditions on one field into one operator document, or use an explicit $and array.

docs.title: Logical operators
docs.text:
db.books.find(
  { $or: [{ rating: { $gte: 4.7 } }, { pages: { $lt: 250 } }] },
  { _id: 0, title: 1, rating: 1, pages: 1 }
)

[
  { title: 'Designing Data-Intensive Applications', pages: 616, rating: 4.8 },
  { title: 'Project Hail Mary', pages: 496, rating: 4.7 },
  { title: 'Thinking in Systems', pages: 240, rating: 4.3 }
]

$and, $or and $nor take arrays of filters; $not negates one operator expression. When every branch of an $or tests the same field for equality, use $in instead — it is shorter and easier for the planner.

docs.title: Negation includes missing fields
docs.text:
db.books.find({ inStock: { $ne: true } }, { _id: 0, title: 1, inStock: 1 })

[
  { title: 'Dune', inStock: false },
  { title: 'Clean Code', inStock: false },
  { title: 'Refactoring' }
]

$ne and $nin match documents where the field is missing, too. Refactoring has no inStock field, so it is "not equal to true". Sometimes that is what you want; often it is a bug in a report. Write { inStock: false } when you mean "explicitly false".

docs.title: Regular expressions
docs.text:
db.books.find({ title: /^the /i }, { _id: 0, title: 1 })

[ { title: 'The Pragmatic Programmer' }, { title: 'The Martian' } ]

Only a case-sensitive regex anchored with ^ can use an index efficiently (as a prefix range). Case-insensitive or unanchored patterns must examine every candidate value. For real search, see Level 3 · 09.

docs.title: Comparing fields with each other: $expr
docs.text:
Ordinary filters compare a field to a constant. To compare two fields of the same document, use $expr with aggregation expressions:

db.books.find({ $expr: { $gt: ["$pages", { $multiply: ["$rating", 100] }] } }, { _id: 0, title: 1 })

[
  { title: 'Designing Data-Intensive Applications' },
  { title: 'Dune' },
  { title: 'Project Hail Mary' },
  { title: 'Clean Code' },
  { title: 'Refactoring' }
]

$expr is powerful but usually can't use an index for the comparison itself. Use it for filters that genuinely need it, not as your default syntax.

docs.title: Projection
docs.text:
The second argument chooses which fields come back. Either include fields ({title: 1}) or exclude them ({reviews: 0}) — not both, with one exception: _id is included by default and may always be excluded.

db.books.find({}, { title: 1, year: 0 })

31254 Cannot do exclusion on field year in inclusion projection

Projection reduces what crosses the network and what your application has to deserialize. It does not make the server read less from disk unless an index alone can answer the query (a covered query, Level 2 · 07).

docs.title: Sort, skip and limit
docs.text:
db.books.find({}, { _id: 0, title: 1 }).sort({ _id: 1 }).skip(3).limit(2)

[ { title: 'Project Hail Mary' }, { title: 'The Martian' } ]

The server always applies them in the order sort → skip → limit, no matter what order you chain them. Without sort(), the order of results is not defined — it often looks like insertion order on a small test collection and then changes after updates, on a different server, or when the plan changes. If order matters, sort, and include a unique field (like _id) as the last sort key so ties are broken deterministically.

skip() still walks over every skipped document, so skip(100000) for page 5,001 of a list is slow. For deep paging use a range on the sort key instead ("give me 20 books with _id greater than the last one I saw").

docs.title: Counting and distinct values
docs.text:
db.books.countDocuments({ inStock: { $ne: true } })   // 3 — runs the query
db.books.estimatedDocumentCount()                      // 10 — reads collection metadata
db.books.distinct("genres")

3
10
[ 'career', 'databases', 'sci-fi', 'software', 'systems' ]

countDocuments() runs a real query and is exact. estimatedDocumentCount() returns the count kept in the collection's metadata without scanning — instant on a billion documents, but it takes no filter and can be slightly off after an unclean shutdown. distinct() unwinds arrays, so each genre appears once even though genres is an array.

findOne() returns the first matching document (or null) instead of a cursor:

db.books.findOne({ author: "Weir" }, { title: 1 })

{ _id: 4, title: 'Project Hail Mary' }

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When a find command arrives, the server parses and normalizes the filter into a tree of match expressions — {year: {$gte: 2000, $lt: 2010}} becomes an AND node with two leaf comparisons. The query planner then looks for indexes that could satisfy some of those leaves. Here there are none except _id, so the only possible plan is a collection scan (COLLSCAN): read every document, evaluate the tree against it, and keep the ones that pass.

Matching documents flow through a pipeline of execution stages: COLLSCAN → SORT (which must see all matches before it can return the first one, and has a memory limit) → SKIP → LIMIT → PROJECTION. Results are packed into a batch of up to 16 MiB (or 101 documents for the first batch by default) and returned with a cursor id if there are more.

Note what this means for sort + limit: without an index on the sort field, finding the top 10 still requires examining every matching document — the server keeps only the best 10 in memory as it goes (a "top-k" sort), but it cannot avoid reading them all. Level 2 is about the indexes that turn these full scans into small, targeted reads, and explain() (Level 2 · 07) shows you which stages a query actually used.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Repeating a key in a filter object — the last one silently wins.
  • Forgetting that $ne/$nin match missing fields.
  • Relying on natural order. Always sort() when order matters, with a unique tie-breaker.
  • Mixing inclusion and exclusion in a projection.
  • Deep pagination with skip(). Use range-based ("keyset") pagination.
  • Using countDocuments({}) for a dashboard total on a huge collection when an estimate would do.
  • Unanchored or case-insensitive regex for search boxes. They scan; use a text or search index.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Using the library.books collection:

  1. Find the titles of in-stock books with more than 400 pages, sorted by pages descending.
  2. Find books in the sci-fi genre published before 1970 or rated at least 4.7 (hint: an AND of one condition and an $or).
  3. Count books where inStock is explicitly false, then count books where it is "not true". Explain the difference in the numbers.
  4. Implement keyset pagination: write a loop that prints the books two at a time ordered by _id, using {_id: {$gt: lastId}} instead of skip().
  5. Use $expr to find books whose title is longer than 15 characters ($strLenCP).

docs.title: 05 · Querying Arrays & Embedded Documents
docs.text: Arrays and embedded documents are why you chose a document database: a student's test results live inside the student, an order's line items inside the order. But array queries follow rules that surprise nearly everyone the first time — a filter that "obviously" means one thing matches documents you didn't expect. This lesson reproduces each surprise so you recognise it in your own data.

docs.title: Sample data
docs.text:
const d = db.getSiblingDB("arrays");
d.students.insertMany([
  { _id: "ana", tags: ["math", "chess"], scores: [72, 95],
    tests: [{ subject: "math", score: 95, year: 2025 }, { subject: "art", score: 60, year: 2026 }],
    address: { city: "Pune", zip: "411001" } },
  { _id: "ben", tags: ["chess"], scores: [88, 81],
    tests: [{ subject: "math", score: 58, year: 2026 }, { subject: "art", score: 91, year: 2025 }],
    address: { city: "Hyderabad", zip: "500001" } },
  { _id: "cy", tags: ["math", "chess", "go"], scores: [55, 62, 99],
    tests: [{ subject: "math", score: 91, year: 2026 }], address: { city: "Pune" } },
  { _id: "dee", tags: [], scores: [], tests: [] },
  { _id: "eve", tags: ["go"], scores: [50, 95], tests: [], address: { city: "Chennai" } }
]);
const ids = q => d.students.find(q, { _id: 1 }).toArray().map(x => x._id).join(",");

The helper ids() prints just the matching _ids so results fit on one line.

docs.title: A scalar condition on an array means "contains"
docs.text:
ids({ tags: "chess" })

ana,ben,cy

When a field holds an array, {field: value} matches if any element equals the value. You never write a loop; the server does it.

docs.title: An array condition means "exactly this array"
docs.text:
ids({ tags: ["math", "chess"] })   // → ana
ids({ tags: ["chess", "math"] })   // → (nothing)

Giving an array as the value asks for an exact match: same elements, same order, same length. Cy has math and chess too, but also go, so it doesn't match. To ask "contains all of these, in any order", use $all:

ids({ tags: { $all: ["chess", "math"] } })

ana,cy

$size matches an exact length — useful for finding empty arrays:

ids({ tags: { $size: 0 } })

dee

$size only takes an exact number. For "at least 3 tags" use {"tags.2": {$exists: true}} (an element at index 2 exists) or $expr with $size.

docs.title: The surprise: several conditions on one array
docs.text:
Which students have a score greater than 90 and less than 60?

ids({ scores: { $gt: 90, $lt: 60 } })

cy

No number is both above 90 and below 60, yet Cy matched. Each condition is checked against the array independently: some element is above 90 (99), and some element — possibly a different one — is below 60 (55). That is sometimes what you want. When you need a single element to satisfy all the conditions, use $elemMatch:

ids({ scores: { $gt: 60, $lt: 90 } })                  // ana,ben,cy,eve
ids({ scores: { $elemMatch: { $gt: 60, $lt: 90 } } })  // ana,ben,cy

Eve's scores are 50 and 95. Neither is between 60 and 90, but 95 is above 60 and 50 is below 90, so the first query matches her and the second does not.

docs.title: The same surprise with arrays of documents
docs.text:
This is where it causes real bugs. "Students who scored at least 90 in math":

ids({ "tests.subject": "math", "tests.score": { $gte: 90 } })

ana,ben,cy

Ben scored 58 in math. He matched because he has a test whose subject is math (the 58) and a test with score ≥ 90 (his 91 in art). Adding a third condition doesn't help:

ids({ "tests.subject": "math", "tests.score": { $gte: 90 }, "tests.year": 2026 })

ana,ben,cy

Each dotted condition can be satisfied by a different element. $elemMatch ties them to one element:

ids({ tests: { $elemMatch: { subject: "math", score: { $gte: 90 }, year: 2026 } } })

cy

Only Cy has one test that is math, ≥ 90 and in 2026. Rule of thumb: if you put two or more conditions on fields of the same array of documents, you almost certainly want $elemMatch.

docs.title: Dot notation for embedded documents and array positions
docs.text:
ids({ "address.city": "Pune" })     // ana,cy — field inside an embedded document
ids({ "scores.0": { $gt: 70 } })    // ana,ben — the first element of the array
ids({ "tests.0": { $exists: false } })  // dee,eve — empty (or missing) tests array

A numeric path component means "the element at this index". Use it sparingly: position-based logic breaks as soon as someone inserts at the front of the array.

Remember from lesson 03 that {address: {city: "Pune"}} (no dot) would only match documents whose entire address is exactly {city: "Pune"} — that matches Cy, but not Ana, whose address also has a zip.

docs.title: Returning only part of an array
docs.text:
By default you get the whole array back. Three projections trim it.

Positional $ returns the first element that matched the query:

d.students.find({ "tests.subject": "art" }, { _id: 1, "tests.$": 1 })

[
  { _id: 'ana', tests: [ { subject: 'art', score: 60, year: 2026 } ] },
  { _id: 'ben', tests: [ { subject: 'art', score: 91, year: 2025 } ] }
]

$elemMatch in a projection returns the first element matching its own condition, independent of the query:

d.students.find({ _id: "ben" }, { _id: 0, tests: { $elemMatch: { score: { $gte: 90 } } } })

[ { tests: [ { subject: 'art', score: 91, year: 2025 } ] } ]

$slice returns a range — here the last two scores:

d.students.find({ _id: "cy" }, { scores: { $slice: -2 }, _id: 0, tags: 0, tests: 0, address: 0 })

[ { scores: [ 62, 99 ] } ]

And a dotted inclusion keeps the array but only that field of each element:

d.students.find({}, { _id: 1, "tests.score": 1 }).limit(2)

[
  { _id: 'ana', tests: [ { score: 95 }, { score: 60 } ] },
  { _id: 'ben', tests: [ { score: 58 }, { score: 91 } ] }
]

Both $ and projection-$elemMatch return only the first matching element. If you need every matching element (all of a student's tests above 90), use the aggregation $filter expression — Level 3 · 02.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The matcher evaluates each leaf of the filter against a path. When it walks a path like tests.score and meets an array along the way, it doesn't stop — it fans out and collects every value reachable through that path: for Ben, tests.score yields {58, 91}. A leaf such as {$gte: 90} is true if any collected value satisfies it. The leaves of an implicit AND are each evaluated separately, with their own fan-out, which is exactly why conditions "jump" between elements.

$elemMatch changes the unit of evaluation: it iterates the array's elements and applies its whole sub-filter to one element at a time, returning true as soon as one element satisfies everything. That is also why it is the only way to express "same element" constraints in an index-friendly way: a multikey index (Level 2 · 06) stores one entry per array element, and the planner can only combine bounds on tests.subject and tests.score tightly when it knows they must come from the same element — which $elemMatch tells it.

When the value in an equality condition is itself an array ({tags: ["math","chess"]}), the matcher first tries to match the whole field as one value (exact array equality) and then tries each element (so a nested array element [["math","chess"]] would also match). That two-step rule is why the array-literal form means "exactly equal" rather than "contains all".

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Multiple dotted conditions on one array of documents without $elemMatch — the Ben bug. It passes tests with simple data and fails with real data.
  • Using an array literal when you mean $all. Order and length must match exactly.
  • Expecting $size to accept ranges. It doesn't; use an index-position $exists or $expr.
  • Expecting positional $ to return all matches. It returns the first only.
  • Index-based paths (scores.0) for meaning like "latest score". Store "latest" explicitly if you query it.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Using the arrays.students collection:

  1. Find students who have both the math and go tags, in any order.
  2. Find students with at least one score from 80 to 89 inclusive. Then write the version without $elemMatch and find a document (insert one if needed) that the two queries disagree on.
  3. Find students who took an art test in 2025 with a score above 90. Prove that your query is correct by inserting a student who would wrongly match a version without $elemMatch.
  4. Return each student's _id and only their highest-indexed (last) test using $slice.
  5. Find students who have an address but no zip inside it.

docs.title: 06 · Update Operators, Upserts & Array Updates
docs.text:
In a relational database you often update a row by reading it, changing it in your program, and writing it back. In MongoDB you usually describe the change instead — "add 1 to views", "append this item", "set the quantity of the pen line to 5" — and the server applies it to the document atomically. Learning the update operators is learning to say exactly that.

All examples run in a database called upd.

docs.title: Why describe the change instead of the result
docs.text:
A small Python program runs 2,000 "add one to qty" operations from 16 threads, twice: once by reading the document and writing back qty + 1, once with $inc.

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pymongo import MongoClient

coll = MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0").upd.stock
coll.delete_many({})
coll.insert_many([{"_id": "read-modify-write", "qty": 0}, {"_id": "inc", "qty": 0}])

def rmw(_):
    doc = coll.find_one({"_id": "read-modify-write"})
    coll.update_one({"_id": "read-modify-write"}, {"$set": {"qty": doc["qty"] + 1}})

def inc(_):
    coll.update_one({"_id": "inc"}, {"$inc": {"qty": 1}})

with ThreadPoolExecutor(16) as pool:
    list(pool.map(rmw, range(2000)))
    list(pool.map(inc, range(2000)))

for d in coll.find().sort("_id", 1):
    print(d)

{'_id': 'inc', 'qty': 2000}
{'_id': 'read-modify-write', 'qty': 400}

Four out of five read-modify-write increments were lost: two threads read the same value, both wrote value + 1, and one increment vanished. The exact number lost will differ on every run; that it loses some will not. $inc was correct every time because the server applies it to the current document under a lock. Every single-document update in MongoDB is atomic — use that.

docs.title: Field operators
docs.text:
The starting document:

db.carts.insertOne({ _id: "c1", user: "ana",
  items: [{ sku: "pen", qty: 2, price: NumberDecimal("1.50") },
          { sku: "ink", qty: 1, price: NumberDecimal("4.00") }],
  tags: ["new"], views: 0 });

db.carts.updateOne({ _id: "c1" },
  { $inc: { views: 1 }, $set: { status: "open" }, $currentDate: { updatedAt: true } })

{ acknowledged: true, insertedId: null, matchedCount: 1, modifiedCount: 1, upsertedCount: 0 }

Run the $set part again and look at the counts:

db.carts.updateOne({ _id: "c1" }, { $set: { status: "open" } })

{ acknowledged: true, insertedId: null, matchedCount: 1, modifiedCount: 0, upsertedCount: 0 }

matchedCount is how many documents the filter found; modifiedCount is how many actually changed. Setting a field to the value it already has is a no-op — nothing is written to disk or to the oplog. Check matchedCount when "did my document exist?" matters, for example to return a 404.

Operator Does Example $set set a field (creating it, and any missing parents) {$set: {"address.city": "Pune"}} $unset remove a field {$unset: {views: ""}} $inc add (negative to subtract) {$inc: {stock: -1}} $mul multiply {$mul: {price: NumberDecimal("1.1")}} $min / $max set only if the new value is lower / higher {$min: {low: 7}} $rename rename a field {$rename: {status: "state"}} $currentDate set to the server's current date {$currentDate: {updatedAt: true}} $setOnInsert set only when an upsert inserts see below

$min and $max are handy for "lowest price seen" and "last activity" fields without reading first:

db.prices.insertOne({ _id: 1, low: 10, high: 10 });
db.prices.updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { $min: { low: 7 }, $max: { high: 8 } });
db.prices.findOne()

{ _id: 1, low: 7, high: 10 }

low became 7 because 7 < 10; high stayed 10 because 8 is not higher.

docs.title: Array operators
docs.text:
db.carts.updateOne({ _id: "c1" }, {
  $push: { items: { sku: "pad", qty: 1, price: NumberDecimal("2.25") } },
  $addToSet: { tags: { $each: ["new", "gift"] } }
});

$push appends. $addToSet appends only values not already present, so "new" was skipped and tags became ['new', 'gift']. $pull removes every element matching a condition, and $pop removes the first or last element.

docs.title: A capped "most recent" list
docs.text:
$push takes modifiers that keep an array bounded. Push five events, keeping only the three with the highest at:

db.feed.insertOne({ _id: 1, recent: [] });
for (const n of [5, 9, 2, 7, 1])
  db.feed.updateOne({ _id: 1 },
    { $push: { recent: { $each: [{ n, at: n }], $sort: { at: -1 }, $slice: 3 } } });
db.feed.findOne().recent.map(x => x.n)

[ 9, 7, 5 ]

This pattern ("last N notifications", "top 3 scores") is one of the cleanest ways to embed a list without letting it grow toward the 16 MB limit.

docs.title: Updating elements inside arrays
docs.text:
There are three ways to target array elements.

Positional $ — the first element matched by the query:

db.carts.updateOne({ _id: "c1", "items.sku": "pen" }, { $inc: { "items.$.qty": 3 } })

All positional $[] — every element:

db.carts.updateOne({ _id: "c1" }, { $set: { "items.$[].checked": false } })

Filtered positional $[name] with arrayFilters — every element matching a condition you name:

db.carts.updateOne({ _id: "c1" },
  { $set: { "items.$[cheap].discount": NumberDecimal("0.10") } },
  { arrayFilters: [{ "cheap.price": { $lt: NumberDecimal("3") } }] })

The cart after these three updates:

{
  user: 'ana',
  items: [
    { sku: 'pen', qty: 5, price: Decimal128('1.50'), checked: false, discount: Decimal128('0.10') },
    { sku: 'ink', qty: 1, price: Decimal128('4.00'), checked: false },
    { sku: 'pad', qty: 1, price: Decimal128('2.25'), checked: false, discount: Decimal128('0.10') }
  ],
  tags: [ 'new', 'gift' ],
  views: 1,
  status: 'open',
  updatedAt: ISODate('2026-10-11T17:28:53.998Z')
}

The pen went from 2 to 5, every item got checked: false, and only the two items under 3.00 got a discount. Positional $ fails if the query didn't match an array element:

db.carts.updateOne({ _id: "c1" }, { $set: { "items.$.qty": 1 } })

2 Plan executor error during update :: caused by :: The positional operator did not find the match needed from the query.

Removing, unsetting and renaming in one update:

db.carts.updateOne({ _id: "c1" },
  { $pull: { items: { sku: "ink" } }, $unset: { views: "" }, $rename: { status: "state" } })

The ink line is gone, views is gone and status is now state.

docs.title: Things an update can't do
docs.text:
Two operators can't touch the same path, or a path and its parent, in one update:

db.k.insertOne({ _id: 1, a: { b: 1 } });
db.k.updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { $set: { a: 1, "a.b": 2 } })

40 Updating the path 'a.b' would create a conflict at 'a'

And an update document without operators is rejected by the driver, which protects you from a classic accident:

db.carts.updateOne({ _id: "c1" }, { user: "bob" })

MongoInvalidArgumentError Update document requires atomic operators

Older APIs (update()) treated a document without operators as a replacement and quietly wiped every other field. If you really mean to replace, use replaceOne (lesson 07).

docs.title: Upserts
docs.text:
An upsert updates the matching document or inserts one if none matches. $setOnInsert sets fields only on the insert:

const hit = () => db.counters.updateOne({ _id: "page:/home" },
  { $inc: { hits: 1 }, $setOnInsert: { createdAt: new Date("2026-10-01") } }, { upsert: true });
hit(); hit();
db.counters.findOne()

The first call reported upsertedCount: 1, insertedId: 'page:/home'; the second matchedCount: 1, modifiedCount: 1. Result:

{ _id: 'page:/home', createdAt: ISODate('2026-10-01T00:00:00.000Z'), hits: 2 }

The inserted document is built from the equality conditions in the filter plus the update — so _id: "page:/home" came from the filter. Upserts with a filter that is not on a unique field can create duplicates when two clients upsert at the same moment; put a unique index on the filter field (Level 2 · 06) and retry on a duplicate-key error.

docs.title: Getting the document back: findOneAndUpdate
docs.text:
updateOne tells you counts. When you need the document — say, the next number from a sequence — use findOneAndUpdate:

db.counters.findOneAndUpdate({ _id: "seq" }, { $inc: { v: 1 } }, { upsert: true, returnDocument: "after" })
db.counters.findOneAndUpdate({ _id: "seq" }, { $inc: { v: 1 } }, { returnDocument: "before" })

{ _id: 'seq', v: 1 }
{ _id: 'seq', v: 1 }

The first call created the counter and returned it after the increment (1); the second returned it before its increment (still 1; it is now 2). The read and the write happen atomically — no other client can increment in between.

docs.title: Updates that use the document's own fields
docs.text:
An update can be an aggregation pipeline (in square brackets), which lets new values be computed from existing fields:

db.people.insertMany([{ _id: 1, first: "Ada", last: "Lovelace" }, { _id: 2, first: "Alan", last: "Turing" }]);
db.people.updateMany({}, [{ $set: { full: { $concat: ["$first", " ", "$last"] } } }]);
db.people.find()

[
  { _id: 1, first: 'Ada', last: 'Lovelace', full: 'Ada Lovelace' },
  { _id: 2, first: 'Alan', last: 'Turing', full: 'Alan Turing' }
]

Inside a pipeline, "$first" means "the value of field first"; in an ordinary $set it would be the literal string "$first". Level 3 covers pipeline expressions.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
For each matching document the server takes a write intent on that document, applies every operator to an in-memory copy, validates the result (size limit, _id unchanged, schema validation if configured) and writes the new version through WiredTiger, which keeps the old version available to readers that started earlier. The read of the current value and the write of the new one happen inside one storage transaction, so no other writer can slip in between: two concurrent $incs are serialized, and if two writers race on the same document WiredTiger detects the write conflict and the server transparently retries the losing operation. That is why $inc never lost an update in the experiment while client-side read-modify-write did.

Atomicity is per document. updateMany matching 1,000 documents applies 1,000 separate atomic updates; another client may see some updated and others not, and if the server crashes halfway, some are done and some are not. When several documents must change together, you either design them into one document (Level 2) or use a transaction (Level 3 · 06).

On a replica set the update is recorded in the oplog not as your operators but as its effect — for $inc the resulting value, for $push with $slice the resulting array or a delta. That makes replaying an oplog entry idempotent: applying it twice gives the same result, which replication depends on.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Read-modify-write in application code for counters and stock levels. Use $inc and conditional filters ({_id, stock: {$gte: 1}} with $inc: {stock: -1}).
  • Unbounded $push. Add $slice, or move the list to its own collection.
  • Positional $ without the array in the query. It errors; use arrayFilters.
  • Upserting on a non-unique field under concurrency, creating duplicates.
  • Ignoring matchedCount and reporting success for an update that touched nothing.
  • Assuming updateMany is all-or-nothing. It isn't.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Using a new upd.inventory collection:

  1. Insert {_id: "widget", stock: 3}. Write a "reserve one" update that decrements stock only if stock is at least 1. Run it four times and inspect matchedCount each time.
  2. Store a product with a priceHistory array. Write one update that pushes a new {price, at} entry and keeps only the 5 most recent.
  3. Given an order with line items, use arrayFilters to set backordered: true on every line whose qty exceeds 10.
  4. Implement an "upsert a daily stats document" pattern: one document per (page, day) with hits incremented and firstSeen set only on insert.
  5. Re-run the lost-update experiment with 4 threads and then with 32 threads. Record how many updates were lost each time, then make the read-modify-write version safe without using $inc (hint: put the value you read into the filter and retry when modifiedCount is 0).

docs.title: 07 · Deletes, Replaces & Bulk Writes
docs.text:
This lesson finishes basic CRUD with the operations that remove or overwrite data, then covers sending many writes at once — which is how imports, sync jobs and batch processes should talk to MongoDB. The interesting part is not the happy path; it is what happens when one write in a batch fails.

Everything runs in a database called bulk.

docs.title: Deleting
docs.text:
db.t.deleteOne({ _id: 12345 })          // first match only
db.t.deleteMany({ batch: true })        // every match

{ acknowledged: true, deletedCount: 0 }
{ acknowledged: true, deletedCount: 3 }

Like updates, deletes report a count rather than failing when nothing matched. If deleting nothing is an error for your application (deleting an order that doesn't exist), check deletedCount yourself.

findOneAndDelete removes one document and returns it, atomically — useful for "take the next job from the queue":

db.t.findOneAndDelete({ batch: true }, { sort: { _id: -1 } })

{ _id: 10, s: 'a', batch: true }

The sort decides which matching document is taken when several match.

docs.title: Before you run a delete
docs.text:
A delete filter is the most dangerous thing you will type. Two habits prevent most disasters:

  1. Run the filter as a countDocuments() or find() first and check the number is what you expect.
  2. Never build a delete filter from user input without validating it isn't empty. In most drivers {} is a perfectly valid filter: deleteMany({}) removes everything, and a filter like { userId: req.query.id } turns into { userId: undefined } when the parameter is missing — which drivers may serialize in surprising ways depending on settings. Validate first.

docs.title: deleteMany({}) versus drop()
docs.text:
Both leave you with no documents. They are very different operations. With 200,000 small documents and one secondary index in each of two collections:

let t = Date.now(); d.a.deleteMany({});
print("deleteMany ms", Date.now() - t, "indexes left", d.a.getIndexes().length);
t = Date.now(); d.b.drop();
print("drop ms", Date.now() - t, "collections:", d.getCollectionNames().join(","));

deleteMany ms 650 indexes left 2
drop ms 7 collections: customers,t,a,orders

deleteMany({}) deletes documents one at a time, writes an oplog entry for each (on a replica set, every secondary repeats the work), and leaves the collection, its indexes, options and validation rules in place. drop() removes the collection's files in one metadata operation; indexes and settings go with it. On a laptop the difference is 650 ms vs 7 ms; on 500 million documents it is hours versus milliseconds — and hours of replication lag. To empty a large collection and keep its definition, it is usually faster to drop and recreate indexes (or create a fresh collection and rename it).

docs.title: Replacing a document
docs.text:
replaceOne swaps the whole document (except _id) for a new one:

db.t.replaceOne({ _id: 2 }, { s: "replaced" });
db.t.findOne({ _id: 2 })

{ _id: 2, s: 'replaced' }

Every field not in the replacement is gone. _id is immutable — try to change it and the server refuses:

66 Plan executor error during update :: caused by :: After applying the update, the (immutable) field '_id' was found to have been altered to _id: 22

And a replacement containing operators is rejected client-side, the mirror image of the protection updateOne gives you:

MongoInvalidArgumentError Replacement document must not contain atomic operators

Use replaceOne when your application owns the whole document and writes it back as a unit (a settings object, a cached API response). Use updateOne with operators when several writers may change different fields — a replace would overwrite their changes with whatever your copy had.

To "change" an _id, insert a new document with the new _id and delete the old one, inside a transaction if nothing may see the in-between state (Level 3 · 06).

docs.title: Batches: ordered by default
docs.text:
insertMany sends many documents in one request. With _ids 1 and 2 already present, insert 3, 1, 4:

try { db.t.insertMany([{ _id: 3 }, { _id: 1 }, { _id: 4 }]) }
catch (e) { print(e.name, "inserted:", e.result.insertedCount,
                  "errors:", e.writeErrors.map(w => w.index + ":" + w.code).join(",")) }
print(db.t.find().toArray().map(x => x._id).join(","))

MongoBulkWriteError inserted: 1 errors: 1:11000
1,2,3

The batch is ordered by default: the server processes it in sequence and stops at the first error. Document 3 was inserted, document 1 failed with a duplicate key (index 1 in the batch, code 11000), and document 4 was never attempted. Nothing was rolled back — 3 stays.

docs.title: Unordered batches keep going
docs.text:
try { db.t.insertMany([{ _id: 5 }, { _id: 2 }, { _id: 6 }, { _id: 1 }, { _id: 7 }], { ordered: false }) }
catch (e) { print(e.name, "inserted:", e.result.insertedCount,
                  "errors:", e.writeErrors.map(w => w.index + ":" + w.code).join(",")) }

MongoBulkWriteError inserted: 3 errors: 1:11000,3:11000
1,2,3,5,6,7

With ordered: false the server attempts every write and reports every failure by its index in the batch. That is what you want for imports and idempotent syncs ("insert these, skip the ones that already exist"). Unordered batches can also be faster, because on a sharded cluster the router can send the writes to different shards in parallel. Use ordered batches only when a later write depends on an earlier one.

Either way, a batch is not a transaction. Writes that succeeded stay applied when later ones fail.

docs.title: bulkWrite: mixed operations in one round trip
docs.text:
bulkWrite batches different kinds of writes against one collection:

const r = db.t.bulkWrite([
  { insertOne:  { document: { _id: 10, s: "a" } } },
  { updateOne:  { filter: { _id: 1 }, update: { $set: { s: "b" } } } },
