  { updateMany: { filter: { _id: { $gte: 5 } }, update: { $set: { batch: true } } } },
  { replaceOne: { filter: { _id: 2 }, replacement: { s: "replaced" } } },
  { deleteOne:  { filter: { _id: 3 } } },
  { updateOne:  { filter: { _id: 99 }, update: { $set: { s: "new" } }, upsert: true } }
]);

{
  acknowledged: true,
  insertedCount: 1,
  insertedIds: { '0': 10 },
  matchedCount: 6,
  modifiedCount: 6,
  deletedCount: 1,
  upsertedCount: 1,
  upsertedIds: { '5': 99 }
}

matchedCount is 6: the first updateOne matched 1, the updateMany matched 4 (5, 6, 7 and 10 — the document inserted earlier in the same ordered batch), and the replaceOne matched 1. The upsert is reported separately with its batch index ('5').

docs.title: Across collections
docs.text:
Since MongoDB 8.0 the server also has a client-level bulkWrite command that mixes collections in one request. mongosh exposes it on the connection:

db.getMongo().bulkWrite([
  { name: "insertOne", namespace: "bulk.orders", document: { _id: 1, total: 20 } },
  { name: "updateOne", namespace: "bulk.customers", filter: { _id: "ana" },
    update: { $inc: { orders: 1 } }, upsert: true }
])

{
  acknowledged: true,
  insertedCount: 1,
  matchedCount: 0,
  modifiedCount: 0,
  deletedCount: 0,
  upsertedCount: 1,
  insertResults: undefined,
  updateResults: undefined,
  deleteResults: undefined
}

It saves round trips; it is still not atomic across the two collections. Driver support for the client-level form arrived over several releases, so check your driver's documentation before relying on it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The driver turns insertMany, bulkWrite and friends into as few server commands as possible. It groups consecutive operations of the same kind (in an ordered batch) or all operations of the same kind (in an unordered one) into insert, update and delete commands, and splits them further so no single command message exceeds the server's limits (maxWriteBatchSize, 100,000 operations, and the 48 MB message size). That is why a 1-million-document insertMany still works: the driver sends it as several commands.

On the server, each write in a command is its own atomic single-document operation. For an ordered command, the server stops at the first failure and returns what it did plus the error; for an unordered one, it records the failure and continues. The driver then merges the per-command replies into one result, translating the indexes back to positions in your list — so writeErrors[i].index always refers to your original array.

A drop is a catalog operation: on a replica set it is replicated as one oplog entry, and the data files are removed after the drop is majority-committed. A deleteMany is N separate document deletes, each with its own oplog entry and index maintenance, which is why its cost scales with the data.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running a delete without counting the filter first.
  • Using replaceOne when other code updates the same document — it silently reverts their fields.
  • Assuming a failed batch rolled back. Ordered or not, successful writes stay.
  • Using ordered batches for imports, so one duplicate stops the whole job half-way.
  • Emptying a huge collection with deleteMany({}) when a drop-and-recreate would do.
  • Reporting "deleted" when deletedCount is 0.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Insert _ids 1–10. Then insertMany a batch of _ids 8–15 ordered, and again unordered. Predict the final contents and the error indexes before running each.
  2. Write a "sync" script that receives a list of products and, with a single bulkWrite, upserts every product by sku, setting updatedAt, and deletes products whose sku is not in the list (use deleteMany with $nin). Print the result counts.
  3. Time deleteMany({}) against drop() on 500,000 documents on your machine. Then check db.getSiblingDB("local").oplog.rs.countDocuments({ns: "bulk.<yourcollection>"}) after each and explain the difference.
  4. Use findOneAndDelete with a sort to build a tiny job queue: insert five jobs with priorities, and take them off in priority order.

docs.title: 08 · Drivers: PyMongo & the Node.js Driver
docs.text:
The shell is for people. Applications talk to MongoDB through a driver — an official library for their language. Drivers all follow the same specifications, so once you understand one, the others differ mainly in syntax. This lesson uses the two most common: PyMongo for Python and the mongodb package for Node.js. (The language basics are covered in the Python and Node.js Mastery Paths.)

Versions used here: PyMongo 4.18.3 on Python 3.14, and the Node.js driver 7.7.0 on Node 26.

python3 -m venv venv && venv/bin/pip install pymongo
npm install mongodb

docs.title: The one rule: create one client and share it
docs.text:
A MongoClient is not a connection. It is a connection pool plus background threads that monitor every server in the deployment. It is expensive to create and designed to be shared by your whole process for its whole life.

To show the cost, this script does 200 reads, first creating a new client for each read (a mistake that appears surprisingly often in web handlers), then with one shared client:

import time
from pymongo import MongoClient

URI = "mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0"

t = time.perf_counter()
for i in range(200):
    with MongoClient(URI) as c:
        c.drivers.items.find_one()
per_request = time.perf_counter() - t

shared = MongoClient(URI)
t = time.perf_counter()
for i in range(200):
    shared.drivers.items.find_one()
reused = time.perf_counter() - t
print(f"new client per operation: {per_request*1000:.0f} ms for 200 reads")
print(f"one shared client:        {reused*1000:.0f} ms for 200 reads")

new client per operation: 307 ms for 200 reads
one shared client:        31 ms for 200 reads

Ten times slower on localhost, where a TCP connection costs almost nothing. Over a real network with TLS and authentication, every new connection adds several round trips plus a password-hashing handshake, and the gap becomes enormous — and the server has to set up and tear down a connection each time. In a web framework, create the client at start-up (module level, an app factory, or a dependency that returns the same instance) and close it at shutdown.

docs.title: Python: PyMongo
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from decimal import Decimal
from bson import Decimal128
from pymongo import MongoClient

client = MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0")
coll = client.drivers.items       # attribute access; client["drivers"]["items"] also works
coll.drop()

res = coll.insert_one({
    "name": "kettle",
    "price": Decimal128(Decimal("29.99")),
    "qty": 3,
    "weight_kg": 1.2,
    "created": datetime(2026, 10, 11, 9, 30, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
    "tags": ["kitchen", "electric"],
})
doc = coll.find_one({"_id": res.inserted_id})
for k, v in doc.items():
    print(f"{k:10} {type(v).__name__:12} {v!r}")

_id        ObjectId     ObjectId('6acbc7ea5646ac91f52b6466')
name       str          'kettle'
price      Decimal128   Decimal128('29.99')
qty        int          3
weight_kg  float        1.2
created    datetime     datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 11, 9, 30)
tags       list         ['kitchen', 'electric']

Method names are snake_case (insert_one, find_one, update_many); filters and update documents are Python dicts with exactly the same operators you used in the shell.

Two type details trip people up:

Decimals. Python's decimal.Decimal is not encoded automatically:

InvalidDocument Invalid document: cannot encode object: Decimal('1.10'), of type: <class 'decimal.Decimal'

Wrap it in bson.Decimal128 on the way in and call .to_decimal() on the way out (or register a custom type codec once).

Datetimes. The document above was stored with a timezone-aware UTC datetime, but it came back naive — datetime(2026, 10, 11, 9, 30) with no tzinfo. BSON dates are always UTC, and by default PyMongo returns them naive. Ask for aware datetimes when you create the client:

aware = MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0", tz_aware=True)
print(aware.drivers.items.find_one()["created"])

2026-10-11 09:30:00+00:00

Mixing naive and aware datetimes in one codebase is a reliable source of off-by-five-and-a-half-hours bugs. Pick tz_aware=True and stick with it.

PyMongo is synchronous. For asyncio applications PyMongo also ships an async API (from pymongo import AsyncMongoClient) with the same method names as coroutines; it replaces the older third-party Motor library, which MongoDB has deprecated.

docs.title: Node.js: the mongodb package
docs.text:
import { MongoClient, Decimal128, MongoServerError } from "mongodb";

const client = new MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0", { maxPoolSize: 10 });
let opened = 0;
client.on("connectionCreated", () => opened++);

const items = client.db("drivers").collection("items");
await items.deleteMany({});
await items.insertMany([
  { name: "kettle", price: Decimal128.fromString("29.99"), qty: 3 },
  { name: "toaster", price: Decimal128.fromString("45.00"), qty: 0 },
  { name: "mug", price: Decimal128.fromString("6.50"), qty: 40 },
]);

for await (const doc of items.find({ qty: { $gt: 0 } }).sort({ name: 1 }).project({ _id: 0 })) {
  console.log(doc.name, doc.price.toString(), typeof doc.qty);
}

kettle 29.99 number
mug 6.50 number

Every operation returns a Promise. Cursors are async iterables, so for await streams results batch by batch without loading them all into memory — prefer it to toArray() for anything large. Forget an await and you get a Promise instead of a document, with no error:

const forgot = items.findOne({ name: "mug" });
console.log("without await:", forgot instanceof Promise);

without await: true

Unlike mongosh, the driver does not hide this for you.

docs.title: The pool in action
docs.text:
The connectionCreated event counted how many connections the client opened while 50 reads ran concurrently:

await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: 50 }, () => items.findOne({ name: "mug" })));
console.log("connections opened for 50 concurrent reads:", opened);

connections opened for 50 concurrent reads: 10

The pool never exceeds maxPoolSize (10 here; the default is 100). The other 40 operations waited for a free connection — each connection runs one operation at a time. Sizing the pool is a trade-off: too small and requests queue in your app; too large across hundreds of app instances and the server spends its memory on idle connections. Level 4 · 08 returns to this.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Both drivers raise typed errors with the server's numeric code:

DuplicateKeyError code 11000                 # PyMongo
true 11000                                   # Node: e instanceof MongoServerError, e.code

Handle by class and code, never by parsing the message. The other error you must expect is "no server available". With the server stopped, PyMongo waits for serverSelectionTimeoutMS (default 30 s; 2 s here) and then raises:

dead = MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27999/", serverSelectionTimeoutMS=2000)
dead.admin.command("ping")

gave up after 2.0s: 127.0.0.1:27999: [Errno 61] Connection refused (configured timeouts: socketTimeoutMS: 20000.0ms

Notice that creating the client did not fail. Clients connect lazily and in the background; the first operation is where you find out. If your application should refuse to start without a database, run a ping command at start-up.

docs.title: Retryable writes and reads
docs.text: Connection strings default to retryWrites=true and retryReads=true. If a write fails with a network error or because the primary stepped down mid-operation, the driver retries it once on the new primary. The server makes this safe by recording each retryable write's transaction number, so a retry of a write that actually succeeded is recognised and not applied twice. This covers single-document writes and insertMany/bulkWrite; updateMany and deleteMany are not retryable, because the server can't tell which documents a half-finished multi-update already touched.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When a client is created, it parses the URI and starts a monitor per seed host. Each monitor connects and sends hello, learns the server's role (primary, secondary, standalone, mongos), the replica set's member list and limits like maxBsonObjectSize, then keeps polling (by default every 10 seconds, or streaming updates on modern servers) so the client always has a current picture of the topology.

Each operation goes through server selection: given the operation type and read preference, pick a suitable server from the current topology — for a write, the primary. If none is suitable (the primary is down mid-election), the client waits and re-checks until serverSelectionTimeoutMS. Then it checks out a connection from that server's pool (creating one, with TLS and auth handshakes, if none is idle and the pool isn't full), encodes the command to BSON, sends it as an OP_MSG wire-protocol message, waits for the reply, decodes it, and returns the connection to the pool.

Everything that makes MongoDB "highly available" from the application's point of view — following a new primary after failover, retrying a write once, reading from secondaries — happens in this layer, which is why using a recent official driver and one long-lived client matters more than most tuning flags.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A new MongoClient per request or per function call. Create one per process.
  • Forgetting await in Node — no error, just a Promise where you expected data.
  • Naive datetimes in Python. Use tz_aware=True and timezone-aware values.
  • Passing decimal.Decimal to PyMongo without Decimal128.
  • toArray() / list(cursor) on unbounded queries. Stream with iteration, or add a limit.
  • Discovering the database is unreachable on the first user request — ping at start-up.
  • Catching errors by message text instead of class and code.
  • Forking after creating a client (e.g. pre-fork servers like Gunicorn): create the client in each worker after the fork; PyMongo warns if a client is used across a fork.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a Python module db.py that exposes one shared client (with tz_aware=True) and a get_collection(name) function. Use it from two other modules and confirm only one client is created.
  2. Reproduce the 200-reads timing on your machine with both drivers. Then repeat it against a server on another machine (or a container) and compare the gap.
  3. In Node, set maxPoolSize: 2, subscribe to the connectionCheckOutStarted and connectionCheckedOut events, and run 20 concurrent find().toArray() calls over a collection of 100,000 documents. Log the time between "started" and "checked out" to watch operations queue for a connection, then raise the pool size and compare.
  4. Insert a document with a Python Decimal price using Decimal128, read it back in Node, and print the price as a string. Then read a Node Decimal128 back in Python and convert it to decimal.Decimal.
  5. Make your Python app fail fast at start-up with a clear message when the database is unreachable.

docs.title: 09 · mongoimport, mongoexport, mongodump & mongorestore
docs.text:
Sooner or later you need to load a spreadsheet, hand data to an analyst, copy a database to your laptop, or take a quick backup before a risky migration. The MongoDB Database Tools cover all four. They come in two pairs that are easy to confuse:

Pair Format Preserves BSON types? Use for mongoimport / mongoexport JSON, CSV, TSV (text) Only with Extended JSON; CSV loses them unless you declare types Exchanging data with other systems and people mongodump / mongorestore BSON (binary) + metadata Yes, exactly, plus indexes and collection options Copies and logical backups between MongoDB deployments

The tools are a separate download from the server and are versioned on their own (100.19.1 here). Every command below ran against the lab replica set with U="mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0".

docs.title: Importing a CSV: what goes wrong by default
docs.text:
sku,name,price,qty,added
P-100,Steel kettle,29.99,3,2026-09-01
P-101,Toaster,45.00,0,2026-09-14
P-102,"Mug, large",6.50,40,2026-10-02
P-103,007 Coffee filter,3.25,120,2026-10-05

mongoimport --uri "$U" --db io --collection naive --type csv --headerline --drop products.csv

2026-10-11T23:03:00.644+0530    dropping: `io.naive`
2026-10-11T23:03:00.676+0530    4 document(s) imported successfully. 0 document(s) failed to import.

It worked — but look at the types:

[ 'P-100', 'Steel kettle', 29.99, 'number', '2026-09-01' ]
[ 'P-101', 'Toaster', 45, 'number', '2026-09-14' ]
...

mongoimport guesses: anything that looks numeric becomes a number (a double for prices — lesson 03 explained why that is bad for money), and dates stay strings. The guessing also destroys data that merely looks numeric:

name,zip
Holtsville,00501

{ name: 'Holtsville', zip: 501 }

The leading zeros are gone. Postal codes, phone numbers, account numbers and product codes are identifiers, not numbers.

docs.title: Importing with declared types
docs.text:
Put the type of each column in the header and pass --columnsHaveTypes:

sku.string(),name.string(),price.decimal(),qty.int32(),added.date(2006-01-02)
P-100,Steel kettle,29.99,3,2026-09-01
...

mongoimport --uri "$U" --db io --collection products --type csv --headerline --columnsHaveTypes --drop products2.csv

{
  sku: 'P-102',
  name: 'Mug, large',
  price: Decimal128('6.50'),
  qty: 40,
  added: ISODate('2026-10-02T00:00:00.000Z')
}

Exact decimals, real dates, and the quoted comma in "Mug, large" handled correctly. The date format uses Go's reference-time layout: 2006-01-02 means "year-month-day" (other layouts: date_go(...), date_ms(...) and date_oracle(...); check mongoimport --help for your version).

For JSON input, mongoimport expects one document per line by default, or a single array with --jsonArray. Extended JSON ({"$date": ...}, {"$numberDecimal": ...}) in the input is converted to the proper BSON types.

Useful flags: --mode upsert --upsertFields sku to update existing documents instead of failing on duplicates, --numInsertionWorkers for parallelism on big files, and --stopOnError if you'd rather fail fast than skip bad lines.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
mongoexport --uri "$U" -d io -c products --sort '{sku:1}' --limit 2 --quiet

{"_id":{"$oid":"6acbc84d1c4469c7f143e675"},"sku":"P-100","name":"Steel kettle","price":{"$numberDecimal":"29.99"},"qty":3,"added":{"$date":"2026-09-01T00:00:00Z"}}
{"_id":{"$oid":"6acbc84d1c4469c7f143e677"},"sku":"P-101","name":"Toaster","price":{"$numberDecimal":"45.00"},"qty":0,"added":{"$date":"2026-09-14T00:00:00Z"}}

This is relaxed Extended JSON: plain numbers where nothing is lost, $oid/$numberDecimal/$date wrappers where a type would otherwise be lost. Feed it back into mongoimport and the types survive. --jsonFormat canonical wraps every value, including ints and dates as epoch milliseconds:

{"_id":{"$oid":"6acbc84d1c4469c7f143e675"},"sku":"P-100","name":"Steel kettle","price":{"$numberDecimal":"29.99"},"qty":{"$numberInt":"3"},"added":{"$date":{"$numberLong":"1788220800000"}}}

CSV export needs an explicit field list, because documents have no fixed columns:

mongoexport --uri "$U" -d io -c products --type csv --fields sku,price,added --sort '{sku:1}' --quiet

sku,price,added
P-100,29.99,2026-09-01T00:00:00.000Z
P-101,45.00,2026-09-14T00:00:00.000Z
P-102,6.50,2026-10-02T00:00:00.000Z
P-103,3.25,2026-10-05T00:00:00.000Z

Arrays and embedded documents end up as JSON text inside a CSV cell — usually a sign you should reshape with an aggregation (Level 3) and export the result instead.

docs.title: mongodump: a logical copy
docs.text:
After adding a unique index on sku:

mongodump --uri "$U" --db io --out dump
find dump | sort

dump
dump/io
dump/io/naive.bson
dump/io/naive.metadata.json
dump/io/prelude.json
dump/io/products.bson
dump/io/products.metadata.json
dump/io/zips.bson
dump/io/zips.metadata.json

For each collection: a .bson file with the documents in raw BSON, and a .metadata.json with its indexes and options. prelude.json records what produced the dump:

{"ServerVersion":"9.0.2","ToolVersion":"100.19.1"}

The metadata contains the index definitions, not the index data — sku_1 will be rebuilt on restore:

{"indexes":[{"v":{"$numberInt":"2"},"key":{"_id":{"$numberInt":"1"}},"name":"_id_",...},{"v":{"$numberInt":"2"},"key":{"sku":{"$numberInt":"1"}},"name":"sku_1","unique":true,...}],...,"collectionName":"products","type":"collection"}

bsondump turns a .bson file into readable JSON when you need to peek inside:

bsondump --quiet dump/io/products.bson | head -1

{"_id":{"$oid":"6acbc84d1c4469c7f143e675"},"sku":"P-100","name":"Steel kettle","price":{"$numberDecimal":"29.99"},"qty":{"$numberInt":"3"},"added":{"$date":{"$numberLong":"1788220800000"}}}

For a single file that is easy to move around, use an archive, optionally compressed:

mongodump --uri "$U" --db io --archive=io.archive.gz --gzip --quiet

The whole database became an 845-byte file. --archive without a file name writes to standard output, so you can pipe a dump straight into mongorestore on another server.

docs.title: mongorestore
docs.text:
Restore into a different database name with namespace remapping — the safe way to inspect a backup without touching the original:

mongorestore --uri "$U" --nsFrom 'io.*' --nsTo 'io_copy.*' dump

2026-10-11T23:03:14.865+0530    no indexes to restore for collection `io_copy.zips`
2026-10-11T23:03:14.989+0530    9 document(s) restored successfully. 0 document(s) failed to restore.

naive,products,zips 4 ["_id_","sku_1"]

All three collections, the four products, and the unique index came back.

Now restore over the existing io.products:

mongorestore --uri "$U" --nsInclude 'io.products' dump

continuing through error: E11000 duplicate key error collection: io.products index: _id_ dup key: { _id: ObjectId('6acbc84d1c4469c7f143e675') }
...
0 document(s) restored successfully. 4 document(s) failed to restore.

mongorestore only inserts; it never overwrites. Documents whose _id already exists are skipped with an error, and documents that exist only in the target are left alone. To replace the collection with the backup's contents, add --drop:

mongorestore --uri "$U" --nsInclude 'io.products' --drop dump

4 document(s) restored successfully. 0 document(s) failed to restore.

--drop drops each collection being restored first — not the whole database, and not collections absent from the dump.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
mongoexport and mongodump are ordinary clients. Each runs a find over every collection (in parallel across collections, controlled by --numParallelCollections) and writes what it receives: mongoexport converts each document to Extended JSON or CSV text; mongodump writes the raw BSON bytes exactly as received, which is why a dump preserves every type for free and is faster to produce. Neither takes a lock or a consistent snapshot of the whole database: collection A is read at a slightly different time from collection B, and documents can change while a large collection is being read. On a replica set, mongodump --oplog (whole-deployment dumps only) also captures the oplog entries written during the dump so mongorestore --oplogReplay can bring everything to a single point in time — Level 4 · 06 covers that and the alternatives.

mongorestore reads the metadata first, creates each collection with its options, inserts documents in batches (with multiple insertion workers), and then builds the indexes from the definitions. Building indexes once at the end is much faster than maintaining them during millions of inserts, but it means a restore of a large, heavily indexed collection spends most of its time in index builds, and a unique index whose constraint is violated by the data fails at the end, not the start.

Because dumps contain only the documents and index definitions, they are smaller than the data directory and portable across server versions and storage settings. The trade-off is time: dumping and restoring hundreds of gigabytes is slow, which is why large production systems rely on physical backups instead (Level 4 · 06).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Importing CSV without declared types, turning money into doubles, dates into strings and postal codes into numbers.
  • Using mongoexport as a backup. It is for data exchange; use mongodump (or better, Level 4's methods), which keeps types, indexes and options.
  • Expecting mongorestore to overwrite. It inserts only; use --drop deliberately.
  • Restoring over a live database to "check" a backup. Restore to a different namespace with --nsFrom/--nsTo, or to a different server.
  • Treating a mongodump of a busy database as a point-in-time snapshot. It isn't, unless you used --oplog on a replica set.
  • Never testing restores. A backup you haven't restored is a hope, not a backup.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Download any public CSV dataset with at least one date column and one identifier column with leading zeros (or create one). Import it naively, inspect the types with $type, then re-import with a typed header and compare.
  2. Export a collection with --jsonFormat canonical, delete the collection, re-import the file and verify with $type that every field has its original type.
  3. Dump the library database from lesson 04 as a gzipped archive, restore it as library_restore using --nsFrom/--nsTo, and compare document counts and index names between the two.
  4. Pipe a dump directly into a restore on a second local server: start another mongod on port 27100 and run mongodump --archive ... | mongorestore --archive --uri mongodb://127.0.0.1:27100.
  5. Find out what happens when you restore a dump into a collection that has a unique index the dumped data violates.

docs.title: 10 · Project — Recipe Box Data Layer
docs.text:
Time to put Level 1 together. You'll build the data layer for a small recipe-box application: the module that the web routes or CLI would call. It uses only what you've learned so far — documents with embedded arrays, query operators, update operators, a unique index, PyMongo, and keyset pagination — and it comes with a test suite that runs against a real server.

The point of a data layer is that the rest of the application never builds MongoDB filters itself. Routes call box.rate("dal-tadka", 5); only this module knows that a rating is two counters updated with $inc.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Each recipe has a URL-friendly slug derived from its title, and slugs must be unique — even when two people add "Masala Omelette" at the same moment.
  2. Find recipes containing all of a list of ingredients, case-insensitively.
  3. Find quick recipes: a tag plus a maximum cooking time, fastest first.
  4. Rate a recipe 1–5 stars and get the new average back. Concurrent ratings must never be lost.
  5. Add tags (no duplicates, kept sorted) and change one ingredient's quantity in place.
  6. Page through all recipes in a stable order without skip().
  7. Delete a recipe, reporting whether it existed.

docs.title: The document shape
docs.text:
{
  _id: ObjectId("..."),
  slug: "masala-omelette",
  title: "Masala Omelette",
  ingredients: [ { name: "egg", qty: "2" }, { name: "onion", qty: null } ],
  steps: ["Beat eggs", "Fry onion", "Cook"],
  tags: ["breakfast", "quick"],
  minutes: 10,
  rating: { count: 0, total: 0 },
  createdAt: ISODate("..."),
  updatedAt: ISODate("...")
}

Design decisions worth noting:

  • Ingredients and steps are embedded. They are always read with the recipe and never shared between recipes, and a recipe has a bounded number of them. (Level 2 · 01 formalises when to embed.)
  • Ingredient names and tags are stored lower-case. Then equality queries are case-insensitive without regexes, and they can use indexes later.
  • The rating is stored as a count and a total, not as an average. An average can't be updated atomically with $inc; a count and a total can, and the average is one division away.
  • _id is an ObjectId, slug has a unique index. The slug is what users see and may in future be editable; _id never changes. Keyset pagination uses _id because it is unique and roughly ordered by creation time.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
Save as recipes.py:

"""Data layer for a small recipe-box app, using only Level 1 features."""
import re
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from bson import ObjectId
from pymongo import ASCENDING, MongoClient, ReturnDocument
from pymongo.errors import DuplicateKeyError


class SlugTaken(Exception):
    pass


def slugify(title: str) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", title.lower()).strip("-")


class RecipeBox:
    def __init__(self, client: MongoClient, db_name: str = "recipebox"):
        self.recipes = client[db_name].recipes
        self.recipes.create_index([("slug", ASCENDING)], unique=True)

    def add(self, title, ingredients, steps, tags=(), minutes=None):
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        doc = {
            "slug": slugify(title),
            "title": title,
            "ingredients": [{"name": i["name"].lower(), "qty": i.get("qty")} for i in ingredients],
            "steps": list(steps),
            "tags": sorted(set(t.lower() for t in tags)),
            "minutes": minutes,
            "rating": {"count": 0, "total": 0},
            "createdAt": now,
            "updatedAt": now,
        }
        try:
            return self.recipes.insert_one(doc).inserted_id
        except DuplicateKeyError:
            raise SlugTaken(doc["slug"]) from None

    def get(self, slug):
        return self.recipes.find_one({"slug": slug})

    def with_all_ingredients(self, names):
        names = [n.lower() for n in names]
        return list(self.recipes.find({"ingredients.name": {"$all": names}},
                                      {"_id": 0, "slug": 1}).sort("slug", ASCENDING))

    def quick(self, tag, max_minutes):
        return list(self.recipes.find({"tags": tag, "minutes": {"$lte": max_minutes}},
                                      {"_id": 0, "slug": 1, "minutes": 1}).sort([("minutes", 1), ("slug", 1)]))

    def rate(self, slug, stars):
        if not 1 <= stars <= 5:
            raise ValueError("stars must be 1-5")
        doc = self.recipes.find_one_and_update(
            {"slug": slug},
            {"$inc": {"rating.count": 1, "rating.total": stars}, "$currentDate": {"updatedAt": True}},
            projection={"_id": 0, "rating": 1},
            return_document=ReturnDocument.AFTER,
        )
        if doc is None:
            raise KeyError(slug)
        r = doc["rating"]
        return round(r["total"] / r["count"], 2)

    def add_tag(self, slug, tag):
        tag = tag.lower()
        # $addToSet would append at the end; this keeps the array sorted and duplicate-free.
        res = self.recipes.update_one(
            {"slug": slug, "tags": {"$ne": tag}},
            {"$push": {"tags": {"$each": [tag], "$sort": 1}}},
        )
        return res.modified_count == 1 or self.recipes.count_documents({"slug": slug}, limit=1) == 1

    def set_qty(self, slug, ingredient, qty):
        res = self.recipes.update_one({"slug": slug, "ingredients.name": ingredient.lower()},
                                      {"$set": {"ingredients.$.qty": qty}})
        return res.modified_count == 1

    def page(self, after_id=None, size=2):
        flt = {"_id": {"$gt": ObjectId(after_id)}} if after_id else {}
        docs = list(self.recipes.find(flt, {"slug": 1}).sort("_id", ASCENDING).limit(size))
        next_cursor = str(docs[-1]["_id"]) if len(docs) == size else None
        return [d["slug"] for d in docs], next_cursor

    def delete(self, slug):
        return self.recipes.delete_one({"slug": slug}).deleted_count == 1

How each requirement maps to Level 1 features:

Requirement Method Feature Unique slugs __init__, add unique index + catching DuplicateKeyError (code 11000) — lesson 08 All ingredients with_all_ingredients dot path into an array of documents + $all — lesson 05 Quick recipes quick array "contains" + range + compound sort with tie-breaker — lessons 04, 05 Ratings rate find_one_and_update with $inc and ReturnDocument.AFTER — lesson 06 Tags add_tag conditional $push with $each + $sort — lesson 06 Quantities set_qty positional $ — lesson 06 Paging page keyset pagination on _id — lesson 04 Delete delete deleted_count — lesson 07

create_index is idempotent: calling it when the index already exists with the same definition does nothing, so it is safe in the constructor for a project this size. Larger applications create indexes in a migration or deployment step instead (Level 4 · 09).

docs.title: The tests
docs.text:
Save as test_recipes.py. The fixture creates a throwaway database for each test and drops it afterwards, so tests can't affect each other or your real data.

import pytest
from pymongo import MongoClient
from recipes import RecipeBox, SlugTaken

URI = "mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0"


@pytest.fixture
def box():
    client = MongoClient(URI, tz_aware=True)
    client.drop_database("recipebox_test")
    b = RecipeBox(client, "recipebox_test")
    b.add("Masala Omelette", [{"name": "Egg", "qty": "2"}, {"name": "Onion"}, {"name": "Chilli"}],
          ["Beat eggs", "Fry onion", "Cook"], tags=["Breakfast", "quick"], minutes=10)
    b.add("Egg Fried Rice", [{"name": "egg", "qty": "2"}, {"name": "rice", "qty": "2 cups"}, {"name": "onion"}],
          ["Scramble", "Add rice"], tags=["dinner", "quick"], minutes=20)
    b.add("Dal Tadka", [{"name": "lentils", "qty": "1 cup"}, {"name": "onion"}, {"name": "ghee"}],
          ["Boil", "Temper"], tags=["dinner"], minutes=40)
    yield b
    client.drop_database("recipebox_test")
    client.close()


def test_slug_is_unique(box):
    with pytest.raises(SlugTaken):
        box.add("masala omelette!", [{"name": "egg"}], ["x"])


def test_ingredient_search_needs_all(box):
    assert box.with_all_ingredients(["EGG", "onion"]) == [{"slug": "egg-fried-rice"}, {"slug": "masala-omelette"}]
    assert box.with_all_ingredients(["egg", "ghee"]) == []


def test_quick_recipes_sorted_by_time(box):
    assert [r["slug"] for r in box.quick("quick", 15)] == ["masala-omelette"]
    assert [r["slug"] for r in box.quick("dinner", 60)] == ["egg-fried-rice", "dal-tadka"]


def test_rating_average(box):
    assert box.rate("dal-tadka", 5) == 5.0
    assert box.rate("dal-tadka", 4) == 4.5
    with pytest.raises(KeyError):
        box.rate("nope", 3)


def test_tags_and_quantities(box):
    assert box.add_tag("dal-tadka", "Comfort")
    assert box.add_tag("dal-tadka", "comfort")
    assert box.get("dal-tadka")["tags"] == ["comfort", "dinner"]
    assert box.set_qty("dal-tadka", "Ghee", "1 tbsp")
    assert not box.set_qty("dal-tadka", "saffron", "a pinch")
    ghee = [i for i in box.get("dal-tadka")["ingredients"] if i["name"] == "ghee"][0]
    assert ghee["qty"] == "1 tbsp"


def test_keyset_pagination(box):
    first, cur = box.page()
    second, cur2 = box.page(cur)
    assert first == ["masala-omelette", "egg-fried-rice"]
    assert second == ["dal-tadka"] and cur2 is None


def test_delete(box):
    assert box.delete("dal-tadka")
    assert not box.delete("dal-tadka")

docs.title: The first run failed
docs.text:
The first version of add_tag used $addToSet:

def add_tag(self, slug, tag):
    res = self.recipes.update_one({"slug": slug}, {"$addToSet": {"tags": tag.lower()}})
    return res.matched_count == 1

FAILED test_recipes.py::test_tags_and_quantities - AssertionError: assert ['d...
1 failed, 6 passed in 1.36s

E       AssertionError: assert ['dinner', 'comfort'] == ['comfort', 'dinner']

$addToSet prevents duplicates but always appends — it doesn't keep tags sorted, which add promised. The fix in the code above is a conditional push: the filter {"tags": {"$ne": tag}} only matches when the tag is absent (so there are no duplicates), and $push with $each and $sort: 1 inserts it in order. Because filter and update are applied atomically to one document, two concurrent add_tag calls with the same tag still can't both add it.

After the fix:

test_recipes.py::test_slug_is_unique PASSED                              [ 14%]
test_recipes.py::test_ingredient_search_needs_all PASSED                 [ 28%]
test_recipes.py::test_quick_recipes_sorted_by_time PASSED                [ 42%]
test_recipes.py::test_rating_average PASSED                              [ 57%]
test_recipes.py::test_tags_and_quantities PASSED                         [ 71%]
test_recipes.py::test_keyset_pagination PASSED                           [ 85%]
test_recipes.py::test_delete PASSED                                      [100%]

docs.title: Checking ratings under concurrency
docs.text:
Unit tests run one thing at a time. Requirement 4 is about concurrency, so check it directly — 400 ratings from 8 threads, cycling through 1–5 stars (80 of each, total 1,200):

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pymongo import MongoClient
from recipes import RecipeBox

client = MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0")
client.drop_database("recipebox_load")
box = RecipeBox(client, "recipebox_load")
box.add("Plain Toast", [{"name": "bread"}], ["Toast it"], minutes=3)

with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as pool:
    list(pool.map(lambda i: box.rate("plain-toast", i % 5 + 1), range(400)))

print(box.get("plain-toast")["rating"])
client.drop_database("recipebox_load")

{'count': 400, 'total': 1200}

Every rating counted. Compare that with lesson 06, where read-modify-write lost 80% of increments under the same kind of load.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Three different mechanisms guarantee correctness here, and it's worth being precise about which one covers which requirement.

The unique index guarantees unique slugs. Checking "does this slug exist?" and then inserting would race: two requests could both see "no" and both insert. With a unique index, the second insert fails inside the storage engine at the moment it tries to add the duplicate key to the index, regardless of timing — the application just translates DuplicateKeyError into SlugTaken.

Single-document atomicity guarantees ratings and tags. find_one_and_update finds the document, applies both $incs and the $currentDate, and returns the new version as one atomic operation. No other write to that document can interleave, so count and total always move together and the average returned is the average including this rating.

A sort key with a unique field guarantees stable paging. Keyset pagination asks for "the next two _ids greater than the last one I saw". Because _id is unique and indexed, the server jumps straight to that position in the _id index and reads two entries — page 1,000 costs the same as page 1, and inserts or deletes between page requests can't cause a recipe to be shown twice or skipped (as they can with skip()).

What the design does not guarantee yet: search by ingredient and by tag are collection scans, because the only indexes are _id and slug. With three recipes that doesn't matter; with three million it would. Level 2 adds the indexes and shows how to prove they're used.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Checking for duplicates in application code instead of with a unique index.
  • Storing an average (or any derived value) that can't be maintained atomically.
  • Leaking MongoDB filters into route handlers, so a schema change touches the whole codebase.
  • Tests that share one database and pass or fail depending on order. Use a fresh database per test.
  • Assuming $addToSet preserves order.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Extend the recipe box:

  1. Add rename(slug, new_title) that changes the title and the slug, raising SlugTaken when the new slug is in use. Write tests for both outcomes.
  2. Add favourite(slug, user_id) and unfavourite(...) storing user ids in a favouritedBy array plus a favouriteCount kept in sync in the same update. Make sure favouriting twice doesn't double-count (hint: filter on favouritedBy: {$ne: user_id}).
  3. Add recently_rated(n) returning the n recipes with the most recent updatedAt, newest first, using a unique tie-breaker.
  4. Dump the test database with mongodump before the fixture drops it (add a flag), and restore it under a new name to inspect what the tests wrote.
  5. Write a concurrency check for add_tag: 20 threads adding the same new tag to one recipe. Assert it appears exactly once.

docs.title: Level 2 · Data Modeling & Indexes
docs.text:
Level 1 taught you to read and write documents correctly. Level 2 is about the two decisions that decide whether a MongoDB application stays fast as it grows: the shape of your documents and the indexes behind your queries. Both are made up front, both are expensive to change later, and both are routinely gotten wrong by people who know the syntax perfectly well.

The lessons measure instead of asserting. You'll watch an embedded comment list hit the 16 MB wall at 180,000 comments, see a bucketed design use 29 times less index than one document per reading, compare three orders of the same compound index on half a million orders (71,514 keys examined versus 219), and watch the planner race four candidate plans. Every number was produced on MongoDB 9.0.2 on a laptop; your absolute timings will differ, the proportions shouldn't.

Prerequisites: Level 1. You'll want the lab replica set running and about 1 GB of free disk for the test collections.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Thinking in Documents: Embed or Reference? — read cost, document growth, the 16 MB wall, duplication and atomicity, measured.
  2. Modeling Relationships — one-to-few through one-to-squillions, many-to-many, and four ways to store a tree.
  3. Schema Design Patterns — computed, subset, extended reference, bucket, attribute, outlier, polymorphic and schema versioning.
  4. Schema Validation with $jsonSchema — validators, error details, cross-field rules, and rolling rules onto existing data.
  5. How Indexes Work & Compound Index Design — B-trees, prefixes, and the Equality-Sort-Range rule.
  6. Multikey, Unique, Partial, TTL, Wildcard & Text Indexes — what each option does and the trap each one hides.
  7. Reading explain() — stages, bounds, keys vs documents examined, covered queries and blocking sorts.
  8. The Query Planner, Plan Cache & Hints — the plan race, cached plans, replanning, hints, query settings and $indexStats.
  9. Time Series & Capped Collections — server-side bucketing and compression for measurements; bounded logs with tailable cursors.
  10. Project — Model & Index a Store Catalog — 100,000 products, a validator, five indexed queries and an automated explain-based budget check.

docs.title: After Level 2
docs.text: Your data has a good shape and your queries hit indexes. Level 3 turns to what you do with the data: the aggregation pipeline for reports and analytics, joins, multi-document transactions, change streams, geospatial queries and text search.

docs.title: 01 · Thinking in Documents: Embed or Reference?
docs.text:
In a relational database, the schema follows the data: you normalise into tables, and queries join them back together. In MongoDB the schema follows the access patterns: you shape documents around how the application reads and writes them. The central decision, made over and over, is whether related data lives inside a document (embedding) or in another document that you point to (referencing).

There is no universal answer, but there is a method — and the trade-offs can be measured. That's what this lesson does.

docs.title: The question to ask first
docs.text:
Before drawing any schema, list the application's operations and how often each runs:

Operation Frequency Data needed Show a blog post page very high post + its comments Show the homepage list very high titles of recent posts Add a comment medium one post Show a user's comment history low comments by one user across posts Rename a user rare every place the name appears

The schema that wins is the one that makes the frequent operations cheap, while keeping the rare ones possible.

docs.title: Experiment: the post page, two ways
docs.text:
A Python script built the same data twice — 2,000 posts with 20 comments each:

  • posts_embedded: each post holds its comments in an array.
  • posts + comments: comments are separate documents with a postId field and an index on {postId: 1, at: 1}.
embedded.append({"_id": p, "title": f"Post {p}", "body": "Lorem " * 200, "comments": cs})
posts.append({"_id": p, "title": f"Post {p}", "body": "Lorem " * 200})
comments.extend({"postId": p, **c} for c in cs)
...
e = timeit(lambda i: db.posts_embedded.find_one({"_id": i}))
r = timeit(lambda i: (db.posts.find_one({"_id": i}),
                      list(db.comments.find({"postId": i}).sort("at", 1))))

3,000 random page views each, on the local lab:

embedded:   0.127 ms per page view (1 query)
referenced: 0.281 ms per page view (2 queries)

Embedding was a little over twice as fast here, and that is with the database on the same machine. Over a network each extra query adds a round trip, so the gap grows with latency. When data is always read together, embedding wins.

But the sizes tell the other side of the story:

posts_embedded  docs=  2000  avgObjSize= 3275 B  size=6.6 MB
posts           docs=  2000  avgObjSize= 1245 B  size=2.5 MB
comments        docs= 40000  avgObjSize=  126 B  size=5.1 MB

Every read of an embedded post — even one that only wants the title — makes the server fetch a 3.2 KB document into memory instead of a 1.2 KB one. Projection reduces what is sent, not what is read:

title only from embedded (projection): 0.120 ms

Almost exactly the cost of fetching the whole thing. For a homepage listing 50 titles, you're pulling the comments of 50 posts into the cache for nothing. When some frequent operation needs the parent without the child data, embedding costs memory.

docs.title: Experiment: what happens when a list never stops growing
docs.text:
One post goes viral. Push comments to it in batches of 10,000:

db.viral.insertOne({ _id: 1, title: "Viral post", comments: [] });
const batch = Array.from({ length: 10000 }, (_, i) =>
  ({ author: "user" + (i % 500), text: "Great point, thanks for sharing this!", at: new Date() }));
let n = 0;
try { while (true) { db.viral.updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { $push: { comments: { $each: batch } } }); n += 10000; } }
catch (e) { print("failed after", n, "comments:", e.code, e.message) }

failed after 180000 comments: 10334 Plan executor error during update :: caused by :: Resulting document after update is larger than 16777216

The 16 MB limit stopped it at 180,000 comments — and from that moment no one can comment on the post. Long before the wall, the document was already a problem. At 16.5 MB:

20 small updates on the huge doc ms: 305
20 small updates on a small doc ms: 103
20 title reads on the huge doc ms: 129
20 title reads on a small doc ms: 7

Reading the title of the huge post was about 18 times slower than reading a normal one, because the whole document is loaded; every change to it rewrites a large document and, on a replica set, can produce large oplog entries. Unbounded arrays are the most common MongoDB modeling mistake.

docs.title: Duplication: the price of embedding things that change
docs.text:
If each embedded comment stores the commenter's display name, renaming a user means updating every comment they ever wrote, across every post. With references, you update one user document. This is the real trade-off behind normalisation, and the question is: how often does the duplicated data change, and does it matter if old copies stay stale?

  • A product's price at the time of an order should be copied into the order and never updated — it is history, not a reference.
  • A user's display name next to their comments probably should update, but a few seconds of inconsistency during a background fix-up is fine.
  • A user's email used for login must exist in exactly one place.

docs.title: Atomicity is a reason to embed
docs.text: A single-document write is atomic (Level 1 · 06). If an order and its line items are one document, "create the order with its items" can't half-succeed, and "change a line's quantity and the order total" is one update. Split them across collections and you need a multi-document transaction (Level 3 · 06) to get the same guarantee. Data that must change together is a strong signal to embed.

docs.title: The rules of thumb
docs.text:
Embed when:

  • the child data is read with the parent most of the time;
  • the relationship is one-to-few, or the number of children is bounded (a product has a few variants; a user has a few addresses);
  • the child doesn't need to be queried or updated independently at high volume;
  • the parent and child should change atomically.

Reference when:

  • the child list is unbounded or can grow large (comments on a public post, log events, orders of a customer over years);
  • the child is shared by many parents and changes (users, products, tags with metadata);
  • frequent operations need the parent without the children, or the children without the parent;
  • the child is large and rarely needed (full-resolution file metadata, raw payloads).

And very often the right answer is both: reference the full data, embed a small, bounded, denormalised subset for the hot read path — the post embeds its latest 10 comments and a comment count; the full history lives in comments. Lesson 03 names that the subset pattern.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The reason embedding is fast and the reason unbounded embedding is slow are the same: the document is the unit of I/O. WiredTiger stores each document as one value in the collection's B-tree. To read any field, the server locates the document via an index (usually _id), loads the page holding it into the cache (decompressing it if necessary), and hands the whole BSON value to the query layer, which then applies the projection. An embedded post with comments is one lookup and one value. A referenced design is one lookup in posts plus an index range scan on comments.postId and twenty document fetches — more work, even though each piece is small.

Writes work the same way. Changing one field of a document creates a new version of the whole document in the cache (WiredTiger is multi-versioned: readers that started earlier still see the old version), and the journal and checkpoint eventually write it out. MongoDB records small diffs in the oplog for updates where it can, but the in-memory and on-disk cost still scales with the document's size. A 16 MB document updated 100 times a second is 1.6 GB per second of document versions for the cache to manage.

The cache is also why size matters for reads that "don't need" most of the document: the cache holds pages of whole documents, so bloated documents mean fewer documents fit in RAM — the working set — and more reads go to disk.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Modeling the data instead of the access patterns. Start from the list of operations.
  • Embedding an unbounded list (comments, events, followers, audit logs).
  • Referencing everything out of relational habit, then doing three round trips for every page view.
  • Duplicating frequently changing data without a plan for keeping copies in sync.
  • Assuming projection makes a big document cheap to read. It doesn't reduce what the server loads.
  • Treating the 16 MB limit as the design limit. Documents should usually be kilobytes.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write the access-pattern table (operation, frequency, data needed) for an online course platform with courses, lessons, students, enrolments and quiz attempts. Decide embed or reference for each relationship and justify each in one sentence.
  2. Re-run the post-page experiment with 200 comments per post instead of 20. Does embedding still win? At what number of comments per post does the referenced design catch up on your machine?
  3. Implement the hybrid: posts embed recentComments (latest 5, via $push with $slice) and commentCount; full comments live in comments. Write the "add comment" function that updates both. What happens if the second write fails? (Keep the answer; Level 3 · 06 returns to it.)
  4. Measure the homepage query — 50 most recent post titles — against both designs.

docs.title: 02 · Modeling Relationships
docs.text: Lesson 01 gave you the embed-or-reference trade-off. This lesson turns it into concrete shapes for every kind of relationship you will meet, with the query that reads each shape and the index it needs. The cardinality labels are borrowed from relational modeling, but MongoDB adds a distinction that matters more than "one" versus "many": how many is many? "A few", "hundreds" and "unbounded" lead to three different designs.

docs.title: One-to-one
docs.text:
A user and their profile settings. Almost always: embed.

{ _id: "u42", email: "ana@example.com",
  settings: { theme: "dark", locale: "en-IN", emailDigest: "weekly" } }

Split it out only when the embedded part is large and rarely read (a 200 KB avatar thumbnail, a verbose audit blob) — then a separate collection keyed by the same _id keeps the hot document small.

docs.title: One-to-few: embed an array
docs.text:
A person's addresses, a product's handful of variants, an order's line items.

{ _id: "u42", addresses: [
    { label: "home", city: "Pune", zip: "411001" },
    { label: "office", city: "Pune", zip: "411014" } ] }

The list is bounded by reality, read with the parent, and changing it atomically with the parent is useful. Query into it with dot notation and $elemMatch (Level 1 · 05); update it with positional operators (Level 1 · 06).

docs.title: One-to-many: reference from the child
docs.text:
A customer's orders, a post's comments, a course's enrolments: potentially thousands, each queried on its own, growing over time. Store the parent's id in the child:

// orders
{ _id: ObjectId("..."), customerId: "u42", placedAt: ISODate("2026-10-01"), total: NumberDecimal("59.90") }

db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1, placedAt: -1 })
db.orders.find({ customerId: "u42" }).sort({ placedAt: -1 }).limit(20)

The compound index serves "this customer's latest orders" directly. Do not also store an array of order ids in the customer: it's an unbounded array (lesson 01), and keeping it in sync is a second write that can fail.

docs.title: One-to-squillions
docs.text: Log lines from a host, sensor readings from a device, events in an analytics stream: millions per parent. The design is the same as one-to-many — child references parent — but now the child collection's volume dominates everything. You will want time series collections or the bucket pattern (lesson 03 and lesson 09), a TTL or archival policy (lesson 06), and, at scale, sharding (Level 4).

docs.title: Many-to-many: arrays of references
docs.text:
Books and authors. Most books have one to three authors (bounded), while a prolific author may have dozens of books. So store the references on the bounded side:

db.authors.insertMany([{ _id: "kl", name: "Martin Kleppmann" }, { _id: "pe", name: "Alex Petrov" },
                       { _id: "co", name: "Co Author" }]);
db.books.insertMany([
  { _id: "ddia", title: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications", authorIds: ["kl"] },
  { _id: "dbi", title: "Database Internals", authorIds: ["pe"] },
  { _id: "joint", title: "A Joint Work", authorIds: ["kl", "co"] }]);
db.books.createIndex({ authorIds: 1 });

Both directions are now a single indexed query. Books by an author ("array contains"):

db.books.find({ authorIds: "kl" }, { _id: 0, title: 1 })

[ { title: 'Designing Data-Intensive Applications' }, { title: 'A Joint Work' } ]

Authors of a book — fetch the book, then $in its ids:

const b = db.books.findOne({ _id: "joint" });
db.authors.find({ _id: { $in: b.authorIds } }, { _id: 0, name: 1 })

[ { name: 'Co Author' }, { name: 'Martin Kleppmann' } ]

Notice the order: the book lists ["kl", "co"] but the authors came back as Co, then Martin. $in does not preserve the order of the list you give it. If author order matters (it does on a book cover), reorder the results in your code using the original array.

Or do the join on the server with $lookup (Level 3 · 03 covers it fully):

db.books.aggregate([
  { $match: { _id: "joint" } },
  { $lookup: { from: "authors", localField: "authorIds", foreignField: "_id", as: "authors" } },
  { $project: { _id: 0, title: 1, "authors.name": 1 } }])

[ { title: 'A Joint Work', authors: [ { name: 'Co Author' }, { name: 'Martin Kleppmann' } ] } ]

Same caveat: the joined array isn't in authorIds order either.

When both sides can be large — students and courses on a platform with thousands of each — don't store arrays on either side. Use a separate link collection (enrolments: {studentId, courseId, enrolledAt, progress}) with an index for each direction. That is also where data about the relationship (enrolment date, progress, grade) naturally lives.

docs.title: Denormalising a little
docs.text:
If book listings always show author names, a second query per page is a cost you pay millions of times to avoid a cost (renaming an author) you pay almost never. Embed a small extended reference:

{ _id: "joint", title: "A Joint Work",
  authors: [ { _id: "kl", name: "Martin Kleppmann" }, { _id: "co", name: "Co Author" } ] }

The _id still links to the full author document; the name is a copy for display. When an author is renamed, an updateMany({"authors._id": "kl"}, {$set: {"authors.$[a].name": ...}}, {arrayFilters: ...}) fixes the copies — rarely, and in the background.

docs.title: Trees
docs.text:
Categories, org charts, folder hierarchies, threaded comments. Four standard shapes, each optimising a different question:

Shape Stores Cheap Expensive Parent reference parent children of a node; moving a node all descendants; the full path Child references children: [...] children of a node parents; unbounded for wide trees Array of ancestors parent, ancestors: [...] all descendants, breadcrumbs moving a subtree Materialized path path: ",a,b,c," descendants via prefix, sorting by path moving a subtree

The ancestors array covers the questions most applications ask. Six categories:

db.cats.insertMany([
  { _id: "electronics", parent: null, ancestors: [], path: ",electronics," },
  { _id: "computers", parent: "electronics", ancestors: ["electronics"], path: ",electronics,computers," },
  { _id: "laptops", parent: "computers", ancestors: ["electronics", "computers"], path: ",electronics,computers,laptops," },
  { _id: "gaming-laptops", parent: "laptops", ancestors: ["electronics", "computers", "laptops"], path: ",electronics,computers,laptops,gaming-laptops," },
  { _id: "phones", parent: "electronics", ancestors: ["electronics"], path: ",electronics,phones," },
  { _id: "kitchen", parent: null, ancestors: [], path: ",kitchen," }]);
db.cats.createIndex({ ancestors: 1 });
db.cats.createIndex({ path: 1 });

children of electronics: computers,phones
all under computers: laptops,gaming-laptops
breadcrumb: electronics > computers > laptops

Those are find({parent: "electronics"}), find({ancestors: "computers"}) and reading one document's ancestors. "Everything under computers" is a single indexed lookup at any depth.

The materialized path answers the same descendant question with an anchored regex:

db.cats.find({ path: /^,electronics,computers,/ })

path prefix: computers,laptops,gaming-laptops

Its explain() showed an IXSCAN with 4 keys examined and 3 documents fetched — a case-sensitive regex anchored with ^ becomes a range scan on the index. The leading and trailing commas stop ,phone from matching ,phones,.

docs.title: Moving a subtree
docs.text:
The price of both shapes is moving a node: every descendant's ancestors and path change. Move laptops from Computers to a new Portables category — one update for the node, one pipeline update for its descendants:

const node = db.cats.findOne({ _id: "laptops" }), newParent = db.cats.findOne({ _id: "portables" });
const newAnc = [...newParent.ancestors, newParent._id];
const oldPrefix = node.path, newPrefix = newParent.path + node._id + ",";
db.cats.updateOne({ _id: "laptops" }, { $set: { parent: "portables", ancestors: newAnc, path: newPrefix } });
db.cats.updateMany({ ancestors: "laptops" }, [{ $set: {
  ancestors: { $concatArrays: [newAnc, ["laptops"],
    { $slice: ["$ancestors", { $add: [{ $indexOfArray: ["$ancestors", "laptops"] }, 1] }, 100] }] },
  path: { $concat: [newPrefix, { $substrCP: ["$path", oldPrefix.length, 1000] }] } } }]);

laptops | electronics>portables | ,electronics,portables,laptops,
gaming-laptops | electronics>portables>laptops | ,electronics,portables,laptops,gaming-laptops,

For a category tree edited a few times a year that's fine. For a tree reorganised constantly (a drag-and-drop folder UI with millions of files), parent references plus $graphLookup (Level 3 · 03) may be the better trade. And note that the node update and the descendants update are two separate writes: a reader between them sees an inconsistent tree. Wrap them in a transaction if that matters.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every relationship query above is fast for one reason: it is an equality or prefix lookup on an index. {customerId: "u42"}, {authorIds: "kl"}, {ancestors: "computers"} and the anchored path regex all translate into a bounded range of keys in a B-tree index, so the cost depends on the number of matching documents, not on the size of the collection.

Array fields get special treatment in indexes: an index on authorIds or ancestors is multikey — it stores one index entry per array element, all pointing to the same document. That is what makes "which books contain author kl?" a direct lookup rather than a scan, and it's why the ancestors-array tree works at any depth: gaming-laptops has three index entries, one for each ancestor. The cost is proportional: a document with 1,000 array elements has 1,000 index entries to maintain on every write — another reason references belong on the bounded side.

$lookup is a join executed inside the server: for each input document it runs a query against the foreign collection (using an index on the foreignField when one exists). It saves round trips, not work. A schema that needs $lookup on every request of its hottest path is usually a sign that some data should be embedded or denormalised.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Storing child ids in the parent for unbounded relationships (customer.orderIds).
  • Storing arrays of references on the unbounded side of a many-to-many.
  • Forgetting the index on the reference field — every "find children" becomes a collection scan.
  • Assuming $in or $lookup return results in your array's order.
  • Unanchored or case-insensitive regex on a materialized path — it can't use the index as a range.
  • Moving tree nodes without updating descendants, or doing it in two steps that readers can observe half-done.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Model a Q&A site: questions, answers, comments on both, votes, tags and users. For each relationship state its cardinality ("few", "many", "squillions") and your design. Create the indexes for: a question page, a user's answer history, and the newest questions with a tag.
  2. Implement students/courses with an enrolments link collection. Write the queries for "courses of student X with progress" and "students of course Y, newest first" and create one index for each.
  3. Build a folder tree with the ancestors-array shape, 4 levels deep. Write moveFolder(id, newParentId) and deleteFolder(id) (deleting the subtree). Run both inside a transaction once you've reached Level 3.
  4. Fix the author-order problem: write a function that returns a book's authors in authorIds order using $in plus client-side reordering, and an aggregation version using $lookup followed by sorting on $indexOfArray.

docs.title: 03 · Schema Design Patterns
docs.text: Experienced MongoDB designers reach for a small set of recurring shapes. They have names — computed, subset, bucket, attribute and so on — and knowing them speeds up design discussions the way knowing "observer" or "factory" speeds up code reviews. Each pattern is an answer to a specific pressure: too many reads, too many documents, too many fields, too much variation. This lesson shows each one, when it applies, and — where it can be measured — what it buys.

docs.title: Computed pattern: do the math on write
docs.text:
Pressure: a value is read far more often than the data it's derived from changes.

The recipe box in Level 1 stored rating: {count, total} instead of recomputing the average from every rating on every page view. Same idea for a product's review count, a forum's post count, an account's balance. Compute it when the inputs change, with an atomic $inc, and reads become free.

db.posts.updateOne({ _id: postId }, { $inc: { commentCount: 1 }, $set: { lastCommentAt: new Date() } })

The price: the derived value is a second source of truth. If you also insert the comment document, the two writes can disagree after a crash in between — either accept a rare off-by-one that a nightly job corrects, or use a transaction (Level 3 · 06).

docs.title: Subset pattern: keep the hot part embedded
docs.text:
Pressure: a document is big because of a list, but readers only need the first few items.

A product page shows the 10 most recent reviews; the "all reviews" page is rare. Embed the latest 10 (bounded with $push + $slice, Level 1 · 06) and keep every review in a reviews collection.

// on new review: two writes
db.reviews.insertOne(review);
db.products.updateOne({ _id: review.productId }, {
  $push: { recentReviews: { $each: [review], $sort: { at: -1 }, $slice: 10 } },
  $inc: { reviewCount: 1 }
});

Lesson 01 measured why: reading a title from a 3.2 KB post with embedded comments cost the same as reading the whole post. The subset keeps the hot document small and the hot read single-query.

docs.title: Extended reference: copy the fields you display
docs.text:
Pressure: a frequent read needs a few fields from a related document.

An order displays the customer's name and shipping address. Instead of joining to customers on every order view, copy those fields into the order: customer: {_id, name, shippingAddress}. Often the copy is not just faster but more correct — the order should show the address it was shipped to, even if the customer moves later. Copy fields that rarely change or that should be frozen as history; never copy things like passwords or balances.

docs.title: Bucket pattern: group many small documents into fewer, larger ones
docs.text:
Pressure: huge numbers of tiny, similar documents — readings, events, metrics — each paying per-document and per-index-entry overhead.

An experiment: 10 sensors reporting one temperature per minute for a week, stored two ways.

  • readings: one document per reading, index on {sensor: 1, at: 1}.
  • buckets: one document per sensor per hour, readings appended to an array, with running aggregates.

The bucket write is an upsert that creates the hour's document on its first reading:

const hour = new Date(Math.floor(r.at.getTime() / 3600000) * 3600000);
db.buckets.updateOne(
  { sensor: r.sensor, hour },
  { $push: { m: { at: r.at, temp: r.temp } },
    $inc: { count: 1, sum: r.temp }, $min: { min: r.temp }, $max: { max: r.temp } },
  { upsert: true });
// with: db.buckets.createIndex({ sensor: 1, hour: 1 }, { unique: true })

The resulting collections:

readings: docs=100800 dataMB=6.3 storageMB=2.3 indexMB=3.79
buckets: docs=1680 dataMB=3.6 storageMB=1.3 indexMB=0.13

The same data in 60× fewer documents, with a little over half the data size and 29× less index. Indexes must fit in RAM to be fast, so that last number is the one that matters at scale.

Then the query "hourly average temperature for sensor s3 on 3 October":

24 24 22.450 22.450 flat ms 14 bucket ms 3
flat docsExamined 1440 bucket docsExamined 24

Both designs give the same 24 hourly averages (22.450 for the sixth hour in both), but the flat design read 1,440 documents and grouped them, while the bucket design read 24 documents and divided two numbers already stored in each. The buckets' pre-computed count, sum, min and max are the computed pattern applied inside the bucket pattern.

The costs: writes are updates to a growing document rather than plain inserts; queries for an individual reading must reach into the array; and you must choose the bucket size up front (an hour of minute data = 60 elements, a sensible size; a year in one bucket would be an unbounded array). MongoDB's time series collections (lesson 09) implement this pattern for you inside the server, and are usually the better choice for pure measurement data. The manual pattern is still useful when buckets need custom contents — pre-aggregates, per-bucket metadata, or grouping that isn't by time.

docs.title: Attribute pattern: many optional fields become key–value pairs
docs.text:
Pressure: documents have many different, sparse fields that you need to query — product specs, where laptops have ram_gb and kettles have watts.

One index per possible field doesn't scale. Instead, move them into an array of {k, v} pairs and index the pair once:

db.products.insertMany([
  { _id: 1, name: "Laptop A", specs: [{ k: "ram_gb", v: 16 }, { k: "screen_in", v: 14 }, { k: "cpu", v: "M-class" }] },
  { _id: 2, name: "Laptop B", specs: [{ k: "ram_gb", v: 32 }, { k: "screen_in", v: 16 }] },
  { _id: 3, name: "Kettle",   specs: [{ k: "litres", v: 1.7 }, { k: "watts", v: 2200 }] },
  { _id: 4, name: "Monitor",  specs: [{ k: "screen_in", v: 27 }, { k: "hz", v: 144 }] }]);
db.products.createIndex({ "specs.k": 1, "specs.v": 1 });
db.products.find({ specs: { $elemMatch: { k: "screen_in", v: { $gte: 15 } } } })

Laptop B, Monitor

The plan uses the one index with tight bounds on both parts:

"indexBounds":{"specs.k":["[\"screen_in\", \"screen_in\"]"],"specs.v":["[15, inf]"]}
2 2 2

Two keys examined, two documents fetched, two returned. The $elemMatch is essential: without it, k and v could come from different pairs (Level 1 · 05), and the index bounds can't be combined. A wildcard index (lesson 06) is an alternative when you'd rather keep specs as ordinary fields.

docs.title: Outlier pattern: design for the normal case, flag the exception
docs.text:
Pressure: 99.9% of documents have a small list, a few have an enormous one — the celebrity with ten million followers, the bestseller with 500,000 buyers.

Don't distort the schema for everyone. Embed normally, and when a document's list passes a threshold, move the overflow elsewhere and set a flag:

{ _id: "book-123", title: "...", buyers: [ /* first 1000 */ ], hasOverflow: true }
// overflow documents: { bookId: "book-123", page: 1, buyers: [ ... next 1000 ... ] }

Application code checks hasOverflow and only then fetches the extra pages. Most reads stay one query.

docs.title: Polymorphic pattern: different shapes in one collection
docs.text:
Pressure: entities that are mostly alike but differ in details — payment methods (card, UPI, bank transfer), notifications (email, SMS, push), catalogue items of different kinds.

Keep them in one collection with a discriminator field, because they're queried together ("all payment methods of this user"):

{ _id: 1, userId: "u42", type: "card", last4: "4242", expiry: "2028-04" }
{ _id: 2, userId: "u42", type: "upi",  vpa: "ana@bank" }

Index the shared fields (userId, type). Validate the variant-specific fields with a oneOf schema (lesson 04).

docs.title: Schema versioning: change shape without downtime
docs.text:
Pressure: the document shape must change, but you can't stop the application to rewrite a billion documents.

Add a schemaVersion field, teach the code to read every version, and upgrade documents lazily as they're touched:

def upgrade(doc):
    """Bring any stored version of a user up to version 2."""
    if doc.get("schemaVersion", 1) == 1:
        first, _, last = doc.pop("name").partition(" ")
        doc.update(firstName=first, lastName=last, schemaVersion=2)
    return doc

def get_user(uid):
    doc = users.find_one({"_id": uid})
    if doc and doc.get("schemaVersion", 1) < 2:
        doc = upgrade(doc)
        # Write back only if nobody else migrated it in the meantime.
        users.replace_one({"_id": uid, "schemaVersion": {"$exists": False}}, doc)
    return doc

With one version-1 user ({_id: 1, name: "Ana Rao"}) and one version-2 user:

{'_id': 1, 'firstName': 'Ana', 'lastName': 'Rao', 'schemaVersion': 2}
{'_id': 2, 'schemaVersion': 2, 'firstName': 'Ben', 'lastName': 'Ito'}
0 documents still on version 1

A background job then migrates the long tail of documents nobody reads, after which the version-1 branch can be deleted. Level 4 · 09 develops this into a full zero-downtime migration procedure.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Most of these patterns trade write-time work for read-time work, and they pay off because of how costs scale inside the server.

Every document carries fixed overhead: its BSON header and field names, a record in the collection's B-tree, and one entry in every index (more for multikey indexes). In the bucket experiment, the flat design had 100,800 records and 100,800 entries in the {sensor, at} index; the bucket design had 1,680 of each. Index size is what decides whether lookups stay in memory, and fewer, larger documents also compress better on disk, since similar values sit next to each other in one block.

Reads are dominated by the number of documents fetched, because each fetch is a separate B-tree lookup and document load. The bucket query fetched 24 documents instead of 1,440; the attribute query fetched exactly the matching documents because the index bounds were tight. Pre-computed values (the computed pattern) move arithmetic from every read to the much rarer writes.

The limit is the document itself: everything in it is read and rewritten together, and it can't exceed 16 MB. Buckets must be bounded, subsets must be capped, outliers must overflow. Every pattern here is a way of making documents as large as the access pattern wants and no larger.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Applying patterns before measuring a need. Start simple; reach for a pattern when a specific pressure appears.
  • Unbounded buckets — a "bucket per sensor" with no time boundary is just an unbounded array.
  • Attribute pattern without $elemMatch in queries, so k and v match different pairs.
  • Computed values updated outside the write that changes their inputs, drifting silently.
  • Extended references to fields that change often, creating constant fan-out updates.
  • Schema versions without a plan to finish the migration, leaving three code paths forever.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build the flat and bucket designs for 50 sensors × 30 days of minute readings. Compare document count, data size and index size, and time "daily min/max per sensor for a month" on both.
  2. Change the bucket size from one hour to one day. What happens to index size, document size and the hourly-average query?
  3. Model a product catalogue with books, laptops and kettles using the polymorphic and attribute patterns together. Write a query for "laptops with at least 16 GB RAM and a screen under 15 inches" that uses one index.
  4. Implement the outlier pattern for a followers array with a threshold of 1,000. Write follow() and followersPage(userId, page).
  5. Write the background migration job for the schema versioning example: process version-1 users in batches of 500 with bulkWrite, safely alongside the lazy migration.

docs.title: 04 · Schema Validation with $jsonSchema
docs.text:
"Schemaless" is the most misleading word ever attached to MongoDB. Every application has a schema — the only question is whether it is written down and enforced in one place, or scattered across the code of every service that writes to the database. A flexible schema is a feature while a design is evolving; in production, a document with tier: "gold" when the code only knows "free", "pro" and "enterprise" is a bug waiting for a customer to find it.

MongoDB lets each collection carry a validator, checked by the server on every insert and update. This lesson builds validators, reads their error reports, and — the part that matters in real systems — adds them to collections that already contain bad data.

docs.title: A first validator
docs.text:
db.createCollection("customers", { validator: { $jsonSchema: {
  bsonType: "object", required: ["email", "name", "tier"],
  properties: {
    email: { bsonType: "string", pattern: "^[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+$", description: "must be an email address" },
    name: { bsonType: "string", minLength: 1 },
    tier: { enum: ["free", "pro", "enterprise"] },
    credit: { bsonType: "decimal", minimum: 0 },
    tags: { bsonType: "array", maxItems: 5, items: { bsonType: "string" }, uniqueItems: true }
  } } } });

$jsonSchema is MongoDB's dialect of JSON Schema (draft 4), with bsonType added so you can require BSON types that JSON doesn't have — decimal, date, objectId, long. Fields not listed under properties are allowed unless you set additionalProperties: false.

A valid document goes in as usual. An invalid one:

db.customers.insertOne({ email: "not-an-email", name: "", tier: "gold", credit: -5 })

121 Document failed validation

Code 121 is the validation error. The exception's errInfo.details explains exactly what failed — every rule, not just the first:

[
  {
    operatorName: 'properties',
    propertiesNotSatisfied: [
      { propertyName: 'email', description: 'must be an email address',
        details: [ { operatorName: 'pattern', specifiedAs: { pattern: '^[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+$' },
                     reason: 'regular expression did not match', consideredValue: 'not-an-email' } ] },
      { propertyName: 'name',
        details: [ { operatorName: 'minLength', specifiedAs: { minLength: 1 },
                     reason: 'specified string length was not satisfied', consideredValue: '' } ] },
      { propertyName: 'tier',
        details: [ { operatorName: 'enum', specifiedAs: { enum: [ 'free', 'pro', 'enterprise' ] },
                     reason: 'value was not found in enum', consideredValue: 'gold' } ] },
      { propertyName: 'credit',
        details: [ { operatorName: 'minimum', specifiedAs: { minimum: 0 },
                     reason: 'comparison failed', consideredValue: -5 },
                   { operatorName: 'bsonType', specifiedAs: { bsonType: 'decimal' },
                     reason: 'type did not match', consideredValue: -5, consideredType: 'int' } ] }
    ]
  }
]

Log errInfo when a write fails with code 121; it turns a vague "validation failed" report into a one-line fix. Note the credit entry: -5 failed twice, because it's below the minimum and it's an int rather than a decimal. Type rules are exact — a validator requiring decimal rejects a perfectly reasonable int, so make sure every writer sends the right type (Level 1 · 08 showed how PyMongo needs Decimal128).

docs.title: Updates are validated too
docs.text:
The server validates the document as it will be after the update:

db.customers.updateOne({ email: "ana@example.com" }, { $set: { tier: "platinum" } })
db.customers.updateOne({ email: "ana@example.com" }, { $unset: { name: "" } })

update: 121 Plan executor error during update :: caused by :: Document failed validation
unset: 121 Plan executor error during update :: caused by :: Document failed validation
