That's the real value of server-side validation: it applies to the admin script someone runs at 2 a.m. just as much as to your carefully reviewed application code.

docs.title: Rules across fields: $expr
docs.text:
$jsonSchema validates fields one at a time. For rules relating fields to each other, combine it with a query expression:

db.createCollection("bookings", { validator: { $and: [
  { $jsonSchema: { required: ["start", "end"],
                   properties: { start: { bsonType: "date" }, end: { bsonType: "date" } } } },
  { $expr: { $lt: ["$start", "$end"] } } ] } });
db.bookings.insertOne({ start: new Date("2026-10-12"), end: new Date("2026-10-10") })

bookings: 121
{
  operatorName: '$and',
  clausesNotSatisfied: [
    { index: 1, details: { operatorName: '$expr', specifiedAs: { '$expr': { '$lt': [ '$start', '$end' ] } },
                           reason: 'expression did not match', expressionResult: false } }
  ]
}

Any query operator can appear in a validator, except a few that need context ($near, $text, $where).

docs.title: Variants: oneOf
docs.text:
For polymorphic collections (lesson 03), oneOf requires a document to match exactly one variant:

db.createCollection("payments", { validator: { $jsonSchema: {
  bsonType: "object", required: ["type"], oneOf: [
    { properties: { type: { enum: ["card"] }, last4: { bsonType: "string", pattern: "^[0-9]{4}$" } }, required: ["last4"] },
    { properties: { type: { enum: ["upi"] }, vpa: { bsonType: "string" } }, required: ["vpa"] } ] } } });
db.payments.insertOne({ type: "upi", vpa: "ana@bank" })     // accepted
db.payments.insertOne({ type: "card", vpa: "ana@bank" })    // 121: a card without last4

docs.title: Adding a validator to a collection that already has data
docs.text:
This is the situation you'll actually be in. A legacy collection has three documents, two of them bad:

db.legacy.insertMany([{ _id: 1, email: "a@x.io", qty: 3 }, { _id: 2, email: "bad", qty: -1 }, { _id: 3, qty: 2 }]);
const schema = { $jsonSchema: { required: ["email"],
  properties: { email: { bsonType: "string", pattern: "@" }, qty: { bsonType: "int", minimum: 0 } } } };

Step 1: find the violators first. A validator is just a query filter, so $nor finds every document that would fail it:

db.legacy.find({ $nor: [schema] })

violating now: 2,3

Step 2: add the rule without breaking existing writes. collMod sets the validator. With validationLevel: "moderate", documents that already violate the rules can still be updated, while valid documents must stay valid and new inserts must be valid:

db.runCommand({ collMod: "legacy", validator: schema, validationLevel: "moderate" });
db.legacy.updateOne({ _id: 2 }, { $set: { note: "still invalid but already was" } })  // modifiedCount 1
db.legacy.updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { $set: { qty: -9 } })                                // 121
db.legacy.insertOne({ _id: 4, email: "nope" })                                         // 121

Or observe before enforcing. validationAction: "warn" accepts invalid writes but logs them:

db.runCommand({ collMod: "legacy", validationAction: "warn" });
db.legacy.insertOne({ _id: 5, email: "nope" })   // acknowledged: true

The server log gained a line with message Document would fail validation (log id 20294). Run in warn mode for a while, grep the log to find which writers send bad data, fix them, then switch to "error".

Step 3: fix the old documents (with a migration, lesson 03's schema-versioning approach or a one-off script), and finally set validationLevel: "strict" so every write is checked.

docs.title: Escape hatches
docs.text:
Users with the bypassDocumentValidation privilege can skip validation per command:

db.runCommand({ insert: "customers", documents: [{ x: 1 }], bypassDocumentValidation: true })

The document {x: 1} went into customers despite having none of the required fields. Restore tools and data-repair scripts sometimes need this; ordinary application users should never have that privilege (Level 4 · 05). Also note that mongorestore validates documents unless told otherwise (--bypassDocumentValidation).

docs.title: Where validation belongs
docs.text: Server-side validation is the last line of defence, not the only one. Validate in the application too (Pydantic, Zod, your framework's forms), because that's where you can give a user a friendly message. The database validator catches what the application misses: other services, scripts, old code paths, and bugs. Keep it to rules that are truly invariant — types, required fields, enums, ranges — and leave volatile business rules in code.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The validator is stored in the collection's catalog entry. On every insert, and on every update after the update has been applied to an in-memory copy, the server evaluates the validator against the new document using the same match-expression engine that runs find() filters — $jsonSchema is compiled into a tree of match expressions, which is why you can combine it with $expr and other query operators, and why find({$nor: [schema]}) finds violators. If the expression evaluates false, the write is rejected before it reaches the storage engine (validationAction: "error") or logged and allowed ("warn").

validationLevel: "moderate" works by evaluating the validator against the document before the update too: if the old version was already invalid, the update is allowed regardless. That is why the update to document 2 succeeded while the update that would have made document 1 invalid failed.

Validation is cheap compared to the write itself, but not free — a large schema with regex patterns is evaluated on every write. And it only applies on writes: changing a validator never re-checks existing documents, so the $nor query is the only way to know what's already in there.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No validator at all on collections written by more than one program.
  • Adding a strict validator to a live collection without checking existing data, then discovering that routine updates to old documents now fail.
  • Requiring double or decimal when writers send integers (or vice versa).
  • additionalProperties: false without listing _id — every insert fails, because _id is a property too.
  • Putting fast-changing business rules in the validator, so every rule change becomes a database change.
  • Giving application users bypassDocumentValidation.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a validator for an orders collection: required customerId (objectId), status (enum), items (non-empty array of {sku: string, qty: int ≥ 1, price: decimal ≥ 0}), and total (decimal). Insert one valid and three different invalid orders and read each errInfo.
  2. Add an $expr rule that shippedAt, if present, must be later than placedAt. (Hint: $or with $exists-like logic using { $eq: [{ $type: "$shippedAt" }, "missing"] }.)
  3. Take the library.books collection from Level 1 · 04, write a schema for it, and list the violators with $nor. Add the validator with moderate + warn, perform some writes, and find the warnings in the log.
  4. Try additionalProperties: false without _id in properties and observe what happens on insert.

docs.title: 05 · How Indexes Work & Compound Index Design
docs.text: Everything in Level 1 ran as a collection scan: to answer a query, the server read every document. With ten books that's instant. With half a million orders it's not — and with fifty million, under load, it's an outage. Indexes are the single biggest performance lever in MongoDB, and compound index design is the skill that separates a database that copes from one that doesn't.

docs.title: A test collection
docs.text:
The script below creates 500,000 orders with a seeded random generator, so you get the same data every time (customerId 0–49,999, five statuses with about 70% delivered and 5% cancelled, placedAt spread across 2025–2026, total up to 500.00):

const d = db.getSiblingDB("idx"); d.orders.drop();
let seed = 42; const rnd = () => { seed |= 0; seed = seed + 0x6D2B79F5 | 0;
  let t = Math.imul(seed ^ seed >>> 15, 1 | seed); t = t + Math.imul(t ^ t >>> 7, 61 | t) ^ t;
  return ((t ^ t >>> 14) >>> 0) / 4294967296; };
const statuses = ["placed","paid","shipped","delivered","cancelled"], weights = [0.05,0.1,0.1,0.7,0.05];
const pick = () => { let r = rnd(), a = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { a += weights[i]; if (r < a) return statuses[i]; } return "delivered"; };
const cities = ["Pune","Mumbai","Delhi","Chennai","Hyderabad","Bengaluru","Kolkata","Jaipur"];
const start = new Date("2025-01-01").getTime(), span = 640 * 86400000;
let batch = [];
for (let i = 0; i < 500000; i++) {
  batch.push({ customerId: Math.floor(rnd() * 50000), status: pick(), city: cities[Math.floor(rnd() * 8)],
    placedAt: new Date(start + Math.floor(rnd() * span)), total: Math.round(rnd() * 50000) / 100,
    items: Math.floor(rnd() * 5) + 1 });
  if (batch.length === 10000) { d.orders.insertMany(batch); batch = []; }
}

(The first version of this generator used a textbook linear congruential formula with a power-of-two modulus. It produced only 5,784 distinct customer ids out of 50,000 — its low bits repeat in short cycles. If your synthetic data looks oddly clumpy, check the generator before blaming the database.)

To compare plans, a small helper prints the plan's stages, how many index keys and documents the server examined, and the time:

const run = (label, q, sort, hint) => {
  let c = o.find(q).sort(sort || {}).limit(20); if (hint) c = c.hint(hint);
  const e = c.explain("executionStats"), s = e.executionStats;
  const stages = []; let p = e.queryPlanner.winningPlan; while (p) { stages.push(p.stage); p = p.inputStage; }
  print(`${label.padEnd(34)} ${stages.join("<-").padEnd(36)} keys=${s.totalKeysExamined} docs=${s.totalDocsExamined} ms=${s.executionTimeMillis}`);
};

Lesson 07 explains explain() in detail; for now, fewer keys and documents examined is better, and the ideal is examining exactly as many as you return.

docs.title: The first index
docs.text:
"Orders of customer 12345":

customer, no index                 LIMIT<-COLLSCAN                      keys=     0 docs=500000 ms=134

db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1 })

customer, {customerId:1}           LIMIT<-FETCH<-IXSCAN                 keys=    11 docs=    11 ms=5

From reading 500,000 documents to reading 11 — the customer's 11 orders. The time difference (134 ms → 5 ms) understates it: the collection scan's cost grows with the collection, the index lookup's cost grows only with the number of results. Building the index took under half a second here (a single-field index on city built in 440 ms on this collection); on large collections builds take longer but don't block reads and writes for their duration.

docs.title: Compound indexes and the order of fields
docs.text:
A compound index sorts entries by its first field, then by the second within equal first values, and so on — like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name. That makes field order decisive. Take a realistic query: the 20 largest cancelled orders placed between March and June 2026.

const q2 = { status: "cancelled", placedAt: { $gte: new Date("2026-03-01"), $lt: new Date("2026-06-01") } };
db.orders.find(q2).sort({ total: -1 }).limit(20)

Three fields: status is an Equality condition, total is the Sort, placedAt is a Range. Three candidate indexes with the same fields in different orders, each forced with hint():

R,E,S {placedAt,status,total}      FETCH<-SORT<-IXSCAN                  keys= 71514 docs=    20 ms=64
E,R,S {status,placedAt,total}      FETCH<-SORT<-IXSCAN                  keys=  3480 docs=    20 ms=3
E,S,R {status,total,placedAt}      LIMIT<-FETCH<-IXSCAN                 keys=   219 docs=    20 ms=0
  • Range first (placedAt, status, total): the index scan covers every order in the three-month range — 71,514 keys, checking each one's status — then sorts the matches in memory (SORT stage).
  • Equality, range, sort: jumps straight to cancelled, scans the 3,480 cancelled orders in the date range, then still has to sort them all in memory to find the top 20.
  • Equality, sort, range: jumps to cancelled, walks the entries already in total descending order, checks each one's date, and stops after finding 20 in range. 219 keys, no SORT stage, no limit on how big the result set could be.

This is the ESR rule: in a compound index, put fields used for Equality first, then the fields you Sort on, then fields with Range conditions. Left to choose for itself with all three indexes available, the planner picked the same one:

planner's own choice               LIMIT<-FETCH<-IXSCAN                 keys=   219 docs=    20 ms=1

ESR is a rule of thumb, not a law. If the range is extremely selective (one minute out of two years) and there's no limit, E-R-S can win because it examines fewer keys in total. Measure with your real data and query shapes.

docs.title: Index prefixes
docs.text:
An index on {a, b, c} can serve queries on {a}, {a, b} and {a, b, c} — its prefixes — but not on {b} or {c} alone, just as a phone book sorted by surname can't find everyone named "Priya":

{status: "cancelled"}          → status_1_placedAt_1_total_-1
{placedAt: {$gte: ...}}        → placedAt_1_status_1_total_-1
{total: {$gt: 400}}            → COLLSCAN

No index starts with total, so the last query scans. Because prefixes are served by longer indexes, a separate index on {status: 1} would be redundant next to {status: 1, total: -1, placedAt: 1} — every extra index costs memory and slows every write.

docs.title: Sort direction
docs.text: For a single-field index, direction doesn't matter: the index can be walked backwards. For compound indexes, the relative directions matter: {status: 1, total: -1} serves sort({status: 1, total: -1}) and its exact reverse sort({status: -1, total: 1}), but not sort({status: 1, total: 1}). Match the index to the sorts you actually run.

docs.title: What indexes cost
docs.text:
{
  _id_: 12439552,
  'placedAt_1_status_1_total_-1': 17547264,
  'status_1_placedAt_1_total_-1': 11968512,
  'status_1_total_-1_placedAt_1': 9293824
}

Each of these is roughly 9–17 MB for 500,000 documents — in the same range as the whole _id index. (Sizes differ partly because of how well each key order compresses: indexes that start with a low-cardinality field like status get excellent prefix compression.) Every index:

  • must be updated on every insert and delete, and on every update that touches an indexed field;
  • competes for the WiredTiger cache — an index that doesn't fit in memory is read from disk;
  • adds to replication and backup work.

A collection with fifteen indexes "just in case" is a slow-writing collection. Create indexes for the queries you actually run, and remove ones nothing uses (lesson 08 shows how to find them with $indexStats).

docs.title: Building indexes on a live system
docs.text:
db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1, placedAt: -1 }, { name: "customer_recent" })

Since MongoDB 4.2 index builds hold an exclusive lock only briefly at the start and end; in between, reads and writes continue. The build still consumes CPU, I/O and cache, so build big indexes off-peak. On a replica set the build runs on all data-bearing members simultaneously and commits once the commit quorum — by default, all voting data-bearing members — is ready (Level 4 · 09 measures one under load). Set name explicitly for important indexes: the auto-generated name changes if you change a field's direction, which makes hints and monitoring brittle.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A MongoDB index is a B-tree (WiredTiger's B+tree variant) whose keys are the indexed values and whose payload is a RecordId — the internal address of the document in the collection's own B-tree. For a compound index the key is the concatenation of the field values in index order, encoded so that a simple byte comparison sorts them correctly (descending fields are encoded inverted).

An IXSCAN computes index bounds from the query — for the ESR index, status: ["cancelled", "cancelled"], total: [MaxKey, MinKey] (all, descending), placedAt: [2026-03-01, 2026-06-01) — seeks to the first key inside the bounds (a tree descent of a few pages), then walks keys in order. For each key it checks the remaining bounds; for passing keys, the FETCH stage uses the RecordId to load the document from the collection and apply any filter conditions the index couldn't check.

That walk is why order matters. Equality fields first means the scan starts in a narrow region. Sort fields next means the keys come out already in the requested order, so no SORT stage is needed and the scan can stop as soon as limit is satisfied. Range fields last means the range is checked per key during the walk instead of fragmenting the scan. A SORT stage, in contrast, must consume all of its input before it can return the first document, and it is limited in memory (100 MB by default before it must spill to disk or, if disk use is disallowed, fail).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Creating single-field indexes on every queried field and hoping the server combines them. It rarely does well; design compound indexes for your query shapes.
  • Putting range fields before sort fields, forcing in-memory sorts.
  • Redundant prefix indexes ({a} next to {a, b}).
  • Low-selectivity single-field indexes alone (an index on status with five values still leaves 350,000 "delivered" documents to fetch).
  • Never removing indexes. Each one taxes every write.
  • Benchmarking with synthetic data that doesn't resemble production — distributions decide which plan wins.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Using idx.orders:

  1. Write the best single index for: "a customer's orders, newest first" and verify that explain shows no SORT stage.
  2. For "delivered orders in Pune with total over 400, sorted by placedAt descending", design the index using ESR and compare it with two alternative orders using hint(). Record keys/docs examined.
  3. Find a query where the E-R-S order beats E-S-R on your data. (Hint: a very narrow date range with no limit.)
  4. Create {status: 1, total: -1} and run sort({status: 1, total: 1}). Is there a SORT stage? What about sort({status: -1, total: 1})?
  5. Measure insert throughput (insert 50,000 documents, time it) with only the _id index, then with five secondary indexes.

docs.title: 06 · Multikey, Unique, Partial, TTL, Wildcard & Text Indexes
docs.text:
Lesson 05 covered the ordinary B-tree index and how to order its fields. The same structure, with a few options switched on, solves a surprising range of problems: enforcing uniqueness, indexing only the documents that matter, expiring old data automatically, and indexing fields you don't know in advance. Each option also has a behaviour that catches people out. This lesson runs into each one on purpose.

All examples use a scratch database, itypes.

docs.title: Multikey indexes: arrays
docs.text:
Index a field that holds arrays and MongoDB creates a multikey index automatically — one entry per element:

db.p.insertMany([{ _id: 1, tags: ["a", "b"], sizes: [1, 2] }, { _id: 2, tags: ["b"], sizes: [3] }]);
db.p.createIndex({ tags: 1 });
db.p.find({ tags: "b" }).explain("executionStats")

The plan reports isMultiKey: true and examined 2 keys for the 2 documents containing "b". You don't declare it; the index becomes multikey the first time an array is inserted, and stays that way.

The restriction: a compound index can include at most one array field per document.

db.p.createIndex({ tags: 1, sizes: 1 })

Index build failed: <uuid>: Collection itypes.p ( <uuid> ) :: caused by :: ... :: caused by :: cannot index parallel arrays [sizes] [tags]

An index on both would need an entry for every combination of elements — the cross product. If the index exists first, the same rule rejects the write instead:

db.p2.createIndex({ tags: 1, sizes: 1 });
db.p2.insertOne({ tags: ["a"], sizes: 5 });        // fine: only one array
db.p2.insertOne({ tags: ["a"], sizes: [5, 6] })    // rejected

171 cannot index parallel arrays [sizes] [tags]

Compound indexes over two fields inside the same array of documents (items.sku and items.qty) are fine — that's one array.

docs.title: Unique indexes and the null trap
docs.text:
db.u.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true });
db.u.insertOne({ name: "no email 1" });
db.u.insertOne({ name: "no email 2" })

unique+missing: 11000 E11000 duplicate key error collection: itypes.u index: email_1 dup key: { email: null }

A document without the field is indexed as null, so only one document may lack it. For optional unique fields (an email that only some accounts have, an external id that arrives later), make the index partial:

db.u2.createIndex({ email: 1 },
  { unique: true, partialFilterExpression: { email: { $type: "string" } } });
db.u2.insertMany([{ name: "a" }, { name: "b" }, { email: "x@y.z" }]);   // all three accepted
db.u2.insertOne({ email: "x@y.z" })                                      // 11000

Uniqueness now applies only among documents that have a string email.

Two more facts about unique indexes. They're the only reliable way to prevent duplicates under concurrency (Level 1 · 10). And you can't create one on a collection that already contains duplicates — find them first with an aggregation ($group by the key, $match count > 1).

docs.title: Partial indexes: index only what you query
docs.text:
Most orders are closed; the application constantly queries open orders by total. Index only those:

db.orders2.createIndex({ total: 1 }, { partialFilterExpression: { status: "open" } });

partial, status open: IXSCAN  no status: COLLSCAN

The index is used only when the query guarantees its results are within the index — here, by including status: "open". A query on total alone can't use it, because the index doesn't contain closed orders and using it would give wrong answers. In exchange, a partial index on 5% of a collection is about 5% of the size and write cost of a full one. Partial indexes are the right tool for "active", "unprocessed", "not deleted" subsets.

docs.title: Sparse indexes
docs.text:
The older way to skip documents: a sparse index omits documents that lack the field. It has a sharp edge:

db.sp.insertMany([{ _id: 1, nick: "zed" }, { _id: 2 }, { _id: 3, nick: "amy" }]);
db.sp.createIndex({ nick: 1 }, { sparse: true });
db.sp.find().sort({ nick: 1 })                     // 2,3,1
db.sp.find().sort({ nick: 1 }).hint({ nick: 1 })   // 3,1  ← document 2 vanished

Forced to use the sparse index, the query silently loses the document without a nick. The planner won't choose a sparse index on its own when that would drop results, but a hint will. Prefer partial indexes with an explicit $exists: true or $type filter — they say what they mean.

docs.title: TTL indexes: data that deletes itself
docs.text:
A TTL index on a date field removes documents a fixed time after that date. Sessions that expire 5 seconds after lastSeen:

db.sessions.createIndex({ lastSeen: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 5 });
db.sessions.insertMany([{ s: 1, lastSeen: new Date(Date.now() - 60000) },
                        { s: 2, lastSeen: new Date() },
                        { s: 3, lastSeen: "not a date" }]);

ttl start: 3 2026-10-11T17:43:12.600Z
2026-10-11T17:43:25.008Z 1,2,3
2026-10-11T17:44:23.745Z 3

Twelve seconds later, nothing had been deleted, even session 1, which expired a minute before it was inserted. About a minute later, sessions 1 and 2 were gone. Session 3 will never be deleted: its lastSeen is a string, and TTL only acts on BSON dates (or arrays of dates, using the earliest).

The delay is the TTL monitor, a background thread that wakes up every 60 seconds by default:

db.adminCommand({ getParameter: 1, ttlMonitorSleepSecs: 1 }).ttlMonitorSleepSecs   // 60

So TTL is for housekeeping, not for exact expiry. If a session must be invalid the instant it expires, check lastSeen in your query as well and let TTL clean up afterwards. Two useful variations:

  • Expire at a specific time: set expireAfterSeconds: 0 and store the expiry moment itself in the field (expiresAt). Each document then chooses its own lifetime.
  • Change the lifetime later with collMod instead of rebuilding the index.

TTL deletes are ordinary deletes: they're replicated, they cost I/O, and a TTL index suddenly applied to a hundred million old documents will generate a hundred million deletes. Roll out TTL on big collections gradually, or delete the backlog in batches first.

docs.title: Wildcard indexes: fields you don't know in advance
docs.text:
For documents with user-defined or highly variable fields, a wildcard index indexes every path under a prefix:

db.w.insertMany([{ attrs: { color: "red", size: "M" } }, { attrs: { color: "blue", weight: 3 } },
                 { attrs: { voltage: 230 } }]);
db.w.createIndex({ "attrs.$**": 1 });
db.w.find({ "attrs.weight": 3 }).explain().queryPlanner.winningPlan.inputStage.keyPattern

{"$_path":1,"attrs.weight":1}

The index stores the path as part of each key ($_path), so a query on any one field under attrs can use it. This is an alternative to the attribute pattern (lesson 03) when you'd rather keep natural field names. Limits: a wildcard index helps queries on one field at a time (it doesn't replace a compound index for multi-field filters, though compound wildcard indexes with fixed prefix fields exist in recent versions), and indexing everything in a document is rarely a good idea for write-heavy collections.

docs.title: Hidden indexes: test a removal safely
docs.text:
Before dropping an index you think is unused, hide it. The planner ignores it, but it's still maintained, so un-hiding is instant:

db.orders2.createIndex({ i: 1 });
db.orders2.hideIndex("i_1");    // plan for {i: 5}: COLLSCAN
db.orders2.unhideIndex("i_1");  // plan for {i: 5}: FETCH (via IXSCAN)

Hide it, watch latency and slow-query logs for a few days, then drop it. Re-creating a dropped index on a large collection can take hours; un-hiding takes milliseconds.

docs.title: Text, geospatial, hashed and others
docs.text:
A few index types belong to later lessons:

  • Text indexes ({ description: "text" }) for word search with stemming and stop words — Level 3 · 09.
  • 2dsphere for geographic queries — Level 3 · 08.
  • Hashed indexes ({ userId: "hashed" }) store a hash of the value; they support equality only and exist mainly for hashed sharding — Level 4 · 04.
  • Collation on an index ({ collation: { locale: "en", strength: 2 } }) for case-insensitive equality and sorting — Level 3 · 09.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
All of these are the same WiredTiger B-tree with different rules about which keys are generated for a document:

  • Multikey: the key generator walks the indexed path, and when it finds an array it emits one key per element (deduplicated). The index's catalog entry records which paths are multikey, which tells the planner where bounds can't be combined.
  • Unique: before inserting a key, the index checks whether that key already exists pointing to a different document, and fails the write if so. Missing fields generate a null key, hence the trap.
  • Partial: the key generator first evaluates partialFilterExpression; documents that fail it get no keys at all. The planner may use the index only if it can prove the query's filter implies that expression.
  • Sparse: documents with none of the indexed fields generate no keys.
  • Wildcard: the generator walks every path under the prefix and emits (path, value) pairs.
  • TTL: an ordinary index plus a catalog flag. The TTL monitor periodically runs, for each TTL index, essentially deleteMany({field: {$lt: now - expireAfterSeconds}}) using that index — which is why it's efficient, why non-date values are never matched, and why deletion is batched rather than instant.
  • Hidden: a catalog flag the planner checks; the index is otherwise fully maintained.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A unique index on an optional field without a partial filter — the second document without it fails.
  • Expecting TTL to delete exactly on time. Filter on the expiry in queries too.
  • Dates stored as strings in a TTL field. Those documents live forever.
  • Querying a partial index's field without the filter condition, then wondering why it isn't used.
  • Hinting a sparse index and silently losing documents.
  • Indexing two arrays in one compound index, which fails at build or at write time.
  • Dropping an index without hiding it first.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create a users collection where username is required and unique, and phone is optional but unique when present. Prove both rules with inserts.
  2. Insert 100,000 tasks where 2% have status: "pending". Create a partial index for pending tasks ordered by dueAt. Compare its size with a full index on {status: 1, dueAt: 1} using collStats.
  3. Build an otpCodes collection where each code expires at its own expiresAt (use expireAfterSeconds: 0). Insert codes expiring in 30, 90 and 150 seconds, and record when each one actually disappears.
  4. Add a wildcard index on attrs to a product collection with 20 different attribute names. Find a query that can't use it efficiently, and explain why.
  5. Hide one of the idx.orders indexes from lesson 05 and rerun the ESR query. What does the planner choose instead?

docs.title: 07 · Reading explain()
docs.text:
An index you think a query uses is worth nothing until explain() confirms it. explain() is how you see what the server actually did: which plan it chose, which index bounds it scanned, how many index keys and documents it touched, and where the time went. Learning to read it quickly is the most practical performance skill in MongoDB.

Everything here runs against the 500,000-document idx.orders collection from lesson 05, with an extra index {customerId: 1, placedAt: -1}.

docs.title: Three verbosity levels
docs.text:
db.orders.find(q).explain()                     // "queryPlanner": chosen plan, not executed
db.orders.find(q).explain("executionStats")     // runs the winning plan and reports counts and times
db.orders.find(q).explain("allPlansExecution")  // also reports the trial runs of rejected plans

queryPlanner is safe on any query because it doesn't run it. executionStats runs the query to completion — fine for reads, but remember that explaining an expensive query costs as much as running it. (Explaining an update or remove with executionStats evaluates it without applying the writes.)

Aggregations use db.orders.explain("executionStats").aggregate([...]) — Level 3 · 05.

docs.title: Anatomy of an explain
docs.text:
"A customer's orders, newest first":

db.orders.find({ customerId: 12345 }).sort({ placedAt: -1 }).explain("executionStats")

The trimmed output, top half:

queryPlanner: {
  namespace: 'idx.orders',
  parsedQuery: { customerId: { '$eq': 12345 } },
  winningPlan: {
    stage: 'FETCH',
    inputStage: {
      stage: 'IXSCAN',
      keyPattern: { customerId: 1, placedAt: -1 },
      indexName: 'customerId_1_placedAt_-1',
      isMultiKey: false,
      direction: 'forward',
      indexBounds: { customerId: [ '[12345, 12345]' ], placedAt: [ '[MaxKey, MinKey]' ] }
    }
  },
  rejectedPlans: [ ]
}

Read the plan from the innermost stage outwards — data flows up. IXSCAN walks the index; FETCH loads each document. There's no SORT stage: the index already delivers placedAt descending. The index bounds say exactly which part of the index was scanned: one customerId value, all placedAt values (MaxKey to MinKey because the field is descending). Bounds are the first thing to check when an indexed query is slow — [MinKey, MaxKey] on your first field means the index is being scanned end to end.

The bottom half:

executionStats: {
  executionSuccess: true,
  nReturned: 11,
  executionTimeMillis: 13,
  totalKeysExamined: 11,
  totalDocsExamined: 11,
  executionStages: {
    stage: 'FETCH', nReturned: 11, works: 12, advanced: 11, needTime: 0, needYield: 0, isEOF: 1,
    docsExamined: 11,
    inputStage: { stage: 'IXSCAN', nReturned: 11, keysExamined: 11, seeks: 1, ... }
  }
}

docs.title: The three numbers that matter
docs.text:
Number Meaning Ideal nReturned documents returned — totalKeysExamined index entries read ≈ nReturned totalDocsExamined documents loaded from the collection ≈ nReturned, or 0 if covered

Here all three are 11: perfect. The ratios tell you what's wrong when it isn't:

  • keys ≫ returned: the index bounds are too wide — wrong field order or a missing equality field.
  • docs ≫ returned, keys ≈ docs: the index finds candidates but a filter applied after the fetch rejects most of them — add that field to the index.
  • docs = collection size, keys = 0: COLLSCAN, no usable index.

executionTimeMillis is useful but noisy (cache state, concurrent load, the first run warming the cache). Trust the examined counts more than the milliseconds.

docs.title: Stages you'll see
docs.text:
Stage What it does COLLSCAN read every document IXSCAN walk a range of an index FETCH load documents by RecordId, apply remaining filters SORT in-memory (blocking) sort LIMIT, SKIP as named PROJECTION_SIMPLE / PROJECTION_DEFAULT apply a projection to fetched documents PROJECTION_COVERED build results from index keys alone — no FETCH OR combine the results of several index scans for an $or SORT_MERGE merge several already-sorted index scans EXPRESS_IXSCAN fast path for an exact _id lookup or a single-result equality match on a unique index (on 9.0.2, find({_id: x}) showed this stage) IDHACK the older servers' name for the _id fast path — you'll still meet it in explains from pre-8.0 deployments

Newer servers may also run eligible queries in the slot-based execution engine (SBE); explain then shows an additional slotBasedPlan section and queryPlanner.winningPlan.queryPlan nesting. The same principles apply: find the scans, check bounds and examined counts.

docs.title: Four plans side by side
docs.text:
Using the same helper as lesson 05:

covered                        PROJECTION_COVERED<-IXSCAN               n=11 keys=11 docs=0 ms=2
not covered (needs total)      PROJECTION_SIMPLE<-FETCH<-IXSCAN         n=11 keys=11 docs=11 ms=0
not covered (_id returned)     PROJECTION_SIMPLE<-FETCH<-IXSCAN         n=11 keys=11 docs=11 ms=0
filter after fetch             FETCH<-IXSCAN                            n=4 keys=11 docs=11 ms=1

The queries:

o.find({ customerId: 12345 }, { _id: 0, customerId: 1, placedAt: 1 }).sort({ placedAt: -1 })   // covered
o.find({ customerId: 12345 }, { _id: 0, placedAt: 1, total: 1 }).sort({ placedAt: -1 })         // needs total
o.find({ customerId: 12345 }, { placedAt: 1 }).sort({ placedAt: -1 })                           // _id included
o.find({ customerId: 12345, items: { $gte: 4 } }).sort({ placedAt: -1 })                       // extra filter

Covered query: every field the query filters on and returns is in the index, so the server builds the results from the index keys and examines zero documents. Note the second and third lines: asking for one field not in the index (total), or forgetting to exclude _id (included by default, and not in this index), forces a fetch of every document. Covered queries are the fastest reads MongoDB can do, and they're often one projection change away. (An index on a multikey field can't cover queries on that field.)

Filter after fetch: items isn't in the index, so 11 documents are fetched and 7 are thrown away. With 11 that's irrelevant; with 11,000 it isn't. If this query is frequent, the index should include items.

docs.title: Blocking sorts
docs.text:
When no index provides the order, a SORT stage collects every input document before returning the first one. All delivered orders sorted by city, then total:

in-memory sort                 SORT<-FETCH<-IXSCAN                      n=349643 keys=349643 docs=349643 ms=861
SORT memLimit 104857600 totalDataSizeSorted 78874594 usedDisk false spills 0

349,643 documents, 79 MB sorted in memory, under the 100 MB limit (the server parameter internalQueryMaxBlockingSortMemoryUsageBytes). To see what happens beyond the limit without generating gigabytes of data, the lab server's limit was lowered to 10 MB for a moment:

db.adminCommand({ setParameter: 1, internalQueryMaxBlockingSortMemoryUsageBytes: 10 * 1024 * 1024 });
o.find({ status: "delivered" }).sort({ city: 1, total: -1 }).allowDiskUse(false).toArray()

31157 Location31157 No viable plan was found because all candidate plans failed.

With disk use disallowed, the sort fails. With the default (allowDiskUseByDefault is true since MongoDB 6.0), it spills to temporary files instead:

usedDisk true spills 9 ms 876

Nine spills to disk — survivable, but it's I/O on the database server for every execution. (The parameter was then set back to 100 MB.) Two better fixes:

  • Add a limit: sort(...).limit(10) turns the blocking sort into a top-k sort that keeps only 10 documents in memory. Its explain showed limitAmount 10 and totalDataSizeSorted 2280 bytes instead of 79 MB — though it still had to read all 349,643 candidates (435 ms).
  • Index the sort: {status: 1, city: 1, total: -1} removes the SORT stage and lets the scan stop after 10 keys.

docs.title: allPlansExecution: why the planner chose what it chose
docs.text:
o.find({ status: "cancelled", placedAt: { $gte: new Date("2026-03-01"), $lt: new Date("2026-06-01") } })
 .sort({ total: -1 }).limit(20).explain("allPlansExecution")

candidates: 3
   status_1_total_-1_placedAt_1 works=219 advanced=20 keys=219
   status_1_placedAt_1_total_-1 works=219 advanced=0 keys=219
   placedAt_1_status_1_total_-1 works=219 advanced=0 keys=219

The planner ran all three candidate plans for the same amount of work (219 units) and compared how many results each produced. The ESR index had already produced all 20; the other two were still scanning and hadn't returned anything (they need to finish scanning before their SORT can output). That trial is the subject of lesson 08.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A query plan is a tree of stages, and execution is pull-based: the root stage asks its child for the next result, which asks its child, down to the scans. Each request is a unit of work; a stage's response is either advanced (here's a result), needTime (I did work but have nothing yet — e.g. an index key that failed a filter), or EOF. That's what the works, advanced and needTime counters in executionStages record, per stage. A SORT stage returns needTime until its child is exhausted, then advances results from its buffer — which is why a blocking sort can't benefit from limit the way an index-ordered scan can.

keysExamined counts index entries the IXSCAN stepped over; seeks counts jumps to a new position in the index (more than one when bounds have several ranges, e.g. an $in list). docsExamined counts FETCH lookups through the collection's B-tree by RecordId. Because every one of those is a potential cache miss and disk read, the examined counts predict how a query will behave on a cold cache or a larger dataset far better than milliseconds measured on a warm laptop.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting that an index is used because it exists. Explain it.
  • Looking only at the winning stage name. An IXSCAN with [MinKey, MaxKey] bounds is a scan in disguise.
  • Comparing milliseconds from single runs instead of examined counts.
  • Forgetting _id: 0 in a projection meant to be covered.
  • Leaving blocking sorts on hot queries because they "fit in memory" on today's data.
  • Running executionStats on a very expensive query in production during peak load.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. For each query, predict the stages and the three numbers, then check with explain("executionStats"): {customerId: 777}; {customerId: 777} projected to be covered; {city: "Pune"}; {status: "paid"} sorted by total descending with limit(5).
  2. Find a query on idx.orders where totalKeysExamined is more than 100 × nReturned. Design an index that brings the ratio close to 1.
  3. Make the "delivered orders by city and total" query run with no SORT stage, and compare its explain with the blocking-sort version above.
  4. Run an $or query on customerId and city with indexes on each and find the OR stage in the plan. What happens to the plan if one branch has no index?

docs.title: 08 · The Query Planner, Plan Cache & Hints
docs.text:
When more than one index could answer a query, MongoDB has to pick. It doesn't use a detailed cost model built on statistics the way PostgreSQL does (see the PostgreSQL Mastery Path for contrast). Instead it runs a short race between the candidate plans and caches the winner for queries of the same shape. That design is simple and usually good — and it has one well-known failure mode. This lesson shows the race, the cache, and the tools for when you need to overrule the planner.

Examples use idx.orders (lesson 05), temporarily with extra single-field indexes on city and total.

docs.title: The race
docs.text:
The query: delivered orders in Pune over 490.

const q = s => ({ status: s, city: "Pune", total: { $gt: 490 } });
db.orders.find(q("delivered")).explain("allPlansExecution")

fresh delivered: status_1_total_-1_placedAt_1 keys 7079 docs 7079 n 906 candidates 4
    status_1_total_-1_placedAt_1 advanced 101 works 815 isEOF 0
    status_1_placedAt_1_total_-1 advanced 2 works 815 isEOF 0
    city_1 advanced 10 works 815 isEOF 0
    total_1 advanced 80 works 815 isEOF 0

Four indexes could serve part of the filter, so the planner built four candidate plans and ran them in round-robin, one unit of work each, until one of them produced 101 results (the default first-batch size) or finished. The {status, total, placedAt} plan got there first: it can apply status and total as index bounds and only has to check city after fetching. The city_1 plan, which bounds only on city, had produced just 10 results in the same number of works.

The winner isn't perfect — it examined 7,079 keys and documents to return 906 — because the ideal index doesn't exist. Given one designed by ESR:

status_1_city_1_total_1 906 906 906

The planner can only choose among the indexes you created. Good index design comes first; the planner then usually picks the right one.

docs.title: The plan cache
docs.text:
Racing costs time, so the winner is cached for the query's shape — the filter, sort and projection structure with the literal values stripped out. After one run:

db.orders.aggregate([{ $planCacheStats: {} }])

entries 1
{"shape":"782ACF54","key":"AD527657","isActive":false,"works":{"high":0,"low":495,...},"idx":"status_1_total_-1_placedAt_1"}

The first run creates an inactive entry recording how much work the winner needed (works: 495). Running the same shape again activates it:

{"isActive":true,"works":{"high":0,"low":495,...}}

From then on, queries of this shape skip the race and use the cached plan. The literal values don't matter — status: "delivered" and status: "cancelled" share the entry:

delivered uses cached? true status_1_total_-1_placedAt_1 keys 7079 n 906
true     ← both queries have the same planCacheShapeHash

docs.title: When the cache goes wrong
docs.text:
Sharing a plan across values is the failure mode. Imagine a shape where the best index depends on the value: for status: "cancelled" (5% of orders) a status-first index is excellent, but for a value covering 70% of the collection a different index would be far better. Whichever value runs first decides the plan, and every query of that shape uses it.

MongoDB defends against this: each time a cached plan runs, the server checks whether it needed much more work than recorded (more than 10 times the cached works by default). If so, it evicts the entry and races again — replanning. That catches the dramatic cases. It doesn't catch plans that are consistently a bit worse than they could be, and repeated replanning shows up as latency spikes and replanned: true in slow-query logs (Level 4 · 07).

The cache is also cleared when indexes are created or dropped on the collection, and on server restart. You can clear it by hand:

db.orders.getPlanCache().clear()

docs.title: hint()
docs.text:
hint() forces an index for one query:

db.orders.find(q("delivered")).hint({ city: 1 }).explain("executionStats")

hint city: keys 62491 docs 62491

Here the hint makes things much worse (62,491 documents examined vs 7,079) — a good reminder that the planner is usually right. Hinting an index that doesn't exist is an error:

2 error enumerating plans for query: ns=idx.ordersTree: $and
    city $eq "Pune"
 ...

Hints live in application code, so they have to be deployed and they break if an index is renamed or dropped. Use them sparingly, name the indexes they refer to explicitly, and document why.

docs.title: Persistent query settings
docs.text:
Since MongoDB 8.0 you can attach settings to a query shape on the server, without changing application code:

db.adminCommand({
  setQuerySettings: { find: "orders", filter: q("delivered"), $db: "idx" },
  settings: { indexHints: { ns: { db: "idx", coll: "orders" }, allowedIndexes: ["city_1"] } } })

setQuerySettings ok: 1
now uses: city_1 {"indexHints":[{"ns":{"db":"idx","coll":"orders"},"allowedIndexes":["city_1"]}]}

The setting was registered with the value "delivered", but the explain above was for status: "placed" — it still applied, because settings attach to the shape. They persist across restarts and are replicated, and $querySettings lists them:

db.getSiblingDB("admin").aggregate([{ $querySettings: {} }])
db.adminCommand({ removeQuerySettings: { find: "orders", filter: q("delivered"), $db: "idx" } })

After removal the planner went back to status_1_total_-1_placedAt_1. Query settings can also reject a shape entirely (reject: true) — a useful emergency brake for a runaway query from a buggy deployment. They replace the older, non-persistent index filters (planCacheSetFilter).

docs.title: Finding indexes nothing uses
docs.text:
Every index taxes writes (lesson 05). $indexStats reports how often each index has been used since the server started (or since the index was created):

db.orders.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }]).toArray().map(i => ({ name: i.name, ops: i.accesses.ops }))

[
  { name: 'total_1', ops: Long('0') },
  { name: 'city_1', ops: Long('0') },
  { name: 'status_1_placedAt_1_total_-1', ops: Long('3') },
  { name: '_id_', ops: Long('0') },
  { name: 'placedAt_1_status_1_total_-1', ops: Long('0') },
  { name: 'status_1_total_-1_placedAt_1', ops: Long('2') },
  { name: 'customerId_1_placedAt_-1', ops: Long('0') }
]

Counters are per server and reset on restart, so look at every member of a replica set (secondaries may serve reads the primary never sees), over a period that includes your monthly reports and batch jobs. Then hide (lesson 06) before dropping.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Planning happens in three steps. Canonicalisation normalises the query (sorting $and children, simplifying nested logic) and computes its shape hash. Enumeration asks, for each predicate, which indexes could provide bounds for it, and builds candidate plans — one per usable index, plus combinations for $or and, rarely, index intersection. The number of candidates is capped so a query with many indexed fields doesn't explode into hundreds of plans.

If there is exactly one candidate, it runs directly. Otherwise the multi-planner runs a trial: it calls each plan's root stage in turn (the works you saw), buffering any results produced, until one plan hits EOF, returns a full batch (101 documents) or the trial reaches its work limit (based on collection size). Each plan is scored mainly by productivity — results advanced per unit of work — with small bonuses for avoiding a fetch or an in-memory sort. The best plan continues from where it left off (its buffered results aren't wasted), and its works count is stored in the plan cache entry.

On later executions the cached plan runs as a CachedPlan stage with a budget proportional to the stored works. If it exhausts the budget without finishing its first batch, the server concludes that the data no longer fits the cached plan, evicts it and runs the multi-planner again. That's replanning — cheap insurance, but not an optimiser with statistics, which is why skewed data plus a shared shape is the classic case where you reach for query settings.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Hinting by habit. The planner is right far more often than intuition; measure first.
  • Hinting by index name in code and then renaming or dropping the index.
  • Ignoring data skew: one shape, values with wildly different selectivity, one cached plan.
  • Reading $indexStats on one member only and dropping an index a secondary depends on.
  • Assuming the plan you saw in development is the one production uses. Different data, different race result.
  • Too many overlapping indexes, which make every race longer and the outcome less predictable.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Clear the plan cache, run {status: "paid", city: "Delhi"} twice and inspect $planCacheStats. Then run the same shape with different values and confirm it reuses the entry.
  2. Create a skewed collection: 1,000,000 documents where type is "a" for 99% and "b" for 1%, with indexes on {type: 1} and {createdAt: 1}. Run find({type, createdAt: {$gte: ...}}) first with "b", then with "a". Use slow-query logging (db.setProfilingLevel(0, {slowms: 0}) and the log) to look for replanning.
  3. Use setQuerySettings to reject a query shape, run the query and record the error. Remove the setting.
  4. List all indexes on idx.orders that have had zero uses since you started your server, hide them, and rerun lesson 05's queries to see whether anything changed.

docs.title: 09 · Time Series & Capped Collections
docs.text: Two kinds of data don't fit the "one document per entity" model well. Measurements over time — sensor readings, metrics, prices, clicks — arrive in huge numbers, are almost never updated, and are queried by time range and source. Rolling logs — the last N events, a recent-activity feed — only matter while they're recent. MongoDB has a special collection type for each.

docs.title: Time series collections
docs.text:
Lesson 03 built the bucket pattern by hand: one document per sensor per hour, readings appended to an array. A time series collection does that for you inside the server, and adds columnar compression on top. You insert ordinary one-reading documents; the server groups them into buckets behind the scenes.

db.createCollection("weather", {
  timeseries: { timeField: "ts", metaField: "sensor", granularity: "minutes" }
});
  • timeField (required) — the BSON date of each measurement.
  • metaField — what identifies the source: a sensor id, a host, a stock symbol. Measurements are bucketed only with others that have an identical metaField value. It can be a sub-document, as here.
  • granularity — "seconds", "minutes" or "hours": roughly how often one source reports. It sets how much time one bucket spans. (You can instead set bucketMaxSpanSeconds and bucketRoundingSeconds explicitly.)

A week of minute readings from 10 sensors, with random-walk temperature and humidity so the data is realistically noisy, inserted into both a time series collection and an ordinary one:

for (let s = 0; s < 10; s++) { let temp = 20 + s, hum = 50;
  for (let m = 0; m < 24 * 60 * 7; m++) {
    temp += (Math.random() - 0.5) * 0.2; hum += (Math.random() - 0.5) * 0.5;
    docs.push({ ts: new Date(start + m * 60000 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 2000)),
                sensor: { id: "s" + s, site: s < 5 ? "north" : "south" },
                temp: Math.round(temp * 100) / 100, hum: Math.round(hum * 10) / 10 }); } }
db.weather.insertMany(docs, { ordered: false });
db.weather_plain.insertMany(docs, { ordered: false });
db.weather_plain.createIndex({ "sensor.id": 1, ts: 1 });
db.adminCommand({ fsync: 1 });   // flush to disk so storage sizes are real

ts:    storageMB 0.37 indexMB 0.025 buckets 110 closedDueToCount 100
plain: storageMB 2.60 indexMB 3.924

The same 100,800 readings take about 7× less disk and over 150× less index in the time series collection. They were stored in 110 buckets; 100 of them were closed because they reached the per-bucket measurement limit (1,000 by default), the rest are still open for new data. On real-world data the ratio depends heavily on how regular your values are — an earlier run of this experiment with perfectly periodic synthetic values compressed far more, which would have been a misleading number to publish.

docs.title: It still looks like documents
docs.text:
db.weather.find({}, { _id: 0 }).sort({ ts: 1 }).limit(1)

{"ts":"2026-10-01T00:00:00.286Z","sensor":{"id":"s9","site":"south"},"hum":50.1,"temp":28.93}

Queries and aggregations see individual measurements; the server unpacks buckets on the fly. Hourly averages for one sensor on one day:

db.weather.aggregate([
  { $match: { "sensor.id": "s3", ts: { $gte: new Date("2026-10-03"), $lt: new Date("2026-10-04") } } },
  { $group: { _id: { $dateTrunc: { date: "$ts", unit: "hour" } }, avg: { $avg: "$temp" }, max: { $max: "$temp" } } },
  { $sort: { _id: 1 } }])

{"_id":"2026-10-03T00:00:00.000Z","avg":20.541999999999998,"max":21.19}
{"_id":"2026-10-03T01:00:00.000Z","avg":20.445833333333333,"max":20.74}
...

(Printed as JSON, first two hours. The data is random, so your numbers will differ.)

The collection was created with an index on {sensor: 1, ts: 1} automatically, and the bucket store is clustered by bucket id, so the explain of the $match showed a CLUSTERED_IXSCAN stage feeding $_internalUnpackBucket — a range scan over buckets rather than over individual readings. Add secondary indexes on measurement fields if you filter on them (createIndex({ "sensor.site": 1, ts: -1 }) works as usual).

docs.title: Expiring old data
docs.text:
Time series collections take expireAfterSeconds directly, and remove whole buckets whose newest measurement is older than the limit:

db.createCollection("weather", { timeseries: { ... }, expireAfterSeconds: 60 * 60 * 24 * 365 * 2 })
// or later: db.runCommand({ collMod: "weather", expireAfterSeconds: ... })

Deleting whole buckets is far cheaper than deleting 100,000 individual documents a day.

docs.title: What doesn't fit
docs.text: Time series collections are optimised for append-mostly data. Updates and deletes of individual measurements are supported (with restrictions in older versions) but are much more expensive than in an ordinary collection, because the server must rewrite a compressed bucket. Choose the metaField carefully: it's the grouping key, every distinct value gets its own buckets, and putting something that varies per reading (like a request id) in it destroys the bucketing. And measurements that arrive badly out of order or far in the past may open extra buckets — check numBucketsClosedDueTo... counters in stats().timeseries if storage looks worse than expected.

docs.title: Capped collections
docs.text:
A capped collection has a fixed maximum size (in bytes, and optionally in documents) and keeps documents in insertion order. When it's full, the oldest documents are overwritten.

db.createCollection("recent_log", { capped: true, size: 1024 * 1024, max: 5 });
for (let i = 1; i <= 8; i++) db.recent_log.insertOne({ n: i, msg: "event " + i });
db.recent_log.find()                                   // natural (insertion) order
db.recent_log.find().sort({ $natural: -1 }).limit(3)   // newest first

4,5,6,7,8
8,7,6

Eight inserts, five kept, the oldest three gone with no delete calls. Sorting by $natural uses insertion order with no index at all.

On this server, deleteOne({n: 6}) succeeded and an update that grew a document by 100 bytes also succeeded. Older versions (before 5.0) rejected deletes and size-changing updates on capped collections, so you'll see advice saying so; check against your deployment's version.

docs.title: Tailable cursors
docs.text:
Capped collections support tailable cursors, which behave like tail -f: after returning the existing documents, the cursor stays open and returns new ones as they're inserted. A Python reader with a writer thread adding three events 0.3 s apart:

cur = db.recent_log.find({}, cursor_type=CursorType.TAILABLE_AWAIT).max_await_time_ms(500)
t0, live = time.time(), 0
while cur.alive and live < 3 and time.time() - t0 < 5:
    for doc in cur:
        print(f"{time.time()-t0:4.1f}s got {doc['n']:>3} {doc['msg']}")
        live += doc["n"] >= 100

 0.0s got   4 event 4
 0.0s got   5 event 5
 0.0s got   6 event 6
 0.0s got   7 event 7
 0.0s got   8 event 8
 0.3s got 100 live 100
 0.6s got 101 live 101
 0.9s got 102 live 102

Existing documents arrived immediately, then each new event about 0.3 s apart, as written. TAILABLE_AWAIT makes the server hold each getMore open for up to max_await_time_ms waiting for new data, instead of the client polling in a tight loop.

Capped collections and tailable cursors were MongoDB's original mechanism for building queues and replication (the oplog is a capped collection). For application-level "notify me when data changes" you'll usually want change streams instead (Level 3 · 07): they work on any collection, survive failovers and can resume after a disconnect. Capped collections remain handy for bounded logs and recent-activity buffers.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A time series collection is really two things: a view with the name you created (weather) and a hidden bucket collection (system.buckets.weather). Inserts go to an in-memory bucket catalog, which finds an open bucket for the measurement's metaField value and time range, or opens a new one. Buckets are closed when they reach the measurement count limit, a size limit, or when a measurement arrives outside their time span — the numBucketsClosedDueTo* statistics count each reason. Each bucket document stores control.min and control.max for every field, the meta value once, and the measurements in a columnar layout: all the ts values together, all the temp values together, compressed with delta and delta-of-delta encoding. Columns of similar, slowly changing numbers compress extremely well, which is where the 7× came from.

When you query, the planner rewrites predicates on timeField and metaField into predicates on the bucket's control.min/control.max and meta, so whole buckets can be skipped without decompressing them, and then unpacks only the surviving buckets (the $_internalUnpackBucket stage you'll see in aggregation explains). That's why queries by source and time range are cheap and queries on arbitrary measurement values without an index are not.

A capped collection is an ordinary collection with a size limit enforced on insert: when an insert would exceed it, the server deletes the oldest documents first. Its documents are stored in insertion order, which is what makes $natural order meaningful and lets a tailable cursor simply remember its position and continue from it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Per-reading values in the metaField, so every measurement gets its own bucket.
  • Wrong granularity — "seconds" for data that arrives hourly creates many tiny buckets.
  • Treating time series collections as general-purpose, with frequent updates and deletes of single measurements.
  • Publishing compression ratios measured on synthetic, perfectly regular data.
  • Using a capped collection as a durable queue. Unread messages are silently overwritten when it fills.
  • Polling a collection in a loop for new data instead of a tailable cursor or a change stream.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create a time series collection for stock ticks (symbol as metaField, granularity "seconds") and insert one day of ticks for 20 symbols with random-walk prices. Compare storage with an ordinary collection.
  2. Repeat with granularity: "hours" and compare bucketCount and query time for "one symbol, one hour".
  3. Write an aggregation that produces OHLC (open, high, low, close) candles per symbol per 5 minutes using $dateTrunc with binSize: 5, $first and $last after sorting by time.
  4. Build a "last 100 audit events" capped collection and a Python tail script that prints events as they're written from mongosh. What happens to the tail if you insert 200 events faster than it reads?

docs.title: 10 · Project — Model & Index a Store Catalog
docs.text: This project takes everything in Level 2 and applies it to one realistic problem: the product catalogue of an online store. You'll model it from its access patterns, enforce its shape with a validator, design one index per hot query, and — the part most teams skip — write a script that proves every query uses its index well, so a future change that breaks a query fails loudly instead of slowly.

docs.title: The access patterns
docs.text: # Operation Frequency Shape Q1 Category page: active products in a category, cheapest first, 24 per page very high equality, equality, sort Q2 Brand page: a brand's active products, best rated first high equality, equality, sort Q3 Spec filter: e.g. laptops with at least 32 GB RAM high equality + attribute range Q4 Product page by SKU very high unique equality Q5 Low-stock report: active products with fewer than 5 in stock a few times a day equality + range + sort on the range

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
{
  sku: "SKU-000123",
  name: "Zen Audio headphones 123",
  category: "headphones",
  brand: { _id: "zen", name: "Zen Audio" },          // extended reference (lesson 03)
  price: Decimal128("129.99"),                       // exact money (Level 1 · 03)
  status: "active",
  stock: 42,
  attrs: [ { k: "wireless", v: true }, { k: "anc", v: false } ],   // attribute pattern (lesson 03)
  rating: { count: 311, avg: 4.12 },                 // computed pattern (lesson 03)
  recentReviews: [ { stars: 5, at: ISODate("...") }, ... ]           // subset pattern, max 5 (lesson 03)
}

Each choice comes from Level 2:

  • Brand is an extended reference. Every product listing shows the brand name, brands are renamed almost never, and brand._id still links to a full brands document for the brand page header.
  • Specs use the attribute pattern. Four categories with different specs (and many more in a real store) share one attrs_kv index instead of one index per spec.
  • Ratings are pre-computed (count + average) and the latest reviews are a bounded subset; the full review history would live in its own reviews collection (lesson 01's referencing rules).
  • SKU has a unique index, and is what URLs use.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
catalog.py creates the collection with its validator and indexes, loads 100,000 products with a seeded random generator, and runs the query budget check. Run it with --no-indexes to see the "before" picture.

"""Level 2 project: model, validate, index and verify a store catalogue."""
import random
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from decimal import Decimal

from bson import Decimal128
from pymongo import ASCENDING, DESCENDING, MongoClient

client = MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0", tz_aware=True)
db = client.catalog

SCHEMA = {"$jsonSchema": {
    "bsonType": "object",
    "required": ["sku", "name", "category", "brand", "price", "status", "attrs"],
    "properties": {
        "sku": {"bsonType": "string", "pattern": "^[A-Z]{3}-[0-9]{6}$"},
        "name": {"bsonType": "string", "minLength": 2},
        "category": {"enum": ["laptop", "phone", "kettle", "headphones"]},
        "brand": {"bsonType": "object", "required": ["_id", "name"],
                  "properties": {"_id": {"bsonType": "string"}, "name": {"bsonType": "string"}}},
        "price": {"bsonType": "decimal", "minimum": 0},
        "status": {"enum": ["active", "discontinued"]},
        "stock": {"bsonType": "int", "minimum": 0},
        "attrs": {"bsonType": "array", "maxItems": 20,
                  "items": {"bsonType": "object", "required": ["k", "v"]}},
        "rating": {"bsonType": "object", "properties": {"count": {"bsonType": "int"}, "avg": {"bsonType": "double"}}},
        "recentReviews": {"bsonType": "array", "maxItems": 5},
    }}}

INDEXES = [
    # Q1 category page: active products in a category, cheapest first
    ([("status", ASCENDING), ("category", ASCENDING), ("price", ASCENDING)], "status_category_price"),
    # Q2 brand page: a brand's active products, best rated first
    ([("brand._id", ASCENDING), ("status", ASCENDING), ("rating.avg", DESCENDING)], "brand_status_rating"),
    # Q3 spec filter: attribute pattern, one index for every spec
    ([("attrs.k", ASCENDING), ("attrs.v", ASCENDING)], "attrs_kv"),
    # Q5 low-stock report: partial index only over the few active products with low stock
    ([("stock", ASCENDING)], "low_stock"),
]

BRANDS = [("acme", "Acme"), ("zen", "Zen Audio"), ("nova", "Nova"), ("kettleco", "KettleCo"), ("orbit", "Orbit")]
ATTRS = {
    "laptop": lambda r: [{"k": "ram_gb", "v": r.choice([8, 16, 32, 64])}, {"k": "screen_in", "v": r.choice([13, 14, 15, 16])},
                         {"k": "weight_kg", "v": round(r.uniform(0.9, 2.5), 2)}],
    "phone": lambda r: [{"k": "storage_gb", "v": r.choice([128, 256, 512])}, {"k": "screen_in", "v": r.choice([6.1, 6.5, 6.7])}],
    "kettle": lambda r: [{"k": "litres", "v": r.choice([1.0, 1.5, 1.7])}, {"k": "watts", "v": r.choice([1500, 2200, 3000])}],
    "headphones": lambda r: [{"k": "wireless", "v": r.random() < 0.7}, {"k": "anc", "v": r.random() < 0.4}],
}


def setup(with_indexes=True):
    client.drop_database("catalog")
    db.create_collection("products", validator=SCHEMA)
    db.products.create_index("sku", unique=True, name="sku_unique")
    if not with_indexes:
        return
    for keys, name in INDEXES[:3]:
        db.products.create_index(keys, name=name)
    db.products.create_index(*[INDEXES[3][0]], name=INDEXES[3][1],
                             partialFilterExpression={"status": "active", "stock": {"$lt": 5}})


def load(n=100_000, seed=11):
    r = random.Random(seed)
    batch = []
    base = datetime(2026, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    for i in range(n):
        cat = r.choice(list(ATTRS))
        bid, bname = r.choice(BRANDS)
        count = r.randint(0, 400)
        batch.append({
            "sku": f"SKU-{i:06d}", "name": f"{bname} {cat} {i}", "category": cat,
            "brand": {"_id": bid, "name": bname},
            "price": Decimal128(Decimal(r.randint(999, 249999)) / 100),
            "status": "active" if r.random() < 0.9 else "discontinued",
            "stock": r.randint(0, 200), "attrs": ATTRS[cat](r),
            "rating": {"count": count, "avg": round(r.uniform(2.5, 5.0), 2) if count else 0.0},
            "recentReviews": [{"stars": r.randint(1, 5), "at": base + timedelta(days=r.randint(0, 280))}
                              for _ in range(min(count, 5))],
        })
        if len(batch) == 5000:
            db.products.insert_many(batch, ordered=False)
            batch = []


QUERIES = {
    "Q1 category page": dict(filter={"status": "active", "category": "laptop"}, sort=[("price", 1)], limit=24),
    "Q2 brand page": dict(filter={"brand._id": "zen", "status": "active"}, sort=[("rating.avg", -1)], limit=24),
    "Q3 laptops 32GB+ RAM": dict(filter={"category": "laptop",
                                         "attrs": {"$elemMatch": {"k": "ram_gb", "v": {"$gte": 32}}}}, limit=24),
    "Q4 product page": dict(filter={"sku": "SKU-000123"}, limit=1),
    "Q5 low stock": dict(filter={"status": "active", "stock": {"$lt": 5}}, sort=[("stock", 1)], limit=50),
}


def stages(plan):
    out = []
    while plan:
        out.append(plan.get("stage"))
        plan = plan.get("inputStage")
    return out


def check():
    ok = True
    for label, q in QUERIES.items():
        cur = db.products.find(q["filter"]).limit(q["limit"])
        if "sort" in q:
            cur = cur.sort(q["sort"])
        ex = cur.explain()
        es = ex["executionStats"]
        st = stages(ex["queryPlanner"]["winningPlan"])
        idx = ex["queryPlanner"]["winningPlan"]
        while idx and "indexName" not in idx:
            idx = idx.get("inputStage")
        idx = idx["indexName"] if idx else "-"
        n, keys, docs = es["nReturned"], es["totalKeysExamined"], es["totalDocsExamined"]
        problems = []
        if "COLLSCAN" in st:
            problems.append("collection scan")
        if "SORT" in st:
            problems.append("blocking sort")
        if docs > max(4 * n, 10):
            problems.append(f"docs examined {docs} > 4x returned")
        ok &= not problems
        print(f"{label:21} {idx:22} {'<-'.join(st):28} n={n:3} keys={keys:6} docs={docs:6} {'OK' if not problems else 'FAIL: ' + ', '.join(problems)}")
    return ok


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys
    setup(with_indexes="--no-indexes" not in sys.argv)
    load()
    print("products:", db.products.estimated_document_count())
    print("all queries within budget:", check())

docs.title: The indexes, query by query
docs.text:
• Q1 {status: 1, category: 1, price: 1} — two equalities then the sort field: pure ESR (lesson 05). The scan starts at "active laptops", walks in price order and stops after 24.
  • Q2 {"brand._id": 1, status: 1, "rating.avg": -1} — same shape. The sort direction matches the query's descending sort.
  • Q3 {"attrs.k": 1, "attrs.v": 1} — the attribute index, used with $elemMatch so k and v bound the scan together (lesson 03).
  • Q4 the unique sku index.
  • Q5 a partial index on stock covering only active products with stock under 5 (lesson 06). The report runs a few times a day; a full index on stock would be maintained on every one of the thousands of stock changes per hour for no benefit. Its query includes status: "active" and stock: {$lt: 5}, so the planner can prove the partial index holds every possible result.

docs.title: Before: no secondary indexes
docs.text:
$ python catalog.py --no-indexes
products: 100000
Q1 category page      -                      SORT<-COLLSCAN               n= 24 keys=     0 docs=100000 FAIL: collection scan, blocking sort, docs examined 100000 > 4x returned
Q2 brand page         -                      SORT<-COLLSCAN               n= 24 keys=     0 docs=100000 FAIL: collection scan, blocking sort, docs examined 100000 > 4x returned
Q3 laptops 32GB+ RAM  -                      LIMIT<-COLLSCAN              n= 24 keys=     0 docs=   165 FAIL: collection scan, docs examined 165 > 4x returned
Q4 product page       sku_unique             EXPRESS_IXSCAN               n=  1 keys=     1 docs=     1 OK
Q5 low stock          -                      SORT<-COLLSCAN               n= 50 keys=     0 docs=100000 FAIL: collection scan, blocking sort, docs examined 100000 > 4x returned
all queries within budget: False

Three of the queries read the entire collection and sorted it in memory to return 24 or 50 documents. Q3 got lucky: laptops with 32 GB or more are common, so the scan found 24 within 165 documents and stopped — on a rarer spec it would have scanned much further. That is exactly the kind of query that looks fine in testing and degrades in production, which is why the budget check fails it anyway.

docs.title: After: the designed indexes
docs.text:
$ python catalog.py
products: 100000
Q1 category page      status_category_price  LIMIT<-FETCH<-IXSCAN         n= 24 keys=    24 docs=    24 OK
Q2 brand page         brand_status_rating    LIMIT<-FETCH<-IXSCAN         n= 24 keys=    24 docs=    24 OK
Q3 laptops 32GB+ RAM  attrs_kv               LIMIT<-FETCH<-IXSCAN         n= 24 keys=    24 docs=    24 OK
Q4 product page       sku_unique             EXPRESS_IXSCAN               n=  1 keys=     1 docs=     1 OK
Q5 low stock          low_stock              LIMIT<-FETCH<-IXSCAN         n= 50 keys=    50 docs=    50 OK
all queries within budget: True

Every query examines exactly as many keys and documents as it returns, with no blocking sort. That's the best possible result short of covered queries.

What it costs:

{'_id_': 1.69, 'sku_unique': 3.58, 'status_category_price': 2.2, 'brand_status_rating': 1.84, 'attrs_kv': 4.58, 'low_stock': 0.07} MB; data 48.4 MB

Under 14 MB of indexes for 48 MB of data. The partial low_stock index is 70 KB — a full index on stock would have been about the size of the others. attrs_kv is the largest because it is multikey: two or three entries per product.

docs.title: The validator at work
docs.text:
db.products.insert_one({"sku": "SKU-1", "name": "Bad", "category": "toaster",
                        "brand": {"_id": "acme", "name": "Acme"}, "price": 9.99,
                        "status": "active", "attrs": []})

sku -> regular expression did not match
category -> value was not found in enum
price -> type did not match

Three mistakes, three precise messages: a malformed SKU, an unknown category, and a price sent as a double instead of Decimal128 — the bug that would otherwise have silently produced 0.30000000000000004-style totals months later.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The budget check works because explain("executionStats") reports what the server did, not what it might do: the winning plan's stages and the exact number of index keys and documents it touched. Checking those numbers against simple rules — no COLLSCAN, no SORT, documents examined close to documents returned — captures the properties that decide how a query scales. A query that examines 24 documents to return 24 will still examine about 24 when the collection has 100 million products; one that examines 100,000 will examine 100 million.

That makes the check suitable for continuous integration: run it against a seeded dataset whenever the schema, indexes or query code change. It catches the three regressions that most often reach production — a query that gains a filter on an unindexed field, an index dropped as "unused", and a sort added without updating the index. The thresholds should be per query (a report can tolerate more than a product page), and the dataset must resemble production's distributions, or the planner may legitimately choose differently.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Designing indexes without listing the queries first.
  • Testing query performance on tiny collections, where every plan is fast.
  • One index per field instead of one compound index per query shape.
  • Full indexes for rare, narrow reports where a partial index would do.
  • No automated check, so the next feature quietly reintroduces a collection scan.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Extend the catalogue:

  1. Add Q6 "search by name prefix within a category" (e.g. names starting with "Acme lap"). Design the index, add the query to QUERIES, and make the budget check pass.
  2. Add a brands collection and a brand page that shows the brand document plus Q2's products. Implement a brand rename that updates the extended references in products with one update_many.
  3. Add a reviews collection and an add_review(sku, stars, text) function that inserts the review and updates rating and recentReviews on the product (computed + subset patterns). What can go wrong between the two writes? Keep your answer for Level 3 · 06.
  4. Make the budget check run each query against every category or brand value and report the worst case, not just one value.
  5. Add "additionalProperties": false to the schema. What else must change for inserts to keep working?

docs.title: Level 3 · Aggregation & Application Features
docs.text:
With a good schema and the right indexes (Level 2), Level 3 turns to what applications do with their data. Most of it is the aggregation pipeline: reports, dashboards, analytics, joins and precomputed rollups. The rest is the set of features that make MongoDB an application platform rather than just a store — multi-document transactions, change streams that push every change to your code, location queries and text search.

The lessons share one seeded dataset — an online shop with 2,000 customers, 200 products and 30,000 orders — so results build on each other. You'll see a $lookup go from examining 300,025 documents to 2,967 by adding one index, a rollup that matched raw data only after its time zones were aligned, eight threads of bank transfers that needed 492 retries and still balanced to the paisa, a change-stream consumer resume after a "crash" without losing an event, and a "local" store placed 7,005 km away by swapping latitude and longitude.

Prerequisites: Levels 1 and 2, the lab replica set (transactions and change streams need one), and Python with PyMongo for lessons 06, 07 and 10.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Aggregation Pipeline Fundamentals — $match, $group, accumulators, $unwind, $sort, $limit, and why stage order matters.
  2. Reshaping Documents with Expressions — $map, $filter, $reduce, conditions, time zones, $replaceWith and safe type conversion.
  3. Joins & Unions: $lookup, $graphLookup, $unionWith — join forms and strategies, the foreign-field index, hierarchies and archives.
  4. Analytics: $facet, $bucket & Window Functions — multi-facet results, histograms, running totals, moving averages, ranks and gap filling.
  5. Pipeline Performance, $out & $merge — what the optimizer does, what blocks it, and incremental rollups.
  6. Multi-Document Transactions — the callback API, isolation, write conflicts and retries, limits and real costs.
  7. Change Streams — event shapes, pre-images, resume tokens, the oplog window and invalidation.
  8. Geospatial Queries — GeoJSON, 2dsphere, $near, $geoNear, zones and the longitude-first trap.
  9. Text Search & Collation — text indexes and their limits; case- and accent-insensitive comparison and sorting.
  10. Project — Order Analytics Backend — a tested dashboard backend with a rollup kept exact by a change-stream worker.

docs.title: After Level 3
docs.text: You can build substantial applications on MongoDB. Level 4 is about running them: replica sets and failover, write and read concerns, sharding, security, backups, monitoring, tuning and upgrades — ending with a secured, sharded cluster built and tested from scratch.

docs.title: 01 · Aggregation Pipeline Fundamentals
docs.text: find() returns documents as they're stored. Everything else — totals, averages, counts per group, reshaped documents, joins, reports — is the job of the aggregation pipeline. A pipeline is a list of stages; documents flow through them in order, each stage transforming the stream it receives. If you know SQL, $match is WHERE, $group is GROUP BY, $sort is ORDER BY, and $project is the SELECT list — but the pipeline lets you chain them in any order, as many times as you like.

docs.title: The Level 3 dataset
docs.text:
Level 3 uses a seeded online-shop database: 2,000 customers, 200 products and 30,000 orders placed between July 2025 and June 2026. Each order embeds its line items with the price paid. The generator, shopgen.py:

"""Seeded sample data for Level 3: customers, products and orders with line items."""
import random
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from decimal import Decimal
from bson import Decimal128
from pymongo import MongoClient

r = random.Random(2026)
client = MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0")
client.drop_database("shop")
db = client.shop

cities = ["Pune", "Mumbai", "Delhi", "Chennai", "Hyderabad", "Bengaluru"]
customers = [{"_id": f"C{i:04d}", "name": f"Customer {i}", "city": r.choice(cities),
              "joined": datetime(2024, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc) + timedelta(days=r.randint(0, 600))}
             for i in range(1, 2001)]
db.customers.insert_many(customers)
