cats = {"books": (199, 1499), "electronics": (999, 59999), "kitchen": (299, 4999), "toys": (149, 2999)}
products = []
for i in range(1, 201):
    cat = r.choice(list(cats))
    lo, hi = cats[cat]
    products.append({"_id": f"P{i:03d}", "name": f"{cat.title()} item {i}", "category": cat,
                     "price": Decimal128(Decimal(r.randint(lo, hi)))})
db.products.insert_many(products)

orders = []
start = datetime(2025, 7, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
for i in range(1, 30001):
    c = r.choice(customers)
    items = []
    for p in r.sample(products, r.choice([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4])):
        items.append({"sku": p["_id"], "category": p["category"], "qty": r.choice([1, 1, 1, 2, 3]), "price": p["price"]})
    orders.append({"_id": i, "customerId": c["_id"], "city": c["city"],
                   "status": r.choices(["delivered", "shipped", "cancelled", "returned"], [80, 10, 7, 3])[0],
                   "placedAt": start + timedelta(minutes=r.randint(0, 60 * 24 * 365)), "items": items})
db.orders.insert_many(orders)
db.orders.create_index([("customerId", 1), ("placedAt", -1)])
db.orders.create_index([("placedAt", 1)])

{'customers': 2000, 'products': 200, 'orders': 30000}

An order looks like this:

{
  _id: 1, customerId: 'C0110', city: 'Hyderabad', status: 'shipped',
  placedAt: ISODate('2026-02-21T11:48:00.000Z'),
  items: [
    { sku: 'P169', category: 'toys', qty: 1, price: Decimal128('254') },
    { sku: 'P055', category: 'kitchen', qty: 1, price: Decimal128('1183') }
  ]
}

Prices are whole rupees stored as Decimal128. Outputs below are printed with JSON.stringify, which shows decimals as {"$numberDecimal": "..."}.

docs.title: $group: one output document per group
docs.text:
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $group: { _id: "$status", orders: { $sum: 1 } } },
  { $sort: { orders: -1 } }
])

{"_id":"delivered","orders":24080}
{"_id":"shipped","orders":2931}
{"_id":"cancelled","orders":2081}
{"_id":"returned","orders":908}

_id is the group key — here the value of status (the $ prefix means "the field", not the literal string). Every other field is an accumulator: $sum: 1 adds one per document. The common accumulators:

Accumulator Result $sum, $avg, $min, $max arithmetic over the group $count number of documents ({ $count: {} }) $first, $last first/last value in the order documents arrive — sort first! $push, $addToSet array of all values / distinct values $top, $bottom, $topN, $bottomN best N by an explicit sortBy, no prior $sort needed $stdDevPop, $median, $percentile statistics

Grouping and counting by one field is so common it has a shortcut, $sortByCount:

db.orders.aggregate([{ $sortByCount: "$city" }])

{"_id":"Pune","count":5242}
{"_id":"Delhi","count":5183}
...

_id: null groups the whole collection into one document:

db.orders.aggregate([{ $group: { _id: null, orders: { $sum: 1 },
  first: { $min: "$placedAt" }, last: { $max: "$placedAt" } } }])

{"_id":null,"orders":30000,"first":"2025-07-01T00:04:00.000Z","last":"2026-06-30T23:43:00.000Z"}

docs.title: $unwind: one document per array element
docs.text:
Revenue lives in the line items, which are an array. $unwind turns one order with three items into three documents, each carrying one item (and all the order's other fields):

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "delivered" } },
  { $unwind: "$items" },
  { $group: { _id: "$city",
              revenue: { $sum: { $multiply: ["$items.qty", "$items.price"] } },
              lines: { $sum: 1 } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } },
  { $limit: 3 }
])

{"_id":"Chennai","revenue":{"$numberDecimal":"135647659"},"lines":8350}
{"_id":"Pune","revenue":{"$numberDecimal":"133519311"},"lines":8198}
{"_id":"Delhi","revenue":{"$numberDecimal":"129433588"},"lines":8330}

Read it top to bottom: keep delivered orders, split into line items, sum quantity × price per city, sort, keep three. Note that lines counts line items, not orders — after $unwind every count is per element. Mixing up the two is the most common aggregation bug. When you need both, count distinct order ids:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "delivered", placedAt: { $gte: new Date("2026-01-01"), $lt: new Date("2026-04-01") } } },
  { $unwind: "$items" },
  { $group: { _id: { $dateTrunc: { date: "$placedAt", unit: "month" } },
              revenue: { $sum: { $multiply: ["$items.qty", "$items.price"] } },
              orders: { $addToSet: "$_id" } } },
  { $project: { _id: 0, month: { $dateToString: { date: "$_id", format: "%Y-%m" } },
                revenue: 1, orders: { $size: "$orders" } } },
  { $sort: { month: 1 } }
])

{"revenue":{"$numberDecimal":"66107008"},"month":"2026-01","orders":2018}
{"revenue":{"$numberDecimal":"55116092"},"month":"2026-02","orders":1832}
{"revenue":{"$numberDecimal":"67508922"},"month":"2026-03","orders":2065}

$dateTrunc rounds each date down to the start of its month (in UTC unless you pass a timezone), giving a group key per month; $project renames and formats the output. The $addToSet of order ids works here because a month has a couple of thousand orders; for very large groups it would build a huge array — lesson 02 shows the leaner way (computing each order's total before unwinding anything).

docs.title: Best-per-group with $top
docs.text:
"The latest order in each city" — without $top you'd $sort by date and take $first. With it:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $group: { _id: "$city", latest: { $top: { sortBy: { placedAt: -1 }, output: { id: "$_id", at: "$placedAt" } } } } },
  { $sort: { _id: 1 } }, { $limit: 2 }
])

{"_id":"Bengaluru","latest":{"id":8581,"at":"2026-06-30T22:08:00.000Z"}}
{"_id":"Chennai","latest":{"id":9799,"at":"2026-06-30T19:23:00.000Z"}}

docs.title: Stage order matters
docs.text:
Stages run in the order you write them. Each one sees only what the previous stage produced:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $group: { _id: "$city", n: { $sum: 1 } } },
  { $match: { status: "delivered" } }
])

This returns nothing. After $group, the documents are {_id: "Pune", n: 5242} — there is no status field left to match. Filter before you group. As a rule, put $match (and $limit, when it's safe) as early as possible: it reduces the work of every later stage, and a $match at the start of a pipeline can use indexes exactly like find() (lesson 05).

Ties also need care: "top customers by order count" sorts on a count, and many customers share a count. Add a unique tie-breaker so results are deterministic:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "delivered" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", orders: { $sum: 1 }, last: { $max: "$placedAt" } } },
  { $sort: { orders: -1, _id: 1 } }, { $limit: 3 }
])

{"_id":"C0227","orders":25,"last":"2026-06-25T18:31:00.000Z"}
{"_id":"C1544","orders":25,"last":"2026-06-18T21:47:00.000Z"}
{"_id":"C0117","orders":24,"last":"2026-06-21T08:24:00.000Z"}

$count is a stage that outputs a single document with the number of documents it received:

db.orders.aggregate([{ $match: { status: "returned" } }, { $count: "returned" }])   // {"returned":908}

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When aggregate arrives, the server parses the stages and runs an optimisation pass over them before executing. It moves $match stages earlier when that can't change the result, merges adjacent $matches, coalesces $sort + $limit into a top-k sort, and pushes as much of the beginning of the pipeline as possible into the query layer — the same planner that serves find(). A leading $match (and $sort, and sometimes $project/$group) therefore becomes an ordinary indexed query whose results stream into the rest of the pipeline.

Execution is a chain of pull-based stages, like the plan stages in Level 2 · 07. Streaming stages ($match, $unwind, $project, $set) handle one document at a time with little memory. Blocking stages ($group, $sort, $bucket) must see all of their input before emitting anything; $group keeps one accumulator state per group in a hash table, so its memory grows with the number of distinct groups, not the number of documents — grouping 30,000 orders by six cities needs six entries. Blocking stages that exceed their memory limit (100 MB per stage by default) spill to disk, which allowDiskUseByDefault permits since 6.0.

Results come back through a cursor, in batches, exactly like find(); the 16 MB limit applies to each output document, not to the whole result set.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Counting after $unwind and calling the result "orders".
  • $match after $group on fields that no longer exist.
  • Using $first/$last without sorting first — the order is undefined. Prefer $top/$bottom.
  • Sorting on non-unique values without a tie-breaker, making pagination and tests flaky.
  • $push-ing every document of a large group into one array and hitting the 16 MB output limit.
  • Forgetting the $ prefix — { _id: "status" } groups everything under the literal string "status".

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Using the shop database:

  1. Count orders per status per city (a compound _id: {city: "$city", status: "$status"}), sorted by city then count.
  2. Find the 5 best-selling SKUs by quantity among delivered orders in 2026.
  3. Compute average order value (sum of line totals per order, then average across orders) for each city. You will need two $group stages — the first per order, the second per city.
  4. For each customer, find the date of their first and last order and the number of distinct cities they ordered to (should be 1 with this data — why?).
  5. Write the same "orders per status" report with $group + $sort and with $sortByCount, and compare their explain() output.

docs.title: 02 · Reshaping Documents with Expressions
docs.text:
Lesson 01 used stages. This lesson is about expressions — the small functional language you write inside stages to compute values: totals from arrays, labels from numbers, local dates from UTC, clean decimals from messy strings. The same expressions work in $project, $set, $group accumulators, $match with $expr, pipeline updates (Level 1 · 06) and validators (Level 2 · 04), so learning them once pays off everywhere.

Examples use the shop database from lesson 01.

docs.title: Syntax in one paragraph
docs.text: An expression is either a field path ("$city", "$items.qty"), a variable ("$$i", "$$NOW", "$$ROOT"), a literal, or an operator document { $operator: [args] }. Operators nest freely: { $multiply: ["$items.qty", "$items.price"] }. Inside array operators you name a variable with as and refer to it with two dollar signs. To use a literal string that starts with $, wrap it: { $literal: "$5 off" }.

docs.title: $set, $unset and $project
docs.text:
• $set (alias $addFields) adds or replaces fields and keeps everything else.
  • $unset removes fields: { $unset: ["items", "city"] }.
  • $project builds the output explicitly: include (field: 1), exclude (field: 0), or compute (field: <expression>).
db.orders.aggregate([{ $match: { _id: 1 } }, { $unset: ["items", "city"] }])

{"_id":1,"customerId":"C0110","status":"shipped","placedAt":"2026-02-21T11:48:00.000Z"}

Use $set when you're adding to documents, $project when you're defining a final output shape.

docs.title: Working on arrays without $unwind
docs.text:
Lesson 01 unwound items to sum them. Often you don't need to: array expressions compute per document, which keeps the number of documents (and the meaning of every count) unchanged.

$map transforms every element:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { _id: { $in: [1, 2] } } },
  { $set: { lineTotals: { $map: { input: "$items", as: "i", in: { $multiply: ["$$i.qty", "$$i.price"] } } } } },
  { $set: { total: { $sum: "$lineTotals" },
            itemCount: { $reduce: { input: "$items", initialValue: 0, in: { $add: ["$$value", "$$this.qty"] } } } } },
  { $project: { _id: 1, lineTotals: 1, total: 1, itemCount: 1 } }
])

{"_id":1,"lineTotals":[{"$numberDecimal":"254"},{"$numberDecimal":"1183"}],"total":{"$numberDecimal":"1437"},"itemCount":2}
{"_id":2,"lineTotals":[{"$numberDecimal":"2549"}],"total":{"$numberDecimal":"2549"},"itemCount":1}

$sum applied to an array (outside $group) adds its elements. $reduce folds an array into one value, with $$value as the accumulator and $$this as the current element — here the total quantity.

$filter keeps matching elements. Orders (among the first eight) containing electronics, with just those SKUs:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { _id: { $in: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] } } },
  { $project: { elec: { $filter: { input: "$items", as: "i", cond: { $eq: ["$$i.category", "electronics"] } } } } },
  { $match: { "elec.0": { $exists: true } } },
  { $project: { skus: "$elec.sku" } }
])

{"_id":6,"skus":["P080"]}
{"_id":8,"skus":["P123"]}

This is how you get all matching elements of an array — Level 1 · 05's positional projection only returned the first. Note the path "$elec.sku" on an array of documents yields an array of the sku values.

Other array operators you'll use: $size, $arrayElemAt (negative indexes count from the end), $first and $last (as expressions), $slice, $concatArrays, $in, $indexOfArray, $sortArray, $zip, and the set operators $setUnion, $setIntersection, $setDifference.

db.orders.aggregate([{ $match: { _id: 1 } }, { $project: {
  first: { $arrayElemAt: ["$items.sku", 0] }, last: { $last: "$items.sku" }, n: { $size: "$items" },
  label: { $let: { vars: { n: { $size: "$items" } },
                   in: { $concat: [{ $toString: "$$n" }, " item(s) for ", "$city"] } } } } }])

{"_id":1,"first":"P169","last":"P055","n":2,"label":"2 item(s) for Hyderabad"}

$let names an intermediate value so you don't repeat a sub-expression.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
$cond is if-then-else; $switch is a chain of cases; $ifNull supplies a default for null or missing. Banding orders by total:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $set: { total: { $sum: { $map: { input: "$items", as: "i", in: { $multiply: ["$$i.qty", "$$i.price"] } } } } } },
  { $set: { band: { $switch: {
      branches: [ { case: { $lt: ["$total", 1000] }, then: "small" },
                  { case: { $lt: ["$total", 10000] }, then: "medium" } ],
      default: "large" } } } },
  { $sortByCount: "$band" }
])

{"_id":"large","count":13737}
{"_id":"medium","count":13664}
{"_id":"small","count":2599}

Branches are evaluated in order and the first true one wins, so ranges can be written as simple upper bounds. Always give $switch a default; without one, a document matching no case is an error.

docs.title: Dates and time zones
docs.text:
BSON dates are UTC. Convert at the edges — for display and for grouping by local day:

db.orders.aggregate([{ $match: { _id: { $in: [1, 3] } } }, { $project: {
  cancelled: { $cond: [{ $eq: ["$status", "cancelled"] }, true, false] },
  coupon: { $ifNull: ["$coupon", "none"] },
  dow: { $dayOfWeek: "$placedAt" },
  local: { $dateToString: { date: "$placedAt", format: "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M", timezone: "Asia/Kolkata" } },
  utc: { $dateToString: { date: "$placedAt", format: "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M" } } } }])

{"_id":1,"cancelled":false,"coupon":"none","dow":7,"local":"2026-02-21 17:18","utc":"2026-02-21 11:48"}
{"_id":3,"cancelled":false,"coupon":"none","dow":5,"local":"2026-01-15 05:56","utc":"2026-01-15 00:26"}

$dayOfWeek returns 1 for Sunday through 7 for Saturday (21 February 2026 is a Saturday). Order 3 was placed at 00:26 UTC — already 05:56 in India. A "daily sales" report grouped by UTC day would put orders placed between midnight and 05:30 IST on the previous day. Pass timezone to $dateTrunc, $dateToString, $dayOfWeek and friends whenever the business day isn't UTC. $dateAdd, $dateDiff and $dateSubtract handle calendar arithmetic (month lengths, leap years) correctly; adding milliseconds by hand does not.

docs.title: Reshaping whole documents
docs.text:
$replaceWith (alias of $replaceRoot: {newRoot: ...}) makes an expression the whole document. Combined with $mergeObjects, it's the cleanest way to flatten a line item with fields from its order:

db.orders.aggregate([{ $match: { _id: 1 } }, { $unwind: "$items" },
  { $replaceWith: { $mergeObjects: [{ orderId: "$_id", city: "$city" }, "$items"] } }])

{"orderId":1,"city":"Hyderabad","sku":"P169","category":"toys","qty":1,"price":{"$numberDecimal":"254"}}
{"orderId":1,"city":"Hyderabad","sku":"P055","category":"kitchen","qty":1,"price":{"$numberDecimal":"1183"}}

That flat shape is what you'd export to CSV (Level 1 · 09) or load into a BI tool.

docs.title: Converting types safely
docs.text:
Imported data is often dirty. $convert converts with fallbacks; the $toX shortcuts don't have them:

db.raw.insertMany([{ v: "12.50" }, { v: "abc" }, { v: null }, { v: 7 }]);
db.raw.aggregate([{ $project: { _id: 0, v: 1,
  asDec: { $convert: { input: "$v", to: "decimal", onError: "BAD", onNull: "MISSING" } } } }])

{"v":"12.50","asDec":{"$numberDecimal":"12.50"}}
{"v":"abc","asDec":"BAD"}
{"v":null,"asDec":"MISSING"}
{"v":7,"asDec":{"$numberDecimal":"7"}}

db.raw.aggregate([{ $project: { x: { $toDecimal: "$v" } } }])

241 Executor error during aggregate command on namespace: shop.raw :: caused by :: Failed to parse number 'abc' in $convert ...

One bad value fails the whole pipeline. In cleanup pipelines, use $convert with onError, then $match the failures into a separate report.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Expressions are parsed once, when the pipeline is built, into a tree of expression objects; for each document, the stage evaluates the tree against that document's fields and the current variable scope. $$ROOT is the whole input document, $$CURRENT the document being processed (usually the same), and $$NOW/$$CLUSTER_TIME are fixed for the whole operation, so every document sees the same "now". Array operators like $map and $filter create a new scope per element with the variable you named, which is why $$i is visible only inside the in/cond expression.

Expressions run inside the server on BSON values, so they preserve types: $multiply of an int and a Decimal128 yields Decimal128 (as in the line totals above), integer overflow promotes to long or double, and comparisons follow the BSON type order from Level 1 · 03. The optimiser also performs constant folding — an expression with no field references is computed once — and can push $set/$project work past $match stages when that's safe.

Per-document expressions are cheap compared to moving documents between stages. Computing an order total with $map/$sum keeps one document per order; $unwind + $group creates one document per line item and then rebuilds groups in a hash table. Reach for $unwind when you need to group by something inside the array (revenue per SKU), not when you only need to aggregate within each document.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• $unwind + $group to compute per-document totals that $map/$sum would compute in place.
  • One $ instead of two inside $map/$filter ("$i.qty" is a field path, "$$i.qty" the variable).
  • Grouping by UTC day when the business operates in another time zone.
  • $switch without a default.
  • $toDecimal/$toInt on dirty data without $convert's onError.
  • Expecting $project to keep fields you didn't list — that's $set's job.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Using the shop database:

  1. Add total and itemCount to every order with one $set using $map, $sum and $reduce, then find the 10 orders with the highest itemCount.
  2. For each order, compute electronicsShare: the fraction of the order total spent on electronics, rounded to two decimals ($round). Return orders where it is between 0.4 and 0.6.
  3. Produce "orders per local (IST) hour of day" for delivered orders, and compare the shape with the same report in UTC.
  4. Flatten orders to one row per line item with orderId, customerId, local date string, sku, qty and lineTotal, and export the first 1,000 rows to CSV with $out + mongoexport (lesson 05 covers $out).
  5. Write a pipeline that classifies each customer as new (first order in the last 90 days of the data), active or lapsed (no order in the last 120 days of the data), using $switch and $dateDiff.

docs.title: 03 · Joins & Unions: $lookup, $graphLookup, $unionWith
docs.text:
Good MongoDB schemas need fewer joins than relational ones (Level 2 · 01), but "fewer" isn't "none": reports combine orders with customers, admin screens show a product with its sales, an org chart needs a manager chain. The pipeline has three stages for combining data: $lookup joins, $graphLookup follows recursive references, and $unionWith concatenates collections. This lesson shows each one and measures the one thing that decides whether a join is fast or a disaster.

Examples use the shop database from lesson 01.

docs.title: $lookup by equality
docs.text:
An order with its customer:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { _id: 1 } },
  { $lookup: { from: "customers", localField: "customerId", foreignField: "_id", as: "customer" } },
  { $set: { customer: { $first: "$customer" } } },
  { $project: { customerId: 1, "customer.name": 1, "customer.joined": 1 } }
])

{"_id":1,"customerId":"C0110","customer":{"name":"Customer 110","joined":"2025-02-12T00:00:00.000Z"}}

$lookup always produces an array (as), because in general several foreign documents can match. For a to-one relationship, unwrap it with $first (or $unwind, which also drops orders with no customer unless you pass preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true). An unmatched lookup gives an empty array, not an error — it's a left outer join.

When localField is an array, $lookup matches any element, and when foreignField is an array field in the foreign documents, it matches if the array contains the value — the usual array semantics from Level 1 · 05.

docs.title: $lookup with a pipeline
docs.text:
The equality form returns every matching document in full. To filter, sort, limit or reshape the joined documents, give $lookup a pipeline. A customer's two most recent delivered orders:

db.customers.aggregate([
  { $match: { _id: { $in: ["C0001", "C0002"] } } },
  { $lookup: { from: "orders", let: { cid: "$_id" }, pipeline: [
      { $match: { $expr: { $eq: ["$customerId", "$$cid"] }, status: "delivered" } },
      { $sort: { placedAt: -1 } }, { $limit: 2 }, { $project: { _id: 1, placedAt: 1 } } ],
    as: "recent" } },
  { $project: { name: 1, recent: 1 } }
])

{"_id":"C0001","name":"Customer 1","recent":[{"_id":9130,"placedAt":"2026-06-14T09:59:00.000Z"},{"_id":19071,"placedAt":"2026-04-30T03:48:00.000Z"}]}
{"_id":"C0002","name":"Customer 2","recent":[{"_id":22622,"placedAt":"2026-06-28T10:44:00.000Z"},{"_id":8738,"placedAt":"2026-05-22T18:15:00.000Z"}]}

let binds fields of the outer document to variables ($$cid), and the inner $match must use $expr to compare a field with a variable. Since MongoDB 5.0 you can combine both forms — localField/foreignField for the join condition plus a pipeline for the rest — which is shorter and lets the server use the equality for an index lookup directly:

db.customers.aggregate([
  { $match: { _id: "C0001" } },
  { $lookup: { from: "orders", localField: "_id", foreignField: "customerId", pipeline: [{ $count: "n" }], as: "stats" } }
])

{"_id":"C0001","name":"Customer 1","city":"Pune","joined":"2024-11-23T00:00:00.000Z","stats":[{"n":12}]}

docs.title: The index on the foreign field is everything
docs.text:
For each input document, $lookup has to find the matching foreign documents. Join 10 products to the orders that contain them (foreignField: "items.sku"), first with no index on items.sku:

const pipe = [{ $match: { category: "books" } }, { $limit: 10 },
  { $lookup: { from: "orders", localField: "_id", foreignField: "items.sku", as: "o" } }];
db.products.explain("executionStats").aggregate(pipe)

2 EQ_LOOKUP(NestedLoopJoin)
ms 85 docsExamined 300025 keysExamined 0

Then after db.orders.createIndex({"items.sku": 1}):

2 EQ_LOOKUP(IndexedLoopJoin)
ms 6 docsExamined 2967 keysExamined 2942

Without the index, the join strategy was a nested loop: for each of the 10 products, scan all 30,000 orders — 300,000 documents examined (plus the 25 products read). With the index, an indexed loop join looks up each SKU in the index and fetches only the orders that contain it. The same join, two orders of magnitude apart, and the gap grows linearly with the foreign collection: with 3 million orders the unindexed version examines 30 million documents for 10 products.

(The 2 is explainVersion 2: the server ran this $lookup in its slot-based execution engine, where it appears as an EQ_LOOKUP stage with a strategy. Lookups that can't be pushed down appear as a $lookup stage in a stages array instead, with indexesUsed and collectionScans fields. Either way, the question is the same: did it use an index on the foreign field?)

Before writing any $lookup, check that foreignField (or the field your inner $match compares) is indexed.

docs.title: Anti-joins and $count's empty output
docs.text:
"Products that have never been ordered" is a lookup followed by a filter on an empty array:

db.products.aggregate([
  { $lookup: { from: "orders", localField: "_id", foreignField: "items.sku", as: "o",
               pipeline: [{ $limit: 1 }, { $project: { _id: 1 } }] } },
  { $match: { o: { $size: 0 } } },
  { $count: "neverOrdered" }
])

This printed nothing at all — not {neverOrdered: 0}. Every product had at least one order, so no document reached $count, and $count emits nothing for empty input. Application code reading result[0].neverOrdered crashes. Handle the empty case (result[0]?.neverOrdered ?? 0). Note the inner $limit: 1: to test existence you need one matching document, not all of them.

docs.title: $graphLookup: recursive references
docs.text:
An org chart where each person stores who they report to (Level 2 · 02's parent-reference tree):

db.staff.insertMany([
  { _id: "asha", title: "CEO", reportsTo: null },
  { _id: "bala", title: "CTO", reportsTo: "asha" }, { _id: "chen", title: "CFO", reportsTo: "asha" },
  { _id: "dev", title: "Eng Manager", reportsTo: "bala" }, { _id: "esha", title: "Engineer", reportsTo: "dev" },
  { _id: "farid", title: "Engineer", reportsTo: "dev" }, { _id: "gita", title: "Accountant", reportsTo: "chen" }]);
db.staff.createIndex({ reportsTo: 1 });

Up the tree — Esha's management chain:

db.staff.aggregate([
  { $match: { _id: "esha" } },
  { $graphLookup: { from: "staff", startWith: "$reportsTo", connectFromField: "reportsTo",
                    connectToField: "_id", as: "chain", depthField: "level" } },
  { $project: { chain: { $sortArray: { input: { $map: { input: "$chain", as: "c",
      in: { who: "$$c._id", level: { $toInt: "$$c.level" } } } }, sortBy: { level: 1 } } } } }
])

{"_id":"esha","chain":[{"who":"dev","level":0},{"who":"bala","level":1},{"who":"asha","level":2}]}

Down the tree — everyone under Bala, at any depth (swap the connect fields):

{ $graphLookup: { from: "staff", startWith: "$_id", connectFromField: "_id",
                  connectToField: "reportsTo", as: "team", depthField: "d" } }

{"_id":"bala","team":["dev","esha","farid"],"size":3}

With maxDepth: 0 only direct reports are returned (["dev"]). $graphLookup does a breadth-first search, issuing one query per level against connectToField — so index that field. Its result array is unordered (hence the $sortArray above), the depth field is a 64-bit integer, and the whole set of visited documents must fit in 100 MB of memory. For large graphs (social networks, deep dependency trees), a dedicated graph database or a precomputed ancestors array (Level 2 · 02) is a better fit.

docs.title: $unionWith: concatenating collections
docs.text:
Many systems move old data into archive collections. $unionWith reads another collection (optionally through its own pipeline) and appends its documents to the stream — SQL's UNION ALL:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { customerId: "C0001" } }, { $project: { _id: 1, placedAt: 1, src: "live" } },
  { $unionWith: { coll: "orders_2024", pipeline: [
      { $match: { customerId: "C0001" } }, { $project: { _id: 1, placedAt: 1, src: "archive" } } ] } },
  { $sort: { placedAt: 1 } }, { $limit: 4 }
])

{"_id":"A2","placedAt":"2024-11-02T00:00:00.000Z","src":"archive"}
{"_id":"A1","placedAt":"2024-12-30T00:00:00.000Z","src":"archive"}
{"_id":9690,"placedAt":"2025-07-01T20:13:00.000Z","src":"live"}
{"_id":20645,"placedAt":"2025-07-02T06:11:00.000Z","src":"live"}

Put the $match inside the union's pipeline, not after the union, so each collection filters with its own indexes before the documents are combined.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
$lookup is executed as a join between the stream of input documents (the outer side) and the foreign collection (the inner side). For each outer document — or, in the slot-based engine, for each batch — the server needs the inner documents whose foreignField equals the outer localField. It picks a strategy when the pipeline is planned:

  • IndexedLoopJoin when a suitable index on the foreign field exists: one index lookup per outer value.
  • HashJoin when there is no index but the foreign collection is small enough: read the foreign collection once, build a hash table keyed on the foreign field, then probe it per outer document.
  • NestedLoopJoin otherwise: scan the foreign collection once per outer document.

The pipeline form with let/$expr and no localField is more general and historically ran the inner pipeline as a separate sub-query per outer document; with localField/foreignField present, the server can use the equality to choose an indexed strategy and then apply the rest of the inner pipeline to the matches. That's why the concise form is usually the faster one.

Join results are embedded in each output document, so each joined document — the input plus its as array — must stay under 16 MB. A product joined to every order it ever appeared in is exactly how pipelines hit that limit; use an inner $limit, $count or $group to keep the joined part small.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No index on the foreign field. The join becomes a scan per input document.
  • Joining before filtering. $match and $limit the outer side first, so fewer lookups run.
  • Pulling whole foreign documents when you need a count or two fields — use a pipeline with $project/$count.
  • Assuming $lookup or $graphLookup return ordered arrays.
  • Reading $count output without handling the empty case.
  • Using $lookup on every request of a hot path where a little denormalisation would remove it.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Using the shop database:

  1. Produce a report of the 10 customers with the highest delivered revenue, including their name and city from customers (group first, then look up only 10 customers).
  2. For each product category, list the 3 products with the most units sold, joined with their names. Check with explain that the lookup uses an index.
  3. Find customers who joined more than 180 days before their first order ($lookup with a $grouped inner pipeline, or group orders first and join customers).
  4. Add 20 more people to the staff collection, 5 levels deep. Write a pipeline that returns each manager with the total number of people under them.
  5. Create an orders_archive collection with orders from 2025 moved out of orders (copy with $merge from lesson 05, then delete). Write a "customer order history" pipeline with $unionWith and confirm both sides use their customerId indexes.

docs.title: 04 · Analytics: $facet, $bucket & Window Functions
docs.text:
Lessons 01–03 produced one result per pipeline: a list of groups, a joined document. Real dashboards and search pages need more: a result list and the category counts down the side and the price histogram, from one request; a running total; a moving average; a rank within each city; a chart with no missing days. This lesson covers the stages built for that kind of analytics.

Examples use the shop database. Several pipelines start by computing an order total as a double, so the numbers are easy to round and print:

const tot = { $set: { total: { $toDouble: { $sum: { $map: { input: "$items", as: "i",
                in: { $multiply: ["$$i.qty", "$$i.price"] } } } } } } };

(For money you'd keep Decimal128; converting to double here is purely for readable charts.)

docs.title: $facet: several pipelines over the same documents
docs.text:
A search results page for "delivered orders in Pune" with a category breakdown, price bands, the newest results and a total count:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { city: "Pune", status: "delivered" } }, tot,
  { $facet: {
      byCategory: [{ $unwind: "$items" }, { $sortByCount: "$items.category" }],
      priceBands: [{ $bucket: { groupBy: "$total", boundaries: [0, 1000, 5000, 20000, 50000],
                                default: "50000+", output: { n: { $sum: 1 } } } }],
      newest: [{ $sort: { placedAt: -1 } }, { $limit: 2 }, { $project: { _id: 1, total: 1 } }],
      count: [{ $count: "n" }] } }
])

{"byCategory":[{"_id":"electronics","count":2181},{"_id":"books","count":2167},{"_id":"kitchen","count":1975},{"_id":"toys","count":1875}],
 "priceBands":[{"_id":0,"n":374},{"_id":1000,"n":1309},{"_id":5000,"n":988},{"_id":20000,"n":547},{"_id":"50000+","n":988}],
 "newest":[{"_id":664,"total":10650},{"_id":20701,"total":2933}],
 "count":[{"n":4206}]}

One round trip, one document, four answers. The documents entering $facet are read once and fed to each sub-pipeline. Two limits to respect:

  • The output is one document, so all facets together must stay under 16 MB. Always $limit list facets.
  • Sub-pipelines can't use indexes — they operate on the documents $facet received. Put the selective $match (and any $sort you want indexed) before $facet.

byCategory counts line items per category (it unwinds); if the side panel should show "orders containing a book", group on distinct order ids or use $addToSet of categories per order first.

docs.title: Histograms: $bucket and $bucketAuto
docs.text:
$bucket (used above) takes explicit boundaries: each document goes in the bucket whose lower bound is the largest boundary ≤ its value; values outside the boundaries go to default (or cause an error if there's no default). It's for ranges that mean something to the business.

$bucketAuto picks boundaries itself to spread documents evenly across N buckets:

db.orders.aggregate([{ $match: { status: "delivered" } }, tot, { $bucketAuto: { groupBy: "$total", buckets: 4 } }])

{"_id":{"min":228,"max":2686},"count":6021}
{"_id":{"min":2686,"max":8231},"count":6020}
{"_id":{"min":8231,"max":46504},"count":6020}
{"_id":{"min":46504,"max":402892},"count":6019}

Those are quartiles of order value: a quarter of delivered orders are under ₹2,686, and the top quarter spans ₹46,504 to ₹402,892 — a long tail typical of baskets containing electronics.

docs.title: Window functions: $setWindowFields
docs.text:
$group collapses documents into groups. Window functions compute values across neighbouring documents while keeping every document — the running total, the moving average, the rank. Daily revenue in Pune for the first nine days of 2026, with a running total and a 3-day moving average:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { city: "Pune", status: "delivered",
              placedAt: { $gte: new Date("2026-01-01"), $lt: new Date("2026-01-10") } } }, tot,
  { $group: { _id: { $dateTrunc: { date: "$placedAt", unit: "day" } }, revenue: { $sum: "$total" } } },
  { $setWindowFields: { sortBy: { _id: 1 }, output: {
      running: { $sum: "$revenue", window: { documents: ["unbounded", "current"] } },
      ma3: { $avg: "$revenue", window: { documents: [-2, 0] } } } } },
  { $project: { _id: 0, day: { $dateToString: { date: "$_id", format: "%m-%d" } },
                revenue: { $round: ["$revenue", 0] }, running: { $round: ["$running", 0] }, ma3: { $round: ["$ma3", 0] } } }
])

{"day":"01-01","revenue":244592,"running":244592,"ma3":244592}
{"day":"01-02","revenue":614289,"running":858881,"ma3":429440}
{"day":"01-03","revenue":119788,"running":978669,"ma3":326223}
{"day":"01-04","revenue":619420,"running":1598089,"ma3":451166}
{"day":"01-05","revenue":102073,"running":1700162,"ma3":280427}
{"day":"01-06","revenue":339622,"running":2039784,"ma3":353705}
{"day":"01-07","revenue":441535,"running":2481319,"ma3":294410}
{"day":"01-08","revenue":156187,"running":2637506,"ma3":312448}
{"day":"01-09","revenue":705777,"running":3343283,"ma3":434500}

The window is defined relative to the current document after sorting: ["unbounded", "current"] is everything up to here (running total); [-2, 0] is the two previous documents and this one. Note the first two moving averages cover fewer than three days — the window is truncated at the start. You can also define windows by value range (range: [-7, 0], unit: "day"), which is the right choice when days might be missing: a document window of 3 "documents" silently spans more than 3 days if a day has no sales.

Window functions run per partition. Rank customers by spend within each city and keep the top two:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "delivered" } }, tot,
  { $group: { _id: { city: "$city", c: "$customerId" }, spend: { $sum: "$total" } } },
  { $setWindowFields: { partitionBy: "$_id.city", sortBy: { spend: -1 }, output: { rank: { $rank: {} } } } },
  { $match: { rank: { $lte: 2 } } }, { $sort: { "_id.city": 1, rank: 1 } }, { $limit: 4 },
  { $project: { _id: 0, city: "$_id.city", customer: "$_id.c", spend: { $round: ["$spend", 0] }, rank: 1 } }
])

{"rank":1,"city":"Bengaluru","customer":"C0649","spend":1055327}
{"rank":2,"city":"Bengaluru","customer":"C1779","spend":1034841}
{"rank":1,"city":"Chennai","customer":"C0481","spend":1252339}
{"rank":2,"city":"Chennai","customer":"C0810","spend":909825}

Other window operators: $denseRank, $documentNumber, $shift (previous/next value — for "change since yesterday"), $derivative, $integral, $expMovingAvg, $covariancePop, plus every $group accumulator applied over a window.

docs.title: Filling gaps: $densify and $fill
docs.text:
Charts lie when days with no data are simply absent. Given counts for 1, 2 and 5 March:

db.daily.insertMany([{ d: new Date("2026-03-01"), n: 5 }, { d: new Date("2026-03-02"), n: 7 }, { d: new Date("2026-03-05"), n: 4 }]);
db.daily.aggregate([
  { $densify: { field: "d", range: { step: 1, unit: "day", bounds: "full" } } },
  { $fill: { sortBy: { d: 1 }, output: { n: { value: 0 } } } },
  { $project: { _id: 0, d: { $dateToString: { date: "$d", format: "%m-%d" } }, n: 1 } }
])

{"n":5,"d":"03-01"}
{"n":7,"d":"03-02"}
{"n":0,"d":"03-03"}
{"n":0,"d":"03-04"}
{"n":4,"d":"03-05"}

$densify inserts documents for the missing dates; $fill sets their values. Zero is right for counts. For measurements (a temperature you didn't record), interpolation may be better:

{ $fill: { sortBy: { d: 1 }, output: { n: { method: "linear" } } } }

{"n":5,"d":"03-01"}
{"n":7,"d":"03-02"}
{"n":6,"d":"03-03"}
{"n":5,"d":"03-04"}
{"n":4,"d":"03-05"}

method: "locf" (last observation carried forward) is the third option. Choose deliberately — filling sales gaps with interpolated numbers invents sales.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
$facet buffers nothing per facet beyond what each sub-pipeline's own stages need: as each input document arrives, it is passed through every sub-pipeline, and at the end each sub-pipeline's results are collected into an array field of the single output document. That's why the inputs aren't re-read, why sub-pipelines can't use indexes (they don't read collections — they read the stream), and why the 16 MB output limit applies to all facets combined.

$setWindowFields first sorts by partitionBy and sortBy (a blocking sort, or an index-provided order if the preceding stages allow it), then walks each partition maintaining the state of each window as it slides: for ["unbounded", "current"] it just keeps adding; for a bounded window it adds the entering document and removes the leaving one, so a moving average over N documents costs O(1) per document rather than O(N). Window operators whose state can't be updated incrementally (like $median over a sliding window) cost more, and windows that must hold many documents in memory are subject to the 100 MB per-stage limit, spilling where supported.

$densify works on the sorted stream too: it remembers the last value of the field (per partition) and generates the missing steps between it and the next value, respecting time-zone-aware units for dates.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Unlimited arrays inside $facet, pushing the single output document over 16 MB.
  • Expecting $facet sub-pipelines to use indexes. Filter before the facet.
  • Document-count windows over data with gaps, so "last 7 days" silently spans weeks. Use range windows or $densify first.
  • Ranking with $rank when you need unique positions — ties share a rank; use $documentNumber.
  • Interpolating values that should be zero.
  • Running analytics pipelines against the primary of a busy OLTP system without thinking about load — consider a secondary with an analytics read preference (Level 4 · 02) or a precomputed rollup (lesson 05).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build a product search facet for the products collection: matching products (top 10 by price), counts per category, and a price histogram with $bucketAuto into 5 buckets.
  2. For each city, compute monthly delivered revenue and the month-over-month change in percent using $shift.
  3. Compute, for every delivered order, the customer's cumulative number of orders up to and including it (their "order number"), using $setWindowFields partitioned by customer. Find how many customers placed a 10th order.
  4. Produce daily order counts for Hyderabad for all of February 2026 with no missing days, then a 7-day moving average defined by a range window. Compare it with a 7-document window.
  5. Rewrite the facet example so byCategory counts orders rather than line items.

docs.title: 05 · Pipeline Performance, $out & $merge
docs.text:
A pipeline that takes 20 ms on 30,000 orders can take 20 minutes on 30 million. Whether it does depends mostly on two things: how much data enters the pipeline (decided by the first stages, and whether they use an index) and whether you recompute the same answer over and over (instead of storing it). This lesson covers both — reading aggregation explains, and building precomputed rollups with $merge.

Examples use the shop database, which has indexes on {customerId: 1, placedAt: -1}, {placedAt: 1} and {"items.sku": 1}.

docs.title: What the optimizer does for you
docs.text:
Units sold per category in June 2026, written two ways — filter first, and (carelessly) filter after $unwind:

const d0 = new Date("2026-06-01"), d1 = new Date("2026-07-01");
const tail = [{ $unwind: "$items" }, { $group: { _id: "$items.category", units: { $sum: "$items.qty" } } }];
db.orders.aggregate([{ $match: { placedAt: { $gte: d0, $lt: d1 } } }, ...tail]);
db.orders.aggregate([{ $unwind: "$items" }, { $match: { placedAt: { $gte: d0, $lt: d1 } } },
                     { $group: { _id: "$items.category", units: { $sum: "$items.qty" } } }]);

match first                              index=placedAt_1  docsExamined=2603 ms=7
match after unwind (optimizer moves it?) index=placedAt_1  docsExamined=2603 ms=7

Identical. The optimizer noticed that the $match only references placedAt, which $unwind doesn't change, moved it to the front, and pushed it into the query layer, where it used the placedAt_1 index. It will even split a $match: with {placedAt: ..., "items.qty": {$gte: 2}} after $unwind, the explain showed

["$cursor","$unwind","$match","$group"]
{"$and":[{"placedAt":{"$lt":"2026-07-01T00:00:00.000Z"}},{"placedAt":{"$gte":"2026-06-01T00:00:00.000Z"}}]}

— the placedAt part moved into the initial $cursor (the indexed query), while the items.qty part stayed after $unwind, where it has to be, because it refers to the unwound element.

docs.title: What the optimizer can't do
docs.text:
It can't move a filter past a stage that creates the field being filtered:

db.orders.aggregate([{ $set: { month: { $month: "$placedAt" } } }, { $match: { month: 6 } }, ...tail])

match on computed field after $set       index=- COLLSCAN docsExamined=30000 ms=20

Every document was read, given a month, and then most were thrown away. Express the filter on the stored field (a placedAt range) and it becomes indexable again. (This version also matches June of every year — another reason to filter on real date ranges.)

The same applies to $group: anything computed by a $group can only be filtered after it, and a $group early in a pipeline reads its whole input:

sort placedAt + limit 5            index=placedAt_1 stages=LIMIT,FETCH,IXSCAN docs=5 ms=1
group, sort, limit                 index=- stages=GROUP,COLLSCAN docs=30000 ms=8

A leading $sort + $limit on an indexed field reads 5 documents. "Top 5 customers by order count" must group all 30,000 orders first — no index can give you the top of a computed count. That's fine for 30,000; for 300 million it's a batch job, which is where rollups come in.

docs.title: Reading an aggregation explain
docs.text: db.orders.explain("executionStats").aggregate(pipeline) returns either a stages array whose first element is $cursor (the part pushed into the query layer, with a normal queryPlanner/executionStats inside), or — when the whole pipeline runs in the slot-based engine — a top-level queryPlanner and executionStats like a find (explainVersion: "2"). In both, look for the same things as Level 2 · 07: which index, how many documents examined, and blocking stages.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
1. $match first, on stored fields, with an index that supports it.
  2. $sort early if it can use an index (and before $group only if you need the order there).
  3. $project/$unset early only to drop big fields you won't use — the optimizer already tracks which fields later stages need, so manual early projections rarely help otherwise.
  4. $limit as early as correctness allows.
  5. $lookup after you've reduced the documents, with an index on the foreign field (lesson 03).
  6. Don't $unwind just to aggregate within a document (lesson 02).

docs.title: Precomputed rollups with $merge
docs.text:
Dashboards ask the same question every few seconds: revenue by day, city and category. Recomputing it from raw orders every time is wasted work. Compute it once into a rollup collection, and update it incrementally:

const rollup = (from, to) => [
  { $match: { status: "delivered", placedAt: { $gte: from, $lt: to } } },
  { $unwind: "$items" },
  { $group: { _id: { day: { $dateTrunc: { date: "$placedAt", unit: "day", timezone: "Asia/Kolkata" } },
                     city: "$city", category: "$items.category" },
              units: { $sum: "$items.qty" },
              revenue: { $sum: { $multiply: ["$items.qty", "$items.price"] } } } },
  { $set: { refreshedAt: "$$NOW" } },
  { $merge: { into: "daily_sales", on: "_id", whenMatched: "replace", whenNotMatched: "insert" } }
];
db.orders.aggregate(rollup(new Date("2025-06-30T18:30:00Z"), new Date("2026-07-01T18:30:00Z")));

The full build took about 200 ms and wrote 8,679 documents — one per (IST day, city, category):

{ _id: { day: ISODate('2026-06-09T18:30:00.000Z'), city: 'Chennai', category: 'kitchen' },
  units: 7, revenue: Decimal128('5645') }

(2026-06-09T18:30Z is midnight on 10 June in India — the day boundary in UTC.)

$merge writes each output document into the target collection: on names the field(s) that identify a document (they need a unique index — _id always has one), whenMatched says what to do if it exists (replace, merge fields, keepExisting, fail, or a custom update pipeline), and whenNotMatched whether to insert, discard or fail.

docs.title: Querying the rollup
docs.text:
Revenue by category for April–June 2026 (IST), from raw orders and from the rollup:

["books=4450184","electronics=169242891","kitchen=12046031","toys=7353295"]
["books=4450184","electronics=169242891","kitchen=12046031","toys=7353295"]
raw docs examined 7548 rollup docs 2167

Same answer, from 2,167 small documents instead of 7,548 orders that also need unwinding. The ratio grows with volume: the rollup has at most days × cities × categories documents no matter how many orders there are.

The first attempt at this comparison did not match. The raw query used UTC month boundaries (2026-04-01T00:00Z) while the rollup's days were IST days, so a few hours of orders at each end fell on different sides — totals differed by a few thousand rupees per category. A rollup and the queries against it must agree on the time zone and boundaries; write that down next to the rollup's definition.

docs.title: Incremental refresh
docs.text:
When orders change — new deliveries, a status correction — re-run the rollup for just the affected window:

db.orders.aggregate(rollup(new Date(day.getTime() - 86400000), new Date(day.getTime() + 86400000)))

That recomputed two days in 12 ms. Because $merge with whenMatched: "replace" overwrites the affected (day, city, category) documents, re-running a window is idempotent — safe to repeat after a failure. The remaining edge case is a group that should now be empty (every order of a day/city/category cancelled): replace won't delete it. Handle it by deleting the window's rollup documents before re-running, or by emitting zero rows for the window.

Typical schedules: re-run "today and yesterday" every few minutes, and a full rebuild nightly. Change streams (lesson 07) can trigger refreshes only for days that actually changed.

docs.title: $out: replace a collection wholesale
docs.text:
$out writes the pipeline's results to a collection, replacing it entirely:

db.orders.aggregate([{ $group: { _id: "$customerId", orders: { $sum: 1 } } }, { $out: "customer_order_counts" }])

That wrote 2,000 documents in 40 ms. The replacement is atomic: $out writes to a temporary collection and renames it over the target at the end, so readers see either the old results or the new ones, never a half-written mix — and if the pipeline fails, the old collection is untouched. Indexes on the target are preserved across runs:

indexes after re-$out: ["_id_","orders_-1"]

Both $out and $merge must be the last stage:

40601 $out can only be the final stage in the pipeline

Use $out for full rebuilds of a derived collection; $merge for incremental updates, for writing into a collection that has other data, or for writing to a different database.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When the server builds an aggregation, it first runs a sequence of rewrites on the stage list: $match stages are swapped ahead of stages that don't modify the fields they reference ($unwind, $sort, $project, $set of other fields, $lookup on other fields), adjacent stages are coalesced ($sort + $limit → top-k; $lookup + $unwind on its output → a single join stage that never materialises the array; $match + $match → one), and dependency analysis records which fields the pipeline actually needs. The longest prefix of the pipeline that the query system can execute — filter, sort, projection, and in the slot-based engine often $group and $lookup too — is pushed down and planned with indexes like a find. Everything after that prefix runs in the document-at-a-time pipeline engine.

$merge performs, for each output document, the equivalent of an update or insert keyed on the on fields, in batches, with the target's unique index enforcing that each key maps to at most one document. It isn't one big transaction: if the pipeline fails half-way, the documents already merged stay. That's why idempotent refresh windows are the right design. $out instead builds a whole new collection and swaps it in with a rename, which gives all-or-nothing replacement at the cost of rewriting everything each time.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Filtering on computed fields that could have been expressed on stored, indexed fields.
  • $group at the start of a hot query on a large collection — it reads everything; precompute instead.
  • Rollups and live queries using different time zones or boundaries.
  • Assuming $merge is atomic. Make refresh windows idempotent.
  • $out into a collection other code writes to — it replaces all of it.
  • Manual $project at the start "for performance" that only makes the pipeline harder to read.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Take three pipelines from lessons 01–04 and explain each one. Which use an index? Rewrite one that doesn't so it does.
  2. Build a monthly_customer_spend rollup with $merge keyed on {customerId, month}. Use it to find each customer's best month.
  3. Simulate late changes: cancel 50 random delivered orders from last week, re-run the rollup for the affected days only, and verify against a fresh full rebuild. Handle the "group became empty" case.
  4. Compare $out and $merge for a full rebuild of daily_sales: time both, and check what a concurrent reader sees during each (run a reader loop in another shell).
  5. Write a $merge with whenMatched as a pipeline that adds new revenue to existing documents instead of replacing them. Why is that version not idempotent?

docs.title: 06 · Multi-Document Transactions
docs.text:
Single-document writes are atomic (Level 1 · 06), and good modeling puts data that changes together in one document (Level 2 · 01). But some operations genuinely span documents: moving money between two accounts, inserting an order and decrementing stock, adding a review and updating the product's rating. Since 4.0 MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions on replica sets (and on sharded clusters since 4.2). This lesson uses them correctly — which mostly means handling the errors they're designed to produce.

Transactions need a replica set or sharded cluster; the course lab is a single-node replica set, which is enough. All examples are Python with PyMongo 4.18.

docs.title: A transfer
docs.text:
from decimal import Decimal
from bson import Decimal128
from pymongo import MongoClient
from pymongo.read_concern import ReadConcern
from pymongo.write_concern import WriteConcern

client = MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0")
db = client.bank
db.accounts.insert_many([{"_id": "ana", "balance": Decimal128("100.00")},
                         {"_id": "ben", "balance": Decimal128("50.00")}])

def transfer(session, src, dst, amount):
    amt = Decimal128(Decimal(amount))
    neg = Decimal128(-Decimal(amount))
    res = db.accounts.update_one({"_id": src, "balance": {"$gte": amt}}, {"$inc": {"balance": neg}}, session=session)
    if res.modified_count != 1:
        raise ValueError(f"insufficient funds in {src}")
    db.accounts.update_one({"_id": dst}, {"$inc": {"balance": amt}}, session=session)
    db.ledger.insert_one({"from": src, "to": dst, "amount": amt}, session=session)

opts = dict(read_concern=ReadConcern("snapshot"), write_concern=WriteConcern("majority"))
with client.start_session() as s:
    s.with_transaction(lambda s: transfer(s, "ana", "ben", "30.00"), **opts)

after transfer 30: {'ana': '70.00', 'ben': '80.00'} ledger: 1

Three things make this a transaction:

  1. A session (client.start_session()), which carries the transaction's identity.
  2. with_transaction(callback), which starts the transaction, runs your callback, and commits.
  3. session=s on every operation inside the callback. An operation without it runs outside the transaction — no error, just silently not part of it. This is the single most common transaction bug.

If the callback raises, the transaction is aborted and every write in it disappears:

rejected: insufficient funds in ben -> {'ana': '70.00', 'ben': '80.00'} ledger: 1

Ben's balance wasn't touched — the conditional $gte failed first — but if it had been decremented before the error, the abort would have undone it, along with any ledger entry.

docs.title: Isolation: nobody sees your changes until commit
docs.text:
s = client.start_session()
s.start_transaction(**opts)
db.accounts.update_one({"_id": "ana"}, {"$inc": {"balance": Decimal128("1000")}}, session=s)
print("inside txn sees:", db.accounts.find_one({"_id": "ana"}, session=s)["balance"],
      "| outside sees:", db.accounts.find_one({"_id": "ana"})["balance"])
s.abort_transaction()

inside txn sees: 1070.00 | outside sees: 70.00
after abort: {'ana': '70.00', 'ben': '80.00'}

Inside the transaction, reads see its own writes; outside, the world sees the last committed state. With read concern "snapshot", every read in the transaction sees data as of one point in time — a consistent snapshot even while other clients commit changes.

docs.title: Write conflicts are normal
docs.text:
Two open transactions update the same document:

s1.start_transaction(**opts); s2.start_transaction(**opts)
db.accounts.update_one({"_id": "ben"}, {"$inc": {"balance": Decimal128("1")}}, session=s1)
db.accounts.update_one({"_id": "ben"}, {"$inc": {"balance": Decimal128("2")}}, session=s2)

second txn: 112 WriteConflict labels: ['TransientTransactionError']
after conflict: {'ana': '70.00', 'ben': '81.00'}

MongoDB doesn't make the second transaction wait for the first: it fails it immediately with code 112 WriteConflict, labelled TransientTransactionError. The label means "the whole transaction may succeed if you retry it from the beginning". Only the first transaction's +1 committed.

This is why you should use with_transaction rather than start_transaction/commit_transaction by hand: it retries the callback on TransientTransactionError, and retries the commit on UnknownTransactionCommitResult (the commit may or may not have happened — e.g. a network error), for up to 120 seconds.

docs.title: Under load: retries happen, invariants hold
docs.text:
Eight threads each make 100 random transfers between five accounts holding 1,000.00 each. The callback counts how often it runs:

def worker(seed, n):
    r = random.Random(seed)
    for _ in range(n):
        src, dst = r.sample(names, 2)
        with client.start_session() as s:
            s.with_transaction(lambda s: transfer(s, src, dst, f"{r.randint(1, 50)}.00"),
                               read_concern=ReadConcern("snapshot"), write_concern=WriteConcern("majority"))

(Here transfer returns False instead of raising when funds are insufficient, so a rejected transfer still commits an empty transaction.)

800 transfers in 1.8s, callback executions: 1292 (retries: 492)
ledger entries: 774 | total balance: 5000.00

With only five accounts, conflicts were constant: the callback ran 1,292 times for 800 transfers. Yet the total is exactly 5,000.00 and the ledger has one entry per successful transfer (26 were rejected for insufficient funds) — retried attempts left no trace. Two lessons:

  • Your callback may run more than once. Everything in it must be safe to repeat: no sending emails, no incrementing in-memory counters you rely on, no calling external APIs. Do those after with_transaction returns.
  • Hot documents make transactions fight. Five accounts shared by eight threads is a worst case; real contention is usually lower, but a single "global counter" document touched by every transaction serialises your whole system.

docs.title: What transactions cost
docs.text:
The same script then ran 300 transfers inside transactions and 300 by calling transfer(None, ...) — the same three writes with no session:

300 transfers: with transaction 2214 ms, without 5330 ms

The transactional version was faster. To see why, a second script compared single updates at two write concerns with transactions of three updates:

300 single updates, w=majority: 1722 ms
300 single updates, w=1: 78 ms
300 transactions of 3 updates (commit w=majority): 1990 ms

The surprise is that the transaction wasn't the expensive part. A single update with write concern majority took about 5.7 ms because the server waits for the write to be journaled (and, on a real replica set, replicated) before acknowledging; with w: 1 the same updates took 0.26 ms each. A transaction of three updates waits for durability once, at commit — so 300 transactions of three updates cost about the same as 300 single durable updates, and the transfer benchmark ran faster with a transaction (2.2 s) than as three separate durable writes (5.3 s). Write concern is covered properly in Level 4 · 02; the point here is to measure before assuming that transactions are slow.

The real costs are elsewhere: transactions hold WiredTiger snapshots open (pressure on the cache), they conflict and retry under contention, and on sharded clusters a transaction touching several shards needs a two-phase commit.

docs.title: Limits and good practice
docs.text:
• Keep them short. By default a transaction that runs longer than transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds — 60 on this server — is aborted. Don't do slow work (HTTP calls, user prompts) inside one.
  • Keep them small. Modifying thousands of documents in one transaction is possible but ties up cache and increases conflict probability. Batch large changes outside transactions, idempotently.
  • Most operations work inside transactions, including creating collections and indexes on empty collections in recent versions, but not everything (e.g. writes to capped collections, some admin commands). Check the docs for your version if something errors.
  • Use read concern snapshot and write concern majority for transactions whose results must survive a failover.
  • Prefer modeling over transactions. If two pieces of data must always change together, ask first whether they belong in one document.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A session is a server-side object identified by a logical session id (lsid). When a transaction starts, every operation sent with that lsid and a transaction number is executed inside one WiredTiger transaction, reading from a snapshot taken at the transaction's start. Writes are applied to the transaction's private view; WiredTiger's multi-version concurrency control keeps other readers on committed versions.

Conflicts are detected eagerly: if a transaction tries to modify a document that another uncommitted transaction has already modified (or that was committed after this transaction's snapshot), WiredTiger reports a write conflict immediately, and MongoDB aborts the transaction with WriteConflict and the TransientTransactionError label rather than blocking. That's optimistic concurrency: no deadlocks, but the application must retry — which the callback API does for you.

At commit, all the transaction's writes are recorded together in the oplog (as a single applyOps entry, or a chain of entries for large transactions) so secondaries apply them atomically too, and the commit is acknowledged according to the write concern. On sharded clusters, a transaction touching several shards uses a coordinator and two-phase commit to make every shard commit or none.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting session=s on one operation, which then silently runs outside the transaction.
  • Non-idempotent side effects in the callback, repeated on every retry.
  • Hand-rolled start_transaction/commit without retry logic for TransientTransactionError and UnknownTransactionCommitResult.
  • Long transactions that hit the 60-second limit or hold snapshots open under load.
  • Using transactions to compensate for a schema that splits data that always changes together.
  • A hot document shared by every transaction (a global counter), serialising all writes.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Implement place_order(customer_id, items) for the shop database: insert the order and decrement each product's stock (add a stock field first), all-or-nothing, rejecting the order if any product is out of stock. Test with an order containing one unavailable item and confirm nothing changed.
  2. Run your place_order from 10 threads against a product with stock 5. Prove that exactly 5 orders succeed.
  3. Revisit the Level 2 · 10 exercise: insert a review and update the product's rating and recentReviews in one transaction. What failure did the transaction remove?
  4. Deliberately add a time.sleep(70) inside a callback and observe what error you get and what with_transaction does with it.
  5. Measure your transfer throughput with 2, 5, 50 and 500 accounts (8 threads). Plot retries per transfer against the number of accounts.

docs.title: 07 · Change Streams
docs.text:
Applications constantly need to react when data changes: push a notification when a ticket is assigned, refresh a cache when a product changes, update a search index, refresh the rollup from lesson 05 only for days that changed, stream changes to another system. Polling (find every few seconds for updatedAt > last) is slow, wasteful and misses deletes. Change streams give you an ordered, resumable feed of every insert, update, replace and delete on a collection, a database or the whole deployment.

They require a replica set or sharded cluster, because they're built on the oplog (Level 4 · 01). Examples use PyMongo against the lab replica set.

docs.title: Watching a collection
docs.text:
import threading, time
from pymongo import MongoClient

client = MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0")
db = client.cs
db.drop_collection("tickets")
db.create_collection("tickets")

def writer():
    time.sleep(0.5)
    db.tickets.insert_one({"_id": 1, "title": "Printer on fire", "status": "open", "priority": "high"})
    db.tickets.insert_one({"_id": 2, "title": "Mouse squeaks", "status": "open", "priority": "low"})
    db.tickets.update_one({"_id": 1}, {"$set": {"status": "in_progress"}, "$inc": {"updates": 1}})
    db.tickets.update_one({"_id": 2}, {"$set": {"status": "closed"}})
    db.tickets.delete_one({"_id": 2})

threading.Thread(target=writer).start()
pipeline = [{"$match": {"operationType": {"$in": ["insert", "update", "delete"]}}}]
with db.tickets.watch(pipeline, full_document="updateLookup", max_await_time_ms=500) as stream:
    seen, t0 = 0, time.time()
    while seen < 5 and time.time() - t0 < 10:
        ch = stream.try_next()
        if ch is None:
            continue
        seen += 1
        desc = ch.get("updateDescription", {})
        print(f"{ch['operationType']:7} _id={ch['documentKey']['_id']}"
              f" updated={desc.get('updatedFields')} full={ch.get('fullDocument')}")

insert  _id=1 updated=None full={'_id': 1, 'title': 'Printer on fire', 'status': 'open', 'priority': 'high'}
insert  _id=2 updated=None full={'_id': 2, 'title': 'Mouse squeaks', 'status': 'open', 'priority': 'low'}
update  _id=1 updated={'status': 'in_progress', 'updates': 1} full={'_id': 1, 'title': 'Printer on fire', 'status': 'in_progress', 'priority': 'high', 'updates': 1}
update  _id=2 updated={'status': 'closed'} full={'_id': 2, 'title': 'Mouse squeaks', 'status': 'closed', 'priority': 'low'}
delete  _id=2 updated=None full=None

Each change event is a document with:

Field Contents _id the resume token — a position in the stream operationType insert, update, replace, delete, plus drop, rename, invalidate and others ns database and collection documentKey the changed document's _id (and shard key on sharded clusters) fullDocument the new document for inserts/replaces; for updates only if requested updateDescription for updates: updatedFields, removedFields, truncatedArrays clusterTime when the change happened

watch() accepts an aggregation pipeline of filtering and reshaping stages ($match, $project, $set, …), applied on the server, so uninteresting events never cross the network. You can watch a collection, db.watch() for a whole database, or client.watch() for everything.

docs.title: updateLookup is "now", not "then"
docs.text: By default an update event carries only the delta. full_document="updateLookup" makes the server look up the document's current version when it sends the event. That's convenient, but note the timing: the lookup happens when the event is delivered, not when the update happened. In the run above, the update to ticket 2 came back with the full document because the lookup happened before the delete; if the consumer had been slower, fullDocument for that update would have been None (the document no longer existed) — and for a document updated twice in quick succession, both events can show the second state. Use updatedFields when you need what changed in this event.

docs.title: Pre-images: what did it look like before?
docs.text:
For deletes there's no current document at all. To see the state before a change, enable pre- and post-images on the collection and ask for them:

db.command("collMod", "events", changeStreamPreAndPostImages={"enabled": True})
db.events.update_one({"_id": 5}, {"$set": {"note": "about to go"}})
with db.events.watch([{"$match": {"operationType": "delete"}}],
                     full_document_before_change="required") as stream:
    db.events.delete_one({"_id": 5})
    ch = stream.next()
    print("deleted", ch["documentKey"], "before:", ch["fullDocumentBeforeChange"])

deleted {'_id': 5} before: {'_id': 5, 'note': 'about to go'}

The server stores a copy of each document's previous version in a system collection when it changes, so this costs extra writes and storage; enable it only on collections that need it, and configure how long pre-images are kept (changeStreamOptions.preAndPostImages.expireAfterSeconds). "required" fails the stream if a pre-image is missing; "whenAvailable" returns null instead.

docs.title: Resuming after a crash
docs.text:
A consumer that restarts must continue exactly where it stopped — not miss events written while it was down, and not reprocess everything. Save the resume token after processing each event, and pass it to watch() on restart:

# 1. A consumer processes two events, saves its resume token after each, then "crashes".
with db.events.watch() as stream:
    db.events.insert_many([{"_id": 1}, {"_id": 2}])
    for _ in range(2):
        ch = stream.next()
        print("consumer A processed", ch["documentKey"]["_id"])
        with open(TOKEN_FILE, "w") as f:
            json.dump(ch["_id"], f)

# 2. Writes happen while no consumer is running.
db.events.insert_many([{"_id": 3}, {"_id": 4}, {"_id": 5}])

# 3. A new consumer resumes from the saved token and gets exactly the missed events.
with open(TOKEN_FILE) as f:
    token = json.load(f)
with db.events.watch(resume_after=token, max_await_time_ms=300) as stream:
    while (ch := stream.try_next()) is not None:
        print("consumer B resumed and got", ch["documentKey"]["_id"])

consumer A processed 1
consumer A processed 2
consumer B resumed and got 3
consumer B resumed and got 4
consumer B resumed and got 5

Nothing lost, nothing repeated. In production, store the token in the same place and transaction as the effect of processing the event (e.g. in the database you're updating), so "processed" and "token saved" can't diverge. If you save the token before processing, a crash loses an event; after, a crash repeats one — so make processing idempotent and save after.

Drivers also resume automatically after transient errors such as a primary failover, using the last token they received. Your code only needs the saved token across process restarts.

docs.title: The oplog window
docs.text: A resume token is a position in the oplog, which is a capped collection (Level 2 · 09) of limited size. If a consumer is down longer than the oplog covers, its position has been overwritten and resuming fails with a ChangeStreamHistoryLost error. Then the only option is a full resync (re-read the collection) followed by a new stream. Monitor how far behind consumers are and size the oplog accordingly (Level 4 · 01).

docs.title: Invalidation
docs.text:
Some events end a stream permanently:

with db.events.watch() as stream:
    db.drop_collection("events")
    for _ in range(2):
        ch = stream.next()
        print("event:", ch["operationType"])
    print("stream alive after invalidate:", stream.alive)

event: drop
event: invalidate
stream alive after invalidate: False

Dropping or renaming a watched collection (or dropping its database) produces an invalidate event and closes the stream. To continue past it, open a new stream with start_after=<invalidate event's token> (not resume_after, which refuses to resume from an invalidate). Database- and deployment-level streams don't invalidate on collection drops — another reason to watch at a higher level and filter by ns.

docs.title: Design notes
docs.text:
• Change streams deliver events in commit order per shard, at least once per resumed position — design consumers to be idempotent.
  • Each stream is a cursor on the server. Hundreds of streams with complex pipelines cost real CPU; prefer a few database-level streams fanned out in your application over one stream per user.
  • A stream sees committed data only, and with the default majority read concern, only data that's durable — a change that's later rolled back during a failover is never delivered.
  • Transactions appear as their individual operations, each carrying the transaction's lsid and txnNumber, all delivered after the transaction commits.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every write on a replica set is recorded in the oplog (local.oplog.rs) on the primary and copied to secondaries. A change stream is an aggregation over the oplog: the server opens a tailable cursor on it, filters entries to the watched namespace, transforms each raw oplog entry into a change-event document (an update's diff becomes updateDescription, for instance), applies your pipeline, and delivers results via getMore — waiting up to maxAwaitTimeMS for new entries, like the tailable cursors of Level 2 · 09.

The resume token encodes the cluster time and position of the event in the oplog. Resuming means reopening the oplog scan at that position, which is why it only works while that position still exists. Because streams read with majority read concern, they only advance over entries replicated to a majority, so events never "un-happen". On a sharded cluster, mongos opens a stream on every shard and merges them in cluster-time order before delivering them to you. fullDocument: "updateLookup" is implemented as an extra find by _id per update event, which is why it returns the document as it is at lookup time, and why it adds read load.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Saving the resume token before processing, losing events on crash.
  • Non-idempotent consumers that break when an event is delivered twice after a restart.
  • Trusting updateLookup to show the state at event time.
  • Enabling pre-images everywhere "just in case", doubling write load.
  • Ignoring invalidate and leaving a consumer silently dead after a collection rename.
  • No monitoring of consumer lag until the oplog window is exceeded.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a consumer that maintains a ticket_counts document ({open: n, in_progress: n, closed: n}) from a change stream on tickets, handling inserts, status updates and deletes (enable pre-images so deletes know which status to decrement). Make it resumable with a saved token.
  2. Kill the consumer with Ctrl+C in the middle of a burst of 1,000 writes, restart it, and verify the counts match a fresh aggregation.
  3. Use a change stream to drive the incremental rollup from lesson 05: collect the days touched by order changes for one second at a time, then re-run the rollup for just those days.
  4. Open a database-level stream with a $match on ns.coll and confirm it survives dropping one collection.
  5. Measure how long a resume token stays valid on your lab: write to another collection in a loop and check db.getReplicationInfo() for the oplog's time window.

docs.title: 08 · Geospatial Queries
docs.text: "Stores near me", "drivers within 2 km", "which delivery zone is this address in", "restaurants inside this map view" — location queries show up in almost every consumer app. MongoDB stores locations as GeoJSON, indexes them with a 2dsphere index that understands the Earth is round, and answers proximity and containment questions with a handful of operators.

docs.title: Storing locations
docs.text:
A location is a GeoJSON object with a type and coordinates:

{ name: "Store 1", type: "pharmacy",
  loc: { type: "Point", coordinates: [73.7035, 18.4336] } }   // [longitude, latitude]

Longitude first, then latitude — x before y. Maps, GPS apps and most people say "lat, long", so this is the most common geospatial bug in existence. Other GeoJSON types — LineString, Polygon, MultiPolygon — store routes and areas.

The lab dataset: 2,000 stores with seeded random positions across a roughly 30 × 24 km box around central Pune (longitude 73.70–74.00, latitude 18.42–18.64). The positions are synthetic, not real businesses.

db.stores.insertMany(docs);
db.stores.createIndex({ loc: "2dsphere" });
const me = { type: "Point", coordinates: [73.8567, 18.5204] };   // a point in central Pune

docs.title: Nearest first: $near
docs.text:
db.stores.find({ type: "pharmacy", loc: { $near: { $geometry: me, $maxDistance: 2000 } } }, { name: 1, _id: 0 }).limit(3)

{"name":"Store 1738"}
{"name":"Store 661"}
{"name":"Store 88"}

$near returns documents sorted by distance, nearest first, optionally limited by $maxDistance (and $minDistance) in metres. It requires a geospatial index. Its explain:

near: stages "stage":"FETCH","stage":"IXSCAN" keys 123 docs 59 n 42

Within 2 km there were 42 stores; the index search examined 123 keys and 59 documents to find them — it searches outward in rings of index cells and fetches only candidates in those cells.

One subtlety: adding .sort() to a $near query replaces the distance ordering. A $near query sorted by name returned "Store 1" — alphabetical order, not proximity. If you need "nearest, then by name", sort in the application or use $geoNear.

docs.title: Distances: $geoNear
docs.text:
To show "407 m away", use the $geoNear aggregation stage, which adds the distance to each document. It must be the first stage of the pipeline:

db.stores.aggregate([
  { $geoNear: { near: me, distanceField: "dist", maxDistance: 1500, query: { type: "cafe" }, spherical: true } },
  { $limit: 3 },
  { $project: { _id: 0, name: 1, metres: { $round: ["$dist", 0] } } }
])

{"name":"Store 173","metres":407}
{"name":"Store 1154","metres":621}
{"name":"Store 1646","metres":640}

Put non-spatial filters in $geoNear's query option rather than a later $match; that way they're applied during the search and $limit gets the nearest cafés, not the nearest stores filtered down afterwards. Distances are computed on a sphere — accurate to well under 1% for app-scale distances, which is plenty for "how far is the shop", but not a surveying tool.

docs.title: Inside an area: $geoWithin
docs.text:
Within a circle (radius in radians: distance divided by the Earth's radius, 6,378.1 km):

db.stores.countDocuments({ loc: { $geoWithin: { $centerSphere: [me.coordinates, 1 / 6378.1] } } })   // 10 within 1 km

Within a polygon — say a delivery zone drawn on a map:

const zone = { type: "Polygon", coordinates: [[
  [73.80, 18.50], [73.88, 18.50], [73.88, 18.56], [73.80, 18.56], [73.80, 18.50] ]] };
db.stores.countDocuments({ loc: { $geoWithin: { $geometry: zone } } })   // 156

A polygon's ring must be closed (first point repeated at the end), and its edges are geodesic — great-circle arcs, not straight lines on a flat map. For small zones the difference is negligible; for a polygon spanning hundreds of kilometres it isn't. $geoWithin doesn't sort, and it works without an index (slowly) as well as with one.

docs.title: Which area contains this point: $geoIntersects
docs.text:
Flip the question: store the zones, query with a point.

db.zones.insertOne({ _id: "central", area: zone });
