db.zones.insertOne({ _id: "east", area: { type: "Polygon", coordinates: [[
  [73.88, 18.50], [73.95, 18.50], [73.95, 18.56], [73.88, 18.56], [73.88, 18.50] ]] } });
db.zones.createIndex({ area: "2dsphere" });
db.zones.find({ area: { $geoIntersects: { $geometry: me } } }, { _id: 1 })

[{"_id":"central"}]

That's how "is this address deliverable, and by which hub?" is answered in one indexed query.

docs.title: The longitude-first trap, measured
docs.text:
A store inserted with its coordinates swapped — [18.5204, 73.8567] — is still a valid point: longitude 18.5°E, latitude 73.9°N, somewhere in the Arctic north of Norway. Nothing fails:

swapped lat/lng distance km: 7005

The "local" store is 7,005 km away and simply never appears in nearby results. Only swaps that produce an impossible latitude are rejected:

db.stores.insertOne({ name: "bad", loc: { type: "Point", coordinates: [73.8, 98.5] } })

510 Could not extract geo keys at path 'loc' for document with _id ObjectId('...'): Longitude/latitude is out of bounds, ...

Validate coordinates at the edge of your system (a $jsonSchema that restricts longitude to [-180, 180] and latitude to [-90, 90] catches only the impossible ones; for a regional app, restrict to your region's bounding box) and name variables lng/lat explicitly in code.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A 2dsphere index maps the sphere onto a hierarchy of cells using Google's S2 geometry library: the Earth is projected onto the six faces of a cube, and each face is recursively divided into four, giving cells at 30 levels of precision, each with a 64-bit id. Nearby cells have nearby ids along a space-filling curve. A point is indexed by the id of its cell at a fine level; a polygon by a covering — a set of cells, at mixed levels, that together cover the shape.

That turns geometry into B-tree range scans. $geoWithin with a polygon computes a covering of the query polygon and scans the index ranges for those cells; the fetched candidates are then checked exactly against the geometry (cells near the edge can contain points just outside it — the extra documents examined). $near starts with the cells around the query point and expands in rings, emitting documents in distance order from each ring once it knows nothing closer can appear in an unexplored ring. That's why $near can stop early after a limit, and why it examined 123 keys to return 42 stores.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Latitude first. GeoJSON is [longitude, latitude].
  • Radians vs metres: $centerSphere takes radians; $near/$geoNear with GeoJSON take metres.
  • Unclosed polygon rings, which are rejected.
  • Filtering after $geoNear instead of using its query option, so $limit gives too few results.
  • Adding sort() to $near and losing distance order.
  • Using the legacy 2d index and coordinate pairs for real-world locations — it treats the Earth as flat. It's only for genuinely flat coordinate systems (a game map, a floor plan).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add a rating to each store. Find the 5 nearest stores with a rating of at least 4, with their distances in metres, within 3 km of a point of your choice.
  2. Draw a polygon around a neighbourhood using a map tool that exports GeoJSON, and count the stores inside it. Make sure the coordinate order matches.
  3. Create three overlapping delivery zones with a priority field. For a given address, return the highest-priority zone that contains it.
  4. Write a $jsonSchema validator for stores.loc that only accepts points inside the bounding box of your city.
  5. Simulate "drivers": 500 documents whose locations update every second (a script with bulkWrite), and a query for the 3 nearest available drivers. Measure query time while the updates run.

docs.title: 09 · Text Search & Collation
docs.text: Two features this lesson covers deal with the fact that human text doesn't compare like bytes. Text indexes let you search for words — "running" should find "runs" — and rank results by relevance. Collations make equality and sorting follow language rules — "zoe" equals "Zoe", "émile" sorts next to "Emile", "item9" comes before "item10". Both are built into the server; both have limits you should know before you promise a product manager "search".

docs.title: Text indexes
docs.text:
Five articles, one text index over title and body, with the title weighted five times higher:

db.articles.insertMany([
  { _id: 1, title: "Running a database in production", body: "Backups, monitoring and running upgrades without downtime." },
  { _id: 2, title: "Indexes explained", body: "How a B-tree index runs range scans. The runner examines keys." },
  { _id: 3, title: "Cooking with cast iron", body: "Seasoning a pan; why food runs off a well-seasoned surface." },
  { _id: 4, title: "Database backups", body: "Logical and physical backup strategies for a production database." },
  { _id: 5, title: "Running shoes reviewed", body: "Road and trail running shoes tested over 500 km." }]);
db.articles.createIndex({ title: "text", body: "text" },
  { weights: { title: 5, body: 1 }, name: "articles_text", default_language: "english" });

Searching, with each result's relevance score:

const S = q => db.articles.find({ $text: { $search: q } }, { score: { $meta: "textScore" }, title: 1 })
  .sort({ score: { $meta: "textScore" } }).toArray().map(d => d._id + ":" + d.score.toFixed(2)).join("  ");

run         -> 1:3.92  5:3.90  3:0.57  2:0.56
database    -> 4:4.33  1:3.33

"run" matched "Running", "running" and "runs" — the index stores stems, so word forms match. Articles 1 and 5 score highest because "Running" is in their (weighted) titles; 2 and 3 only have "runs" in the body. Note what didn't match: "runner" in article 2's body is a different stem, so article 2 matched only through "runs".

"production database" -> 4:4.92
running -shoes        -> 1:3.92  3:0.57  2:0.56
datab (partial)       ->
the (stop word)       ->
  • A quoted phrase must appear exactly (article 1 has both words, but not as the phrase "production database").
  • A minus excludes a term.
  • No partial words: "datab" matches nothing. Text indexes are not autocomplete.
  • Stop words ("the", "a", "and") aren't indexed, so searching for them returns nothing.

Space-separated terms are OR'ed (any term matches), with documents matching more terms scoring higher.

The plan is an index scan per term, OR'ed together, then fetched and matched:

text explain: "stage":"TEXT_MATCH","stage":"FETCH","stage":"OR","stage":"IXSCAN"

docs.title: Limits worth knowing
docs.text:
• One text index per collection. Creating a second fails — every text index has the same internal key pattern, so the server reports it as a conflict:
85 IndexOptionsConflict An equivalent index already exists with a different name and options. Requested index: { v: 2, key: { _fts: "text", _fts ...

Include every field you'll want to search in that one index (or use {"$**": "text"} for all string fields). - No fuzzy matching, typo tolerance, synonyms or autocomplete. - Scoring is simple term-frequency weighting, not a modern relevance model. - Stemming is per language (default_language, or a language field per document); "none" disables stemming and stop words.

For a search box that users will judge against web search engines, MongoDB offers a separate full-text engine built on Apache Lucene: Atlas Search on MongoDB Atlas, and in recent releases a self-managed search process (mongot) that brings the $search aggregation stage to Community and Enterprise deployments. It adds fuzzy matching, autocomplete, synonyms, facets and better relevance. It wasn't part of this course's lab setup, so it isn't demonstrated here; check MongoDB's current documentation for availability on your deployment type. Text indexes remain a good fit for simple keyword search inside an application: admin tools, internal search, tagging.

docs.title: Collation: language-aware comparison
docs.text:
By default, strings compare by their bytes (UTF-8 binary order). That's fast and predictable, and wrong for people:

db.people.insertMany([{ n: "émile" }, { n: "Zoe" }, { n: "adam" }, { n: "Émile" }, { n: "zoe" }, { n: "Adam" },
                      { n: "item10" }, { n: "item9" }]);
db.people.find().sort({ n: 1 })                                  // binary
db.people.find().sort({ n: 1 }).collation({ locale: "en" })      // English rules

binary sort:      Adam,Zoe,adam,item10,item9,zoe,Émile,émile
en sort:          adam,Adam,émile,Émile,item10,item9,zoe,Zoe

Binary order puts all capitals before all lower-case letters and accented letters after z. The English collation sorts the way a person expects. Add numericOrdering and digit sequences compare as numbers:

numericOrdering:  item9,item10

docs.title: Strength: what counts as "equal"
docs.text:
db.people.countDocuments({ n: "zoe" })                                                    // 1
db.people.countDocuments({ n: "zoe" }, { collation: { locale: "en", strength: 2 } })      // 2
db.people.countDocuments({ n: "emile" }, { collation: { locale: "en", strength: 1 } })    // 2

strength: 2 ignores case (zoe = Zoe); strength: 1 also ignores accents (emile = émile = Émile). The default is 3, which distinguishes both.

docs.title: Indexes must have the same collation
docs.text:
A case-insensitive lookup is only fast if an index with the same collation exists and the query asks for it:

db.people.createIndex({ n: 1 }, { collation: { locale: "en", strength: 2 }, name: "n_ci" });

query with matching collation: "stage":"FETCH","stage":"IXSCAN"
query without collation:       "stage":"COLLSCAN"
regex /^zoe$/i plan:           "stage":"COLLSCAN"

The query without a collation uses binary comparison, which the n_ci index can't answer. And the classic workaround, a case-insensitive regex, can't use an index efficiently at all.

The simplest way to make collation automatic is to set it on the collection; every index and query then defaults to it. Case-insensitive unique emails:

db.createCollection("users", { collation: { locale: "en", strength: 2 } });
db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true });
db.users.insertOne({ email: "Ana@Example.com" });
db.users.insertOne({ email: "ana@example.com" })              // 11000 duplicate key
db.users.countDocuments({ email: "ANA@EXAMPLE.COM" })          // 1

The alternative — storing a normalised emailLower field alongside the original — works everywhere and is easier to reason about across languages and tools; a collection collation is neater when the whole collection is about human-facing text.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A text index is a B-tree whose keys are (term, weight) pairs: when a document is indexed, each indexed string field is tokenised, lower-cased, stop words are dropped, each token is reduced to its stem with a Snowball stemmer for the document's language, and one key per distinct stem is written with a weight derived from the term's frequency and the field's weight. A $text query applies the same processing to the search string, does one index scan per stem (the OR of IXSCANs), and accumulates each document's score; phrases and negations are checked afterwards against the fetched document (TEXT_MATCH). Because the index stores whole stems, prefixes and typos can't be matched.

A collation is implemented with ICU, the Unicode library: each string is converted into a sort key — a byte string whose binary order is the collation order for that locale and strength. An index with a collation stores sort keys instead of raw strings, which is why equality and range scans on it are fast, and why a query must use the same collation to use the index: its comparison values have to be converted the same way. Sort keys at strength 2 don't encode case, so "Zoe" and "zoe" produce the same key — that's what makes the unique index above case-insensitive.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Promising "search" with a text index and then being asked for autocomplete and typo tolerance.
  • Trying to add a second text index instead of including all fields in one.
  • Searching for partial words ($text matches whole stems only).
  • Case-insensitive regex for lookups on large collections — use a collation index or a normalised field.
  • Index and query collations that differ, silently falling back to a collection scan.
  • Sorting user-visible names in binary order.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build a text index over a recipes collection (title weighted 10, ingredients 3, steps 1). Search for "tomato -garlic", for a phrase, and print the scores. Explain each score ordering.
  2. Insert some recipes with language: "spanish" and search them with $language: "spanish". What changes in the matched stems?
  3. Create a products collection with an English collation at strength 1 and a unique index on name. Which of "Café", "cafe", "CAFE" can coexist?
  4. Sort 1,000 strings like "file1" … "file1000" with and without numericOrdering and print the first 12 of each.
  5. Measure a case-insensitive lookup on 100,000 users three ways: /^…$/i regex, a collation index, and a normalised emailLower field with an ordinary index. Compare keys and documents examined.

docs.title: 10 · Project — Order Analytics Backend
docs.text: The Level 3 project builds the backend of a sales dashboard over the shop database from lesson 01. It pulls together most of the level: aggregation stages and expressions, a $lookup, a $facet dashboard with a window function, a $merge rollup, and a change-stream worker that keeps the rollup correct as orders change — with a test suite that proves the rollup always agrees with the raw data.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. A dashboard query for a date range (and optional city): total revenue and units, revenue by category, and daily revenue with a 7-day moving average. It runs every few seconds per open dashboard, so it must not scan raw orders.
  2. Best-selling products for a range, with product names.
  3. Days are Indian Standard Time days, everywhere.
  4. The dashboard must reflect changes within seconds: new deliveries, cancellations, returns, deletions, and late corrections to old orders.
  5. The numbers must be exactly right — the rollup must equal an aggregation over raw orders.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• daily_sales is a rollup keyed by {day, city, category} with units, revenue and distinct orders — the lesson 05 rollup plus an order count. The dashboard reads only this collection (requirement 1).
  • refresh_days(days) recomputes whole IST days. It deletes the days' rollup documents first, then re-runs the rollup pipeline for them with $merge. Deleting first fixes the "group became empty" edge case from lesson 05; working in whole days makes refreshes idempotent.
  • RollupWorker is a change-stream consumer on orders (lesson 07). For each batch of events it collects the IST days of the affected orders — from the post-image for inserts and updates and from the pre-image for deletes (and for updates that moved an order's date) — and refreshes just those days.
  • top_products aggregates raw orders (it's requested rarely) and uses $lookup with the concise localField/foreignField + pipeline form to fetch only product names (lesson 03).

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
analytics.py:

"""Level 3 project: an order-analytics backend over the `shop` database.

- daily_sales: rollup per (IST day, city, category), maintained with $merge
- RollupWorker: change-stream consumer that refreshes only the days that changed
- dashboard(): one $facet query over the rollup for the UI
- top_products(): best sellers joined with product names via $lookup
"""
import threading
from decimal import Decimal
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

from pymongo import MongoClient

TZ = "Asia/Kolkata"
IST = timezone(timedelta(hours=5, minutes=30))


def ist_day_start(dt):
    """Start of the IST calendar day containing dt, as a UTC datetime."""
    local = dt.astimezone(IST)
    return local.replace(hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0).astimezone(timezone.utc)


class Analytics:
    def __init__(self, client: MongoClient, db="shop"):
        self.db = client[db]

    # ---- rollup -------------------------------------------------------------
    def _rollup_pipeline(self, start, end):
        return [
            {"$match": {"status": "delivered", "placedAt": {"$gte": start, "$lt": end}}},
            {"$unwind": "$items"},
            {"$group": {"_id": {"day": {"$dateTrunc": {"date": "$placedAt", "unit": "day", "timezone": TZ}},
                                "city": "$city", "category": "$items.category"},
                        "units": {"$sum": "$items.qty"},
                        "revenue": {"$sum": {"$multiply": ["$items.qty", "$items.price"]}},
                        "orders": {"$addToSet": "$_id"}}},
            {"$set": {"orders": {"$size": "$orders"}}},
            {"$merge": {"into": "daily_sales", "on": "_id", "whenMatched": "replace", "whenNotMatched": "insert"}},
        ]

    def refresh_days(self, days):
        """Recompute the rollup for whole IST days (idempotent)."""
        for day in sorted(set(days)):
            start, end = day, day + timedelta(days=1)
            # remove the window first so groups that became empty disappear
            self.db.daily_sales.delete_many({"_id.day": {"$gte": start, "$lt": end}})
            self.db.orders.aggregate(self._rollup_pipeline(start, end))

    def rebuild(self):
        self.db.daily_sales.drop()
        first = self.db.orders.find_one(sort=[("placedAt", 1)])["placedAt"].replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
        last = self.db.orders.find_one(sort=[("placedAt", -1)])["placedAt"].replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
        self.db.orders.aggregate(self._rollup_pipeline(ist_day_start(first), ist_day_start(last) + timedelta(days=1)))

    # ---- queries ----------------------------------------------------------------
    def dashboard(self, start, end, city=None):
        match = {"_id.day": {"$gte": start, "$lt": end}}
        if city:
            match["_id.city"] = city
        res = list(self.db.daily_sales.aggregate([
            {"$match": match},
            {"$facet": {
                "totals": [{"$group": {"_id": None, "revenue": {"$sum": "$revenue"}, "units": {"$sum": "$units"}}}],
                "byCategory": [{"$group": {"_id": "$_id.category", "revenue": {"$sum": "$revenue"}}},
                               {"$sort": {"revenue": -1}}],
                "byDay": [{"$group": {"_id": "$_id.day", "revenue": {"$sum": "$revenue"}}}, {"$sort": {"_id": 1}},
                          {"$setWindowFields": {"sortBy": {"_id": 1}, "output": {
                              "ma7": {"$avg": "$revenue", "window": {"range": [-6, 0], "unit": "day"}}}}}],
            }}]))[0]
        dec = lambda v: v.to_decimal() if hasattr(v, "to_decimal") else Decimal(v)   # Decimal128 -> Decimal
        totals = res["totals"][0] if res["totals"] else {"revenue": 0, "units": 0}
        return {"revenue": dec(totals["revenue"]), "units": totals["units"],
                "byCategory": [{"category": c["_id"], "revenue": dec(c["revenue"])} for c in res["byCategory"]],
                "byDay": [{"day": d["_id"], "revenue": dec(d["revenue"]), "ma7": dec(d["ma7"])} for d in res["byDay"]]}

    def top_products(self, start, end, n=5):
        return list(self.db.orders.aggregate([
            {"$match": {"status": "delivered", "placedAt": {"$gte": start, "$lt": end}}},
            {"$unwind": "$items"},
            {"$group": {"_id": "$items.sku", "units": {"$sum": "$items.qty"}}},
            {"$sort": {"units": -1, "_id": 1}}, {"$limit": n},
            {"$lookup": {"from": "products", "localField": "_id", "foreignField": "_id",
                         "pipeline": [{"$project": {"_id": 0, "name": 1}}], "as": "p"}},
            {"$project": {"_id": 0, "sku": "$_id", "units": 1, "name": {"$first": "$p.name"}}},
        ]))


class RollupWorker(threading.Thread):
    """Watches `orders` and refreshes the rollup for the IST days touched by each batch of changes."""

    def __init__(self, analytics: Analytics):
        super().__init__(daemon=True)
        self.a = analytics
        self.stop_flag = threading.Event()
        self.ready = threading.Event()
        self.batches = 0

    def run(self):
        pipeline = [{"$match": {"operationType": {"$in": ["insert", "update", "replace", "delete"]}}}]
        with self.a.db.orders.watch(pipeline, full_document="updateLookup",
                                    full_document_before_change="whenAvailable",
                                    max_await_time_ms=200) as stream:
            self.ready.set()
            while not self.stop_flag.is_set():
                days = set()
                while (ch := stream.try_next()) is not None:
                    for doc in (ch.get("fullDocument"), ch.get("fullDocumentBeforeChange")):
                        if doc:
                            days.add(ist_day_start(doc["placedAt"].replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)))
                if days:
                    self.a.refresh_days(days)
                    self.batches += 1

    def stop(self):
        self.stop_flag.set()
        self.join()

docs.title: A failure on the way
docs.text:
The first version of dashboard() returned the rollup's values as they came from PyMongo, and one test failed:

E       TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'Decimal128' and 'int'
FAILED test_analytics.py::test_dashboard_shape - TypeError: '>' not supported...

bson.Decimal128 is a storage type, not a number: Python can't compare or add it. A backend should hand its callers real decimal.Decimal values (or strings, for JSON), so the final version converts every money value with to_decimal() at the boundary — the dec helper above.

docs.title: The tests
docs.text:
test_analytics.py regenerates nothing itself — run python shopgen.py from lesson 01 first. The module fixture enables pre-images on orders and rebuilds the rollup.

import random, time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from decimal import Decimal

import pytest
from bson import Decimal128
from pymongo import MongoClient

from analytics import Analytics, RollupWorker

client = MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0", tz_aware=True)
A = Analytics(client)
APR, JUL = datetime(2026, 3, 31, 18, 30, tzinfo=timezone.utc), datetime(2026, 6, 30, 18, 30, tzinfo=timezone.utc)


def raw_revenue_by_category(start, end):
    rows = client.shop.orders.aggregate([
        {"$match": {"status": "delivered", "placedAt": {"$gte": start, "$lt": end}}},
        {"$unwind": "$items"},
        {"$group": {"_id": "$items.category", "revenue": {"$sum": {"$multiply": ["$items.qty", "$items.price"]}}}}])
    return {r["_id"]: r["revenue"].to_decimal() for r in rows}


def rollup_revenue_by_category(start, end):
    return {r["category"]: r["revenue"] for r in A.dashboard(start, end)["byCategory"]}


@pytest.fixture(scope="module", autouse=True)
def built():
    client.shop.command("collMod", "orders", changeStreamPreAndPostImages={"enabled": True})
    A.rebuild()


def test_rollup_matches_raw():
    assert rollup_revenue_by_category(APR, JUL) == raw_revenue_by_category(APR, JUL)


def test_dashboard_shape():
    d = A.dashboard(APR, JUL, city="Pune")
    assert d["revenue"] > 0 and len(d["byCategory"]) == 4
    assert len(d["byDay"]) == 91                       # every IST day of April-June had Pune sales
    assert all("ma7" in x for x in d["byDay"])


def test_empty_range_returns_zero():
    d = A.dashboard(datetime(2030, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc), datetime(2030, 2, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc))
    assert d["revenue"] == 0 and d["byCategory"] == []


def test_top_products_have_names():
    top = A.top_products(APR, JUL, n=3)
    assert len(top) == 3 and all(t["name"] for t in top)
    assert top[0]["units"] >= top[1]["units"] >= top[2]["units"]


def test_worker_keeps_rollup_in_sync():
    w = RollupWorker(A); w.start(); w.ready.wait(5)
    r = random.Random(5)
    orders = client.shop.orders
    ids = [d["_id"] for d in orders.find({"placedAt": {"$gte": APR, "$lt": JUL}}, {"_id": 1})]
    for oid in r.sample(ids, 40):                      # status flips in both directions
        new = r.choice(["delivered", "cancelled", "returned"])
        orders.update_one({"_id": oid}, {"$set": {"status": new}})
    for oid in r.sample(ids, 5):
        orders.delete_one({"_id": oid})
    orders.insert_one({"_id": 999999, "customerId": "C0001", "city": "Pune", "status": "delivered",
                       "placedAt": datetime(2026, 5, 15, 12, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
                       "items": [{"sku": "P001", "category": "books", "qty": 2, "price": Decimal128(Decimal("500"))}]})
    deadline = time.time() + 10
    while time.time() < deadline:
        if rollup_revenue_by_category(APR, JUL) == raw_revenue_by_category(APR, JUL):
            break
        time.sleep(0.2)
    w.stop()
    assert rollup_revenue_by_category(APR, JUL) == raw_revenue_by_category(APR, JUL)
    assert w.batches >= 1

The important test is the last one. It starts the worker, then makes 40 random status changes, 5 deletions and one new delivered order, and waits (up to 10 seconds) for the rollup to agree with a fresh aggregation over raw orders, to the rupee, for every category.

docs.text:
a = Analytics(MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0", tz_aware=True))
APR, JUL = datetime(2026, 3, 31, 18, 30, tzinfo=timezone.utc), datetime(2026, 6, 30, 18, 30, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
d = a.dashboard(APR, JUL, city="Pune")

On a freshly generated dataset:

revenue: 34645411 units: 3431
byCategory: [('electronics', '30280520'), ('kitchen', '2316538'), ('toys', '1268685'), ('books', '779668')]
first days: [('2026-04-01', '490473'), ('2026-04-02', '783530'), ('2026-04-03', '668140')]
top: [{'units': 135, 'sku': 'P162', 'name': 'Books item 162'}, {'units': 128, 'sku': 'P140', 'name': 'Kitchen item 140'}, {'units': 127, 'sku': 'P047', 'name': 'Electronics item 47'}]

APR and JUL are midnight IST on 1 April and 1 July expressed in UTC (18:30 the previous day) — requirement 3 in practice. The first days' values are the 7-day moving averages, which are short windows at the start of the range.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Correctness comes from three properties working together.

Idempotent refresh. refresh_days doesn't add or subtract deltas; it recomputes a day from the source of truth and replaces whatever was there. Running it once, twice, or after a crash half-way through always converges on the right answer. That's what makes it safe to drive from an at-least-once event source.

Complete change capture. The worker must learn about every day whose numbers could have changed. Inserts and updates carry the new document (updateLookup); deletes carry nothing about the document except its _id — which is why the collection has pre-images enabled and the worker reads fullDocumentBeforeChange. An update that changes an order's placedAt affects two days, the old and the new, and pre- plus post-images give both.

Batching. The worker drains all available events, collects the distinct days, and refreshes each once. A burst of 1,000 changes to today's orders becomes one refresh of one day, not 1,000.

What this design doesn't yet do: persist its resume token (a restarted worker would miss changes made while it was down — lesson 07 shows the fix; a nightly full rebuild() is a cheap safety net), or survive running two workers at once (both would refresh the same days — harmless because refreshes are idempotent, but wasteful).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Applying deltas ($inc revenue on each event) instead of recomputing — any missed or duplicated event corrupts the rollup permanently.
  • Ignoring deletes because the change event has no document.
  • Mixing UTC and local days between the rollup, the refresh and the queries.
  • Returning Decimal128 to application code that expects numbers.
  • Testing a rollup only right after a rebuild, never after changes.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Persist the worker's resume token in a worker_state collection, updated after each batch, and resume from it on start. Test it by stopping the worker, making changes, and restarting.
  2. Add an orders count and average order value to dashboard()'s totals (the rollup's orders field counts distinct orders per day/city/category — think about why summing it across categories over-counts, and fix it).
  3. Add a customer_monthly rollup (customer, IST month → orders, revenue) maintained by the same worker, and a top_customers(month) query.
  4. Make top_products fast for wide date ranges by maintaining a daily_product_sales rollup instead of aggregating raw orders.
  5. Write a load test: a thread that updates 50 random orders per second for 30 seconds while the worker runs. Measure the maximum time between a change and the rollup reflecting it.

docs.title: Level 4 · Operations & Production
docs.text:
Levels 1–3 were about using MongoDB well. Level 4 is about running it: keeping data safe when machines fail, choosing the guarantees each operation needs, scaling past one machine, locking the doors, recovering from mistakes, and changing a live system without stopping it.

Every lesson breaks something on purpose and measures what the application saw. You'll kill a primary in the middle of a stream of writes and find the driver hid it completely — then turn off retryable writes and watch the same failure surface as an error. You'll force a rollback and find five acknowledged writes in a BSON file in the data directory. You'll see w: 3 beat w: "majority" (and learn why that's not the good news it looks like), a restore come back 42 units short of a bank's total because it skipped the oplog, a sharding balancer stop with the cluster "unbalanced" because the donor's counts included orphans, and a capstone acceptance script fail twice before passing — once because cluster users don't exist on shards, which had left every shard's localhost exception open.

Prerequisites: Levels 1–3. These lessons run several mongod processes at once (up to ten in the capstone), so close other labs and cap each server's cache with --wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 0.25. Python with PyMongo is used for anything involving concurrency or timing; OpenSSL for certificates.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Replica Sets: Elections, the Oplog & Failover — a three-node set, oplog entries read directly, step-down vs kill -9, retryable writes, and a real rollback.
  2. Write Concern, Read Concern & Read Preference — the price of each write concern, stale secondaries, causal sessions, and majority versus local reads.
  3. Sharding Architecture — mongos, config servers and shards; the routing table; targeted and broadcast queries; the balancer and orphans.
  4. Choosing & Changing a Shard Key — cardinality, frequency, monotonicity; indivisible chunks; unique indexes; reshardCollection and refineCollectionShardKey.
  5. Authentication, Roles & TLS — the localhost exception, built-in and custom roles, TLS and mutual TLS, x.509 users, and keyFile member authentication.
  6. Backup, Restore & Point-in-Time Recovery — consistent dumps under load, recovery to the operation before a bad deleteMany, and file-level copies.
  7. Monitoring & the Profiler — serverStatus, mongostat, mongotop, the slow-query log, the profiler, and killing runaway operations.
  8. Performance Tuning: WiredTiger, Memory & Connections — cache sizing and the working set, compression trade-offs, connection pools, and OS settings.
  9. Upgrades, FCV & Online Schema Migrations — rolling restarts under load, featureCompatibilityVersion, online index builds, and idempotent batched migrations.
  10. Capstone — A Secured Sharded Cluster — ten processes with TLS, keyFile and least-privilege roles, accepted by a 12-check script including a live failover.

docs.title: What wasn't run
docs.text: Managed services (MongoDB Atlas), Ops Manager and Cloud Manager, and Enterprise-only features (auditing, encryption at rest, LDAP and Kerberos authentication) aren't part of the Community server used here, so they are described where relevant but never shown with output. Only one server version was installed, so the version upgrade lesson performs the rolling procedure and FCV changes for real but not a binary swap between releases.

docs.title: After Level 4
docs.text: You've finished the course. The best next step is to take the capstone's acceptance-script idea back to a real system: write down what your MongoDB deployment is supposed to guarantee — durability, failover, access, recovery time — and write a test for each one. Related courses in the series: System Design for where MongoDB fits in larger architectures, Kubernetes and Docker for running it in containers, and PostgreSQL for the relational side of the same problems.

docs.title: 01 · Replica Sets: Elections, the Oplog & Failover
docs.text:
Every lab so far has used a single-node replica set — enough to unlock transactions and change streams, but with none of the reason replica sets exist. A real replica set is several mongod processes holding copies of the same data: one primary accepts writes, the secondaries copy them, and if the primary disappears the survivors elect a new one within seconds. This lesson builds a three-node set on one machine, reads the log that carries every change between nodes, and then breaks it on purpose: a clean step-down, a hard kill in the middle of a stream of writes, and a failure that makes acknowledged writes vanish.

Everything here ran on MongoDB 9.0.2 with PyMongo 4.18.3 on a laptop. Election timings depend on the defaults shown below, not on hardware, so yours should be close.

docs.title: Three nodes on one machine
docs.text:
Each member is an ordinary mongod with its own port, its own data directory and the same --replSet name:

mkdir -p n1 n2 n3
for p in 1 2 3; do
  mongod --replSet rs4 --port 2730$p --dbpath n$p --bind_ip 127.0.0.1 \
         --wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 0.25 --oplogSize 64 --logpath n$p.log &
done

--wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 0.25 stops three servers from each claiming half the laptop's memory (Lesson 08 explains the default), and --oplogSize 64 keeps the replication log small for a lab. The processes start but refuse writes until the set is initiated — once, on one member:

rs.initiate({_id: "rs4", members: [
  {_id: 0, host: "127.0.0.1:27301"},
  {_id: 1, host: "127.0.0.1:27302"},
  {_id: 2, host: "127.0.0.1:27303"}]})

{ ok: 1, ... }
127.0.0.1:27301 SECONDARY
127.0.0.1:27302 SECONDARY
127.0.0.1:27303 PRIMARY

All three started as secondaries; within a few seconds one called an election and won. Which one wins is not something to rely on — here it was the third. The host names in the config are what members use to reach each other and what drivers are told to connect to, so in a real deployment they must be names every client can resolve. 127.0.0.1 only works because everything is on one machine.

Applications connect with a seed list and the set name, never to one host:

mongodb://127.0.0.1:27301,127.0.0.1:27302,127.0.0.1:27303/?replicaSet=rs4

The driver contacts any seed, asks it for the current topology (hello), and from then on sends writes to whoever is primary and tracks changes itself. Any one reachable seed is enough.

docs.title: The settings that decide failover speed
docs.text:
const c = rs.conf()

{
  protocolVersion: Long('1'),
  electionTimeoutMillis: 10000,
  heartbeatIntervalMillis: 2000,
  catchUpTimeoutMillis: -1,
  chainingAllowed: true
}

Members send each other heartbeats every 2 seconds. A secondary that hasn't heard from a primary for electionTimeoutMillis — 10 seconds — calls an election. That number is the floor for unplanned failover: lowering it makes failover faster and false alarms (a GC pause, a busy network, a laptop going to sleep) more likely. chainingAllowed lets a secondary copy from another secondary instead of the primary.

docs.title: The oplog: replication is replaying a log
docs.text:
The primary records every write in a capped collection, local.oplog.rs; secondaries copy entries from it and apply them to their own data. A few writes:

const app = db.getSiblingDB("app")
app.stock.insertMany([{_id: "pen", qty: 10}, {_id: "ink", qty: 4}, {_id: "pad", qty: 7}])
app.stock.updateMany({}, {$inc: {qty: -1}})
app.stock.deleteOne({_id: "pad"})
db.getSiblingDB("local").oplog.rs.find({ts: {$gte: start}}).sort({$natural: 1})

c app.$cmd    {"create":"stock","idIndex":{"v":2,"key":{"_id":1},"name":"_id_"}}
c admin.$cmd  {"applyOps":[{"op":"i","ns":"app.stock",...,"o":{"_id":"pen","qty":10},...},{"op":"i",...
u app.stock   {"$v":2,"diff":{"u":{"qty":9}}}
u app.stock   {"$v":2,"diff":{"u":{"qty":3}}}
u app.stock   {"$v":2,"diff":{"u":{"qty":6}}}
d app.stock   {"_id":"pad"}

Four details explain most of replication's behaviour:

  • One updateMany became three entries, one per document. The oplog is per-document, so a multi-document update of a million documents is a million oplog entries — and a million things for every secondary to apply.
  • $inc: {qty: -1} was recorded as "set qty to 9". Oplog entries are rewritten into an idempotent form: applying the same entry twice gives the same result. That property lets a secondary that crashes mid-batch simply re-apply from a safe point.
  • The batched insert became one applyOps command containing all three inserts, applied atomically on secondaries.
  • The collection's own creation is an entry too. Index builds, drops and renames all replicate as commands.

A full entry also carries ts (a timestamp plus counter that orders every entry in the set), t (the election term), wall (wall-clock time), and for retryable writes the session id and txnNumber:

{ lsid: { id: UUID('6a4d4626-...') }, txnNumber: Long('2'), op: 'd', ns: 'app.stock',
  ui: UUID('768e247c-...'), o: { _id: 'pad' }, stmtId: 0,
  ts: Timestamp({ t: 1791829347, i: 6 }), t: Long('1'), v: Long('2'),
  wall: ISODate('2026-10-12T18:22:27.209Z') }

The oplog is capped by size, so it covers a window of time that depends on write volume. rs.printReplicationInfo() reports it; a secondary that falls further behind than that window cannot catch up and must be resynced from scratch. Size the oplog for hours or days of writes, not minutes.

docs.title: Failure 1: a planned step-down
docs.text:
A Python writer inserts a numbered document every 20 ms, timing each insert, while the primary is asked to step down — what happens during maintenance or a rolling upgrade:

client = MongoClient(URI, serverSelectionTimeoutMS=30000)
...
MongoClient(f"mongodb://127.0.0.1:{old}/?directConnection=true").admin.command("replSetStepDown", 30)

stepping down primary on port 27301 with replSetStepDown at t=2.00s
inserts acknowledged: 208, errors raised to the app: 0 []
longest single insert: 0.03s (started at t=0.00s)
new primary: 27302
documents stored: 208 | gaps in sequence: 0

Nothing visible happened. A stepping-down primary waits for a secondary to catch up, then that secondary wins an election immediately — no 10-second timeout, because nobody had to notice a failure. The slowest insert was the very first one (opening connections), not one during the switch.

docs.title: Failure 2: kill -9 the primary
docs.text:
Same writer; this time the primary process is killed with SIGKILL — a crash, a power cut, a kernel panic:

killing primary on port 27303 (pid 86990) with SIGKILL at t=2.00s
inserts acknowledged: 197, errors raised to the app: 0 []
longest single insert: 10.33s (started at t=2.00s)
new primary: 27301
documents stored: 197 | gaps in sequence: 0

The application saw no error, but one insert took 10.33 seconds. The new primary's log shows where the time went:

23:52:52.360  Starting an election, since we've seen no PRIMARY in election timeout period  10000
23:52:52.374  Election succeeded, assuming primary role
23:52:52.387  Transition to primary complete; database writes are now permitted

Ten seconds of noticing, then 27 ms of electing. Meanwhile the driver kept the in-flight insert waiting for a new primary (up to serverSelectionTimeoutMS) and then retried it once — retryable writes are on by default in modern drivers. The retry is safe because the write carries a session id and transaction number (visible in the oplog entry above): if the old primary had already applied it before dying, the new primary would recognise the number and not apply it twice.

The same test with retryWrites=false in the connection string:

killing primary on port 27302 (pid 86988) with SIGKILL at t=2.00s
inserts acknowledged: 172, errors raised to the app: 1 ['AutoReconnect']
longest single insert: 11.17s (started at t=2.04s)
new primary: 27303
documents stored: 172 | gaps in sequence: 1

Now the in-flight insert surfaced as an AutoReconnect error and left a gap. Worse, the application cannot know whether that write happened — here it didn't, but a write that reached the primary just before the kill would have replicated and been stored. Leave retryable writes on, and make sure anything you retry by hand is idempotent.

A restarted old primary simply rejoins as a secondary and copies what it missed:

127.0.0.1:27301 PRIMARY    2026-10-12T18:22:57.000Z
127.0.0.1:27302 SECONDARY  2026-10-12T18:22:57.000Z
127.0.0.1:27303 SECONDARY  2026-10-12T18:22:57.000Z

docs.title: Failure 3: acknowledged writes that disappear
docs.text:
What if the primary accepts writes that never reach a secondary, then dies? To force it: kill both secondaries, write with w: 1 (acknowledge as soon as the primary has it), kill the primary, and bring the two secondaries back first so they elect a leader from the data they have.

majority write ok                                  # _id 0, written while all three were up
both secondaries killed
w:1 acknowledged: 5 | still primary: true          # _id 1..5, acknowledged to the client
old primary killed
127.0.0.1:27301 PRIMARY
127.0.0.1:27302 (not reachable/healthy)
127.0.0.1:27303 SECONDARY
orders on new primary: [0]
new write with _id 1 ok                            # a different document, same _id

Five writes the client was told succeeded are not on the new primary, and an application has already reused one of their _ids. When the old primary restarts, it finds its history has diverged from the set's and rolls back:

Transition to ROLLBACK
Finding common point
...
Preparing to write deleted documents to a rollback file
Rolling back to the stable timestamp
Operations reverted by rollback
Rollback complete
Rollback summary
Transition to SECONDARY

orders on old primary now: [{"_id":0,"note":"before"},{"_id":1,"note":"written after failover"}]
n2/rollback/3e0fa3a6-82f5-4131-8eae-ac5f3a0d44ee/removed.2026-10-12T18-25-30.1.bson

The five documents are gone from the database; the only trace is a BSON file in the data directory:

bsondump --quiet n2/rollback/3e0fa3a6-*/removed*.bson

{"_id":{"$numberInt":"2"},"note":"w:1 only"}
{"_id":{"$numberInt":"3"},"note":"w:1 only"}
{"_id":{"$numberInt":"5"},"note":"w:1 only"}
{"_id":{"$numberInt":"4"},"note":"w:1 only"}
{"_id":{"$numberInt":"1"},"note":"w:1 only"}

Nobody is alerted; someone has to notice the file and decide what to do with it. The fix is not "watch for rollback files" but write concern majority: a write acknowledged by a majority is on a node that will win any future election, and cannot be rolled back. That is the next lesson's subject, and the reason majority is the default write concern since 5.0. This demonstration had to override it explicitly.

A first attempt that didn't roll back — and why it matters

The first version of this experiment paused the secondaries with SIGSTOP instead of killing them. The "w:1 only" writes — and even a majority write that failed with WriteConcernTimeout — all survived on the new primary: the secondaries' replication cursors had already been sent the data, which sat in socket buffers until the processes resumed. Two lessons: failure tests must actually cut the path, and a write-concern timeout does not mean the write failed — only that confirmation didn't arrive in time.

docs.title: Priorities, arbiters and hidden members
docs.text:
Members can be weighted. Giving one node priority: 2 makes it take over whenever it's healthy and caught up:

c.members[2].priority = 2; rs.reconfig(c)

Starting an election for a priority takeover
127.0.0.1:27303 PRIMARY

Other member options, briefly:

  • priority: 0 — never becomes primary (a node in a distant data centre, or a reporting node).
  • hidden: true (requires priority 0) — invisible to drivers; used for backups or analytics.
  • secondaryDelaySecs — a deliberately lagging copy, a safety net against a bad deleteMany (hidden, priority 0).
  • votes: 0 — doesn't vote. A set has at most 7 voting members (and 50 total).
  • Arbiters hold no data and only vote. They make a two-data-node set "elect-able", but a primary-plus-arbiter set with one secondary down can't acknowledge majority writes. Prefer three data-bearing members.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
MongoDB's replication protocol (protocol version 1) is a Raft-style consensus design. Time is divided into terms; each election increments the term, and each member votes at most once per term, for a candidate whose oplog is at least as up to date as its own. A candidate needs votes from a strict majority of voting members, which is why two halves of a partitioned set can never both elect a primary, and why a write acknowledged by a majority survives: any future majority must include at least one member that has it, and the up-to-date-log voting rule guarantees the winner has it too.

Secondaries pull: each runs an oplog fetcher that keeps a tailable, awaitData cursor open on its sync source's oplog, receives batches, and hands them to an applier that applies them in parallel (grouped so writes to the same document stay ordered). Each secondary reports how far it has applied back upstream; that's how the primary knows when a write has reached a majority and moves the majority commit point forward.

Rollback is the consequence of a primary accepting writes beyond the commit point. When a former primary rejoins, it compares its oplog with its sync source's, walks back to the last common entry, then uses WiredTiger's stable timestamp — a point no later than the majority commit point, which the storage engine can restore to directly — to discard everything after it, writing the affected documents to rollback files first. The sleep anecdote from building this lab is the same machinery seen from the other side: an earlier three-node lab left running on a laptop overnight had been through 104 elections by morning, because every sleep froze heartbeats for longer than 10 seconds.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Connecting to a single host instead of a seed list with replicaSet= — writes fail as soon as that host is no longer primary.
  • Two data nodes and no third voter. Losing either node loses the majority, so the survivor can't become primary.
  • Member host names clients can't resolve (container-internal names, localhost in a multi-machine set).
  • An oplog sized for minutes, so a secondary down for maintenance can't catch up and needs a full resync.
  • Turning off retryable writes, or retrying non-idempotent writes by hand.
  • Using w: 1 for data you can't afford to lose, and never checking for rollback files.
  • Treating WriteConcernTimeout as failure and re-inserting, creating duplicates.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build the three-node set. Run the kill test three times, killing a different member each time (including a secondary). How long is the stall when a secondary dies?
  2. Set electionTimeoutMillis to 2000 with rs.reconfig and repeat the kill test. Then pause the primary with kill -STOP for 3 seconds and resume it. What happened, and what does that tell you about low timeouts?
  3. Add a fourth member with priority: 0, hidden: true, secondaryDelaySecs: 120. Run deleteMany({}) on a collection and recover its documents from the delayed member within two minutes.
  4. Reproduce the rollback, then write a short script that restores the documents from the rollback file into an orders_recovered collection for human review.
  5. Insert one million small documents with insertMany, then run one updateMany({}, {$set: {flag: true}}). Check how many oplog entries it produced and how long the secondaries took to catch up (rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo()).

docs.title: 02 · Write Concern, Read Concern & Read Preference
docs.text:
Lesson 01 ended with five acknowledged writes being rolled back. Whether that can happen to your data is decided by three knobs that every MongoDB operation carries, whether you set them or not:

  • Write concern — how many members must have a write before the server says "done".
  • Read concern — which version of the data a read may return: the newest, or only what can never be rolled back.
  • Read preference — which member the driver sends a read to.

The defaults are sensible. This lesson measures what each alternative costs and shows, on the same three-node set, exactly what each one lets you see. All numbers come from MongoDB 9.0.2 and PyMongo 4.18.3 on a laptop where all three members share one SSD; on real networks the gaps between options grow, but their order doesn't.

docs.title: Write concern: the options and their price
docs.text:
client = MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27301,127.0.0.1:27302,127.0.0.1:27303/?replicaSet=rs4")
print("default write concern:", client.admin.command("getDefaultRWConcern")["defaultWriteConcern"])

def bench(label, wc, n=300):
    coll = db.get_collection("t", write_concern=wc)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    for i in range(n):
        coll.insert_one({"i": i})
    ...

bench("w=0 (unacknowledged)", WriteConcern(w=0))
bench("w=1", WriteConcern(w=1))
bench("w=1, j=true", WriteConcern(w=1, j=True))
bench("w=majority", WriteConcern(w="majority"))
bench("w=3", WriteConcern(w=3))

default write concern: {'w': 'majority', 'wtimeout': 0}
w=0 (unacknowledged)   300 inserts in    10.9 ms  (0.04 ms each)
w=1                    300 inserts in   131.6 ms  (0.44 ms each)
w=1, j=true            300 inserts in  2857.9 ms  (9.53 ms each)
w=majority             300 inserts in  2893.4 ms  (9.64 ms each)
w=3                    300 inserts in   288.5 ms  (0.96 ms each)

A second run gave the same shape (9.33 ms per majority insert, 1.04 ms per w=3). Reading it row by row:

  • w: 0 doesn't wait for any reply. The driver can't even tell you about a duplicate key. Almost never right.
  • w: 1 waits until the primary has applied the write in memory. Fast, and exactly what was rolled back in Lesson 01.
  • j: true waits for the primary's journal to be flushed to disk. That's where the time goes on this machine: about 9 ms per fsync.
  • w: "majority" costs the same as j: true, because with writeConcernMajorityJournalDefault: true (the default) a majority acknowledgement means "journaled on a majority".
  • w: 3 — all three members — was faster than majority, which surprises most people. A numeric w only waits for the members to apply the write, not to journal it; three in-memory copies are not the same as durable copies. If you want "every member, on disk", write {w: 3, j: true}.

This is why batching matters for durable writes: one insert_many of 300 documents pays for one majority acknowledgement, not 300. The transaction benchmark in Level 3 · 06 was the same effect.

docs.title: When members are missing
docs.text:
One secondary is killed, then each write concern is tried with a 3-second wtimeout:

for label, wc in [("w=majority", WriteConcern(w="majority", wtimeout=3000)),
                  ("w=3", WriteConcern(w=3, wtimeout=3000))]:
    try:
        db.get_collection("t", write_concern=wc).insert_one({"tag": label})
    except WriteConcernError as e:
        ...
print("documents tagged w=3 that exist anyway:", db.t.count_documents({"tag": "w=3"}))

w=majority: ok in 349 ms
w=3: WTimeoutError after 3015 ms -> {'w': 3, 'wtimeout': 3000, 'provenance': 'clientSupplied'}
documents tagged w=3 that exist anyway: 1

majority (two of three) still succeeds. w: 3 can't, and without wtimeout it would wait forever — the default wtimeout is 0, meaning no limit. And the failed write exists: it was applied on the primary and the surviving secondary. A write concern error means "I couldn't confirm the level you asked for", never "the write was undone". Code that re-inserts on WTimeoutError creates duplicates; use idempotent writes (upserts on a natural key) if you need to retry.

This is also why w should be majority rather than the number of members: it keeps working through the loss of a minority, which is the whole point of having replicas.

docs.title: Read preference: where reads go
docs.text:
By default every read goes to the primary, so you read what you (or anyone) last wrote. Read preferences primaryPreferred, secondary, secondaryPreferred and nearest let the driver use secondaries — and secondaries can be behind.

To make lag visible, the experiment freezes one secondary with fsync + lock, which stops it applying the oplog, and tags members so a read can be aimed at a specific node:

const c = rs.conf(); c.members.forEach((m, i) => m.tags = {node: "n" + (i + 1)}); rs.reconfig(c)

from_n1 = client.shop.get_collection("prices", read_preference=Secondary(tag_sets=[{"node": "n1"}]))

n1.admin.command("fsync", lock=True)                            # n1 stops applying the oplog
prices.update_one({"_id": "widget"}, {"$set": {"price": 120}})  # majority = primary + n2
print("primary:", prices.find_one()["price"], "| secondary n1:", from_n1.find_one()["price"])

primary: 120 | secondary n1: 100

The update succeeded with the default majority write concern — the primary and n2 were enough — and a read routed to n1 returned the old price. Nothing errors; the data is simply older. Real lag comes from heavy write bursts, a slow disk, an index build, or a member in another region.

Tag sets are also how you route reads deliberately — {dc: "mumbai"} for local reads, {use: "reporting"} for an analytics node — and maxStalenessSeconds tells the driver to skip secondaries estimated to be too far behind. It has a floor, which the driver enforces:

ConfigurationError maxStalenessSeconds must be at least heartbeatFrequencyMS + 10 seconds.
maxStalenessSeconds is set to 10, heartbeatFrequencyMS is set to 10000.

(The server-selection specification sets the minimum at 90 seconds.) It's a coarse guard against a badly lagging node, not a freshness guarantee.

docs.title: Causal consistency: reading your own writes from a secondary
docs.text:
A causally consistent session tracks the cluster time of your last operation and sends it with the next one as afterClusterTime. A member that hasn't reached that point waits rather than answering with older data:

with client.start_session(causal_consistency=True) as s:
    prices.update_one({"_id": "widget"}, {"$set": {"price": 130}}, session=s)
    try:
        from_n1.find_one({}, session=s, max_time_ms=2000)
    except ExecutionTimeout:
        print(...)
    ok = client.shop.get_collection("prices", read_preference=Secondary(tag_sets=[{"node": "n2"}]))
    print("causal read on caught-up n2:", ok.find_one({}, session=s)["price"])

causal read on lagging n1 waited, then timed out after 2.0s
causal read on caught-up n2: 130

The frozen secondary could not show this session its own write, so it blocked until max_time_ms expired; the caught-up one returned 130. Within one session you never go backwards in time — but only within that session, and the guarantee only holds across failures if writes use majority and reads use majority read concern.

docs.title: Read concern: newest or durable?
docs.text:
Both secondaries are now frozen and the primary takes a w: 1 write — the exact situation that produced a rollback in Lesson 01:

n2.admin.command("fsync", lock=True)
prices.with_options(write_concern=WriteConcern(w=1)).update_one({"_id": "widget"}, {"$set": {"price": 999}})
local = prices.with_options(read_concern=ReadConcern("local")).find_one()["price"]
major = prices.with_options(read_concern=ReadConcern("majority")).find_one()["price"]

on the primary -> local: 999 | majority: 130
after unlock -> majority: 999 | n1: 999

On the same server, at the same moment:

  • local (the default for reads) returned 999 — the newest data, which could still be rolled back.
  • majority returned 130 — the newest version acknowledged by a majority, which can never be rolled back.

Once the secondaries resumed and caught up, majority advanced to 999. Use majority reads when acting on data that must not "un-happen" — a payment status, an inventory reservation, anything you show the user as final.

The other levels: available (like local, relevant for sharded clusters where it can return orphaned documents), snapshot (a consistent point-in-time view, used in transactions — Level 3 · 06), and linearizable, which confirms with a majority that the primary is still primary before returning:

linearizable read on primary ok
NotWritablePrimary cannot satisfy linearizable read concern on non-primary node

It only works on the primary, adds a round trip, and should be paired with maxTimeMS.

docs.title: A sensible default set
docs.text:
Situation Write concern Read concern Read preference Most application data majority (default) local (default) primary (default) Must-not-lose and must-not-un-happen (payments, orders) majority majority primary Read-your-writes from secondaries majority majority secondary* + causal session Analytics / reports that tolerate minutes of lag n/a local secondary with tags Logs or metrics you can afford to lose w: 1 local primary

Reading from secondaries is not a free scaling strategy: every secondary applies every write, so read capacity added by secondaries comes with stale reads, and if one member fails the remaining ones must absorb its reads. Scale reads with indexes and caching first; scale writes with sharding (Lessons 03–04).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every write gets an oplog timestamp. Each secondary continuously reports to its sync source the timestamps it has applied, written to its journal, and so on; the primary combines these into a majority commit point — the newest timestamp that a majority of voting members have durably. A write waiting for w: "majority" is parked until the commit point passes its timestamp; a write waiting for w: 3 is parked until three members report having applied it.

Reads use WiredTiger's multi-version storage. A local read uses the newest data. A majority read uses a storage snapshot at the majority commit point — the server keeps enough old versions in its cache (and the history store) to serve it, which is why a set whose majority can't advance accumulates cache pressure. Causal consistency rides on the cluster time: every response carries operationTime, the driver remembers the largest it has seen in the session and sends it as afterClusterTime, and the receiving member waits until its own applied oplog has reached that timestamp. Read preference, finally, is purely client-side: the driver monitors every member (hello every heartbeatFrequencyMS, 10 seconds by default), keeps a round-trip average for each, and picks from eligible members within a latency window (localThresholdMS, 15 ms by default) of the fastest.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• w: <number of members> instead of majority, so one failed node stops all writes (or hangs them, with no wtimeout).
  • Treating WTimeoutError as failure and retrying a non-idempotent insert.
  • Believing w: 3 means three durable copies. Add j: true if that's what you need.
  • Reading from secondaries to "scale" and then being surprised by stale data, for example a user who doesn't see the comment they just posted.
  • Using majority writes but local reads for decisions that must not be reversed.
  • linearizable reads without maxTimeMS, which can hang during a partition.
  • Per-operation overrides scattered through code. Set concerns once on the client or collection and override rarely, on purpose.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Re-run the write-concern benchmark with insert_many batches of 100. How much does majority cost per document now?
  2. Change the cluster-wide default to w: 1 with setDefaultRWConcern, confirm getDefaultRWConcern reports it, and change it back. When would a cluster-wide override be justified?
  3. With one secondary frozen, run a loop that writes and immediately reads back from secondaryPreferred without a causal session. How often does the read miss the write? Repeat with a causal session.
  4. Write a function read_final_status(order_id) that returns an order's status only if it can never be rolled back. Prove it with the frozen-secondaries setup: a w: 1 status change must not be visible through it.
  5. Add a fourth member tagged {use: "reporting"} with priority: 0, and route an aggregation to it with a tag set. What happens to that aggregation when the reporting member is down, with secondary versus secondaryPreferred?

docs.title: 03 · Sharding Architecture
docs.text:
A replica set copies all the data to every member, so it scales reads (with caveats) and survives failures, but every member still has to hold — and write — everything. When one machine can no longer keep up with the data size or the write rate, MongoDB shards: it splits a collection by a shard key into ranges and spreads the ranges over several replica sets. Applications keep talking to what looks like one database.

This lesson builds a complete sharded cluster on one laptop, then looks at how it routes every query, what the "split pipeline" of an aggregation is, and how the balancer moves data around. The next lesson is about the decision that determines whether any of this works well: choosing the shard key.

Versions: MongoDB 9.0.2. Sharding behaviour changed substantially across 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (how chunks are split, how the balancer measures imbalance, how many chunks a new collection starts with); what follows is what this version did, and older material you find online may describe the previous rules.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
Component What it does In this lab Shards Each shard is a replica set holding a subset of the data. shA, shB, shC (single-node replica sets) Config servers A replica set storing the cluster's metadata: which shards exist, which collections are sharded, which ranges live where. cfg (one node) mongos Stateless router. Applications connect to it; it caches the routing table and forwards each operation to the right shard(s). port 27400

In production every shard and the config server set have three members each, and you run several mongos (often one per application host). For learning, single-node replica sets behave the same way for everything in this lesson.

docs.title: Building it
docs.text:
O="--bind_ip 127.0.0.1 --wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 0.25 --oplogSize 64"
mongod --configsvr --replSet cfg --port 27401 --dbpath cfg $O --logpath cfg.log &
mongod --shardsvr  --replSet shA --port 27411 --dbpath a   $O --logpath a.log &
mongod --shardsvr  --replSet shB --port 27412 --dbpath b   $O --logpath b.log &
mongod --shardsvr  --replSet shC --port 27413 --dbpath c   $O --logpath c.log &

(In zsh, write ${=O} instead of $O — zsh doesn't split variables into words, and mongod will refuse to start with one giant argument. That cost a failed first attempt here.)

Initiate each replica set — the config server's with configsvr: true — then start the router pointing at the config server set and register the shards through it:

// on 27401
rs.initiate({_id: "cfg", configsvr: true, members: [{_id: 0, host: "127.0.0.1:27401"}]})
// on 27411, 27412, 27413
rs.initiate({_id: "shA", members: [{_id: 0, host: "127.0.0.1:27411"}]})   // and shB, shC

mongos --configdb cfg/127.0.0.1:27401 --port 27400 --bind_ip 127.0.0.1 --logpath mongos.log &

// on 27400 (mongos)
sh.addShard("shA/127.0.0.1:27411"); sh.addShard("shB/127.0.0.1:27412"); sh.addShard("shC/127.0.0.1:27413")
db.adminCommand({listShards: 1}).shards.forEach(s => print(s._id, s.host))

shA shA/127.0.0.1:27411
shB shB/127.0.0.1:27412
shC shC/127.0.0.1:27413

From here on, everything goes through mongos. Connecting directly to a shard to read or write application data bypasses routing and is how people end up seeing duplicate or missing documents.

docs.title: Sharding a collection
docs.text:
Collections are not sharded by default — each unsharded collection lives entirely on its database's primary shard. Sharding one is a single command naming the key:

sh.shardCollection("shop.orders", {customerId: "hashed"})

The load script then inserted 200,000 orders (customerId 1–20,000, a city, a date, a total) in batches of 5,000:

inserted 200000 in 2942 ms

db.getSiblingDB("shop").orders.getShardDistribution()

Shard shC   docs: 68352, chunks: 1
Shard shA   docs: 67150, chunks: 1
Shard shB   docs: 64498, chunks: 1
Totals      docs: 200000, chunks: 3

A hashed key spreads documents by a hash of the value, so the collection was created with one chunk per shard and the inserts landed evenly from the first document.

docs.title: The routing table
docs.text:
The config database records each chunk — a contiguous range of shard-key values — and its owner:

cfg.chunks.find({uuid: coll.uuid}, {_id: 0, shard: 1, min: 1, max: 1, lastmod: 1}).sort({min: 1})

{ min: { customerId: MinKey() },                  max: { customerId: Long('-3074457345618258602') }, shard: 'shC', lastmod: Timestamp({ t: 1, i: 0 }) }
{ min: { customerId: Long('-3074457345618258602') }, max: { customerId: Long('3074457345618258602') }, shard: 'shA', lastmod: Timestamp({ t: 1, i: 1 }) }
{ min: { customerId: Long('3074457345618258602') },  max: { customerId: MaxKey() },                 shard: 'shB', lastmod: Timestamp({ t: 1, i: 2 }) }

For a hashed key the ranges are over the 64-bit hash, cut into thirds. MinKey and MaxKey are special BSON values smaller and larger than everything, so the ranges cover every possible value. To route customer 4242, mongos hashes it:

convertShardKeyToHashed(4242)

Long('-6212294558869892362')

That is below −3,074,457,345,618,258,602, so customer 4242 lives on shC. lastmod is the chunk's version; whenever ownership changes it increases, which is how routers and shards detect that a cached routing table is out of date.

docs.title: Targeted and broadcast operations
docs.text:
Every query falls into one of two classes, and explain on mongos shows which:

function ex(label, f) {
  const e = f(), qp = e.queryPlanner.winningPlan;
  const shards = (e.executionStats.executionStages.shards || []).map(s => s.shardName + ":" + s.totalDocsExamined);
  print(label, qp.stage, "returned", e.executionStats.nReturned, "examined per shard", JSON.stringify(shards));
}

find({customerId: 4242})                            SINGLE_SHARD      returned 11   examined per shard ["shC:11"]
find({customerId: {$in: [1, 2, 3]}})                SHARD_MERGE       returned 28   examined per shard ["shB:10","shA:18"]
find({customerId: {$lt: 50}})                       SHARD_MERGE       returned 512  examined per shard ["shC:109","shA:173","shB:230"]
find({city: 'Pune'}).sort({placedAt: -1}).limit(5)  SHARD_MERGE_SORT  returned 5    examined per shard ["shB:5","shA:5","shC:5"]
  • An equality on the shard key goes to exactly one shard (SINGLE_SHARD) — the only shard that can hold matching documents. This is the query shape a sharded cluster scales best.
  • An $in goes only to the shards owning those values — here two of the three.
  • A range on a hashed key can't be targeted: consecutive customer ids hash to scattered places, so every shard is asked. A range on a ranged key would be targeted (next lesson).
  • A query without the shard key is broadcast — "scatter-gather". With sort + limit, each shard returns its own top 5 and mongos merge-sorts them (SHARD_MERGE_SORT). The {city: 1, placedAt: -1} index existed on every shard, so each one examined only 5 documents.

Broadcast queries aren't wrong. They're fine for occasional reports; the problem is when the busiest query in the application is one, because then every shard does work for every request and adding shards adds no capacity for it.

Aggregations are split in two:

const agg = shop.orders.explain().aggregate([{$match: {city: "Pune"}}, {$group: {_id: "$items", revenue: {$sum: "$total"}}}])

aggregate split -> shardsPart: ["$match","$group"] mergerPart: ["$mergeCursors","$group"] merge on: router

Each shard runs $match and a partial $group; the router merges the partial groups with a second $group. Stages that need all the data at once (a $sort of everything, a $group on high-cardinality keys, some $lookups) move work to the merging side, which may be mongos or a chosen shard.

docs.title: The balancer, observed
docs.text:
To see data move, the next collection is sharded by range on a timestamp — a monotonically increasing key — with the chunk size lowered to 1 MB (the default is 128 MB; never do this in production):

cfg.settings.updateOne({_id: "chunksize"}, {$set: {value: 1}}, {upsert: true})
sh.shardCollection("logs.events", {ts: 1})
// insert 200,000 events with increasing ts

primary shard of logs: shB
after inserts      chunks ["shB:1"]                 | docs ["shB=200000"]
after 30s          chunks ["shA:7","shB:1","shC:7"] | docs ["shA=61159","shB=200000","shC=61159"]
after 60s          chunks ["shA:7","shB:1","shC:7"] | docs ["shA=61159","shB=200000","shC=61159"]

A range-sharded empty collection starts as one chunk on the primary shard, so all 200,000 inserts went to shB. Within 30 seconds the balancer had moved fourteen ranges to shA and shC — and then stopped, with the cluster still unbalanced by these counts. Two separate things are going on:

1. The donor still holds the moved documents. Those per-shard counts come from $collStats, which counts what is physically stored. After a migration commits, the documents left behind on the donor are orphans, removed later by a background range deleter:

countDocuments via mongos: 200000 | estimatedDocumentCount via mongos: 322318
shB local count: 200000
pending range deletions on shB: 14
orphanCleanupDelaySecs: 3600

countDocuments through mongos is correct, because each shard filters out documents it doesn't own. estimatedDocumentCount reads collection metadata and counts orphans, overstating by 122,318. On this version the range deleter waits an hour (orphanCleanupDelaySecs) before deleting, so queries still running against the old owner can finish.

2. The balancer balances data size, not chunk counts. In recent versions it compares each shard's amount of data for a collection and only migrates when the difference exceeds a threshold derived from the chunk size; chunks are split as part of migrating. With shA and shC each holding about 61,000 documents and shB owning the rest, the remaining difference was under the threshold.

New writes show the real problem with this key:

shA returned 0
shC returned 0
shB returned 10000

Every new event has a larger ts than anything before it, so all 10,000 fell into the last range — ts up to MaxKey — owned by shB. With a monotonically increasing key, one shard takes all inserts, and the balancer spends its life moving yesterday's data away from it. That is the central lesson of shard-key choice.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
mongos holds a cached copy of each sharded collection's routing table, loaded from the config servers. Every operation it sends carries the shard version it believes is current. The receiving shard compares that with the version it knows; if the router is behind — because a migration just changed ownership — the shard rejects the operation with a stale-config error, the router refreshes its table and retries. That's why routers can be stateless and why there's no global lock on routing: correctness is checked at the shard on every request.

A migration copies a range from donor to recipient while the donor keeps serving reads and writes, streams the changes made meanwhile, then enters a brief critical section where writes to that range block, commits the new ownership to the config servers (bumping the version), and leaves the critical section. Queries arriving with the old version are bounced and retried. The donor's copy then becomes orphaned and is scheduled for deletion. The balancer itself runs on the config server primary, in rounds, choosing a donor/recipient pair per collection and issuing these moves.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sharding too early. A sharded cluster is several replica sets plus config servers plus routers to operate. Vertical scaling, indexes and schema fixes come first.
  • Connecting applications to shards directly instead of to mongos.
  • Trusting estimatedDocumentCount or per-shard stats on a cluster with recent migrations.
  • Making the busiest query a broadcast, then adding shards that don't help it.
  • Monotonically increasing range keys (timestamps, ObjectIds, sequence numbers) for insert-heavy collections.
  • Tiny chunk sizes copied from tutorials into production, causing endless migrations.
  • Ignoring the primary shard: unsharded collections in a database all live there and can make it the hottest node.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build the cluster and shard shop.orders on {customerId: "hashed"}. Use explain to find a query shape that is targeted to two shards.
  2. Run find({customerId: 4242, city: "Pune"}) and find({city: "Pune"}) from 10 parallel clients for 30 seconds each. Compare throughput. Then stop one shard and run each again. What does each query do?
  3. With the 1 MB chunk size, watch logs.events for longer and record when the balancer next moves data. Lower orphanCleanupDelaySecs (lab only) and confirm shB's local count drops.
  4. Use sh.moveChunk (or moveRange) to move a range of logs.events by hand. Read the donor's log for the critical section duration.
  5. Explain an aggregation with a $sort on total followed by $limit: 10, and one with $group on customerId. Where does each pipeline split, and which does more work on the merging side?

docs.title: 04 · Choosing & Changing a Shard Key
docs.text:
The shard key decides three things at once: where each document lives, which shards each query must ask, and where each new write lands. A good key spreads writes, keeps the common queries on one shard, and lets data divide into as many pieces as you'll ever need. A bad key creates one overloaded shard, broadcasts every query, or produces chunks too big to move — and before MongoDB 5.0 it was effectively permanent.

This lesson evaluates keys against the criteria, then runs every failure and remedy on the cluster from Lesson 03 (MongoDB 9.0.2, three shards, shop.orders with 200,000 orders from 20,000 customers).

docs.title: The three properties
docs.text:
Cardinality — how many distinct values the key can have. Each chunk holds a range of key values, and a chunk containing a single value can't be split. A key with 8 possible values can never be spread across more than 8 chunks, however much data arrives.

Frequency — how evenly documents are distributed over those values. If 40% of orders come from one enterprise customer, customerId alone puts 40% of the data in a single unsplittable value.

Monotonicity — whether new values always increase (timestamps, ObjectIds, auto-increment numbers). Range sharding on a monotonic key sends every insert to the chunk ending at MaxKey, on one shard. Lesson 03 showed it: 10,000 new events, all 10,000 on shB.

And the property people forget: query isolation. The key should appear in the equality filters of the application's most frequent queries, so they target one shard.

docs.title: Low cardinality: chunks that can't be divided
docs.text:
lab.bycity is the orders data sharded on {city: 1} — eight cities, each with about 21,500 orders — with the lab's 1 MB chunk size:

Bengaluru:21577 Chennai:21417 Delhi:21372 Hyderabad:21421 Jaipur:21331 Kochi:21468 Kolkata:21719 Pune:21550

shC  MinKey     -> Chennai
shB  Chennai    -> Delhi
shB  Delhi      -> Hyderabad
shC  Hyderabad  -> Jaipur
shB  Jaipur     -> Kochi
shA  Kochi      -> Pune
shA  Pune       -> MaxKey

Each city's orders are about 2 MB — double the chunk size — yet asking MongoDB to split a one-city chunk fails:

sh.splitFind("lab.bycity", {city: "Chennai"})

split Chennai chunk: CannotSplit - Unable to find median in chunk because chunk is indivisible.

Every document in that chunk has city: "Chennai"; there is no boundary to cut at. At production scale these become jumbo chunks: too large to migrate, so they stay wherever they are, and a popular city's shard grows without limit. Adding shards beyond the number of distinct values achieves nothing.

docs.title: Comparing candidate keys for orders
docs.text:
The application's main queries are "orders for customer X" and "customer X's orders in a date range". Four candidates:

Key Write distribution "Orders for customer X" "Customer X, last 30 days" Divisibility {_id: 1} (ObjectId) all inserts to one shard (monotonic) broadcast broadcast fine {city: 1} 8 hot spots broadcast broadcast 8 chunks max {customerId: "hashed"} even one shard one shard fine, but no range targeting on customerId {customerId: 1, placedAt: 1} spread across customers one shard one shard fine — a big customer splits by date

The compound key wins for this workload: customerId gives distribution and isolation, and placedAt as a suffix lets one very active customer's orders be split by time, solving the frequency problem. {customerId: "hashed"} is a reasonable runner-up and the safer choice if customer ids were themselves monotonic (assigned sequentially to new sign-ups who then order heavily).

docs.title: Changing your mind: reshardCollection
docs.text:
shop.orders was sharded on {customerId: "hashed"} in Lesson 03. Resharding to the compound key is one command, run through mongos — but the first attempt failed:

db.adminCommand({reshardCollection: "shop.orders", key: {customerId: 1, placedAt: 1}})

MongoServerError: Recipient shard shB reached an unrecoverable error :: caused by :: can't shard collection
'shop.orders' with unique index on { customerId: 1, orderNo: 1 }, proposed shard key { customerId: 1, placedAt: 1 }
and collation {}. Uniqueness can't be maintained unless shard key is a prefix and has simple collation

A unique index created earlier (below) was valid for the old key but not the new one. After dropping it:

reshard ok: 1 in 332184 ms
new key: {"customerId":1,"placedAt":1}
count: 200000

Five and a half minutes for 200,000 small documents is not the copy speed — it's a deliberate floor. While it ran, $currentOp showed each shard both donating and cloning:

shB cloning elapsed Long('183') remaining est Long('166') copied Long('69752')
shB donating-initial-data elapsed Long('183') ...
minimum duration ms: 300000

reshardingMinimumOperationDurationMillis is 300,000 on this version: resharding takes at least five minutes so that the oplog the recipients must catch up on stays bounded. Afterwards the collection had 30 chunks per shard and the queries were targeted as designed:

find({customerId: 4242})                                SINGLE_SHARD  returned 10    ["shB:10"]
find({customerId: {$gte: 100, $lt: 150}})               SINGLE_SHARD  returned 493   ["shC:493"]
find({customerId: 4242, placedAt: {$gte: 2026-06-01}})  SINGLE_SHARD  returned 6     ["shB:6"]
find({placedAt: {$gte: 2026-09-01}})                    SHARD_MERGE   returned 20035 ["shA:59747","shB:69752","shC:70501"]
