The customer range query that was a broadcast under the hashed key is now single-shard. The date-only query is still a broadcast — and examined every document on every shard because no index starts with placedAt. No key serves every query; choose for the frequent ones and index for the rest.

Resharding rewrites the entire collection: each recipient needs room for its new share, there's extra write load throughout, and writes are blocked during a short critical section at the end — if it can't finish within reshardingCriticalSectionTimeoutMillis (5,000 ms on this version) the whole operation is aborted. Plan it for a quiet period on a cluster with headroom.

docs.title: A cheaper change: refining the key
docs.text:
If the key is right but not divisible enough, refineCollectionShardKey appends fields, without moving data. For logs.events on {ts: 1}:

refine without index: InvalidOptions - Please create an index that starts with the proposed shard key before refining the collection's shard key.
refine ok: 1 | key now {"ts":1,"level":1}
refine changing prefix: InvalidOptions - refineCollectionShardKey shard key { level: 1, ts: 1 } does not extend the current shard key { ts: 1, level: 1 }

It needs a supporting index, and it can only extend the existing key as a suffix. Refining helps a key with frequency problems (many documents per value) become splittable. It does nothing for monotonicity: {ts, level} still sends every new event to the last chunk.

docs.title: Rules that come with a shard key
docs.text:
Unique indexes must start with the shard key. Each shard enforces uniqueness only on its own data, so a cluster-wide unique constraint is only possible when equal values are guaranteed to live on the same shard:

CannotCreateIndex: ... cannot create index with 'unique' or 'prepareUnique' option over { orderNo: 1 } with shard
key pattern { customerId: "hashed" } and collation {}
unique {customerId: 1, orderNo: 1}: "customerId_1_orderNo_1"

An order number unique per customer was allowed; globally unique wasn't. For globally unique values on a sharded collection, use _id (unique per shard plus generated values like ObjectIds that don't collide), or a separate small collection sharded on the unique field as a "claim" table.

A document's shard key value can change, and the document moves to the owning shard:

before: 4242 on [ 'shC' ]
set customerId to 4247 (hashed 3529713213878061024) modified: 1 | now on [ 'shB' ]

The update had to be a retryable write or run in a transaction. Through PyMongo with retryWrites=false:

20 None - Plan executor error during update :: caused by :: Must run update to shard key field in a
multi-statement transaction or with retryWrites: true.
inside a transaction: ok, now 4242

Under the hood it's a delete on one shard and an insert on another, which must be atomic. It works, but if your design changes key values often, the key is probably wrong.

Single-document operations without the shard key (updateOne({_id: ...})) are accepted on recent versions — updateOne by _id only, modified: 1 — but mongos has to ask every shard to find the document. Include the shard key in filters on hot paths.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A shard key value maps to exactly one chunk because chunks are contiguous, non-overlapping ranges over the key's sort order (or over the 64-bit hash for hashed keys) covering MinKey to MaxKey. A split can only place a boundary between two distinct key values, which is why a range holding one value is indivisible, and why appending a field (refining) creates new possible boundaries: {city: "Chennai", customerId: 17} and {city: "Chennai", customerId: 18} are distinct values of {city, customerId}.

Resharding builds the new layout alongside the old. The coordinator (on the config server primary) chooses new chunk boundaries from a sample of the data; each recipient shard creates a temporary collection, clones its share from every donor at a fixed timestamp, then tails every donor's oplog to apply changes made since. When the recipients are caught up and the minimum duration has passed, donors block writes briefly, recipients apply the last changes, and the coordinator atomically swaps the temporary collections in and installs the new routing table. The old collection's data is then dropped. That's why it needs roughly double the space while it runs.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sharding on a timestamp or ObjectId with range sharding for an insert-heavy collection.
  • Low-cardinality keys (status, country, type) that cap the number of chunks and create jumbo chunks.
  • A key absent from the main queries, turning the hottest path into a broadcast.
  • Hashing a key you need ranges on, losing range targeting.
  • Forgetting unique indexes when planning a reshard — or designing on globally unique secondary fields.
  • Resharding a cluster without headroom in disk and write capacity.
  • Picking the key from the schema, not the workload. Pull the real query mix (profiler, slow logs, $queryStats where available) before deciding.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. For a ride-hailing trips collection (fields: tripId, riderId, driverId, city, startedAt, status), list the three most frequent queries you'd expect, then propose and justify a shard key. What goes wrong with {city: 1, startedAt: 1}?
  2. Shard a copy of the orders on {_id: 1} (ObjectIds) and insert 50,000 new orders. Show where they land. Then reshard to {_id: "hashed"} and repeat.
  3. Create a data set where one customerId has 30% of all orders. Shard on {customerId: 1} with a small chunk size and find the indivisible chunk. Fix it with refineCollectionShardKey and show it splitting.
  4. Implement globally unique orderNo on a collection sharded by customerId, using a second collection sharded on orderNo and a transaction that inserts into both.
  5. Run reshardCollection while a writer inserts continuously. Measure the writer's longest pause and look in the logs for the critical section.

docs.title: 05 · Authentication, Roles & TLS
docs.text:
Every lab in this course so far has run without authentication, bound to 127.0.0.1. That is fine on a laptop and catastrophic anywhere else: for years, automated scanners have found MongoDB servers exposed to the internet with no authentication, copied or deleted their data, and left ransom notes in its place. None of those attacks needed an exploit — only a server that accepted connections from anyone and trusted everyone who connected.

This lesson turns on the three defences that matter most — authentication (who are you?), authorization (what may you do?) and encryption in transit (can anyone read or alter the traffic?) — and shows the exact errors you'll hit along the way, because most of the real work of securing MongoDB is understanding those errors. Everything ran on MongoDB 9.0.2 Community with OpenSSL 4.0 for certificates. Passwords in the examples are throwaway lab values; in real use, prompt for them (passwordPrompt() in mongosh) or load them from a secret store.

docs.title: Turning on authentication
docs.text:
Start mongod with --auth (or security.authorization: enabled in the config file):

mongod --port 27501 --dbpath db --bind_ip 127.0.0.1 --auth --logpath sec.log &

There are no users yet, so nothing is permitted:

before any user: Unauthorized - not authorized on shop to execute command { find: "orders", filter: {}, limit: 1, ... }

The localhost exception solves the chicken-and-egg problem: while a server has no users, a client connecting from the same machine may create one user in the admin database. Make it a user administrator, not an all-powerful root:

db.getSiblingDB("admin").createUser({user: "ops", pwd: passwordPrompt(),
                                     roles: ["userAdminAnyDatabase", "clusterMonitor"]})

created first user through the localhost exception
second createUser without auth: Unauthorized

The exception closed the moment the first user existed. From now on, even on localhost, you must authenticate.

docs.title: Users live in a database
docs.text:
A user is defined in an authentication database — admin for administrators, or the application's own database — and its roles can grant privileges on any database:

const shop = db.getSiblingDB("shop")
shop.createUser({user: "shop_app", pwd: passwordPrompt(), roles: [{role: "readWrite", db: "shop"}]})

Clients must name the authentication database when they connect (authSource, or the path in the URI):

mongodb://shop_app:<password>@127.0.0.1:27501/shop
mongodb://ops:<password>@127.0.0.1:27501/admin

Passwords are stored as SCRAM credentials (salted, iterated hashes), never in plain text:

["SCRAM-SHA-1","SCRAM-SHA-256"]

A failed login is logged with the mechanism and reason — useful when debugging, and worth alerting on in bulk:

"msg":"Failed to authenticate","attr":{"client":"127.0.0.1:54067", ... "mechanism":"SCRAM-SHA-256",
"user":"reporter","db":"shop","error":"AuthenticationFailed: SCRAM authentication failed, storedKey mismatch"}

docs.title: What the built-in roles actually allow
docs.text:
Roles are often assigned by name without anyone checking what the name permits. Three surprises from this lab:

ops (userAdminAnyDatabase) inserting: Unauthorized
shop_app reading admin.system.users: Unauthorized
shop_app dropped orders?  [ 'customers' ]
  • userAdminAnyDatabase can't read or write data, only manage users and roles. But it can grant itself any role — it is effectively root with one extra step, so guard it as carefully.
  • readWrite includes dropping collections. The application user deleted the whole orders collection with one call. If your application never drops collections, readWrite is more than it needs.
  • Users in one database can't see another's data unless granted — the app user can't read admin.

The common built-in roles:

Role Scope Can read / readWrite one database query / query, insert, update, delete, create and drop collections and indexes dbAdmin one database indexes, stats, profiler, validation — but not read data userAdmin / userAdminAnyDatabase one / all databases create users and roles, grant roles (including to itself) clusterMonitor cluster read-only monitoring commands (serverStatus, replSetGetStatus, …) backup / restore cluster what mongodump / mongorestore need root everything everything

docs.title: Custom roles for least privilege
docs.text:
A reporting service should read orders and nothing else. A custom role lists exact actions on exact resources:

shop.createRole({role: "ordersReporter",
  privileges: [{resource: {db: "shop", collection: "orders"}, actions: ["find"]}],
  roles: []})
shop.createUser({user: "reporter", pwd: passwordPrompt(), roles: ["ordersReporter"]})

reporter find orders: 2
reporter find customers: Unauthorized
reporter update orders: Unauthorized
200
reporter $lookup into customers: Unauthorized

The find action covers queries and aggregation on that collection (the 200 is a $group total), but a $lookup into customers is refused: every collection a pipeline reads is checked. Writing roles this narrowly takes a few minutes per service and turns a leaked credential from "attacker has the database" into "attacker can read one collection".

A sensible set for most applications:

  • one user administrator (stored in a password manager, rarely used);
  • one application user per service, with a custom role covering only the collections and actions it uses (often find, insert, update, remove — without dropCollection);
  • a migration user with index and collection management, used only by the deploy pipeline;
  • read-only users for humans and reporting; backup for the backup job; clusterMonitor for monitoring.

docs.title: TLS: encrypting the connection
docs.text:
Without TLS, every query, result and SCRAM exchange crosses the network in readable form. A lab certificate authority and server certificate with OpenSSL — the server's certificate must name the host clients will use, in its Subject Alternative Name:

openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 30 -subj "/CN=Lab CA" -keyout ca.key -out ca.pem
openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -subj "/CN=127.0.0.1" -keyout server.key -out server.csr
printf "subjectAltName=IP:127.0.0.1,DNS:localhost\nextendedKeyUsage=serverAuth" > san.ext
openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -days 30 -extfile san.ext -out server.crt
cat server.crt server.key > server.pem

mongod --port 27502 --dbpath tlsdb --bind_ip 127.0.0.1 --tlsMode requireTLS \
       --tlsCertificateKeyFile server.pem --tlsCAFile ca.pem --logpath tls.log &

Then four attempts to connect, each failing for a different, instructive reason:

--- plain connection:
MongoServerSelectionError: connection <monitor> to 127.0.0.1:27502 closed
--- TLS without trusting the CA:
MongoNetworkError: unable to get local issuer certificate
--- TLS with CA:
MongoServerSelectionError: connection <monitor> to 127.0.0.1:27502 closed

The first is requireTLS refusing plain text. The second is the client refusing a certificate signed by an authority it doesn't trust — exactly what should happen. The third is the surprise: the client trusted the server, but the server's log says why it hung up:

"msg":"SSL peer certificate validation failed; connection rejected","attr":{"error":"No SSL certificate provided by peer"}

Giving mongod a --tlsCAFile also makes it require client certificates signed by that CA. That's a strong setting (mutual TLS) but it's a choice. If clients should authenticate with passwords over TLS instead, add --tlsAllowConnectionsWithoutCertificates. And the CA file can't simply be left out — this version refuses to start:

"errmsg":"The use of TLS without specifying a chain of trust is no longer supported. See https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-72839 for details."

Host name verification is the other half of TLS. A server whose certificate names db.lab.internal, reached as 127.0.0.1:

MongoServerSelectionError: Hostname/IP does not match certificate's altnames: IP: 127.0.0.1 is not in the cert's list:
--- same with tlsAllowInvalidHostnames:
connected 9.0.2

tlsAllowInvalidHostnames (and its cousin tlsAllowInvalidCertificates) make the error go away by turning off the check that stops a man-in-the-middle. Fix the certificate or the connection string instead.

docs.title: x.509: certificates as identities
docs.text:
With mutual TLS in place, the client certificate can be the credential. A certificate for a service:

openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -subj "/O=Lab/OU=apps/CN=billing-svc" -keyout client.key -out client.csr
printf "extendedKeyUsage=clientAuth" > cli.ext
openssl x509 -req -in client.csr -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -days 30 -extfile cli.ext -out client.crt
cat client.crt client.key > client.pem
openssl x509 -in client.pem -noout -subject -nameopt RFC2253

subject=CN=billing-svc,OU=apps,O=Lab

The user is created in the virtual $external database, named by the certificate's subject exactly as RFC 2253 prints it:

db.getSiblingDB("$external").createUser({user: "CN=billing-svc,OU=apps,O=Lab",
                                         roles: [{role: "read", db: "billing"}]})

mongodb://127.0.0.1:27502/?tls=true&tlsCAFile=ca.pem&tlsCertificateKeyFile=client.pem&authMechanism=MONGODB-X509&authSource=$external
[ { user: 'CN=billing-svc,OU=apps,O=Lab', db: '$external' } ]

No password exists to leak; revoking access means removing the user or letting the certificate expire. The cost is running a certificate authority properly — issuing, rotating and revoking. (This TLS server ran without --auth to keep the experiment focused on TLS; in production you'd combine both.)

docs.title: Replica sets and clusters: member authentication
docs.text:
Members of a replica set or sharded cluster must authenticate to each other. With --auth, that's not optional:

BadValue: security.keyFile is required when authorization is enabled with replica sets

The simplest mechanism is a keyFile: a shared secret every member reads.

openssl rand -base64 756 > keyfile && chmod 400 keyfile
mongod --replSet rs4 --keyFile keyfile ...      # --keyFile implies --auth

Every mongod and mongos in the deployment needs the same file. In production, x.509 member certificates (--clusterAuthMode x509) are stronger: no shared secret, and each member has its own identity. Lesson 10 builds a cluster with keyFile auth end to end.

docs.title: Beyond the basics
docs.text:
• Network exposure is the first control: bindIp only on private interfaces, firewall rules or security groups allowing only application hosts, never a public address.
  • Encryption at rest (WiredTiger's encrypted storage engine), auditing, LDAP and Kerberos authentication are MongoDB Enterprise / Atlas features — not in the Community server used here, so not demonstrated. Community deployments usually rely on encrypted disks at the OS or cloud level.
  • Client-side field level encryption and Queryable Encryption encrypt chosen fields in the driver so the server never sees plaintext; they need extra libraries and key management, and parts depend on edition and version — check current documentation before designing around them.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
SCRAM (Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism) never sends the password. The server stores a salt, an iteration count, and two keys derived from the password (StoredKey, ServerKey). On login the client and server exchange nonces; the client proves it knows the password by sending a proof computed from the salted password and the conversation, and the server proves it knows the stored credential by returning a signature the client checks. A stolen user document allows offline guessing (which the salt and iterations slow down) but not direct login — that's what "storedKey mismatch" in the log refers to.

After authentication the connection has a set of users, each with roles; roles resolve (recursively, through inherited roles) into privileges — pairs of a resource (cluster, database, collection) and a list of actions. Every command declares which actions on which resources it needs; before running it, the server checks the connection's privilege set. An aggregation's check includes every namespace it touches, which is why the $lookup failed. TLS happens a layer below all of this: the TLS handshake (certificate validation on both sides when client certificates are required) completes before MongoDB's wire protocol starts, so a failed handshake never reaches authentication at all — which is why the "TLS with CA" attempt showed only a closed connection on the client and the real reason only in the server log.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Exposing mongod on a public address, with or without auth.
  • Giving applications root or dbOwner, or one shared user for every service.
  • Assuming readWrite is harmless — it can drop collections.
  • Treating userAdminAnyDatabase as low-risk. It can grant itself anything.
  • Disabling host name or certificate checks (tlsAllowInvalidHostnames, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates) to silence errors.
  • Forgetting the authentication database (authSource), then debugging "Authentication failed" for an hour.
  • Passwords in connection strings committed to git, or special characters in passwords not URL-encoded.
  • Copying one keyFile into a container image shared across environments.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Start a fresh mongod --auth, create the user administrator through the localhost exception, and confirm you can't create a second user without logging in.
  2. Write a custom role shopService with find, insert, update and remove on shop.orders and find on shop.products — and nothing else. Prove that it can't drop a collection, create an index, or read customers.
  3. Rotate the shop_app password with db.changeUserPassword while a Python client stays connected. Do existing connections break? Do new ones work with the old password?
  4. Set up TLS with a CA, a server certificate and --tlsAllowConnectionsWithoutCertificates. Connect with PyMongo using tlsCAFile. Then capture traffic with tcpdump (or Wireshark) with and without TLS and compare what you can read.
  5. Convert your three-node replica set from Lesson 01 to keyFile authentication with a rolling restart (start with transitionToAuth on each member, then without it), keeping a writer running throughout.

docs.title: 06 · Backup, Restore & Point-in-Time Recovery
docs.text:
Replication is not a backup. A replica set faithfully copies every change to every member — including the deleteMany({}) someone ran against production instead of staging, which reaches all secondaries within milliseconds. A backup is a copy from before the mistake, plus a way to get from that copy to the moment you actually need.

Level 1 · 09 introduced mongodump and mongorestore for moving data around. This lesson uses them as a backup system on a live replica set: taking a consistent dump while transactions are running, proving why the oplog matters by restoring without it, recovering to the exact second before a destructive command, and taking a file-level copy. Tools: MongoDB 9.0.2 and Database Tools 100.19.1, on the three-node set from Lesson 01.

docs.title: The test: an invariant that must survive
docs.text:
A bank.accounts collection holds 500,000 accounts with a balance of 1,000 each. A Python writer moves 7 units between random accounts inside transactions, so the total must always be exactly 500,000,000. Any backup that restores to a different total captured a state that never existed.

while time.time() < end:
    x, y = random.sample(range(500000), 2)
    with c.start_session() as s:
        s.with_transaction(lambda s: (a.update_one({"_id": x}, {"$inc": {"balance": -7}}, session=s),
                                      a.update_one({"_id": y}, {"$inc": {"balance": 7}}, session=s)))

docs.title: Dumping a live replica set with --oplog
docs.text:
With the writer running, dump from a secondary (keeping the load off the primary):

mongodump --uri "mongodb://127.0.0.1:27301,127.0.0.1:27302,127.0.0.1:27303/?replicaSet=rs4" \
          --readPreference secondary --oplog --out dump2

done dumping `bank.accounts` (500000 documents)
writing captured oplog to ``
    dumped 812 oplog entries
writer transfers: 1216

A dump is not instantaneous: it reads each collection with a cursor while writes continue, so different documents are copied at different moments. --oplog fixes that. Before starting, mongodump notes the newest oplog timestamp; when it finishes, it also copies every oplog entry written during the dump into oplog.bson. Replaying those entries on restore rolls every document forward to the same moment — the end of the dump.

Restoring the same dump into two empty servers, once without and once with replay:

mongorestore --port 27601 --nsInclude 'bank.*' dump2
mongorestore --port 27602 --oplogReplay dump2

500000 document(s) restored successfully. 0 document(s) failed to restore.
applied 1624 oplog entries
27601 total balance: 499999958
27602 total balance: 500000000

Without replay, the restored bank is 42 units short: the dump caught six transfers half-way, with one side copied before the transfer and the other after. With replay, the total is exact. (812 oplog entries became 1,624 applied operations because each transaction's entry carries both of its updates.)

Honesty note: the first attempt used 50,000 accounts, and that dump finished in 0.4 seconds — both restores balanced, because no transfer happened to straddle a copied pair. A small test passing doesn't prove consistency; the larger dump did.

Two operational details:

  • --oplog works only on a whole-instance dump (no --db/--collection), and the restore refuses filters with replay: Failed: cannot use --oplogReplay with includes specified. Restore everything to a scratch server, then copy out what you need.
  • --oplog gives a consistent snapshot of a replica set. For a sharded cluster, mongodump through mongos can't produce a cluster-wide consistent point; sharded clusters need coordinated snapshots (managed services, Ops Manager, or careful file-level procedures).

docs.title: Point-in-time recovery
docs.text:
The dump finished at 18:44:43 UTC. Life goes on — 309 more transfers — and then:

db.getSiblingDB("bank").accounts.deleteMany({_id: {$lt: 1000}})

OOPS deleted: 1000
writer transfers: 311
live now: 499000 docs, total 498999993

Restoring last night's dump would lose every transfer since. What you want is the database as it was one operation before the delete. That's the dump plus the oplog up to that operation.

Step 1: find the bad operation in the oplog. Note where the dump's own oplog ends, then search after it. In this version a multi-document delete is written as applyOps batches, so search inside them:

// last entry of dump2/oplog.bson: {'$timestamp': {'t': 1791830683, 'i': 93}}
db.getSiblingDB("local").oplog.rs.find({ts: {$gt: Timestamp(1791830683, 93)}, "o.applyOps.op": "d"})
  .sort({$natural: 1}).limit(3)

1791830713:1 c admin.$cmd ops in entry: 10 first: {"_id":9}  lsid? false 2026-10-12T18:45:13.472Z
1791830713:2 c admin.$cmd ops in entry: 10 first: {"_id":19} lsid? false 2026-10-12T18:45:13.473Z
1791830713:3 c admin.$cmd ops in entry: 10 first: {"_id":29} lsid? false 2026-10-12T18:45:13.473Z
delete-bearing entries: 100

The delete begins at timestamp 1791830713:1 — 100 entries of 10 deletes each. In a real incident you'd narrow the search by wall time ("around 18:45 UTC") and by namespace.

Step 2: save the oplog since the dump — before it rolls over, since the oplog is a fixed-size buffer:

mongodump --host rs4/127.0.0.1:27301,127.0.0.1:27302 --readPreference secondary -d local -c oplog.rs \
  --query '{"ts": {"$gt": {"$timestamp": {"t": 1791830683, "i": 93}}}}' --out oplogdump
mkdir replay && cp oplogdump/local/oplog.rs.bson replay/oplog.bson

done dumping `local.oplog.rs` (1046 documents)

Step 3: restore the dump to a scratch server, then replay up to — not including — the bad timestamp:

mongorestore --port 27603 --oplogReplay dump2
mongorestore --port 27603 --oplogReplay --oplogLimit 1791830713:1 replay

applied 1624 oplog entries
501679 document(s) restored successfully. 0 document(s) failed to restore.
replaying oplog
applied 1236 oplog entries
recovered: 500000 docs, total 500000000 | _id<1000 present: 1000

All 500,000 accounts, the exact total, and every transfer up to the moment of the delete. --oplogLimit replays entries strictly before the given timestamp.

Step 4: put the lost documents back, copying only them from the scratch server to production:

mongodump --port 27603 -d bank -c accounts --query '{"_id": {"$lt": 1000}}' --out fix
mongorestore --uri "$PROD_URI" fix

done dumping `bank.accounts` (1000 documents)
1000 document(s) restored successfully. 0 document(s) failed to restore.
live after putting them back: 500000 docs, total 499999993

Every account is back — and production is 7 units short. Between the delete and the fix, a transfer touched one of the deleted accounts: update_one on a missing document matched nothing and silently did nothing, while the other half of the transfer succeeded. Restoring data cannot undo what applications did because data was missing. The real fix was in the writer — check matched_count and abort the transaction if it isn't 1 — and the recovery runbook should include reconciling anything written during the incident window.

docs.title: File-level copies
docs.text:
For large databases, copying data files is much faster than dumping documents. The files must be consistent; on a secondary you can briefly stop writes to disk with fsyncLock:

db.fsyncLock()      // on a secondary: flush and block writes

cp -R rs/n1 snap    # copy the whole dbpath

db.fsyncUnlock()

Long('1')
unlock lockCount: Long('0')
locked for 1.4s
73M
snapshot copy (standalone): 500000 docs, total 499999993
still has replset config: 1

The copy started as a standalone server with all data. Notes:

  • Copy the entire dbpath, including WiredTiger*, journal/, and every collection-*/index-* file. A partial copy is unusable.
  • While locked, the secondary falls behind; keep it short, and never lock the primary.
  • The copy still contains the replica set config in local. To use it as a seed for a new member that's fine; to use it as an independent server, start it without --replSet (as here).
  • Filesystem or volume snapshots (LVM, ZFS, cloud disk snapshots) are the production form of this technique. If the journal is on the same volume, an atomic snapshot is consistent even without fsyncLock because WiredTiger recovers from its journal at startup, just as after a crash.

docs.title: Choosing a strategy
docs.text:
Method Good for Weak at mongodump --oplog Small-to-medium replica sets; logical copies portable across versions Slow for large data; restore rebuilds every index; not consistent for sharded clusters Volume snapshots Large data; fast restore Tied to storage; must cover the whole dbpath atomically Oplog archiving + base backup Point-in-time recovery to any second Must keep the oplog archive continuous — a gap breaks the chain Managed backups (Atlas, Ops Manager) Sharded clusters, scheduled PITR Not available in a plain Community install; not demonstrated here

Whatever you use, the rule is the same as for every database: a backup you haven't restored is a hope, not a backup. Schedule restore tests, measure how long they take (that's your real recovery time), and check invariants like the bank total — not just that the restore "succeeded".

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
mongodump is an ordinary client: it lists collections and reads each with a cursor, writing BSON to files and index definitions to metadata JSON. With --oplog it first reads the newest oplog entry's timestamp, dumps collections, then queries local.oplog.rs for everything after that starting timestamp and writes it to oplog.bson. Each document in the dump reflects some moment between start and end. Because oplog entries are idempotent (Lesson 01) — "set balance to 993", not "subtract 7" — replaying entries over documents that already include some of those changes is harmless, and every document ends at the state as of the last replayed entry. Point-in-time recovery is the same mechanism with more oplog and a stop point.

mongorestore inserts documents in batches, then builds indexes from the metadata (index builds dominate restore time for large collections), then — with --oplogReplay — applies the entries with applyOps. A file copy skips all of that: WiredTiger's files are the database. At startup it finds the last checkpoint, then replays its journal to recover anything written after it, which is why a crash-consistent snapshot of the whole dbpath restores cleanly.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating replicas as backups. They replicate the mistake too.
  • Dumping a busy replica set without --oplog, or restoring without --oplogReplay, producing states that never existed.
  • An oplog window shorter than your detection time, so the operations you need to replay are already gone. Archive the oplog continuously if you need PITR.
  • Never testing restores, or testing only that the tool exits successfully.
  • File copies of a running primary without a lock or atomic snapshot.
  • Restoring over production instead of into a scratch server and copying out what's needed.
  • Forgetting side effects during the incident window — writes that failed or did nothing because data was missing.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the invariant test: dump a busy bank.accounts without --oplog and with it, restore both, and compare totals. Make the collection large enough that the difference shows up.
  2. Write a script pitr.sh <dump_dir> <limit_ts> <scratch_port> that performs steps 2 and 3 automatically. Test it by recovering from an accidental updateMany({}, {$set: {balance: 0}}).
  3. Fix the writer so that a transfer involving a missing account aborts its transaction, rerun the incident, and show the total is exact after the fix.
  4. Measure: how long do mongodump and mongorestore take for your 500,000 accounts, and how much of the restore is index building? Add two secondary indexes and measure again.
  5. Write a nightly job outline that keeps a dump plus a continuous oplog archive, with a retention policy and a monthly automated restore test that checks an invariant.

docs.title: 07 · Monitoring & the Profiler
docs.text:
When a MongoDB application gets slow, the database usually already knows why. It counts every operation, times them, logs the slow ones with their plans, tracks its cache and its connections, and will list what's running right now. Monitoring is mostly knowing where those numbers live and which ones to watch.

This lesson reads them from the three-node set (MongoDB 9.0.2, Database Tools 100.19.1) while the bank-transfer writer from Lesson 06 generates load. Hosted monitoring (Atlas charts, Ops Manager, commercial APM tools) reads the same server metrics and isn't covered here.

docs.title: serverStatus: the counters behind every dashboard
docs.text:
const s = db.serverStatus()

A few fields, as read from the primary after the previous lessons' experiments:

uptime s: 1500 | connections: {"current":24,"available":104833,"totalCreated":121}
opcounters: insert 554003, query 52, update 4905, delete 9, getmore 16484, command 34992, aggregate 4518
opLatencies (micros total / ops): reads 187us avg over 16513, writes 2347us avg over 7874, commands 684us avg over 34844
WT cache: 131.0 MB used of 256 MB | dirty 6.8 MB | pages read into cache 3797

What each tells you, and what to alert on:

  • connections — current against what you expect from your application fleet. A steady climb usually means a client creating a new MongoClient per request (Level 1 · 08). totalCreated racing upward means connection churn, which is expensive (each new connection does a TLS handshake and authentication).
  • opcounters — cumulative counts since startup. Dashboards plot their rate. Note the replicated operations a secondary applies are counted separately (opcountersRepl).
  • opLatencies — cumulative microseconds and operation counts for reads, writes and commands; the change in latency divided by the change in ops over an interval is average latency. Writes averaging 2.3 ms here reflects majority write concern (Lesson 02). Averages hide outliers; histograms are available with serverStatus({opLatencies: {histograms: true}}).
  • WiredTiger cache — bytes currently in the cache against maximum bytes configured, and dirty bytes. When dirty data stays high (WiredTiger aims to keep it well below the cache size) application threads get drafted into evicting pages, and latency jumps. pages read into cache rising fast means the working set doesn't fit in memory. Lesson 08 explains the mechanics.
  • queues.execution — admission tickets for reads and writes. This server reported 8 read and 8 write tickets available with throughput probing on, meaning the server adjusts concurrency itself; operations queueing for a ticket show up as queueLength above zero.

Everything in serverStatus is also recorded continuously, about once per second, into the diagnostic.data directory in the dbpath (FTDC — "full-time diagnostic data capture"):

metrics.2026-10-12T18-22-04Z-00000
metrics.2026-10-12T18-23-06Z-00000

Those compressed files are what MongoDB support asks for after an incident; keep them when you collect logs.

docs.title: mongostat and mongotop: the live view
docs.text:
mongostat prints one line per second of rates from serverStatus:

mongostat --host 127.0.0.1:27303 -n 4 1

insert query update delete getmore command dirty  used flushes vsize  res qrw arw net_in net_out conn set repl                time
    *0    *0    190     *0     381   675|0  3.6% 67.9%       0  467G 134M 0|0 0|0   853k    792k   27 rs4  SLV Oct 13 00:21:44.348
    *0    *0    214     *0     428   750|0 12.5% 68.5%       0  467G 110M 0|0 0|0   953k    860k   27 rs4  SLV Oct 13 00:21:45.347
    *0    *0    208     *0     416   732|0 11.2% 68.7%       0  467G 132M 0|0 0|0   926k    845k   27 rs4  SLV Oct 13 00:21:46.347
    *0    *0    209     *0     419   730|0 10.2% 68.7%       0  467G 133M 0|0 0|0   929k    846k   27 rs4  SLV Oct 13 00:21:47.349

About 200 updates per second — 100 transfers, two updates each. dirty and used are WiredTiger cache percentages; qrw/arw are queued and active readers|writers; getmore here is mostly secondaries pulling the oplog. vsize is virtual address space and means little on 64-bit systems; res (resident memory) matters more.

One honest oddity: rs.status() reported 27303 as PRIMARY at this moment, yet this mongostat labelled it SLV, and mongostat --discover against the set listed only the two secondaries. The tools and server are versioned separately, and this tools release appears to misread the 9.0 server's role. The rate columns were right; for roles, trust rs.status() or db.hello().

mongotop shows where time is spent per collection:

mongotop --host 127.0.0.1:27303 -n 1 2

                     ns    total    read    write
         local.oplog.rs     21ms    21ms      0ms
          bank.accounts     12ms     0ms     12ms
config.image_collection     12ms    12ms      0ms
    config.transactions      6ms     6ms      0ms

Reading the oplog (secondaries fetching) was the busiest namespace, followed by the transfers' writes. config.transactions and config.image_collection are internal: the server records retryable-write and transaction state there.

docs.title: The slow-query log
docs.text:
Any operation slower than slowms (100 ms by default) is written to the server log with its full details. One unindexed query:

db.getSiblingDB("bank").accounts.find({owner: "nobody"}).toArray()

"msg":"Slow query", ... {"type": "command", "ns": "bank.accounts", "command": {"find": "accounts",
"filter": {"owner": "nobody"}, ...}, "planSummary": "COLLSCAN", "planningTimeMicros": 495, "keysExamined": 0,
"docsExamined": 500000, "nreturned": 0, "numYields": 10,
"queryShapeHash": "5F869006B0C736375D7D96EDFAF043B6745867B9A6E0375A18A3AA18E38D3B27", "durationMillis": 179}

Everything needed to diagnose it is on one line: a collection scan examined 500,000 documents to return none. docsExamined far above nreturned is the classic signature of a missing index (Level 2 · 07). The queryShapeHash groups all queries of the same shape regardless of the literal values, so you can count how often this pattern runs rather than chasing individual instances.

Because the log is structured JSON, it's easy to aggregate: ship it to whatever log system you use and chart slow queries by queryShapeHash, ns and planSummary.

docs.title: The profiler
docs.text:
The profiler records operations into the capped system.profile collection of a database, where you can query them. Level 1 records operations slower than slowms:

const bank = db.getSiblingDB("bank")
bank.setProfilingLevel(1, {slowms: 20})

{ was: 0, slowms: 100, slowinprogms: Long('5000'), sampleRate: 1, ok: 1 }

Three operations followed: the unindexed find, a lookup by _id, and an unindexed updateMany:

bank.system.profile.find({}, {op: 1, ns: 1, command: 1, planSummary: 1, keysExamined: 1, docsExamined: 1,
                              nreturned: 1, nModified: 1, millis: 1, numYield: 1}).sort({ts: -1})

update bank.accounts COLLSCAN keys 0 docs 500000 returned 3 millis 130 yields 8 | filter {"balance":{"$gt":1010}}
query  bank.accounts COLLSCAN keys 0 docs 500000 returned 0 millis 179 yields 10 | filter {"owner":"nobody"}
profile entries: 2 | capped: true

The _id lookup was too fast to record. Both slow operations scanned the whole collection; the update modified 3 documents after reading 500,000.

Profiler guidance:

  • Level 1 with a sensible slowms is safe in production for short investigations; sampleRate (0–1) records only a fraction of slow operations on very busy systems.
  • Level 2 records everything and adds a write for every operation. Use it only briefly on a test system.
  • It's per database and per mongod: on a replica set, enable it on the member whose traffic you're investigating; on a sharded cluster, on the shards.
  • system.profile is a small capped collection (1 MB by default), so old entries vanish. Copy out what you need.
  • Setting it at level 0 still changes the slowms threshold used for the log.

docs.title: What's running right now: $currentOp and killOp
docs.text:
A report someone started with a pathological pipeline — a $lookup that scans the whole collection 200 times:

db.getSiblingDB("bank").accounts.aggregate([
  {$group: {_id: {$mod: ["$_id", 200]}}},
  {$lookup: {from: "accounts", let: {k: "$_id"},
             pipeline: [{$match: {$expr: {$eq: [{$mod: ["$_id", 200]}, "$$k"]}}}, {$count: "c"}], as: "same"}}
], {comment: "monthly-report"})

From another shell, find operations running longer than 2 seconds:

db.getSiblingDB("admin").aggregate([{$currentOp: {}}, {$match: {ns: /^bank\./, secs_running: {$gte: 2}}}])

opid 307201 | op command | ns bank.accounts | secs_running Long('5') | planSummary COLLSCAN | comment monthly-report | app mongosh 2.13.0

db.killOp(307201)

killOp ok: 1
long query ended: Interrupted - Executor error during aggregate command on namespace: bank.accounts :: caused by :: operation was interrupted

Two habits make this much easier in a real incident: set appName in every application's connection string so $currentOp shows which service an operation came from, and pass a comment on expensive queries so you can recognise them. Better still, prevent runaway queries with maxTimeMS on anything user-triggered.

(Two earlier versions of this "long query" finished too fast or failed outright — one built an array over the 100 MB per-array limit and died with ExceededMemoryLimit. Aggregations have guard rails; the $count sub-pipeline keeps arrays tiny.)

docs.title: What to put on a dashboard
docs.text: Signal Source Why Operation rates and latencies by type opcounters, opLatencies load and the first sign of trouble Slow queries per shape slow log / profiler (queryShapeHash) which query to fix Replication lag per secondary rs.status() optimes stale reads, failover risk, oplog window Oplog window (hours) rs.printReplicationInfo() how long a member can be down Cache used / dirty, pages read wiredTiger.cache working set vs memory Connections current / created connections pool misconfiguration, churn Queued operations, tickets queues.execution saturation Disk space, IOPS, CPU OS everything else depends on them Elections log, rs.status().term instability (Lesson 01's laptop had 104 overnight)

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every operation passes through a CurOp object that accumulates its statistics as it runs — keys and documents examined, yields, locks, time spent waiting. $currentOp reads the live CurOps; when an operation finishes, the same object is used to decide whether to log it (duration above slowms, subject to sampleRate) and whether to write a profiler document. Long-running operations periodically check whether they've been interrupted — at yield points, between batches — which is how killOp and maxTimeMS work: they set a flag that the operation notices at its next check, then it cleans up and returns Interrupted or MaxTimeMSExpired.

serverStatus gathers counters maintained by each subsystem, many as lock-free per-CPU counters so that counting millions of operations doesn't itself become a bottleneck. FTDC samples serverStatus, replSetGetStatus and a few others on a timer and stores them with delta compression, which is why a day of once-per-second samples takes only megabytes.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Monitoring only CPU and memory and missing replication lag, cache pressure and queueing.
  • Profiler level 2 in production.
  • Looking at averages only. One slow query shape at the 99th percentile is invisible in a mean.
  • No appName, no comment, so $currentOp shows anonymous connections.
  • Killing operations blindly, including internal ones (replication, balancer, index builds).
  • Discarding diagnostic.data and logs after an incident.
  • Alerting on a single sample of a noisy metric instead of a sustained condition.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a script that samples serverStatus every 5 seconds and prints per-second rates for inserts, updates and queries, plus average read and write latency over the interval.
  2. Run the transfer writer and a deliberately unindexed query loop. Find the query in the slow log, then group all slow log lines from the run by queryShapeHash and count them. Add the index and repeat.
  3. Enable profiling at level 1 with sampleRate: 0.1 and slowms: 0 for one minute under load. Use the profile collection to find the three most expensive query shapes by total millis.
  4. Start a long aggregation with appName=reports in its connection string. Write a "kill switch" script that kills only operations from that app running longer than 30 seconds.
  5. Design the alert thresholds for the dashboard table above for a hypothetical service handling 2,000 operations per second, and write down what an on-call engineer should check first for each alert.

docs.title: 08 · Performance Tuning: WiredTiger, Memory & Connections
docs.text:
Most MongoDB performance problems are solved by the work in Levels 2 and 3 — the right indexes, a schema that matches the queries, pipelines that filter early. This lesson covers what's left once those are done: how the storage engine uses memory, what compression costs and saves, how connections behave, and which server and OS settings matter. Every claim is backed by a measurement on this course's lab, with an honest note on how a laptop differs from a production server.

Lab: MongoDB 9.0.2 on a laptop with 8 GB of RAM and 8 cores, PyMongo 4.18.3.

docs.title: The WiredTiger cache
docs.text:
WiredTiger keeps recently used data and index pages in its own cache, uncompressed. Its default size is the larger of 256 MB and 50% of (RAM − 1 GB). Started with no cache option on the 8 GB machine:

RAM MB: Long('8192') cores: 8
default cache MB: 3584

(8,192 − 1,024) × 0.5 = 3,584 MB — exactly the formula. The rest of memory isn't wasted: the operating system's file cache holds recently read compressed data files, and every connection, sort, aggregation and index build uses memory outside the cache.

Two consequences:

  • Never run two mongods on one host with default settings. Each claims half the RAM. That's why every lab in this course sets --wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 0.25.
  • In containers, set the cache explicitly (or make sure the container's memory limit is visible to mongod). A cache sized from the host's RAM inside a small container gets the process killed.

docs.title: Working set: what has to fit
docs.text:
The working set is the data and indexes your workload touches regularly. The test server has a 256 MB cache and a collection of 1.2 million documents with 400 random characters each:

loaded 1200000 docs in 27s | data 490 MB | on disk 497 MB | _id index 13 MB

Random characters don't compress, so the collection is almost twice the cache. After a restart (empty WiredTiger cache), 20,000 random _id lookups, first restricted to 5% of the documents, then across all of them:

def run(label, hi, n=20000):
    r = random.Random(1); p0, _ = cache(); t = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n):
        coll.find_one({"_id": r.randrange(hi)})
    ...

hot 5% (60k docs), cold cache         9014 reads/s | pages read into cache   1280 | cache used    29 MB
hot 5% (60k docs), warm               9567 reads/s | pages read into cache      0 | cache used    29 MB
whole collection (1.2M docs)          4644 reads/s | pages read into cache  14524 | cache used   209 MB
whole collection, again               7774 reads/s | pages read into cache  12855 | cache used   218 MB
  • The hot 5% (about 25 MB) fit easily: after the first pass it was entirely cached and no pages were read.
  • Reading across the whole collection, the cache filled to about 210–220 MB — WiredTiger keeps it around 80% full and evicts to stay there — and kept reading pages in: 12,855 page reads on the second pass, because the working set no longer fits. Each read evicts something that may be needed again soon.

The honest caveat: the gap here (about 7,800 vs 9,600 reads/s once warm) is small because this laptop's operating system had the whole 497 MB file in its own memory, so a cache miss cost a copy and decompression rather than a disk read. On a server whose data is many times larger than RAM, a miss is a real disk I/O — tens or hundreds of microseconds on SSDs, milliseconds on network storage — and the same pattern becomes an order-of-magnitude slowdown. Watch pages read into cache per second: if it stays high under normal load, the working set doesn't fit, and you need more memory, smaller documents, better indexes (fewer pages touched), or sharding.

Indexes deserve special attention: an index used by every query must stay in memory to be fast. Compare totalIndexSize across collections with the cache size; unused indexes (find them with $indexStats) cost cache and write time for nothing.

docs.title: Compression: disk versus CPU
docs.text:
WiredTiger compresses data blocks on disk with snappy by default; zstd, zlib and none are options per collection. The same 200,000 order-like documents in each:

p.createCollection("c_" + c, {storageEngine: {wiredTiger: {configString: "block_compressor=" + c}}})

none    data 40.0 MB | on disk 41.7 MB | ratio 0.96 | insert 5417 ms
snappy  data 40.0 MB | on disk 13.3 MB | ratio 3.00 | insert 5393 ms
zlib    data 40.0 MB | on disk 7.2 MB | ratio 5.55 | insert 5404 ms
zstd    data 40.0 MB | on disk 8.6 MB | ratio 4.65 | insert 5391 ms

On this repetitive, text-heavy data, snappy cut disk use by two-thirds, and zstd and zlib by over 80% — with zlib slightly ahead at default levels on this sample. The insert times didn't differ because the mongosh script generating documents was the bottleneck, not the server; compression CPU cost is real but small next to everything else in this test. The random-character collection above, by contrast, didn't compress at all (497 MB on disk for 490 MB of data). Measure with your own documents.

Choosing:

  • snappy (default): cheap and fast; a fine default.
  • zstd: noticeably smaller files for modest extra CPU; good for large, cold or archival collections, and for network compression between client and server (compressors=zstd in the connection string).
  • none: rarely worth it.
  • Compression affects disk and the OS file cache, not the WiredTiger cache — pages are decompressed in memory. Smaller files mean more data fits in the OS file cache, which itself improves performance when the working set overflows WiredTiger's cache.

docs.title: One client per process, not per request
docs.text:
200 lookups, new client each:    298 ms, connections created: 602
200 lookups, shared client:       24 ms

Creating a MongoClient per request was twelve times slower and opened about three connections per client (the driver's monitoring connection, its round-trip-time monitor, and one for the operation). Add TLS and authentication and each new client costs several round trips plus CPU on both sides. A MongoClient is thread-safe and maintains a pool; create it once at startup and share it. In serverless functions, create it outside the handler so warm invocations reuse it.

docs.title: Pool size is not a throughput dial
docs.text:
64 Python threads doing random lookups through one client, with different pool limits:

maxPoolSize=1       8154 reads/s  (server connections now: 6)
maxPoolSize=4       9512 reads/s  (server connections now: 9)
maxPoolSize=16      8653 reads/s  (server connections now: 21)
maxPoolSize=100     8885 reads/s  (server connections now: 69)

Throughput was flat: the bottleneck was the Python client (one interpreter, the GIL), not connections, so more connections just meant more idle sockets. In other languages or with more client processes the curve rises further before flattening, but the shape is universal: beyond the server's ability to execute operations in parallel (bounded by cores and storage), more connections add memory and contention, not speed.

Budget connections across the fleet: 40 application instances × maxPoolSize 100 is 4,000 potential connections per mongod, each with its own memory. Size pools from measured concurrency, set maxIdleTimeMS so bursts don't leave thousands of idle sockets, and set waitQueueTimeoutMS / timeoutMS so a saturated pool fails fast rather than queueing forever.

docs.title: Server and OS settings worth knowing
docs.text:
These follow MongoDB's production notes; the details change between versions, so check the notes for the version you run. None were benchmarked here — a laptop can't meaningfully test them.

  • File system: XFS is recommended for WiredTiger on Linux.
  • ulimit: raise open files and processes (MongoDB suggests 64,000); each connection and each data/index file uses descriptors.
  • Swappiness: keep it low (often 1) so the kernel doesn't swap out the cache.
  • Transparent huge pages: the recommendation reversed in MongoDB 8.0 — older versions said disable THP; 8.0 and later, with an upgraded TCMalloc, recommend enabling it. A runbook copied from an older guide gets this backwards.
  • NUMA: on multi-socket machines, use interleaved memory allocation (numactl --interleave=all).
  • Read-ahead: small values (around 8–32 sectors) on data volumes; large read-ahead wastes the file cache.
  • Clock sync: NTP/chrony on every member; replication and logs depend on sane clocks.
  • Disks: SSDs, and separate volumes for data and logs if your platform's I/O is shared.

mongod checks several of these at startup and prints warnings in the log (and in mongosh's startup banner). Read them rather than suppressing them.

docs.title: A tuning method
docs.text:
1. Find the expensive operations — slow log and profiler grouped by query shape (Lesson 07).
  2. Fix the query or index first. A COLLSCAN turned into an IXSCAN beats any server setting.
  3. Check the working set: cache usage, dirty percentage, pages read per second.
  4. Check connections and queues: tickets in use, queued operations, connection counts and churn.
  5. Check replication: lag, and whether majority writes are waiting on a slow secondary.
  6. Change one thing, measure again, on production-like data and load.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
WiredTiger stores each collection and index as a B-tree in its own file. Pages on disk are compressed blocks; when a page is needed, it's read (from the OS file cache or disk), decompressed and expanded into an in-memory format in the cache. Updates create new versions of records in memory (that's how readers get consistent snapshots without locks), making pages dirty. Checkpoints (every 60 seconds by default) write dirty pages back as new compressed blocks, and the journal records changes between checkpoints for crash recovery.

Background eviction threads keep the cache below its targets: they start evicting clean pages when usage passes about 80% (eviction_target) and work harder on dirty content past its own threshold. If the cache reaches its hard triggers (around 95% used, or too much dirty data), application threads are made to do eviction before their operations proceed — the moment latency suddenly spikes in an overloaded system. That's why the test above settled at about 210–220 MB of a 256 MB cache: eviction holding it near the target while new pages arrived.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Tuning server knobs before fixing queries and indexes.
  • Default cache settings for several mongods on one host, or inside a memory-limited container.
  • Ignoring index size relative to memory; keeping unused indexes.
  • A new MongoClient per request or per function invocation.
  • Huge pool sizes on many app instances, multiplying into tens of thousands of server connections.
  • Applying THP and other OS advice from a guide written for a different MongoDB version.
  • Benchmarking on a laptop and extrapolating to production storage. Use laptops to compare alternatives, as this lesson does, and production-like hardware to size.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Load a collection 3× larger than a 256 MB cache. Measure random-read throughput and pages read per second for hot ranges of 1%, 10%, 25% and 50%. Plot where performance falls off.
  2. Repeat the compression comparison with your own application's documents (or a public data set). Add a read test: time a full collection scan for each compressor after a restart.
  3. Write a "client per request" and a "shared client" version of a small web endpoint (Flask or FastAPI) and load test both. Count totalCreated connections on the server for each.
  4. Run the pool-size test from Node.js with the async driver and 200 concurrent promises. Does the curve differ from Python's?
  5. Read every startup warning your mongod prints, look up each in the production notes for your version, and decide which apply to your deployment.

docs.title: 09 · Upgrades, FCV & Online Schema Migrations
docs.text:
A production database is never finished. Servers need upgrades and patches, workloads need new indexes, and schemas change as the application does. With a replica set and a little discipline, all of these happen while the application keeps running. This lesson does each one on the three-node lab set with a writer running throughout, measuring what the application actually experienced.

Lab: MongoDB 9.0.2, PyMongo 4.18.3. One limitation up front: only one server version was installed for this course, so the binary swap in a version upgrade was not performed here. The rolling procedure below is identical with or without a new binary, and it was run for real; the featureCompatibilityVersion steps were run on 9.0.2 itself.

docs.title: Rolling restarts: the core procedure
docs.text:
Patching the OS, changing a startup option, rotating certificates, upgrading MongoDB — all follow the same pattern: one member at a time, secondaries first, primary last.

  1. Restart one secondary (with its new binary or configuration). Wait until it's SECONDARY and caught up.
  2. Repeat for every other secondary.
  3. Step the primary down (replSetStepDown), wait for a new primary, restart the old one.

A script did exactly that while a thread inserted a document every 20 ms:

for p in (27301, 27302, 27303):
    if p != primary:
        log(f"restarting secondary {p}"); restart(p)        # shutdown, start mongod, wait for state 1 or 2
log(f"stepping down primary {primary}")
direct(primary).admin.command("replSetStepDown", 60)
restart(primary)

t=  2.0s  restarting secondary 27301
t= 18.8s  27301 back as SECONDARY
t= 18.8s  restarting secondary 27302
t= 35.9s  27302 back as SECONDARY
t= 35.9s  stepping down primary 27303
t= 36.0s  new primary 127.0.0.1:27301; restarting 27303
t= 52.6s  27303 back as SECONDARY
t= 67.7s  primary now 127.0.0.1:27303
inserts: 2037, errors: 0 []
slowest inserts: 0.07s at t=28.2s, 0.05s at t=0.0s, 0.04s at t=35.1s

Every member restarted, there were two elections, and the application saw zero errors and no insert slower than 70 ms. Two details:

  • The stepped-down member came back and took over again (t = 67.7 s). It had priority: 2 from Lesson 01, so a priority takeover followed as soon as it caught up — a second, unplanned-looking election. Harmless here, but know your priorities before maintenance so the last step doesn't surprise you.
  • Most of each member's ~17 seconds was a clean shutdown and startup. Wait for each member to be healthy and caught up (rs.status() optimes) before touching the next; restarting two at once drops below a majority.

For a sharded cluster, the order is: stop the balancer, upgrade the config server replica set (rolling), then each shard (rolling), then the mongos routers, then re-enable the balancer.

docs.title: Version upgrades and featureCompatibilityVersion
docs.text:
Upgrades go one major release at a time (for example 7.0 → 8.0 → 9.0, never skipping), using the rolling procedure to replace binaries. But new binaries alone don't turn on new features that change on-disk formats or replication behaviour. That's controlled by the featureCompatibilityVersion (FCV):

db.adminCommand({getParameter: 1, featureCompatibilityVersion: 1})

binary: 9.0.2 | FCV: {"version":"9.0"}

The safe sequence:

  1. Rolling-upgrade all members to the new binaries. FCV stays at the old version, so the new binaries behave compatibly with the old ones — you can still roll back to the old binaries.
  2. Run the application on the new binaries for a while (days, typically).
  3. Raise FCV: db.adminCommand({setFeatureCompatibilityVersion: "9.0", confirm: true}). New features become available; rolling back the binaries now requires lowering FCV first.

Lowering FCV on the 9.0.2 server:

without confirm: Location7369100 - To proceed with the FCV downgrade, please re-run this command with 'confirm: true'.
downgrade ok: 1 in 16 ms | FCV: {"version":"8.0"}
to 7.0: Location4926900 - Invalid feature compatibility version value '7.0'. Expected one of the following versions: ''9.0', '8.3', '8.0'. ...
upgrade ok: 1 | FCV: {"version":"9.0"}

The confirm: true requirement exists because FCV changes are hard to undo in practice. The server accepts only the adjacent versions it can interoperate with — here 8.0, 8.3 (a rapid release) and 9.0 — and on an empty standalone the change took 16 ms. On a large deployment, changing FCV can rewrite metadata and take longer; read the release notes' compatibility section for every version you cross, since each release documents what its FCV gates and which features must be removed before a downgrade.

Before any upgrade: check driver compatibility with the new server, read the compatibility-changes page, test the application against the new version in staging, take (and test) a backup, and confirm the oplog window is long enough to cover a member being down for its restart.

docs.title: Online index builds
docs.text:
Adding an index to a large collection used to be a planned outage. Since 4.2 index builds take an exclusive lock only briefly at the start and end, and replica sets build on all data-bearing members at once, committing when a commit quorum (by default all voting data-bearing members) is ready.

A writer updating random accounts in bank.accounts (500,000 documents), before and during a new index build:

a.create_index([("owner", 1), ("balance", -1)], name="vip_balance")

before  updates:   523 | median  9.53 ms | p99  15.57 ms | max   23.3 ms
during  updates:   146 | median 10.04 ms | p99  27.33 ms | max   40.5 ms
index build (all 3 members, commit quorum) took 1.6s

"msg":"Index build: commit quorum satisfied"
"msg":"Index build: done building"
"msg":"Index build: completed successfully"

Writes continued throughout; the tail latency roughly doubled (the build competes for CPU, cache and disk), and the median barely moved. On a collection hundreds of times larger the build runs for minutes or hours, so the practical advice is: build during quieter periods, watch replication lag, and make sure every member has the disk space. Hiding a new index from the planner first is possible too — hideIndex makes an existing index invisible to queries without dropping it, which is the safe way to test whether an index can be removed.

docs.title: Online schema migrations
docs.text:
MongoDB doesn't need ALTER TABLE, but data still has a shape the code depends on. Changing it safely is an application-level process. The example: 200,000 users stored as

{"_id": 4242, "name": "Ravi Shah", "phone": "9895420477"}

must become

{"_id": 4242, "name": {"first": "Ravi", "last": "Shah"}, "phones": ["9895420477"], "schemaVersion": 2}

without stopping the application. The steps:

1. Deploy code that understands both shapes. Here the code that adds a phone number checks the document's version and writes the matching shape — and checks that its update still matched, because the migration may have converted the document between the read and the write:

def add_phone(uid, phone):
    while True:
        doc = users.find_one({"_id": uid}, {"schemaVersion": 1})
        if doc.get("schemaVersion") == 2:
            res = users.update_one({"_id": uid, "schemaVersion": 2}, {"$addToSet": {"phones": phone}})
        else:   # still v1: write the v1 shape; the migration will carry it over
            res = users.update_one({"_id": uid, "schemaVersion": {"$exists": False}}, {"$set": {"phone": phone}})
        if res.matched_count == 1:
            return
        races[0] += 1           # migrated between our read and our write: read again

2. Migrate in batches, each an update-with-pipeline that transforms a document in one atomic step, filtered so that already-migrated documents are skipped:

to_v2 = [{"$set": {
    "name": {"first": {"$arrayElemAt": [{"$split": ["$name", " "]}, 0]},
             "last":  {"$arrayElemAt": [{"$split": ["$name", " "]}, 1]}},
    "phones": ["$phone"], "schemaVersion": 2}}, {"$unset": "phone"}]

while True:
    ids = [d["_id"] for d in users.find({"_id": {"$gt": last_id}}, {"_id": 1}).sort("_id", 1).limit(2000)]
    if not ids: break
    users.update_many({"_id": {"$gte": ids[0], "$lte": ids[-1]}, "schemaVersion": {"$exists": False}}, to_v2)
    last_id = ids[-1]
    time.sleep(0.01)          # throttle: leave room for the application and for replication

v1 users: 200000
app writes that lost the race and retried: 0
migrated 200000 in 100 batches, 7.6s, while the app made 620 writes
left on v1: 0 | v2 docs with a stray 'phone' field: 0
sample: {'_id': 4242, 'name': {'first': 'Ravi', 'last': 'Shah'}, 'phones': ['9895420477'], 'schemaVersion': 2}
re-running the migration modifies: 0

Every document converted, concurrent application writes landed in the right shape, and re-running the migration changed nothing — it's idempotent, so a crash halfway is fixed by running it again. In this run the race the retry loop guards against never fired (0 of 620 writes), because the window between read and write is tiny; an earlier version of the code without the matched_count check would have silently dropped a phone number whenever it did. Rare is not never.

3. Lock in the new shape with validation once nothing writes v1 any more:

c.app.command("collMod", "users", validator={"$jsonSchema": {"required": ["schemaVersion", "name", "phones"], ...}},
              validationLevel="strict", validationAction="error")

v1-shaped insert after validation: WriteError

4. Remove the v1 code paths in a later deploy.

Why batches and not one updateMany({}, ...)? A single huge update produces one oplog entry per document in a burst that secondaries must absorb (Lesson 01), can't be throttled or paused, and holds resources for its whole duration. Batches let you watch replication lag and slow down. For the very large migrations, an alternative is lazy migration: convert each document whenever the application next writes it, plus a slow background job for the rest.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A rolling restart works because each member can be absent without losing the majority, and because drivers treat a restart like any other failover: they notice the topology change, rediscover the primary, and retry the write once. A step-down is gentler than a crash because the primary first waits for a secondary to catch up, then that secondary wins an election immediately.

FCV is stored as a document in the admin.system.version collection, replicated like any other write. New code paths in the server check the FCV before using new on-disk formats or protocol features, so a set at the old FCV writes nothing an old binary can't read. Raising FCV runs an upgrade procedure that may convert metadata; lowering it runs the reverse and refuses if data exists that the old version couldn't handle.

Hybrid index builds scan the collection without holding an exclusive lock, while concurrent writes to the collection are recorded in a side table; at the end, the build applies the side table and takes a brief exclusive lock to commit. In a replica set the primary writes a startIndexBuild oplog entry so every member starts building, each member votes when it's ready, and the primary writes commitIndexBuild once the commit quorum is met.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Restarting two members at once, or the primary first.
  • Skipping major versions or raising FCV the moment new binaries are in, removing the easy rollback.
  • Forgetting the balancer during sharded-cluster maintenance.
  • Big-bang updateMany migrations on large collections in production.
  • Non-idempotent migrations that double-transform documents when re-run.
  • Code that only understands the new shape, deployed before the migration finishes.
  • Read-then-write without checking matched_count, silently losing writes during the migration.
  • Dropping an index without hiding it first to check nothing depends on it.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write your own rolling-restart script that refuses to proceed if any member is unhealthy or lagging more than 10 seconds. Run it with a writer going, and add a deliberate failure (a member that doesn't come back) to check it stops.
  2. Before Lesson 01's priority change, what would the end of the rolling restart have looked like? Reset all priorities to 1 and run it again.
  3. Hide vip_balance with hideIndex, run a query that would use it and check explain, then unhide it.
  4. Migrate bank.accounts.balance from integers to Decimal128 in batches while the transfer writer from Lesson 06 runs. Prove the total is unchanged afterwards.
  5. Implement the lazy-migration variant for the users example: convert on every write, plus a background job limited to 500 documents per second. How long until no v1 documents remain?

docs.title: 10 · Capstone — A Secured Sharded Cluster
docs.text:
This capstone puts Level 4 together. You'll build a sharded cluster the way it's built for production — every component a three-member replica set, TLS required on every connection, members authenticating to each other, least-privilege users for each client — and then accept it the way production systems should be accepted: with a script that tries to break each guarantee and reports PASS or FAIL.

The finished cluster is ten processes on one machine:

Component Members Ports Config server replica set cfg 3 27901–27903 Shard replica set shardA 3 27911–27913 Shard replica set shardB 3 27921–27923 Router mongos 1 27900

Everything below was run on MongoDB 9.0.2 with PyMongo 4.18.3 and OpenSSL 4.0, including two mistakes that turned into the most useful parts of the lesson. On a laptop the ten processes use a few hundred MB each with the cache capped at 0.25 GB; close other labs first.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. All three replica sets have three data-bearing members; losing any one member loses nothing and stops nothing.
  2. Every connection uses TLS; plain-text connections are refused.
  3. Members authenticate to each other; clients must authenticate; no anonymous access.
  4. Three client identities: a cluster administrator, an application user that can read and write orders (but not drop or index them, or touch other collections beyond reading products), and a read-only reporting user.
  5. shop.orders is sharded on {customerId: 1, placedAt: 1} (Lesson 04), spread across both shards, with customer queries targeted to one shard.
  6. An acceptance script verifies all of the above, including a shard primary killed during writes.

docs.title: Step 1: secrets and certificates
docs.text:
openssl rand -base64 756 > keyfile && chmod 400 keyfile

openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 30 -subj "/CN=Capstone CA" -keyout ca.key -out ca.pem
openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -subj "/O=Capstone/OU=cluster/CN=127.0.0.1" -keyout member.key -out member.csr
printf "subjectAltName=IP:127.0.0.1,DNS:localhost\nextendedKeyUsage=serverAuth,clientAuth\n" > member.ext
openssl x509 -req -in member.csr -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -days 30 -extfile member.ext -out member.crt
cat member.crt member.key > member.pem && chmod 600 member.pem ca.key

The member certificate carries both serverAuth and clientAuth, because members are clients of each other when they replicate and heartbeat. In production every host gets its own certificate naming its own DNS name; one certificate for 127.0.0.1 works here only because every member shares that address.

docs.title: Step 2: one configuration file per member
docs.text:
Command-line flags are fine for experiments; production uses configuration files, which are reviewable and repeatable. The file for a1:

storage:
  dbPath: /path/to/cap/data/a1
  wiredTiger:
    engineConfig:
      cacheSizeGB: 0.25
systemLog:
  destination: file
  path: /path/to/cap/logs/a1.log
  logAppend: true
net:
  port: 27911
  bindIp: 127.0.0.1
  tls:
    mode: requireTLS
    certificateKeyFile: /path/to/cap/member.pem
    CAFile: /path/to/cap/ca.pem
    allowConnectionsWithoutCertificates: true
security:
  keyFile: /path/to/cap/keyfile
  authorization: enabled
replication:
  replSetName: shardA
  oplogSizeMB: 64
sharding:
  clusterRole: shardsvr

A small shell function generated all nine, varying the name, port, clusterRole (configsvr or shardsvr) and replica set name. allowConnectionsWithoutCertificates lets clients authenticate with passwords over TLS (Lesson 05 explains why CAFile alone would demand client certificates).

docs.title: Step 3: start and initiate
docs.text:
for f in cfg1 cfg2 cfg3 a1 a2 a3 b1 b2 b3; do mongod --config $f.conf & done

A plain-text connection is already refused:

MongoServerSelectionError: connection <monitor> to 127.0.0.1:27901 closed

With no users anywhere, the localhost exception lets you initiate each replica set over TLS:

// mongosh --host 127.0.0.1 --port 27901 --tls --tlsCAFile ca.pem
rs.initiate({_id: "cfg", configsvr: true, members: [{_id: 0, host: "127.0.0.1:27901"},
  {_id: 1, host: "127.0.0.1:27902"}, {_id: 2, host: "127.0.0.1:27903"}]})
// likewise shardA on 27911 and shardB on 27921 (without configsvr)

27901=PRIMARY 27902=SECONDARY 27903=SECONDARY
27911=PRIMARY 27912=SECONDARY 27913=SECONDARY
27921=PRIMARY 27922=SECONDARY 27923=SECONDARY

docs.title: Step 4: router, first administrator, shards, roles
docs.text:
mongos.conf has the same net.tls and security.keyFile sections and sharding.configDB: cfg/127.0.0.1:27901,127.0.0.1:27902,127.0.0.1:27903. Through mongos, the localhost exception creates the first user — stored on the config servers, so it is a cluster user:

db.getSiblingDB("admin").createUser({user: "clusterAdmin", pwd: passwordPrompt(), roles: ["root"]})

Then, authenticated as clusterAdmin:

sh.addShard("shardA/127.0.0.1:27911,127.0.0.1:27912,127.0.0.1:27913")
sh.addShard("shardB/127.0.0.1:27921,127.0.0.1:27922,127.0.0.1:27923")

const shop = db.getSiblingDB("shop")
shop.createRole({role: "shopService", roles: [], privileges: [
  {resource: {db: "shop", collection: "orders"},   actions: ["find", "insert", "update", "remove"]},
  {resource: {db: "shop", collection: "products"}, actions: ["find"]}]})
shop.createUser({user: "shop_app", pwd: passwordPrompt(), roles: ["shopService"]})
db.getSiblingDB("admin").createUser({user: "reporter", pwd: passwordPrompt(), roles: [{role: "read", db: "shop"}]})

sh.shardCollection("shop.orders", {customerId: 1, placedAt: 1})
shop.orders.createIndex({status: 1, placedAt: -1})

docs.title: Mistake 1: a secrets file that changed every time it was read
docs.text:
The scripted version of this step generated passwords into a secrets.env file — written as ADMIN_PW="cap-admin-$(openssl rand -hex 6)". Every time the file was sourced, the command substitution ran again and produced a new password. The users were created with one set of values; the next script read another. Nobody could log in, and the localhost exception was gone because a user existed.

The way back in was the keyFile. Members authenticate to each other as the internal __system user, whose password is the keyFile's contents — so anyone holding the keyFile can authenticate as __system directly. Users created through mongos live on the config servers, so that's where to connect:

mongosh "mongodb://127.0.0.1:27901,127.0.0.1:27902,127.0.0.1:27903/?replicaSet=cfg&tls=true&tlsCAFile=ca.pem" \
  -u __system -p "$(tr -d '\n' < keyfile)" --authenticationDatabase local

passwords reset as __system on the config server
clusterAdmin login ok: clusterAdmin

(Trying it through mongos first failed with Can't use 'local' database through mongos.) Two lessons. The fixed secrets file contains literal values, generated once. And the keyFile is equivalent to root on every member: protect it like the most privileged password you have — file permissions, a secrets manager, never in images or repositories. That's one reason production clusters prefer x.509 member certificates.

docs.title: Step 5: distribute the data
docs.text:
A new range-sharded collection starts as one chunk on the database's primary shard, and with the default 128 MB chunk size the balancer won't move a small collection. Pre-splitting puts half the customers on each shard before loading:

sh.splitAt("shop.orders", {customerId: 10000, placedAt: MinKey})
db.adminCommand({moveRange: "shop.orders", min: {customerId: 10000, placedAt: MinKey}, toShard: "shardB"})

primary shard of shop: shardA
moveRange to shardB 1
shardA {} -> 10000
shardB 10000 -> {}

({} is how JSON.stringify prints MinKey/MaxKey.) Pre-splitting is standard practice before a bulk load into a range-sharded collection; otherwise one shard takes the whole load and the balancer moves it later.

docs.title: Step 6: the acceptance script
docs.text:
verify.py connects as each identity and checks every requirement. Its building blocks:

CA = os.path.abspath("ca.pem")
def client(user=None, pw=None, source="admin", tls=True, **kw):
    auth = dict(username=user, password=pw, authSource=source) if user else {}
    return MongoClient("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27900", tls=tls, tlsCAFile=CA if tls else None,
                       serverSelectionTimeoutMS=3000, **auth, **kw)

def denied(fn):
    try: fn(); return False, "allowed"
    except OperationFailure as e: return e.code == 13, e.details.get("codeName")   # 13 = Unauthorized

The checks, in order: plain-text connection refused; unauthenticated read refused; the app user inserts 60,000 orders; the app user is denied four things its role doesn't grant; the reporter reads but can't write; the orders are on both shards; a customer query is SINGLE_SHARD; and finally a writer runs as the app user while the shardA primary is killed with SIGKILL:

prim = shard_a.admin.command("hello")["primary"].split(":")[1]
pid = subprocess.check_output(["pgrep", "-f", f"a{int(prim) - 27910}.conf"]).decode().split()[0]
os.kill(int(pid), signal.SIGKILL); time.sleep(15)

docs.title: Mistake 2: cluster users don't exist on the shards
docs.text:
The first run:

The first eleven checks passed; the last one didn't:

     (could not ask shardA for its primary: AuthenticationFailed )
FAIL  shardA primary killed: no write errors  (53 inserts, slowest 0.12s, errors [])

To find the shard's primary, the script connected directly to the shard as clusterAdmin — and failed. Users created through mongos are stored on the config servers; a shard has its own, separate user database, which was empty. Which also meant something worse:

shardA before: Unauthorized
